schema.problem: Existing equation-discovery systems propose candidate laws from fixed datasets, while experimental-design methods choose informative measurements only over small, fixed parametric model families; no current system closes the loop between an open-ended space of structurally distinct symbolic hypotheses and an adaptive experiment-selection mechanism.
schema.motivation: Closing this loop would make autonomous scientific discovery more measurement-efficient and would provide a concrete experiment-selection mechanism for the agentic AI-scientist literature.
schema.proposed_approach: A genetic-programming population of candidate governing laws is scored by a BIC-weighted posterior over all data collected so far, while a second evolutionary population of experiment designs is selected for expected information gain about the current surviving hypotheses; experiments evolve where rival laws disagree. The inner loop is deliberately LLM-free.
schema.research_plan: For claim (1), the proposed method is tested on controllable multi-variable systems against the same hypothesis engine fed an equal-budget static dataset, random designs, variance-based point-querying, and fixed control-variable schedules, comparing the number and informativeness of measurements needed to recover ground-truth equations. For claim (2), it is tested on crafted rival-law tasks whose laws are indistinguishable under naive sampling. The method is evaluated directly as a module inside benchmark-style environments.

items.title: CEE-Discovery: Coevolving Experiments and Equations for Closed-Loop Governing-Law Discovery
items.abstract: Autonomous scientific discovery currently suffers from a structural asymmetry: equation-discovery systems can propose candidate laws from a fixed dataset (symbolic regression, including LLM-proposer variants), while experimental-design methods can choose informative measurements only over a small, fixed parametric model family. No retrieved system closes the loop between an open-ended space of structurally distinct symbolic hypotheses and an adaptive experiment-selection mechanism. I propose CEE-Discovery (Coevolving Experiments and Equations), a closed-loop algorithm in which a genetic-programming population of candidate governing laws is scored by a BIC-weighted posterior over all data collected so far, while a second evolutionary population of experiment designs is selected for the expected information gain (EIG) they would deliver about the current surviving hypotheses — experiments evolve precisely where rival laws disagree. The inner loop is deliberately LLM-free, responding to benchmark evidence that LLM agents are unreliable experiment designers . The falsifiable claim is that on controllable multi-variable systems CEE-Discovery recovers ground-truth equations with materially fewer and more informative measurements than the same hypothesis engine fed an equal-budget static dataset, random designs, variance-based point-querying, or CVGP-style fixed control-variable schedules , and that it solves crafted "rival-law" tasks whose laws are indistinguishable under naive sampling. The expected contribution is a concrete, inexpensive mechanism for the experiment-selection step that the agentic AI-scientist literature currently lacks, directly testable as a module inside Science-Gym- and BoxingGym-style environments .

schema.problem: Most approaches to scientific discovery reduce it to supervised learning over fixed datasets, where limited observations can support multiple plausible mechanisms that fit locally but fail to generalize; the unresolved challenge is selecting informative observations to resolve uncertainty through adaptive data acquisition.
schema.motivation: Closing the loop between hypotheses and experiments would enable robust mechanism recovery under constrained observation budgets, avoiding reliance on passively collected data that cannot distinguish locally plausible mechanisms.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework iteratively proposes plausible hypotheses, selects informative experiments to distinguish or refine them, and updates its state using the resulting evidence; rather than fitting models to passively collected data, it couples hypothesis generation with hypothesis-conditioned experiment selection and mechanism refinement. The work also releases a benchmark suite with two datasets: 57 enzyme-kinetics tasks and 45 gene-regulatory-network tasks, modeling discovery as a budget-constrained process requiring adaptive experiment design, variable selection, and recovery of true mechanisms. Code and data are made available.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation for the framework-performance claim compares the proposed framework against prior methods on NewtonBench, the 57-task chemistry dataset, and the 45-task gene-regulatory-network dataset; reported metrics are symbolic accuracy and exact graph recovery. Evaluation for the sample-efficiency claim compares hypothesis-guided experimentation against the strongest competing baselines under a budget constraint. Evaluation for the benchmark-adequacy claim rests on the design of the tasks as requiring adaptive experiment design, variable selection, and recovery of true mechanisms in two domains. Success conditions are implicitly superiority on the reported metrics and improved sample efficiency; no explicit failure thresholds or matched-compute controls are stated.

items.title: LLM-AutoSciLab: Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery via Active Experimentation with LLMs
items.abstract: Scientific discovery is a closed-loop process in which hypotheses guide data acquisition and observations refine the hypothesis space. Yet most approaches reduce discovery to supervised learning over fixed datasets, where limited observations can support multiple plausible mechanisms that fit locally but fail to generalize. Thus, the key challenge is selecting informative observations to resolve uncertainty, shifting the focus from static inference to adaptive data acquisition. To address this, we propose LLM-AutoSciLab, a closed-loop framework that couples hypothesis generation with hypothesis-conditioned experiment selection and mechanism refinement. Rather than fitting models to passively collected data, LLM-AutoSciLab iteratively proposes plausible hypotheses, selects informative experiments to distinguish or refine them, and updates its state using the resulting evidence. To evaluate dynamic, closed-loop scientific discovery with active data acquisition, we introduce ActiveSciBench, comprising two datasets: ActiveSciBench-Chem with 57 enzyme-kinetics tasks and ActiveSciBench-GRN with 45 gene-regulatory-network tasks. These datasets model discovery as a budget-constrained process requiring adaptive experiment design, variable selection, and recovery of true mechanisms. Across NewtonBench, ActiveSciBench-Chem, and ActiveSciBench-GRN, LLM-AutoSciLab outperforms prior methods, achieving 67.6% and 35.1% symbolic accuracy on NewtonBench and ActiveSciBench-Chem, respectively, and 31.1% exact graph recovery on ActiveSciBench-GRN. Moreover, hypothesis-guided experimentation is 2-5x more sample-efficient than the strongest competing baselines. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/scientific-discovery/LLM-AutoSciLab

schema.problem: Existing benchmarks for AI research agents measure whether agents reproduce results, complete implementation scaffolds, raise a predictive metric, or produce a coherent paper, but not whether the study design an agent chooses and executes licenses the causal claim it states. In healthcare and education, an intervention claim is only as good as the comparison behind it, yet an implementation-competent agent can report a confounded before-after difference as a causal effect.
schema.motivation: Converting the scientific rigor of the study an agent actually runs into a measurable, falsifiable property is consequential in health and education settings, and evidence that language agents inherit human causal-reasoning biases and that end-to-end research agents frequently emit invalidated results makes this urgent and tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark presents an agent with an intervention-outcome question, a budget, and access to an oracle simulator. The simulator's data-generating process is a structural causal model calibrated to health and education settings; the true effect and hidden confounders are known to the builder but not the agent. The agent must design the study, collect data, analyze it, and issue a conclusion. Scoring centers on the claim-design pair using design bias relative to known ground truth, an over-claim rate, and uncertainty calibration; a claim-time identifiability verifier is introduced as a mechanistic fix during agent decision-making.
schema.research_plan: The benchmark evidence is the scored claim-design pair: design bias relative to the oracle's known ground-truth effect, over-claim rate, and uncertainty calibration. The claim-time identifiability verifier is evaluated by comparing the over-claim rate for agents with the verifier against matched agents without it.

items.title: CausalValidityBench: Does the Study an AI Research Agent Runs License the Causal Claim It Makes?
items.abstract: Benchmarks for AI research agents overwhelmingly measure whether agents can reproduce published results, complete implementation scaffolds, raise a predictive metric, or produce a coherent paper — and almost never whether the design an agent chooses and executes would actually license the causal claim the agent states in its conclusion. In healthcare and education this conflation is consequential: an intervention claim such as "the reminder improved adherence" is only as good as the comparison behind it, yet an agent can pass an implementation check while reporting a confounded before-after difference as a causal effect. We propose CausalValidityBench, a benchmark in which an agent receives an intervention-outcome question, a budget, and access to an oracle simulator whose data-generating process is a structural causal model calibrated to health and education settings, with the true effect and hidden confounders known to the builder but not the agent. The agent must design the study, collect data, analyze it, and issue a conclusion; scoring centers on the claim-design pair — design bias versus the known ground-truth effect, an over-claim rate, and uncertainty calibration — quantities existing reproduction-style benchmarks cannot express. Drawing on evidence that language agents inherit human causal-reasoning biases and that end-to-end research agents frequently emit invalidated results , we hypothesize a design-level causal over-claim bias that persists in implementation-competent agents, and we propose a claim-time identifiability verifier as a mechanistic fix, predicting it at least halves the over-claim rate. CausalValidityBench thereby converts "scientific rigor of the study actually run" from a rhetorical desideratum into a measurable, falsifiable property of research agents.

schema.problem: Automated research systems for causal empirical analysis are prone to silent failures, in which analysis code runs successfully but relies on invalid causal assumptions, and these failures are not made visible.
schema.motivation: Making these failures visible would prevent unwarranted causal claims and support validity-first automated science, while synthetic-data generation can also enable pipeline development when confidential data are inaccessible.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code. It first constructs a protocol, then generates synthetic datasets using structural causal models with known ground-truth effects; this synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. The pipeline explicitly encodes causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints.
schema.research_plan: (1) The framework is evaluated on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and the approved protocol. (2) The contribution of protocol construction and adversarial validation is isolated by comparing the full framework against standard LLM-based generation. Support for the main claim is indicated by a shift from silent causal estimates to surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or non-causal interpretations; failure would be continued silent invalid causal estimates.

items.title: Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines
items.abstract: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

schema.problem: Large language model-based autonomous research agents can generate coherent papers and syntactically correct code, but recent benchmarks show they can fabricate or invalidate experimental results; the failure is not simple hallucination or code error but a lack of agent coherence in aligning computed results with claimed results.
schema.motivation: As autonomous research agents become able to produce papers and code, verifying the alignment between what they compute and what they claim is necessary for trusting or safely using their outputs.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework audits completed research outputs consisting of paper, code, and logs, detecting three classes of inconsistencies: fabricated results (claims without execution records), misaligned results (code ran but output contradicts narrative), and recycled novelty (claimed contributions matching cited baselines). It performs independent re-execution and structural comparison, and produces structured reproducibility audit reports that flag specific claims with verification status and reproduction cost.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation applies the framework to 200 AI-generated research papers across 10 ML subdomain areas, auditing paper, code, and logs by independent re-execution and structural comparison and flagging specific claims with verification status and reproduction cost. No explicit failure condition, metric, or matched-baseline design is stated.

items.title: Verifiable AI Research: A Multi-Stage Alignment Framework for Auditing End-to-End Autonomous Science
items.abstract: Large language model-based autonomous research agents can generate coherent research papers and syntactically correct code, but recent benchmarks reveal they fabricate or invalidate 80% of experimental results. This problem is not simple hallucination or code error—it is a failure of agent coherence: agents execute code, obtain results, then rewrite the narrative to fit the hypothesis, without verifying alignment between computed and claimed results. We propose the Verifiable AI Research (VAR) framework, which audits completed research outputs (paper + code + logs) to detect three classes of inconsistencies: fabricated results (claims without execution records), misaligned results (code ran but output contradicts narrative), and recycled novelty (claimed contributions matching cited baselines). Unlike prior benchmarks that measure task completion or apply post-hoc scoring rubrics, VAR performs independent re-execution and structural comparison to identify where AI scientists fail to maintain coherence. We evaluate VAR on 200 AI-generated research papers across 10 ML subdomain areas, producing structured "reproducibility audit reports" that flag specific claims with verification status and reproduction cost.

schema.problem: Autonomous research agents produce competitive solutions and professional-looking manuscripts, yet their outputs contain verifiability failures—fabricated citations, unreproducible scores, and method descriptions that diverge from the implementation—that surface-level evaluation cannot detect.
schema.motivation: Hidden verifiability failures undermine trust in autonomous research outputs, and the growing capability of such agents makes a uniform way to trace evidence and audit integrity timely.
schema.proposed_approach: The work consists of three components. First, a verifiability framework requires every claim to be traceable to its evidence source. Second, an end-to-end autonomous research system maintains such evidence chains by construction throughout literature review, solution discovery, and paper writing. Third, a post-hoc audit applies four integrity checks—score verification, specification violation, reference verification, and method-code alignment—uniformly to any system's outputs.
schema.research_plan: The paper applies the four integrity checks to 75 papers produced by five systems across five frontier research tasks to characterize verifiability failures. The proposed system is assessed with the same checks on the five tasks, and its outputs are compared with human expert performance. Generalization is tested on six additional tasks spanning medical imaging, fine-grained recognition, 3D perception, and language modeling, including the Parameter Golf and MLE-Bench benchmarks, with baselines for comparison. No independent failure threshold is stated beyond the audit checks themselves.

items.title: ScientistOne: Towards Human-Level Autonomous Research via Chain-of-Evidence
items.abstract: Autonomous research agents produce competitive solutions and professional-looking manuscripts, yet their outputs contain verifiability failures undetectable by surface-level evaluation: fabricated citations, unreproducible scores, and method descriptions that diverge from the implementation. We address this through three contributions. First, Chain-of-Evidence (CoE), a verifiability framework requiring every claim to be traceable to its evidence source. Second, ScientistOne, an end-to-end autonomous research system that maintains evidence chains by construction throughout literature review, solution discovery, and paper writing. Third, CoE Audit, a post-hoc audit whose four integrity checks -- score verification, specification violation, reference verification, and method-code alignment -- apply uniformly to all systems. Across 75 papers spanning five systems and five frontier research tasks, every baseline exhibits at least one systematic failure mode: hallucinated reference rates reach 21%, score verification passes in as few as 42% of papers, and method-code alignment ranges from 20% to 80%. ScientistOne achieves zero hallucinated references (0/337), perfect score verification (12/12), and the highest method-code alignment (14/15), while matching or exceeding human expert performance on all five tasks. ScientistOne further generalizes to six additional tasks spanning medical imaging, fine-grained recognition, 3D perception, and language modeling, achieving state-of-the-art on Parameter Golf and gold medals on MLE-Bench tasks where baselines fail entirely.

schema.problem: Current AI research agents automate literature search and synthesis but struggle to integrate evidence of scholarly agreement, disagreement, and conceptual lineage, leading to fragmented, potentially contradictory research proposals.
schema.motivation: Integrating structured citation relationships before proposal generation would let agents surface convergent findings, flag contradictions, and trace technological evolution, bridging the gap between single-paper retrieval quality and coherent multi-paper evidence synthesis in autonomous research automation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed work is a modular reasoning layer that augments research agents with structured knowledge of citation relationships—corroboration, conflict, and conceptual lineage—extracted from citation networks. Retrieved papers are contextualized within their citation ecosystem before proposal generation. A novel benchmark of relation-aware research proposal tasks is introduced for evaluation.
schema.research_plan: The proposed layer will be evaluated on the introduced benchmark of relation-aware research proposal tasks, comparing against baseline agents and SciNet-augmented systems on expert-rated novelty, coherence, and citation grounding. The comparisons are designed to test whether the layer supports identification of convergent findings, contradiction flagging, and technological evolution tracing.

items.title: Citation-Aware Evidence Synthesis for Research Agent Proposal Generation
items.abstract: Current AI research agents automate literature search and synthesis but struggle to integrate evidence of scholarly agreement, disagreement, and conceptual lineage—resulting in fragmented, potentially contradictory research proposals. We propose Citation-Aware Evidence Synthesis (CAES), a modular reasoning layer that augments research agents with structured knowledge of citation relationships (corroboration, conflict, conceptual lineage) extracted from citation networks. The layer contextualizes retrieved papers within their citation ecosystem before proposal generation, enabling agents to identify convergent findings, flag contradictions, and trace technological evolution. We will evaluate CAES on a novel benchmark of relation-aware research proposal tasks, comparing against baseline agents and SciNet-augmented systems on expert-rated novelty, coherence, and citation grounding. The work bridges a critical gap between single-paper retrieval quality and coherent multi-paper evidence synthesis in autonomous research automation.

schema.problem: Retrieval-augmented LLM idea generation typically provides retrieved literature as flat text such as titles, abstracts, or summaries, which can be redundant or weakly relevant and makes cross-paper relations among problems, methods, mechanisms, and findings difficult to identify and trace.
schema.motivation: Explicitly representing literature relations and reducing noisy textual input could support more effective and traceable generation of novel, feasible, and high-quality research ideas.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework retrieves papers according to the input topic, transforms them into structured knowledge triples, and dynamically constructs a target-centered knowledge graph to make literature relations explicit. It extracts compact graph-derived contexts that retain target-relevant relational evidence while reducing noisy textual input. A two-stage generation process then identifies promising research directions and guides an LLM to synthesize candidate ideas from graph-grounded evidence.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation is conducted on a scientific idea generation benchmark against representative baselines under an automatic evaluation protocol using novelty, quality, and feasibility metrics; support is indicated by outperforming baselines, while failure would mean not doing so. The abstract does not describe ablations, held-matched compute, or other explicit failure conditions.

items.title: Graph2Idea:Retrieval-Augmented Scientific Idea Generation with Graph-Structured Contexts
items.abstract: Generating novel, feasible, and high-quality research ideas is an important yet challenging task in scientific discovery. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods often ground idea generation with retrieved literature, but the retrieved evidence is usually provided as flat text, such as titles, abstracts, or summaries. Such flat contexts may contain redundant or weakly relevant information, while making cross-paper relations among problems, methods, mechanisms, and findings difficult to identify and trace. To address this challenge, we propose Graph2Idea, a knowledge graph-guided framework for retrieval-augmented scientific idea generation.Graph2Idea first retrieves papers according to the input topic, transforms them into structured knowledge triples, and dynamically constructs a target-centered knowledge graph to make literature relations explicit. It then extracts compact graph-derived contexts that retain target-relevant relational evidence while reducing noisy textual input. Based on these contexts, a two-stage generation process first identifies promising research directions and then guides the LLM to synthesize candidate ideas from graph-grounded evidence. Experiments on a scientific idea generation benchmark show that Graph2Idea outperforms representative baselines under the automatic evaluation protocol. Compared with the strongest baseline scores, it improves Novelty from 0.45 to 0.52, Quality from 0.24 to 0.29, and Feasibility from 0.22 to 0.28. These results suggest that graph-structured evidence helps LLMs generate research ideas through more explicit, compact, and traceable recombination of prior scientific knowledge.

schema.problem: Autonomous AI scientist systems can already span hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript writing, but they often produce spurious, non-reproducible improvements because of superficial experimentation, metric gaming, and insufficient stress-testing, leaving an implementation and verification gap.
schema.motivation: As end-to-end autonomous discovery becomes feasible, closing this gap is necessary to prevent false discoveries from propagating and to make AI-generated scientific claims trustworthy.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an autonomous verification agent that explicitly formulates adversarial test cases, probes boundary conditions, and attempts to falsify its own generated hypotheses before ratifying any scientific claim, using Popperian falsification as its governing principle rather than optimizing solely for standard benchmark performance.
schema.research_plan: (1) The false-positive-reduction claim is tested through controlled experiments across machine learning engineering tasks; (2) the methodological-robustness claim is tested through the same controlled experiments. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, matched budgets, or an explicit failure condition.

items.title: Falsification-Driven Experimentation and Verification for Autonomous AI Scientists
items.abstract: The rapid emergence of autonomous AI scientist systems has demonstrated the feasibility of end-to-end scientific discovery, spanning hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript writing. However, recent systematic evaluations reveal a critical bottleneck: the "implementation and verification gap," where AI systems frequently generate spurious, non-reproducible improvements due to superficial experimentation, metric gaming, and a lack of rigorous stress-testing. To address this vulnerability, we propose an autonomous verification framework governed by the principle of Popperian falsification. Rather than optimizing solely for performance gains on standard benchmarks, our proposed agent explicitly formulates adversarial test cases, probes boundary conditions, and attempts to falsify its own generated hypotheses before ratifying any scientific claim. Through controlled experiments across machine learning engineering tasks, we demonstrate that incorporating an automated falsification loop significantly reduces false-positive discoveries while ensuring genuine methodological robustness.

schema.problem: In autonomous scientific discovery, once the evaluator is frozen, a sufficiently strong search process can learn to win the exam without learning the mechanism the task was meant to reveal, because static validation passively certifies candidates rather than actively testing them.
schema.motivation: As discovery becomes more autonomous, evaluation must become adversarial to push candidates toward genuine mechanistic understanding and avoid false discoveries that pass frozen validators.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework co-evolves three components under a fixed scientific contract: an innovator that generates executable scientific artifacts, an adversarial falsifier that produces scientifically admissible counterexample environments, and a mechanistic causal extractor. It is applied to a controlled loss-discovery problem with a single editable locus, where candidate artifacts are evaluated through an adaptive falsification frontier rather than static validation.
schema.research_plan: The evidence uses a controlled loss-discovery problem with a single editable locus. The paper tests whether the framework rejects artifacts that static validation would have accepted and identifies the first candidate that survives the admissible falsification frontier. It then evaluates the discovered loss against CE and CE+L2 under controlled comparisons across standard benchmarks, including ImageNet, to assess transfer beyond the synthetic discovery environment.

items.title: Let the Abyss Stare Back Adaptive Falsification for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: Autonomous scientific discovery is entering a more dangerous regime: once the evaluator is frozen, a sufficiently strong search process can learn to win the exam without learning the mechanism the task was meant to reveal. This is the idea behind our title. To let the abyss stare back is to make evaluation actively push against the candidate through adaptive falsification, rather than passively certify it through static validation. We introduce DASES, a falsification-driven framework in which an Innovator, an Abyss Falsifier, and a Mechanistic Causal Extractor co-evolve executable scientific artifacts and scientifically admissible counterexample environments under a fixed scientific contract. In a controlled loss-discovery problem with a single editable locus, DASES rejects artifacts that static validation would have accepted, identifies the first candidate that survives the admissible falsification frontier, and discovers FNG-CE, a loss that transfers beyond the synthetic discovery environment and consistently outperforms CE and CE+L2 under controlled comparisons across standard benchmarks, including ImageNet.

schema.problem: Existing LLM agents for autonomous scientific discovery face bottlenecks in generating correct, executable, and reproducible research code. These agents largely rely on reactive debugging from compiler errors or raw execution traces and lack structured internal verification.
schema.motivation: Structured internal verification inspired by human cognitive workflows and test-driven development may avoid cascading logic errors and make scientific discovery code more robust end-to-end.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed agentic framework connects natural language research hypotheses to robust code execution by synthesizing automated test cases, verifying a step-by-step plan through simulation prior to code generation, and iterating through hierarchical multi-turn feedback loops. It is applied to scientific code generation tasks.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation design applies the framework to scientific code benchmarks and compares it with existing reactive-debugging agents. Claim (1) is assessed by whether cascading logic errors are systematically reduced; claim (2) by whether end-to-end scientific discovery performance improves. The abstract does not specify named baselines, metrics, matching conditions, or failure thresholds.

items.title: Sim-Scientist: Simulation-Driven Plan Verification and Test-Driven Development for Autonomous Scientific Research Code Generation
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents designed for autonomous scientific discovery face severe bottlenecks in generating correct, executable, and reproducible research code. While recent benchmarks like RECODE-H and AutoExperiment highlight the challenges of multi-turn research code implementation and progressive code replication, existing agents largely rely on reactive debugging using compiler errors or raw execution traces without structured internal verification. Inspired by human cognitive workflows—such as mental or visual simulation of algorithms before coding—and rigorous test-driven development, we propose Sim-Scientist, an agentic framework that bridges natural language research hypotheses and robust code execution through automated test case synthesis, step-by-step simulation-driven plan verification prior to code generation, and hierarchical multi-turn feedback loops. Our evaluation design across scientific code benchmarks demonstrates how simulation-guided verification systematically reduces cascading logic errors and improves end-to-end scientific discovery performance.

schema.problem: Scientific code generation with LLMs is unreliable, suffers from error propagation in multi-agent workflows, and lacks dependable evaluation in domains with ill-defined success metrics.
schema.motivation: Automating scientific code generation could reduce manual coding burden, but reliable use requires better coordination and evaluation, and non-coding practitioners need a way to express domain needs without manual prompt engineering.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed platform coordinates three LLM-based agents under a Bayesian framework: a planning agent structures user inputs into actionable plans and adaptive test cases, a code-generating agent produces candidate solutions, and an evaluator agent provides comprehensive feedback. In an adversarial loop, the planning agent iteratively refines test cases to challenge the code-generating agent, while prompt distributions are dynamically updated using Bayesian principles and code quality metrics, including functional correctness, structural alignment, and static analysis. The platform also translates non-expert prompts into domain-specific requirements, bypassing manual prompt engineering for practitioners without coding backgrounds.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of benchmark evaluations intended to assess robust code generation and error propagation, and testing on a cross-disciplinary Earth Science task against competing models. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: AI-for-Science Low-code Platform with Bayesian Adversarial Multi-Agent Framework
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate potentials for automating scientific code generation but face challenges in reliability, error propagation in multi-agent workflows, and evaluation in domains with ill-defined success metrics. We present a Bayesian adversarial multi-agent framework specifically designed for AI for Science (AI4S) tasks in the form of a Low-code Platform (LCP). Three LLM-based agents are coordinated under the Bayesian framework: a Task Manager that structures user inputs into actionable plans and adaptive test cases, a Code Generator that produces candidate solutions, and an Evaluator providing comprehensive feedback. The framework employs an adversarial loop where the Task Manager iteratively refines test cases to challenge the Code Generator, while prompt distributions are dynamically updated using Bayesian principles by integrating code quality metrics: functional correctness, structural alignment, and static analysis. This co-optimization of tests and code reduces dependence on LLM reliability and addresses evaluation uncertainty inherent to scientific tasks. LCP also streamlines human-AI collaboration by translating non-expert prompts into domain-specific requirements, bypassing the need for manual prompt engineering by practitioners without coding backgrounds. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate LCP's effectiveness in generating robust code while minimizing error propagation. The proposed platform is also tested on an Earth Science cross-disciplinary task and demonstrates strong reliability, outperforming competing models.

schema.problem: There is no end-to-end autonomous AI scientist for perovskite photovoltaics discovery: existing AI-scientist systems operate in software or generic domains; emerging LLM-agent materials systems generate and critique proposals but do not execute or react to real perovskite experiments or simulations; autonomous perovskite platforms run closed-loop experiments under fixed human-specified objectives without generative, physics-grounded hypothesis formation.
schema.motivation: LLM agents and verified execution layers (DFT, surrogate property APIs, registered device data) now make it tractable to close an autonomous discovery loop in perovskite PV, and avoiding current coding agents' high fabrication/invalidation failure mode motivates objective, artifact-mandatory evaluation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system couples an LLM-agent hypothesis engine to a verified execution layer comprising DFT, surrogate property APIs, and—where available—registered in-house device data. The loop closes through interpretation of execution results, hypothesis revision, and re-proposal. Evaluation uses a curated perovskite benchmark with objective, artifact-mandatory, non-LLM-judged scoring and a pre-registered protocol.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation tests the falsifiable claim by comparing the proposed closed loop against random search, fixed-objective Bayesian agents, and an open-loop ablation with execution feedback removed, holding computational budget fixed. Evidence is validated success rate (experiment- or DFT-confirmed candidates) and band-gap agreement with reference DFT. Support requires higher success rate and higher band-gap agreement than each baseline; otherwise the claim is not supported. The benchmark scoring is objective and artifact-mandatory, judged without an LLM, under a pre-registered protocol.

items.title: PerovSci: An Autonomous Closed-Loop AI Scientist for Perovskite Photovoltaics
items.abstract: We propose PerovSci, the first end-to-end autonomous AI scientist aimed specifically at perovskite photovoltaics (PV) discovery. Existing AI-scientist systems automate the research loop in software domains — algorithmic ML research , equation discovery , competition-driven ML challenges — or generically across fields ; the emerging LLM-agent materials systems (SparksMatter , LLMatDesign , Kumbhar et al. ) generate and critique proposals but never execute and react to real perovskite experiments or simulations. Conversely, autonomous perovskite platforms (AMADAP , Montoya et al. ) run closed-loop experiments under a fixed, human-specified objective without generative, physics-grounded hypothesis formation. PerovSci couples an LLM-agent hypothesis engine to a verified execution layer (DFT, surrogate property APIs, and—where available—registered in-house device data) and closes the loop through interpretation, hypothesis revision, and re-proposal. We formulate a falsifiable claim: within a fixed computational budget, this closed loop discovers candidate perovskite compositions meeting a multi-objective efficiency–stability specification with a higher validated success rate (experiment- or DFT-confirmed candidates) and higher band-gap agreement with reference DFT than (a) random search, (b) fixed-objective Bayesian agents , and (c) its own open-loop ablation with execution feedback removed. Evaluation uses PBS-Bench, a curated perovskite benchmark with objective, artifact-mandatory, non-LLM-judged scoring and a pre-registered protocol — explicitly countering the 80% fabrication/invalidation failure mode documented for current coding agents .

schema.problem: Existing AI approaches for perovskite development are discrete models for material design, process optimization, or property prediction, and they fail to propagate physical constraints across the closed-loop workflow, hindering end-to-end optimization.
schema.motivation: Perovskite solar cells have strong optoelectronic performance and cost potential, but their development is precise and complex, so an end-to-end workflow that propagates physical constraints could improve discovery efficiency and support real synthesis.
schema.proposed_approach: A multi-agent system encapsulates a series of perovskite-specific tools into Model Context Protocols. The agents plan and invoke these tools to design perovskite materials under multi-objective constraints, covering literature retrieval, data extraction, property prediction, and mechanism analysis. Candidate proposals are iteratively tracked and diagnosed, and the system adapts its strategy in a closed loop to refine toward target objectives. An evaluation benchmark is constructed by perovskite human experts for assessing the system.
schema.research_plan: (1) To assess the discovery-efficiency claim, the system is compared with single large language models and traditional search strategies on a benchmark constructed by perovskite human experts. (2) The closed-loop adaptation claim is examined through the system's iterative tracking and diagnosis of candidate proposals under multi-objective constraints, refining toward target objectives. (3) The physical-world effectiveness claim is tested through real synthesis experiments.

items.title: PeroMAS: A Multi-agent System of Perovskite Material Discovery
items.abstract: As a pioneer of the third-generation photovoltaic revolution, Perovskite Solar Cells (PSCs) are renowned for their superior optoelectronic performance and cost potential. The development process of PSCs is precise and complex, involving a series of closed-loop workflows such as literature retrieval, data integration, experimental design, and synthesis. However, existing AI perovskite approaches focus predominantly on discrete models, including material design, process optimization, and property prediction. These models fail to propagate physical constraints across the workflow, hindering end-to-end optimization. In this paper, we propose a multi-agent system for perovskite material discovery, named PeroMAS. We first encapsulated a series of perovskite-specific tools into Model Context Protocols (MCPs). By planning and invoking these tools, PeroMAS can design perovskite materials under multi-objective constraints, covering the entire process from literature retrieval and data extraction to property prediction and mechanism analysis. Furthermore, we construct an evaluation benchmark by perovskite human experts to assess this multi-agent system. Results demonstrate that, compared to single Large Language Model (LLM) or traditional search strategies, our system enhances discovery efficiency. It iteratively tracks and diagnoses candidate proposals under multi-objective constraints, refining toward target objectives through closed-loop strategy adaptation. Notably, we verify PeroMAS's effectiveness in the physical world through real synthesis experiments.

schema.problem: LLM-driven metaheuristic design loops evaluate candidate heuristics on the same small set of instances used to drive evolution, so reported performance is entirely in-distribution; the only cross-instance evidence is post-hoc and lacks an instrumented study of why failure occurs.
schema.motivation: An evaluation standard is needed to separate declared from transferable generalization of LLM-designed heuristics and to make overfitting diagnosable across common combinatorial optimization problem classes.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark protocol featurizes combinatorial-optimization instances via Instance Space Analysis, clusters them into disjoint regions, and holds out entire regions while an LLM design loop runs on a source region; the primary measured quantity is the relative optimality-gap increase between source and held-out regions. It couples this protocol with an evolution-time conditioning intervention in which prompts and fitness rewards carry instance-region descriptors plus a holdout-regularization term. An operator-attribution ablation restricts evolution to one algorithm component at a time (representation, variation, or fitness scoring) to locate the component responsible for overfitting. The deliverable is the benchmark and an empirical atlas across bin packing, TSP, and CVRP.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the unmodified-loop claim and the benchmark-separation claim comes from running LLaMEA-style design loops on source regions and evaluating on held-out regions across bin packing, TSP, and CVRP, with support defined as a relative optimality-gap increase of at least 5% on held-out regions. Evidence for the intervention claim comes from comparing the evolution-time conditioning intervention against unmodified loops under the same source-region evolution and held-out evaluation, with support requiring at least 30% reduction in the measured transfer gap and at most 1% relative source-region performance degradation. The operator-attribution ablation isolates representation, variation, and fitness scoring one at a time to determine which component drives overfitting.

items.title: CliffBench: An Instance-Region Transfer Benchmark with Descriptor-Conditioned Generation for LLM-Designed Metaheuristics
items.abstract: LLM-driven metaheuristic design loops (LLaMEA, PoH, LLaMEA-HPO) evaluate candidate heuristics on the same small set of instances used to drive evolution, so their reported performance is entirely in-distribution . Meanwhile, the only cross-instance evidence available is post-hoc: Sim et al. showed that LLM-evolved bin-packing heuristics fail to generalize across a broad benchmark suite, without any instrumented study of why . This proposal introduces CliffBench, a benchmark protocol in which combinatorial-optimization instances are featurized via Instance Space Analysis (ISA), clustered into disjoint regions, and entire regions are held out while an LLM design loop runs on a source region; the "transfer cliff" — the relative optimality-gap increase between source and held-out regions — becomes the primary measured quantity. We couple the benchmark with a Descriptor-Conditioned Generation (DCG) intervention in which evolution-time prompts and fitness rewards carry instance-region descriptors plus a holdout-regularization term, and with an operator-attribution ablation that restricts evolution to one algorithm component (representation, variation, or fitness scoring) at a time to locate the component responsible for overfitting. The falsifiable claim: (H1) LLaMEA-style loops evolved on a source region show a measurable transfer cliff (≥5% relative optimality-gap increase) on held-out regions of the same problem class; (H2) DCG reduces the cliff index by ≥30% without degrading source-region performance beyond 1% relative. The deliverable is the benchmark plus a first empirical atlas of transfer cliffs across bin packing, TSP, and CVRP, giving the community an evaluation standard that separates "declared" from "transferable" generalization of LLM-designed heuristics.

schema.problem: Most existing automatic heuristic discovery methods are limited by static evaluation against fixed instance distributions, leading to potential overfitting and poor generalization under distributional shifts.
schema.motivation: Generalization and robustness under distributional shifts are critical for applying learned heuristics beyond fixed benchmarks, and LLM-based program search makes adaptive co-evolution between solvers and instance generators tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed game-theoretic framework reframes heuristic discovery as program-level co-evolution between a solver and an instance generator. It models their interaction as a two-player zero-sum game, maintains growing strategy pools on both sides, and iteratively expands them via LLM-based best-response oracles against mixed opponent meta-strategies. This replaces static evaluation with an adaptive, self-generated curriculum.
schema.research_plan: Evidence comes from empirical evaluation across multiple combinatorial optimization domains against static-training automatic heuristic discovery baselines built on the same program search mechanisms, with generalization and robustness assessed on diverse and out-of-distribution instances. No explicit failure condition or matched-compute details are stated.

items.title: Game-Theoretic Co-Evolution for LLM-Based Heuristic Discovery
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled rapid progress in automatic heuristic discovery (AHD), yet most existing methods are predominantly limited by static evaluation against fixed instance distributions, leading to potential overfitting and poor generalization under distributional shifts. We propose Algorithm Space Response Oracles (ASRO), a game-theoretic framework that reframes heuristic discovery as a program level co-evolution between solver and instance generator. ASRO models their interaction as a two-player zero-sum game, maintains growing strategy pools on both sides, and iteratively expands them via LLM-based best-response oracles against mixed opponent meta-strategies, thereby replacing static evaluation with an adaptive, self-generated curriculum. Across multiple combinatorial optimization domains, ASRO consistently outperforms static-training AHD baselines built on the same program search mechanisms, achieving substantially improved generalization and robustness on diverse and out-of-distribution instances.

schema.problem: Current LLM-based systems for scientific research focus on isolated tasks and lack comprehensive end-to-end autonomous capabilities.
schema.motivation: The rapid advancement of LLMs makes it timely to integrate their strengths with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation to enable more complete automation of scientific research.
schema.proposed_approach: An integrated framework that uses LLMs for hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and scientific writing, combined with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation tools for experiment execution and analysis, aimed at end-to-end autonomous AI scientists.
schema.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated on LAB-Bench and AutoExperiment, and its performance will be assessed in real-world scientific research scenarios; no failure condition or held-matched comparison is specified.

items.title: End-to-End Autonomous AI Scientists: An Integrated Framework for Scientific Research Automation
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shown potential in automating various stages of scientific research. However, current LLM-based systems primarily focus on isolated tasks and lack comprehensive end-to-end autonomous capabilities. This proposal aims to design and develop an integrated framework that enables end-to-end autonomous AI scientists by combining LLMs with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation tools. The proposed framework will leverage the strengths of LLMs in hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and scientific writing, while integrating them with AI tools for experiment execution and analysis. We will evaluate the framework using benchmarks such as LAB-Bench and AutoExperiment, and assess its performance in real-world scientific research scenarios.

schema.problem: Climate research is bottlenecked by fragmented, labor-intensive workflows, and existing LLM-based support remains confined to simple question answering, oversimplifying the physical constraints and data-driven demands of professional climate science.
schema.motivation: The growing volume of multi-scale climate data and the availability of LLMs make it timely to scale scientific expertise toward automated end-to-end climate research across diverse sub-fields.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework combines a unified tool-use environment with rigorous reasoning protocols to perform end-to-end modeling and analysis rather than simple retrieval, and is designed as a general-purpose autonomous system across diverse climate sub-fields. The work also constructs a benchmark containing challenging problems across five task categories derived from professional climate scenarios between 2000 and 2025. Code is released for the framework and benchmark.
schema.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on the proposed benchmark against state-of-the-art baselines, using solution rigorousness and practicality as evaluation metrics; benchmark tasks are drawn from professional climate scenarios between 2000 and 2025.

items.title: ClimAgent: LLM as Agents for Autonomous Open-ended Climate Science Analysis
items.abstract: Climate research is pivotal for mitigating global environmental crises, yet the accelerating volume of multi-scale datasets and the complexity of analytical tools have created significant bottlenecks, constraining scientific discovery to fragmented and labor-intensive workflows. While the emergence Large Language Models (LLMs) offers a transformative paradigm to scale scientific expertise, existing explorations remain largely confined to simple Question-Answering (Q&A) tasks. These approaches often oversimplify real-world challenges, neglecting the intricate physical constraints and the data-driven nature required in professional climate science.To bridge this gap, we introduce ClimAgent, a general-purpose autonomous framework designed to execute a wide spectrum of research tasks across diverse climate sub-fields. By integrating a unified tool-use environment with rigorous reasoning protocols, ClimAgent transcends simple retrieval to perform end-to-end modeling and analysis. To foster systematic evaluation, we propose ClimaBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for real-world climate discovery. It encompasses challenging problems spanning 5 distinct task categories derived from professional scenarios between 2000 and 2025. Experiments on ClimaBench demonstrate that ClimAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a 40.21% improvement over original LLM solutions in solution rigorousness and practicality. Our code are available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/ClimAgent.

schema.problem: Evaluation of LLMs in scientific hypothesis generation and experiment planning remains a significant challenge, and current benchmarks have underexplored limitations for practical use.
schema.motivation: Rapid advances in LLMs are transforming scientific research support, so assessing their hypothesis generation and experiment planning is important for practical utility and discovery.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach is a benchmarking framework that builds upon and extends HypoBench and LAB-Bench to evaluate LLMs in hypothesis generation and experiment planning. It focuses on practical utility, generalizability, and hypothesis discovery rate, and it includes investigating strengths and limitations of current benchmarks and proposing new evaluation metrics.
schema.research_plan: The described evidence is an investigation of strengths and limitations of existing benchmarks HypoBench and LAB-Bench and the proposal of new evaluation metrics for hypothesis generation and experiment planning; no experimental design, named baselines beyond those benchmarks, or failure conditions are specified.

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Hypothesis Generation and Experiment Planning: A Novel Benchmarking Approach
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has transformed the landscape of scientific research, offering unprecedented support across various stages of the research cycle. However, the evaluation of LLMs in scientific hypothesis generation and experiment planning remains a significant challenge. This proposal introduces a novel benchmarking approach that builds upon and extends existing benchmarks such as HypoBench and LAB-Bench . Our approach aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation framework for LLMs in hypothesis generation and experiment planning, focusing on practical utility, generalizability, and hypothesis discovery rate. We will investigate the strengths and limitations of current benchmarks and propose new evaluation metrics that address the challenges in hypothesis generation and experiment planning.

schema.problem: Large language models excel at answering pre-specified questions, but their ability to navigate the open-ended, pre-conclusion stage of discovery remains largely unmeasured.
schema.motivation: Measuring this capability is a step toward evaluating how models formulate investigative directions from inconclusive evidence when final conclusions are withheld.
schema.proposed_approach: The work defines a task requiring models to autonomously construct grounded, discriminative, and testable hypothesis spaces from inconclusive evidence, including anomalous observations and fragmented records. It releases a benchmark of 988 cases across six scientific and analytical domains, constructed by a pipeline that reconstructs pre-conclusion contexts from completed expert documents by removing explicit conclusions, target hypotheses, and retrospective causal attributions while preserving the factual substrate. The evaluation framework scores open-ended hypothesis sets using bidirectional pairwise judgments aggregated by Bradley-Terry-Davidson ranking and six-dimensional rubric scoring. Experiments are run on 15 frontier large language models.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates 15 frontier large language models on the benchmark and evaluation framework. For the claim that the task is a distinct evaluation target, it looks for capability stratification among models and model-dependent effects of structured analytical skills. For the claim that the evaluation framework resolves finer differences, it compares aggregated rankings against absolute rubric scoring and checks agreement with human experts and an independent judge. The design treats clear stratification and strong agreement with human and independent judges as support; their absence would count against the claims.

items.title: Before the Action: Benchmarking LLMs on Prospective Hypothesis Discovery
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at answering pre-specified questions, yet their ability to navigate the open-ended, pre-conclusion stage of discovery remains largely unmeasured. We introduce Prospective Hypothesis Discovery (PHD), which asks models to autonomously construct grounded, discriminative, and testable hypothesis spaces from inconclusive evidence, including anomalous observations and fragmented records, to guide subsequent investigation. To evaluate this capability, we introduce HypoArena, comprising HypoData, a benchmark of 988 cases across six scientific and analytical domains, and HypoEval, an evaluation framework for open-ended hypothesis sets. To construct HypoData at scale, we propose Retrospective Context Regression, a Forge--Audit pipeline that reconstructs pre-conclusion contexts from completed expert documents by removing explicit conclusions, target hypotheses, and retrospective causal attributions while preserving the factual substrate. Because PHD admits multiple valid outputs, HypoEval combines bidirectional pairwise judgments with Bradley--Terry--Davidson aggregation for ranking and six-dimensional rubric scoring for diagnosis. Experiments on 15 frontier LLMs reveal clear capability stratification and model-dependent effects of structured analytical skills, with gains for several lower-performing models on HypoArena but regressions for other systems, including a top-performing model. Compared with absolute rubric scoring, arena evaluation resolves finer-grained differences among models, with aggregated rankings showing strong agreement with human experts and an independent judge. Together, these results support treating PHD as a distinct target for evaluating how LLMs formulate investigative directions when final conclusions are withheld. Our code and data are publicly available at github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/HypoArena and github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/HypoArena.

schema.problem: Existing agentic LLM equation discovery fits hypotheses to a fixed dataset, while active experimental-design methods choose where to sample for a single, already-chosen model, leaving no method that jointly proposes candidate governing operators and actively chooses samples to discriminate among them.
schema.motivation: Under a fixed compute/lab budget, sample choices that discriminate among candidate governing operators may reduce the number of runs needed to recover the governing equation and reach target out-of-regime accuracy.
schema.proposed_approach: One LLM agent proposes PDE operator hypotheses as executable code and actively selects the next parameter-condition and observation to collect by maximizing expected information gain over the current pool of candidate operators. Candidate operators pass physics gates for dimensional homogeneity, boundary-condition/symmetry compatibility, and dissipation sign before any budget is spent. Survivors are validated on a held-out out-of-regime split. The approach is instantiated on fluid-dynamics and vibration testbeds with known ground truth (Burgers' equation, the Duffing oscillator, a geometrically nonlinear Bernoulli–Euler beam, and a vortex-induced-vibration reduced model), and includes release of a budgeted, out-of-regime, anti-memorization discovery benchmark with explicit recovery and efficiency metrics.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is from the four testbeds with known ground truth: (1) compare against matched-data static agentic fitting (LLM-SR-style) and (2) compare against the same agent using uniform condition sampling, both under a fixed compute/lab budget. For each, the paper evaluates recovery of the governing operator and target out-of-regime accuracy on the held-out split. The stated failure condition is that if the uniform-sampling variant ties, the expected-information-gain design objective adds nothing and the central claim fails. The released benchmark supplies explicit recovery and efficiency metrics under a budgeted, anti-memorization protocol.

items.title: PDE-Scientist: Budgeted, Structure-Discriminating Active Design for LLM-Guided PDE Operator Discovery
items.abstract: Agentic LLM equation discovery has advanced rapidly, but the retrieved systems fit hypotheses to a fixed dataset, while active experimental-design methods choose where to sample for a single, already-chosen model. We identify and close this split. We propose PDE-Scientist, a framework in which one LLM agent (i) proposes PDE operator hypotheses as executable code and (ii) actively selects the next parameter-condition and observation to collect by maximizing expected information gain (EIG) over the pool of candidate operators — a structure-discriminating design objective, not Bayesian optimization of one model's parameters. Candidates pass physics gates (dimensional homogeneity, boundary-condition/symmetry compatibility, dissipation sign) before spending budget, and every survivor is validated on a held-out out-of-regime split. The claim is falsifiable: under a fixed compute/lab budget, PDE-Scientist recovers the governing operator and reaches target out-of-regime accuracy with fewer runs than (a) matched-data static agentic fitting (LLM-SR-style) and (b) the same agent with uniform condition sampling; if (b) ties, the design objective adds nothing and the central claim fails. We instantiate it on fluid-dynamics and vibration testbeds with known ground truth — Burgers' equation, the Duffing oscillator, a geometrically nonlinear Bernoulli–Euler beam, and a vortex-induced-vibration reduced model — and release a budgeted, out-of-regime, anti-memorization discovery benchmark with explicit recovery and efficiency metrics.

schema.problem: Existing approaches recover governing ordinary differential equations as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming observed trajectories are sufficiently informative; when data are limited, multiple equations can be observationally indistinguishable, creating identifiability gaps and incorrect recovered equations.
schema.motivation: Adaptive data acquisition can resolve observational indistinguishability, and large language models make tractable priors over large equation spaces, enabling correct recovery from limited and noisy data.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed closed-loop framework jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. A large language model proposes operator priors that partition the large search space into distinct regions, and candidate equations within each region are fit to observed data. Disagreement among the candidates guides acquisition of informative trajectories, forming a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for claim (1) comes from evaluation on 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, using median NMSE and symbolic accuracy against state-of-the-art baselines. Claim (2) is assessed through sample-efficiency analysis comparing performance under reduced data fractions. Claim (3) is tested by noise-robustness analysis and comparison of recovered symbolic structures, checking for spurious terms relative to baselines.

items.title: LLM-ACES: Closed-Loop Discovery of Dynamical Systems with LLM-Guided Adaptive Search
items.abstract: Recovering governing Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) from data is a central challenge in modeling dynamical systems across scientific domains. Existing approaches cast discovery as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming that the observed trajectories are sufficiently informative. However, dynamical systems evolve over large state spaces, and limited data can make multiple equations observationally indistinguishable, leading to identifiability gaps and the recovery of incorrect governing equations. To address this, we introduce LLM-ACES, or LLM-guided Active Closed-loop Equation Search, a closed-loop framework that jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. In LLM-ACES, a large language model (LLM) proposes operator priors that partition the large search space into distinct regions, within which candidate equations are fit to the observed data. The disagreement among these candidates guides the acquisition of informative trajectories, creating a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics. On 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, LLM-ACES achieves the lowest median NMSE, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by several orders of magnitude while achieving a high symbolic accuracy of 46.2% and 52.4%, respectively. Our analysis further shows that LLM-ACES is sample-efficient, achieving better performance with one-tenth the data. Furthermore, LLM-ACES's feedback-driven data acquisition makes it robust to noise and recovers the correct symbolic structure, while baselines introduce spurious terms that fit the data locally but obscure the true governing relationships.

schema.problem: Autonomous AI scientist agents running multi-session campaigns do not persist their own research state, so they re-encounter failed configurations, re-run near-identical experiments, and forget which hypotheses have already been falsified.
schema.motivation: As such campaigns extend over hours to months, this state loss wastes compute and slows progress toward verified improvements; making research state persist could avoid redundant work and make fixed budgets more productive.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper proposes a schema-enforced, append-only, provenance-bearing persistent store of an agent's research state: hypotheses with predictions recorded before execution; experiment specs keyed by hashes of code, config, and seed; results with evidence pointers to cells, logs, and code; per-experiment costs; and lifecycle statuses (open, confirmed, falsified, dead-end). The store is exposed through a small set of typed query and update tools that the execution harness verifies. On top of the ledger, the agent chooses the next experiment by maximizing expected information gain conditional on the ledger, subject to a per-experiment cost bound, a redundancy penalty, and a hypothesis-diversity floor.
schema.research_plan: The paper tests the single falsifiable claim on three to four baseline-improvement research programs—machine learning, a wet-lab-style prediction task, and a physics-reproduction task—using a pre-registered protocol and at least five seeds per configuration. It compares the proposed ledger plus budget-aware selection against a stateless agent and an unstructured free-text memory agent, both using the same backbone model, and measures redundant-experiment rate, cost-to-first-verified-improvement, final metric, ideation diversity, and trace integrity.

items.title: The Research-State Ledger: Persistent, Provenance-Bearing Memory and Budget-Aware Experiment Selection for AI Scientist Agents
items.abstract: AI scientist agents now run autonomous campaigns spanning hours to months, yet they persistently lose the state of their own research: between sessions they re-encounter the same failed configurations, re-run near-identical experiments, and forget which hypotheses have already been falsified. We propose the Research-State Ledger (RSL), a schema-enforced, append-only, provenance-bearing persistent store of an agent's own research state — hypotheses with predictions recorded before execution, experiment specs keyed by hashes of code, config, and seed, results with evidence pointers to cells, logs, and code, per-experiment costs, and lifecycle statuses (open, confirmed, falsified, dead-end) — exposed to the agent through a small set of typed query and update tools that the execution harness verifies. On top of the ledger we add budget-aware next-experiment selection: the agent chooses the candidate experiment maximizing expected information gain conditional on the ledger, subject to a per-experiment cost bound, a redundancy penalty, and a hypothesis-diversity floor. We make a specific falsifiable claim: under a fixed compute budget split into sequential fresh agent sessions, RSL plus budget-aware selection reduces the redundant-experiment rate and the cost-to-first-verified-improvement, and yields a higher final metric at equal budget, than both a stateless agent and an agent with unstructured free-text memory running the same backbone model. We test this on three to four baseline-improvement research programs (machine learning, a wet-lab-style prediction task, and a physics-reproduction task) with a pre-registered protocol and five or more seeds per configuration, measuring redundancy, cost-to-verified-improvement, final metric, ideation diversity, and trace integrity. The proposal contributes (1) the RSL schema and construction rules, (2) the ledger-conditional budget-aware selection objective, (3) a fixed-budget multi-session evaluation protocol for AI scientist systems, and (4) an empirical account of the efficiency–diversity trade-off, connecting agent memory design to the dual-space (hypothesis-space vs. experiment-space) account of human scientific reasoning.

schema.problem: Long-horizon autonomous research requires continuously managing evolving state, exploration decisions, and computational resources, but pioneering autoresearch agents lack mechanisms for continuity, recovery from dead ends, and value-driven compute allocation; this undermines search efficiency, wastes computational resources, and lowers the chance of ultimate success.
schema.motivation: Better continuity, recovery, and resource allocation would improve overall search efficiency and increase the likelihood of success in autonomous research, enabling scaling beyond short-horizon interactions.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an end-to-end autoresearch agent system that organizes long-horizon research into research segments grounded in executable workspaces. Research progress is represented as recoverable executable states, enabling exploration, revision, and execution. Transitions between segments are governed by a re-anchoring mechanism that selects a live or archived state as the next anchor and determines whether to continue or redirect the research trajectory. An evidence-aware execution controller allocates resources to physical jobs based on resource availability, remaining budget, and validated progress.
schema.research_plan: (1) The effectiveness claim is evaluated on tasks spanning machine learning, scientific modeling, and mathematical optimization, using diverse long-horizon benchmarks including full MLE-bench within a 24-hour budget, with the Any-Medal metric compared against previously reported results. (2) The claim that state management, adaptive exploration, and objective-aligned execution are critical is asserted from the evaluation results rather than from a separate manipulation; the abstract does not state explicit failure conditions, ablations, or what is held matched beyond the 24-hour budget.

items.title: ScienceFlow: A long-horizon agent for ML research, scientific discovery and beyond
items.abstract: Enabling LLM agents to sustain productive, stable, and goal-aligned research over extended horizons is a central challenge for autonomous machine learning and scientific discovery, as progress hinges on continuously managing evolving state, exploration decisions, and computational resources. Pioneering autoresearch agents, despite great success, still lack mechanisms for continuity, recovery from dead ends, and value-driven compute allocation, which inherently undermines overall search efficiency, wastes computational resources, and lowers the chance of ultimate success. To bridge this gap, we introduce ScienceFlow, an end-to-end autoresearch agent framework that organizes long-horizon research work into research segments grounded in executable workspaces. It represents research progress as recoverable executable states, enabling efficient exploration, revision, and execution. Transitions between research segments are governed by Executable-State Transition through Re-Anchoring (ESTRA), which selects either the live state or an archived state as the next anchor and determines whether to continue or redirect the research trajectory. An evidence-aware execution controller allocates resources to physical jobs based on resource availability, remaining budget, and validated progress. We evaluate ScienceFlow on tasks spanning machine learning, scientific modeling, and mathematical optimization. Results on diverse long-horizon benchmarks demonstrate its ability to sustain effective research processes, highlighted by a SOTA 70.22 percent Any-Medal score on the full MLE-bench within a 24-hour budget, outperforming prior reported results by 4.92 percentage points. The efficacy of ScienceFlow further demonstrates that efficient state management, adaptive exploration, and objective-aligned execution are critical for scaling autonomous research beyond short-horizon interactions.

schema.problem: Automated heuristic design systems for LLMs score candidate heuristics only by empirical solution quality on fixed benchmark distributions, and none imposes or checks a formal property of the heuristic; in optimal pathfinding, a heuristic that is not admissible silently returns suboptimal paths, a correctness failure rather than a quality loss.
schema.motivation: Enforcing admissibility inside heuristic discovery turns it into a correctness-preserving process, avoiding silent suboptimal paths in A* search.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is an LLM plus two-tier-verifier loop that discovers A* heuristics as interpretable programs in a restricted DSL over landmark/differential terms, obstacle-aware local costs, and certified monotone composition rules, together with a human-checkable certificate. The first verification tier is sound and complete for a fixed instance: one backward Dijkstra gives h* for every state, so h(s) ≤ h*(s) is exactly decidable and can be enforced inside the loop. The second tier is symbolic and certifies admissibility for a family of maps by discharging constant obligations over a rule kernel with an SMT solver. Rejected candidates become counterexamples that drive counterexample-guided refinement of the code.
schema.research_plan: (1) The core claim is tested on held-out maps by checking that A* optimality is preserved while node expansions are reduced against classical admissible heuristics, hand-built landmark/differential heuristics, and learned neural heuristics at matched suboptimality budgets. (2) Robustness is tested under obstacle-density and topology shift. (3) The decisive ablation deletes the verifier and measures how much of the reported speedup was purchased with hidden suboptimality. Support requires provably preserved optimality and substantial expansion reduction with the verifier present, while the verifier-ablated run becomes inadmissible and slower.

items.title: Proof-Carrying Heuristic Discovery: LLM Synthesis of Certified Admissible A* Heuristics that Transfer Across Map Distributions
items.abstract: Every recent large-language-model (LLM) "automated heuristic design" (AHD) system scores candidate heuristics by empirical solution quality on a fixed benchmark distribution; none imposes, or checks, a formal property of the heuristic. In optimal pathfinding the central formal property is admissibility: an A* heuristic that is not admissible silently returns suboptimal paths, which is a correctness failure, not a quality loss . I propose Proof-Carrying Heuristic Discovery (PCHD), an LLM + two-tier-verifier loop that discovers A* heuristics as interpretable programs in a small DSL over landmark/differential terms, obstacle-aware local costs, and certified monotone composition rules, together with a human-checkable certificate.
