Tier 1 is sound and complete for a fixed instance: one backward Dijkstra gives h* for every state, so h(s) ≤ h*(s) is exactly decidable and can be enforced inside the loop. Tier 2 is symbolic: it certifies admissibility for a family of maps by discharging constant obligations over a rule kernel with an SMT solver. Rejected candidates become counterexamples that drive counterexample-guided refinement of the code. Core falsifiable claim: PCHD finds heuristics that provably preserve A* optimality on every held-out map while still cutting node expansions substantially against classical admissible heuristics, hand-built landmark/differential heuristics, and learned neural heuristics evaluated at matched suboptimality budgets — and that retain this advantage under obstacle-density and topology shift, where the same LLM search run without the verifier becomes both inadmissible and slower. The decisive ablation deletes the verifier and measures how much of the reported speedup was purchased with hidden suboptimality.

schema.problem: Existing end-to-end AI-scientist benchmarks ask whether an agent can produce research artifacts that score well on an LLM judge or performance metric, but they do not measure whether an agent can detect that an apparent improvement is an artifact of an engineered confound and report honestly, including null results.
schema.motivation: Agents fabricate or invalidate their own results, LLM-judged innovation misaligns with objective performance, and audits show failure to execute verification procedures; a benchmark is needed to convert epistemic-reliability failure from an anecdotal concern into a directly measurable capability and a controlled test of self-correction mechanisms.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark consists of tasks that ask an agent to determine whether its own proposed improvement is an artifact of an engineered confound — data leakage, a sabotaged baseline, or a spurious shortcut — and to report honestly up to and including a null result. Spurious tasks are calibrated so that the claimed effect is large, seed-reproducible, and entirely false, while genuine-improvement control tasks prevent indiscriminate null-reporting. Grading is objective and execution-grounded rather than LLM-judged. The benchmark is used to evaluate a structured adversarial falsification stage in which an independent refuter agent is rewarded for overturning the proposer's claim via executed diagnostic controls, compared with prompted self-correction.
schema.research_plan: The first claim would be tested by running state-of-the-art research agents on the benchmark and measuring false-discovery rate on confounded tasks, with support requiring a rate above 50% and failure being a rate at or below 50%. The second claim would be tested by comparing false-discovery rate under prompted self-correction and under the structured adversarial falsification stage, with support requiring the refuter to reduce the rate by at least 25 percentage points and prompted self-correction not to achieve that reduction. Grading would be objective and execution-grounded across conditions.

items.title: ConfoundBench: Measuring Whether AI Research Agents Can Detect That Their Own "Improvements" Are Spurious
items.abstract: Every end-to-end AI-scientist benchmark built to date asks whether an agent can produce research artifacts — ideas, implementations, executed experiments, and papers — that score well on an LLM judge or a performance metric. The retrieved evidence shows this framing is one-sided: agents fabricate or invalidate their own experimental results at striking rates , LLM-judged innovation misaligns with objective performance , and independent audits converge on agents' failure to execute the verification procedures that would expose a wrong conclusion . I propose ConfoundBench, a benchmark that inverts the question: each task asks whether an agent can detect that its own proposed improvement is an artifact of an engineered confound — data leakage, a sabotaged baseline, or a spurious shortcut — and report the result honestly, up to and including a null result. Spurious tasks are calibrated so that the claimed effect is large, seed-reproducible, and entirely false; genuine-improvement control tasks make indiscriminate null-reporting unviable; and grading is objective and execution-grounded rather than LLM-judged. Two falsifiable claims follow: that state-of-the-art research agents will assert confounded improvements as genuine findings in the large majority of tasks (false-discovery rate above 50%), and that a structured adversarial falsification stage — an independent refuter agent rewarded for overturning the proposer's claim via executed diagnostic controls — reduces that rate by at least 25 percentage points, while prompted self-correction does not. ConfoundBench thus converts epistemic-reliability failure from an anecdotal concern into a directly measurable capability and provides a controlled test of when, and with what mechanism, self-correction can make research agents trustworthy.

schema.problem: In autonomous AI research systems, scheduling asynchronous experiments to maximize convergence toward performance targets is suboptimal when experiment durations and information gains are unknown, and current approaches either use static reinforcement-learning policies or ignore runtime uncertainty.
schema.motivation: Efficient scheduling is valuable because wasted effort on slow, low-value experiments directly delays progress toward performance targets in autonomous research systems.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed scheduler maintains a Bayesian model of experiment runtime distributions learned from execution traces and dynamically reschedules tasks as experiments complete and uncertainty reduces. It prioritizes experiments likely to finish quickly and produce high-value results, and revises priorities online as new data arrives.
schema.research_plan: The scheduler is evaluated against static RL schedulers, classical list-scheduling heuristics, and uncertainty-agnostic baselines on synthetic benchmarks and traces from real autonomous research systems, using time-to-convergence as the metric. Support requires faster convergence than fixed policies and competitive or better performance relative to classical heuristics.

items.title: Adaptive Bayesian Scheduling for Autonomous Research Workflows
items.abstract: Autonomous AI research systems must schedule asynchronous experiments to maximize convergence speed toward performance targets. Current approaches either use static reinforcement-learning policies or ignore runtime uncertainty, leading to suboptimal scheduling when experiment durations and information gains are unknown. We propose AdaBS (Adaptive Bayesian Scheduler), an online scheduling algorithm that maintains a Bayesian model of experiment runtime distributions learned from execution traces, and dynamically reschedules tasks as experiments complete and uncertainty reduces. AdaBS combines two key insights: (1) runtime prediction enables prioritization of experiments likely to finish quickly and produce high-value results, and (2) online adaptation allows the scheduler to revise priorities as new data arrives, reducing wasted effort on slow, low-value tasks. We evaluate AdaBS against static RL schedulers, classical list-scheduling heuristics, and uncertainty-agnostic baselines on synthetic benchmarks and traces from real autonomous research systems. We hypothesize that adaptive Bayesian scheduling achieves >15% faster time-to-convergence compared to fixed policies, while remaining competitive with or outperforming classical heuristics.

schema.problem: Autonomous AI agents orchestrating multi-step workflows lack structured data management infrastructure; in particular, they lack machine-readable dataset discovery mechanisms, systematic real-time validation of data quality, and action-indexed versioning for downstream agent reasoning and reproducibility.
schema.motivation: As autonomous agents accelerate scientific discovery, providing them structured data management is needed to make their complex multi-step workflows reliable and reproducible.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is implemented as middleware compatible with existing agent frameworks and integrates FAIR principles with agent-queryable metadata catalogs, executable validation rules, and agent-action-indexed versioning. It is designed for evaluation on multi-agent chemistry and materials-science workflows.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation on multi-agent chemistry and materials-science workflows, with success for the claim measured by agent discovery accuracy, error detection rate, reproducibility fidelity, and failure-mode prevention. The abstract does not name baselines or specify failure thresholds.

items.title: Research Data Management for Autonomous AI Agents: Enabling Discovery, Validation, and Reproducibility in Multi-Agent Scientific Workflows
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are accelerating scientific discovery by orchestrating complex multi-step workflows, yet they operate without structured data management infrastructure. Agents lack machine-readable dataset discovery mechanisms, systematic real-time validation of data quality, and action-indexed versioning that supports downstream agent reasoning and reproducibility. We propose RDM4Agents, a data management system that integrates FAIR principles with agent-queryable metadata catalogs, executable validation rules, and agent-action-indexed versioning. Implemented as middleware compatible with existing agent frameworks, RDM4Agents will be evaluated on multi-agent chemistry and materials-science workflows. Success is measured by agent discovery accuracy, error detection rate, reproducibility fidelity, and failure-mode prevention—expected to substantially improve performance on realistic multi-agent tasks where dataset discovery is essential.

schema.problem: Dynamic advanced manufacturing and logistics environments face unforeseen disturbances such as machine breakdowns, rush orders, and fluctuating inventory constraints. Conventional dispatching rules rely on rigid heuristics, while deep reinforcement learning and genetic programming methods require extensive task-specific reward engineering and heavy computational training overheads; existing LLM-driven scheduling approaches either treat shopfloor scheduling as a static sequence generation task or lack rigorous physical constraint validation, leading to invalid or brittle policies in complex multi-objective settings.
schema.motivation: Recent large language models show emergent capabilities in combinatorial optimization and automated algorithm design, making autonomous discovery and refinement of scheduling heuristics tractable without task-specific reward engineering or heavy training.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework orchestrates specialized LLM agents, including an inductive idea generator, a physical constraint validator, a discrete-event simulation evaluator, and a self-reflective refiner. These agents iteratively synthesize, validate, evaluate, and refine scheduling code using discrete-event simulation feedback and explicit constraint-aware reasoning, without pre-training or manual hyperparameter tuning.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the framework on established dynamic flexible job shop scheduling benchmarks, comparing it against traditional priority dispatching rules, genetic programming hyper-heuristics, and vanilla LLM code-generation baselines. The evaluation measures makespan minimization and adaptability under severe shopfloor uncertainty. The abstract does not report ablations, robustness checks, or an explicit failure condition.

items.title: ManufAI-Opt: Automated Discovery of Robust Dispatching Rules and Routing Heuristics for Dynamic Advanced Manufacturing via Constraint-Aware LLM Multi-Agent Feedback
items.abstract: Dynamic advanced manufacturing and logistics (AML) environments are characterized by unforeseen disturbances such as machine breakdowns, sudden rush orders, and fluctuating inventory constraints. Conventional dispatching rules rely on rigid heuristics, while end-to-end deep reinforcement learning and genetic programming methods often require extensive task-specific reward engineering and heavy computational training overheads. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent capabilities in combinatorial optimization and automated algorithm design. However, existing LLM-driven scheduling approaches either treat shopfloor scheduling as a static sequence generation task or lack rigorous physical constraint validation, leading to invalid or brittle policies in complex multi-objective settings. To address this gap, we propose ManufAI-Opt, a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously discovers, validates, and refines scheduling heuristics and dispatching rules using discrete-event simulation feedback and explicit constraint-aware reasoning. By orchestrating specialized agents—including an inductive idea generator, a physical constraint validator, a discrete-event simulation evaluator, and a self-reflective refiner—ManufAI-Opt iteratively synthesizes robust scheduling code without requiring pre-training or manual hyperparameter tuning. Extensive evaluations on established dynamic flexible job shop scheduling benchmarks demonstrate that ManufAI-Opt significantly outperforms traditional priority dispatching rules, genetic programming hyper-heuristics, and vanilla LLM code-generation baselines in makespan minimization and adaptability under severe shopfloor uncertainty.

schema.problem: Automated reviewer agents can flag critical flaws in a paper yet assign high scores, because their scoring is influenced by stylistic biases and lacks factual substantiation; this misalignment leaves automated scientific evaluation vulnerable to unverified or fabricated papers.
schema.motivation: As large language models enter autonomous research loops and peer review, aligning reviewer scores with textual critiques is necessary to defend against score inflation and unverified AI-driven publication loops.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach is a structured multi-stage review framework. It constructs claim-evidence graphs from research execution artifacts, conducts independent logical checks, and applies monotonic score penalties whenever unresolved technical or integrity concerns are present. Reviewer scores are thereby made conditional on verified textual critique.
schema.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on automated paper review benchmarks, using flawed or fabricated papers as the test condition. Support would be a reduction in score inflation for flawed or fabricated papers; the abstract does not state baselines, metrics, or a failure threshold.

items.title: Verifiable Scientific Auditing: Mitigating Concern-Acceptance Conflict in Automated LLM Peer Review and Research Loops
items.abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into autonomous research loops and peer review introduces significant vulnerabilities, notably the "concern-acceptance conflict" where reviewer agents flag critical flaws yet assign high scores due to stylistic biases and lack of factual substantiation. In this paper, we propose Verifiable Scientific Auditing (VSA), a structured multi-stage framework designed to align reviewer scoring with textual critique in automated scientific evaluation. VSA enforces strict verification by constructing claim-evidence graphs from research execution artifacts, conducting independent logical checks, and enforcing monotonic score penalties when unresolved technical or integrity concerns are present. Through rigorous evaluation on automated paper review benchmarks, VSA demonstrates substantial reductions in score inflation for flawed or fabricated papers, providing a robust defense against unverified AI-driven publication loops.

schema.problem: Current automated research-idea generation loops gate ideas through novelty assessors but discard the retrieved counter-evidence behind a rejection, regenerating or re-planning until a score passes instead of using that evidence to repair the rejected proposal. Existing assessors also lack calibration against adversarial paraphrases of published work, so optimism bias can remain hidden behind recency-proxied benchmarks.
schema.motivation: Repairing rejected ideas with the rejection evidence could preserve the original problem premise and avoid discarding otherwise promising proposals; closing the loop safely also requires knowing whether novelty assessors are fooled by adversarial paraphrases.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed module conditions typed, schema-constrained plan edits — hypothesis refinement, control addition, scope narrowing, and method substitution — on the exact retrieved counter-examples that caused rejection, so a rejected idea is repaired rather than abandoned. It is paired with a calibration benchmark of adversarial paraphrases of published work carrying gold non-novel labels. The system is compared against matched-compute baselines that regenerate at rejection, using SciMON-style re-suggestion and Nova-style re-planning of retrieval, while preserving the original problem premise.
schema.research_plan: (1) The system claim is tested by comparing the proposed revision module against matched-compute regeneration baselines (SciMON-style re-suggestion and Nova-style re-planning of retrieval) using independent blind-judge novelty on a 5-point scale, with success requiring the revision condition to exceed the baselines by the pre-specified margin while preserving the original problem premise. (2) The benchmark prediction is tested by applying existing assessors — RAG-based LLM judges, density-based scorers, and off-the-shelf LLM judges — to adversarial paraphrases of published work carrying gold non-novel labels; support is a large share labeled novel, and failure is no evidence of optimism bias beyond what recency-proxied benchmarks already reveal.

items.title: Revising from Rejection: Evidence-Conditioned Plan Editing at the Novelty Gate of Autonomous Research Ideation, with an Adversarial Paraphrase Calibration Benchmark
items.abstract: Automated research-idea generation systems now routinely gate candidates through automated novelty assessors, and several systems close a quality loop by re-sampling when the gate fails — regenerating or re-planning ideas until a novelty score is passed. We argue this loop is broken at a specific point: a novelty assessor's retrieved counter-evidence (the prior papers that triggered rejection) is discarded instead of being used to edit the rejected proposal. We propose ECPE (Evidence-Conditioned Plan Editor), a revision module that conditions typed, schema-constrained plan edits — hypothesis refinement, control addition, scope narrowing, and method substitution — on the exact retrieved counter-examples that caused rejection, so that a rejected idea is repaired rather than abandoned. Our falsifiable system claim is that evidence-conditioned revision yields at least 1 point higher independent blind-judge novelty (5-point scale) than matched-compute baselines that regenerate at rejection (SciMON-style re-suggestion; Nova-style re-planning of retrieval), while preserving the original problem premise. Because any such loop is only as good as its gate, we pair ECPE with ParaNovel, a calibration benchmark of adversarial paraphrases of published work carrying gold non-novel labels; we predict that existing assessors — RAG-based LLM judges, density-based scorers, and off-the-shelf LLM judges alike — label a large share of these paraphrases novel, exposing systematic optimism bias that recency-proxied benchmarks cannot reveal. To our knowledge this is the first work that (i) uses novelty-rejection counter-evidence as a direct conditioning signal for structural plan editing inside the ideation loop, and (ii) evaluates novelty assessors on an adversarial paraphrase calibration set with behavioral gold labels.

schema.problem: Topic-model construction is currently approached as either single-pass LLM generation or fixed hyperparameter optimization, leaving structural design choices such as embedding model, dimensionality reduction, clustering algorithm, number of topics, and labels unexamined as sequential, revisable decisions.
schema.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents make it feasible to explore this structured design space iteratively, and explicit multi-criteria feedback offers a way to balance quality dimensions that fixed pipelines often trade off.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a tool-using LLM agent that, given a corpus, an optional gold or human-annotated concept set, and a quality specification, proposes and executes one atomic design action per cycle—choosing or changing the embedding model, dimensionality reduction, clustering algorithm, number of topics via explicit merge/split decisions over existing clusters, or natural-language labels. A harness executes the resulting pipeline and computes a multi-criteria report card covering coherence, topic diversity, outlier rate, and agreement with gold labels, then decides whether to continue, which component to change, or when to stop. The agent is implemented in two flavors: a ReAct-style tool loop and a tree-search planner over design decisions with a structured design-trace world model. It is evaluated on a new benchmark that pairs standard corpora with gold human label/concept standards.
schema.research_plan: The proposal compares the agent against single-pass LLM topic generation and black-box hyperparameter search on the joint objective of coherence, diversity, and purity, using the benchmark's gold human label/concept standards. It also specifies ablations that remove merge/split actions or self-critique. The core claim is supported if the full agent outperforms both baselines on the joint objective and the advantage disappears in those ablation conditions; otherwise the claim is refuted.

items.title: TopicAgent: A Self-Evaluating LLM Agent for End-to-End Iterative Topic Model Construction
items.abstract: We propose TopicAgent, a tool-using LLM agent that treats topic-model construction as a sequential decision problem rather than a single-pass generation or a fixed hyperparameter optimization. Given only a text corpus, a gold or human-annotated concept set where available, and a quality specification, TopicAgent iteratively proposes and executes one atomic design action per cycle — choosing or changing the embedding model, dimensionality reduction, clustering algorithm, the number of topics (via explicit merge_topics/split_topic decisions over existing clusters), or natural-language labels — with the harness executing the pipeline, computing a multi-criteria report card (coherence, topic diversity, outlier rate, agreement with gold labels), and deciding whether to continue, which component to change, or when to stop. The agent is implemented in two flavors (a ReAct-style tool loop and a tree-search planner over design decisions with a structured design-trace world model) and evaluated on a new benchmark, TopicAgent-Bench, pairing standard corpora with gold human label/concept standards. Our falsifiable core claim: an agent that reasons over the structural design space of topic models and iterates under explicit multi-criteria self-evaluation outperforms both single-pass LLM topic generation and black-box hyperparameter search on the joint objective (coherence × diversity × purity), and this advantage disappears when the agent is denied merge/split actions or self-critique. The proposal defines the benchmark, the agent architecture, the evaluation protocol, and the ablations that would confirm or refute the claim.

schema.problem: Existing LLM-based methods for vehicle routing optimization often rely on fixed performance metrics and benchmark datasets, which may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios.
schema.motivation: Vehicle routing optimization has significant economic and environmental implications, making real-time adaptation to new, unseen scenarios valuable for logistics and transportation.
schema.proposed_approach: An adaptive LLM-based system that learns from existing vehicle routing data, adapts to new, unseen scenarios, and optimizes routes in real-time; its evaluation uses dynamic performance metrics and benchmark datasets.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation will use dynamic performance metrics and benchmark datasets, with no stated baselines, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: LLM-Based Vehicle Routing Optimization with Adaptive Performance Metrics
items.abstract: Vehicle routing optimization is a critical problem in logistics and transportation, with significant economic and environmental implications. Recent studies have explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve the efficiency of vehicle routing. However, existing LLM-based methods often rely on fixed performance metrics and benchmark datasets, which may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios. This proposal introduces an adaptive LLM-based system that learns from existing vehicle routing data and adapts to new, unseen scenarios, optimizing routes in real-time. The system will utilize a set of dynamic performance metrics and benchmark datasets to evaluate its performance.

schema.problem: Existing LLM-based systems for clinical trial data analysis are task-specific and not adaptable to diverse clinical trial tasks.
schema.motivation: Clinical trials are crucial for drug development but are time-consuming and have high failure rates, so automating data analysis could reduce these burdens.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is an LLM-based framework that unifies three clinical trial analysis tasks: data extraction, patient-trial matching, and trial outcome prediction. It will use advanced LLM architectures and fine-tuning strategies that include synthetic data distillation and parameter-efficient tuning.
schema.research_plan: The work will develop and evaluate the proposed system on the three named tasks, aiming for state-of-the-art performance. The abstract does not specify datasets, baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: A Comprehensive LLM-based System for Automating Clinical Trial Data Analysis
items.abstract: Clinical trials are crucial for drug development but are often time-consuming and have high failure rates. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating clinical trial data analysis, but existing systems are task-specific and not adaptable to diverse clinical trial tasks. This proposal aims to develop and evaluate a comprehensive LLM-based system for automating clinical trial data analysis, including data extraction, patient-trial matching, and trial outcome prediction. The proposed system will leverage advanced LLM architectures and fine-tuning strategies, such as synthetic data distillation and parameter-efficient tuning, to achieve state-of-the-art performance.

schema.problem: Genome mining has made microbial natural-product discovery data-intensive, but converting predicted biosynthetic gene clusters into defensible structure-and-activity hypotheses remains manual, and large language models applied to this interpretive task hallucinate.
schema.motivation: Automating the interpretive core would scale discovery and reduce manual effort; self-verification against domain databases offers a route to curb hallucination in emitted claims.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed multi-agent system treats deterministic genome-mining tools (BGC detection, dereplication, gene-to-molecule and activity predictors) as instruments. It decomposes findings into atomic claims—backbone type, tailoring-enzyme calls, structural features, bioactivity—and runs a verifier agent that cross-checks each claim against domain databases (BGC entries, NPASS activity records, sequence indices) under an explicit abstain policy. The accompanying benchmark removes gold clusters and their close sequence neighbors from the databases the agent may query, eliminating lookup shortcuts; it provides three tracks: annotation accuracy, gene-to-molecule/activity prediction, and a novelty track whose primary metric is claim-level hallucination rate. Expected releases include the benchmark as a community resource, a reference agent and tool suite, and an error analysis linking agentic failure modes to genome-mining stages.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the novelty-track claim, compare the full agent against a RAG-only agent on the benchmark with gold clusters and close neighbors removed from queryable databases; the primary metric is claim-level hallucination rate, and a Verifier ablation checks whether self-verification drives the reduction. (2) For the accuracy claim, compare the full agent to a deterministic detection + classification pipeline on backbone-type and product-class accuracy. The stated failure conditions—no significant hallucination reduction in the Verifier ablation, or loss to the deterministic pipeline—would refute the design principle. An error analysis ties agentic failure modes to specific genome-mining stages.

items.title: Self-Verification Turns LLM Agents into Reliable Natural-Product Scientists: BGC-Scientist and the Contamination-Controlled BGC-Bench Benchmark
items.abstract: Genome mining has turned microbial natural-product (NP) discovery into a data-throughput problem, but the interpretive core — converting a predicted biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) into a defensible structure-and-activity hypothesis — remains manual, and large language models applied to this task hallucinate. We propose BGC-Scientist, a self-verifying LLM multi-agent system that treats deterministic genome-mining tools (BGC detection, dereplication, gene-to-molecule and activity predictors) as instruments, decomposes every finding into atomic claims (backbone type, tailoring-enzyme calls, structural features, bioactivity), and runs a Verifier agent that cross-checks each claim against domain databases (BGC entries, NPASS activity records, sequence indices) under an explicit abstain policy. We also introduce BGC-Bench, a benchmark whose holdout construction removes gold clusters — and their close sequence neighbors — from the very databases the agent may query, eliminating lookup shortcuts and yielding three tracks: annotation accuracy, gene-to-molecule/activity prediction, and a novelty track on which claim-level hallucination rate is the primary metric. Our central, falsifiable claim is that self-verification against domain databases reduces the hallucination rate of emitted structure/activity claims by ≥30% relative to a RAG-only agent, while the full agent matches or beats a deterministic detection + classification pipeline on backbone-type and product-class accuracy. We state the failure conditions in advance — no significant hallucination reduction in the Verifier ablation, or loss to the deterministic pipeline — under which this design principle is refuted. Expected outputs: BGC-Bench as a community resource, a reference agent and tool suite, and an error analysis tying agentic failure modes to specific genome-mining stages.

schema.problem: AI scientist agents accumulate a heterogeneous, rapidly growing research state — competing hypotheses, code and diffs, experiment logs, result tables, equations, citations, and provenance links — that overflows the finite context window of the LLM driving them. Existing compression research optimizes generic perplexity or token length, and existing agent-memory research optimizes storage and retrieval, so neither provides a science-fact-preserving compressor with explicit per-artifact budget allocation.
schema.motivation: Budget-limited compression that preserves critical scientific facts could keep the research state usable for downstream AI-scientist decisions such as hypothesis ranking, experiment interpretation, error diagnosis, and result-to-claim faithfulness.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed compressor parses the research state into typed artifacts, assigns each type a task-conditional fidelity weight, and solves a budget allocation. It keeps a small set of verbatim facts — identifiers, units, statistical estimates, failure signatures, equations, citation keys, provenance pointers — lossless while lossily summarizing the remainder. To make the claims testable, the work also constructs a fixed-budget benchmark of real research-agent trajectories with annotated critical facts and decision points, so that the effect of the compressor is isolated from the effect of retrieval.
schema.research_plan: To test claim (1), the evaluation uses the fixed-budget benchmark of real research-agent trajectories with annotated critical facts and decision points, comparing the proposed compressor against truncation, LLMLingua/LongLLMLingua, generic summarization, and gist-memory baselines at matched context budgets of 10–25% of original. Support for claim (1) requires retaining the stated critical-fact threshold and improving downstream capability across hypothesis ranking, experiment interpretation, error diagnosis, and result-to-claim faithfulness; the abstract announces explicit conditions that would falsify the proposal but does not enumerate them. Claim (2) is evaluated by fixing the budget in the benchmark so that the effect of the compressor is isolated from the effect of retrieval.

items.title: SciRD: Rate-Distortion Context Compression for Token-Budget-Limited AI Scientist Agents
items.abstract: AI scientist agents accumulate a heterogeneous, rapidly growing research state — competing hypotheses, code and diffs, experiment logs, result tables, equations, citations, and provenance links — that soon overflows the finite context window of the LLM driving them. Existing compression research optimizes generic perplexity or token length, and existing agent-memory research optimizes storage and retrieval, so neither provides a science-fact-preserving compressor with an explicit per-artifact budget allocation. We propose SciRD, a rate-distortion context compressor that (i) parses the research state into typed artifacts, (ii) assigns each type a task-conditional fidelity weight, and (iii) solves a budget allocation that keeps a small set of verbatim "anchor facts" (identifiers, units, statistical estimates, failure signatures, equations, citation keys, provenance pointers) lossless while lossily summarizing the remainder. Our falsifiable claim: at matched context budgets (10–25% of the original), SciRD retains >90% of labeled critical scientific facts and improves downstream AI-scientist capability — hypothesis ranking, experiment interpretation, error diagnosis, and result-to-claim faithfulness — over truncation, LLMLingua/LongLLMLingua, generic summarization, and gist-memory baselines. To make the claim testable we build SciRD-Bench, a fixed-budget benchmark of real research-agent trajectories with annotated critical facts and decision points, so that the effect of the compressor is isolated from the effect of retrieval. We also state explicitly what would falsify the proposal.

schema.problem: Automated scientific discovery planners that select actions by maximizing a myopic score cannot value constructive actions—actions that acquire an epistemic capability whose worth appears only in later available actions—so when the least-cost route to a confident answer requires a chain of such constructions, such planners fail to reach the goal.
schema.motivation: This limitation is structural rather than a matter of tuning the score, and it makes some solvable discovery problems unreachable; recognizing it opens the way to planners that reason about future action availability instead of only immediate information.
schema.proposed_approach: The work formalizes goal-directed discovery as a stochastic shortest-path problem in belief space in which constructive experiments modify the downstream action graph. It proves lower bounds via a lemma that within the horizon acquiring a capability can be observationally indistinguishable from paying for a null action. It also introduces an incremental replanner whose cost-to-go heuristic adds a capability-aware term to an expected-experiment term.
schema.research_plan: The theoretical claims are supported by constructed instances for each lookahead depth d, showing unbounded approximation ratio and non-reachability for myopic planners; the mechanism is isolated by the indistinguishability lemma. The planner is evaluated in a controlled testbed comparing myopic and capability-aware planning under conditions that vary whether capability acquisition is required, the fixed horizon length, and whether near-miss hypotheses are produced by a data-consistent proposer. The implied failure conditions are that the performance gap would not appear only under capability acquisition requirements, would not persist across fixed horizons, or would not track the data-consistent proposer condition.

items.title: Capability-Gated Planning: Cost-to-Goal Discovery and the Limits of Myopic Experiment Selection
items.abstract: Systems that automate scientific discovery must repeatedly decide which experiment to run, which hypothesis to test, which tool to build, and when to stop. Many systems make these decisions by maximizing a myopic score such as expected information gain per unit cost or a learned plausibility score. We identify a structural limitation of this approach. Some actions are constructive: they acquire an epistemic capability (an instrument, assay, pipeline, simulator, or abstraction) whose value lies not in the information returned immediately but in the future actions it makes available. When the least-cost route to a confident answer requires a chain of such constructions, a planner that scores actions only by information obtainable within a bounded horizon cannot value the first construction: it yields no information within the horizon and is dominated by any measurement with positive information, however small. We formulate goal-directed discovery as a stochastic shortest-path problem in belief space in which constructive experiments change the downstream action graph, and prove that for every lookahead depth d there is an instance on which every myopic information-maximizing planner has an unbounded approximation ratio, and a related instance on which it never reaches the goal. The mechanism is a capability-indistinguishability lemma: within the horizon, acquiring a capability can be observationally indistinguishable from paying for a null action. This establishes capability gating as a reachability axis of difficulty distinct from curvature (submodularity) and information order (adaptivity gaps). We introduce CG-Plan, an incremental replanner with a capability-aware cost-to-go heuristic h = h_cap + h_exp. In a controlled testbed, the performance gap appears only under gating, persists for every fixed horizon, and arises when near-miss hypotheses come from a data-consistent proposer.

schema.problem: Automated research systems use experimental scores from single runs to decide which ideas to retain, transfer, and pursue, but one run scores only one implementation of an idea, so an idea-level conclusion may depend on which plausible implementation was sampled.
schema.motivation: As automated research pipelines increasingly make branching, transfer, and memory decisions from experimental scores, it becomes necessary to know how much single-implementation scores can mislead idea-level conclusions before relying on them.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed procedure validates and freezes candidate cards, samples fresh-session implementations for each candidate, obtains outcome-blind fidelity labels, reruns saved artifacts, and decomposes variance using an intraclass correlation and leave-one-implementation-out winner reversal. It is applied to tabular tasks, coding-agent setups, and an exploratory set of materials-regression workflows with a deterministic evaluator.
schema.research_plan: The main estimate covers 312 assignments across 13 tabular tasks and two coding-agent setups, comparing implementation variance with same-artifact rerun variance and measuring leave-one-implementation-out winner reversal. Persistence is tested under two outcome-blind card-level review rules. An exploratory diagnostic on three materials-regression workflows with a deterministic evaluator checks whether implementation variation dominates the variance decomposition. The design holds reruns of saved artifacts as a baseline and treats reversal under repeated implementations as evidence against the sufficiency of single-implementation scores.

items.title: One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery in Automated Research
items.abstract: Automated research systems use experimental scores both to deliver artifacts and to decide which ideas to retain, transfer, and pursue. Yet one run scores one implementation of an idea. Crediting that realization-level score as evidence about the parent mechanism creates the \emph{implementation lottery}, in which an idea-level conclusion depends on which plausible implementation was sampled. The mismatch is structural whenever one run updates beliefs about a mechanism. We estimate its magnitude. The \emph{Idea Reliability Audit} measures \emph{idea reliability} by validating and freezing candidate cards, sampling fresh-session implementations, using outcome-blind fidelity labels, and rerunning saved artifacts. It reports idea ICC and leave-one-implementation-out (LOO) winner reversal. Prior work generally repeats the task; we repeat the idea. Across 312 assignments on 13 tabular tasks and two coding-agent setups, implementation variance was more than five and ten times same-artifact rerun variance, respectively, and the winner from one implementation draw differed from the winner under the other-two mean in 25.6\% and 43.6\% of decisions. Reversal survives card-level filtering under two outcome-blind review rules. An exploratory diagnostic on three materials-regression workflows with a deterministic evaluator also finds implementation variation dominating the decomposition. These findings distinguish idea reliability from best-of-$N$ artifact utility. Before a score guides idea-level branching, transfer, or research memory, evidence should cover multiple implementations.

schema.problem: Broader adoption of single-cell genomics in plant biology is limited by plant-specific technical constraints, fragmented tools, and inconsistent analytical practices.
schema.motivation: Addressing these limits would transform isolated plant single-cell studies into an interoperable ecosystem that accelerates discovery and crop improvement.
schema.proposed_approach: A community workshop convened researchers to define shared needs and design solutions, yielding five priority challenge areas. A community-curated web portal aggregates protocols, datasets, and tutorials, and conceptual roadmaps are outlined for cross-species integration, multimodal trajectory and gene regulatory network inference, spatially anchored visualization, and AI scientist agents that dynamically coordinate analytical tools and literature; both scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq are considered for regulatory inference and cross-species analysis.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is a structured community workshop process in which researchers identified priority challenge areas and designed shared solutions; support for the claims would be participant consensus on those areas and roadmaps, while no quantitative evaluation or failure condition is described.

items.title: Cross-species plant single-cell analysis: community challenges and shared solutions
items.abstract: Single-cell genomics is rapidly reshaping plant biology, yet broader adoption is limited by plant-specific technical constraints, fragmented tools, and inconsistent analytical practices. Here we report outcomes from the 2025 Summer Workshop for Plant Single-Cell Analysis, which convened researchers to define community needs and design shared solutions. Participants identified five priority challenge areas: (1) improving data quality through imputation, simulation, and deep generative modeling; (2) developing automated, phylogenetically aware cell-type annotation frameworks; (3) reconstructing developmental trajectories and gene regulatory networks from single-cell and single-nucleus profiles; (4) creating visualization approaches that embed transcriptional states into anatomically grounded plant organ contexts; and (5) using Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents and foundation models to orchestrate end-to-end single-cell workflows. In response, we established PlantSCHub, a community-curated web portal that aggregates protocols, datasets, and tutorials to support reproducible plant single-cell analysis. We outline conceptual roadmaps for cross-species integration, multimodal trajectory and Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs) inference, spatially anchored visualization, and AI scientist agents that dynamically coordinate analytical tools and literature. We discuss both scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq that are important for regulatory inference and cross-species analysis. Together, these efforts aim to transform isolated plant single-cell studies into an interoperable, evolving ecosystem that accelerates discovery and crop improvement.

schema.problem: Neural simulation-based inference typically requires the user to specify a simulator encoding a fixed model structure, so it cannot jointly select among model structures and estimate parameters.
schema.motivation: It is now possible to combine large language models with neural simulation-based inference to infer over model families from natural language descriptions, avoiding fixed simulator assumptions.
schema.proposed_approach: Given a natural language description of the system and data under investigation, a large language model proposes candidate simulator programs. These candidates are iteratively refined via feedback-driven mutation and evaluated using neural density estimation, enabling simulation-based inference over a pool of models.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates on benchmarks spanning deterministic dynamics, stochastic epidemic models, and dark matter substructure inference from gravitational-lensing images, assessing whether the method identifies plausible model families from open-ended prompts. The abstract states that the resulting accuracy reflects the information content of the data and identifiability of candidate models, but it does not specify baselines, metrics, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: Program Synthesis for Simulation-Based Inference: Joint Model Selection and Parameter Estimation
items.abstract: Neural simulation-based inference enables parameter estimation for complex models, but typically requires the user to specify a simulator encoding a fixed model structure. We present a framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation that combines large language models for program synthesis with neural simulation-based inference. Given a natural language description of the system and data under investigation, an LLM proposes candidate simulator programs which are iteratively refined via feedback-driven mutation and evaluated using neural density estimation. The approach enables simulation-based inference over a pool of models, not just parameters within a fixed model. On benchmarks spanning deterministic dynamics, stochastic epidemic models, and dark matter substructure inference from gravitational-lensing images, the method identifies plausible model families from open-ended prompts, with accuracy that reflects the information content of the data and identifiability of candidate models.

schema.problem: Procedural memory is increasingly used to improve LLM agents on recurring workplace tasks, but whether and how the skills it produces transfer across tasks, roles, and model backbones remains poorly understood.
schema.motivation: Clarifying skill transferability would provide practical guidance for building, evaluating, and deploying procedural memory systems in production agent platforms.
schema.proposed_approach: The work constructs a benchmark of 382 realistic enterprise tasks spanning six professional roles and 22 procedural skills. It defines controlled evaluation settings for local improvement, cross-task transfer, cross-role transfer, and cross-model generalization. Evaluations use procedural memory with single refinement rounds and skills evolved from multi-model execution traces.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim that procedural memory yields consistent gains is tested by measuring aggregate performance on the benchmark after a single refinement round across the six roles and 22 skills. (2) The claim about multi-model trace sources is tested by comparing cross-model test accuracy for skills evolved from diverse multi-model execution traces against each single-model trace source. (3) The claim about heterogeneous transferability is examined by evaluating learned skills across tasks, roles, and model backbones and identifying which generalize broadly versus become role-specific. The abstract does not state explicit failure thresholds or matched compute/parameter budgets.

items.title: Managing Procedural Memory in LLM Agents: Control, Adaptation, and Evaluation
items.abstract: Procedural memory is increasingly used to improve LLM agents on recurring workplace tasks, yet its ability to produce reusable skills remains poorly understood. We introduce AFTER, a benchmark of 382 realistic enterprise tasks spanning six professional roles and 22 procedural skills, designed to evaluate how skills transfer across tasks, roles, and model backbones. The benchmark includes controlled evaluation settings for local improvement, cross-task transfer, cross-role transfer, and cross-model generalization. Experiments show that procedural memory delivers consistent gains in industrial workflows: a single refinement round improves aggregate performance by 3.7-6.7 points, while skills evolved from diverse multi-model execution traces achieve 73.1% cross-model test accuracy, outperforming all single-model trace sources. We further find that some skills generalize broadly across tasks and models, whereas others become specialized to role-specific workflows and lose effectiveness under transfer. These results provide practical guidance for building, evaluating, and deploying procedural memory systems in production agent platforms.

schema.problem: The research profession lacks a principled account of which activities within each stage of the research pipeline can be delegated to AI agents; existing framings treat delegation as between sequential stages rather than as a property of the underlying cognitive tasks.
schema.motivation: AI agents can now read files, run code, query databases, search the web, and invoke domain-specific skills, making autonomous multi-step research workflows newly possible and raising the stakes for deciding what should be delegated.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper constructs a cognitive task framework that classifies research activities along two dimensions: codifiability and tacit knowledge requirement. It uses a 26-skill plugin for Claude Code, covering 18 orchestrated phases with 53 quality gates, as an illustrative case spanning the research pipeline from idea to submission. From this framework it derives a cognitive delegation boundary and then analyzes implications for the profession, ending with five principles for responsible use of AI agents in research.
schema.research_plan: The paper supports its claims through conceptual argument and an illustrative case: the 26-skill Claude Code plugin is used to instantiate the framework and to show where the cognitive delegation boundary falls. The claim about agent strengths and weaknesses is argued analytically, without experimental benchmarks. The implications and principles are developed as conceptual analysis. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions, baselines, or matched comparisons.

items.title: Vibe Researching as Wolf Coming: Can AI Agents with Skills Replace or Augment Social Scientists?
items.abstract: AI agents -- systems that execute multi-step reasoning workflows with persistent state, tool access, and specialist skills -- represent a qualitative shift from prior automation technologies in social science. Unlike chatbots that respond to isolated queries, AI agents can now read files, run code, query databases, search the web, and invoke domain-specific skills to execute entire research pipelines autonomously. This paper introduces the concept of vibe researching -- the AI-era parallel to vibe coding -- and uses scholar-skill, a 26-skill plugin for Claude Code covering the full research pipeline from idea to submission across 18 orchestrated phases with 53 quality gates, as an illustrative case. I develop a cognitive task framework that classifies research activities along two dimensions -- codifiability and tacit knowledge requirement -- to identify a delegation boundary that is cognitive, not sequential: it cuts through every stage of the research pipeline, not between stages. I argue that AI agents excel at speed, coverage, and methodological scaffolding but struggle with theoretical originality and tacit field knowledge. The paper concludes with an analysis of three implications for the profession -- augmentation with fragile conditions, stratification risk, and a pedagogical crisis -- and proposes five principles for responsible vibe researching.

schema.problem: Existing algorithms for accelerating drug development depend heavily on expert design and labor-intensive task-specific optimization, and no system autonomously evolves algorithms across the entire multi-stage pipeline.
schema.motivation: Since AI-driven acceleration of drug development is recognized as a cumulative, often synergistic effect across multiple stages, holistic advancement requires autonomous evolution of existing algorithms across the entire pipeline.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is a multi-role large language model system that realizes a closed-loop evolution process through three collaborating role domains covering research, engineering, and analysis. It iteratively designs, implements, evaluates, and refines algorithms by leveraging scientific knowledge and accumulated evolutionary experience. It is applied to eleven representative tasks spanning target identification, drug discovery, preclinical study, and clinical trial.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation of the evolved task-specific algorithms on 120 benchmark test sets across the eleven tasks spanning target identification, drug discovery, preclinical study, and clinical trial. Generalization is assessed across heterogeneous data modalities, namely biological sequence, graph, molecular topology, and textual language. The evaluation covers both predictive and generative tasks. The abstract does not state baselines, metrics, failure conditions, or what is held matched for trade-off claims.

items.title: An AI System for Autonomous Algorithm Evolution in Drug Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly permeating the drug development pipeline. Numerous algorithms for accelerating this multi-stage and multi-task process have been constructed, which depends heavily on expert design and labor-intensive task-specific optimization. Given that AI-driven acceleration of drug development is recognized as a cumulative, often synergistic, effect across multiple stages, the autonomous evolution of existing algorithms across the entire pipeline is demanded to achieve a holistic advancement. Here, we present DrugEvolve, a multi-role large language model system for systematic and autonomous algorithm evolution in drug development. DrugEvolve realizes a closed-loop evolution process by incorporating Researcher , Engineer , and Analyst domains, and enables an iterative design, implementation, evaluation, and refinement of algorithm by leveraging scientific knowledge and accumulated evolutionary experience. Across eleven representative tasks spanning target identification, drug discovery, preclinical study, and clinical trial, DrugEvolve autonomously evolved the corresponding task-specific algorithms and achieved substantial performance enhancement on 120 benchmark test sets. Moreover, it showed robust generalizabilities across heterogeneous data modalities (ranging from biological sequence and graph to molecular topology and textual language), and realized gains in both predictive and generative tasks. Collectively, this AI system can serve not only as an algorithmic infrastructure for drug development, but also as a transferable paradigm for broader scientific domains.

schema.problem: Single-reference electronic structure methods such as Hartree–Fock and density-functional theory require iterative self-consistent field convergence to obtain molecular orbital coefficients and total energies, and alternative algorithms that approximate these results without any self-consistent field iterations are lacking.
schema.motivation: Avoiding the self-consistent field loop reduces computational cost, and the invariance of molecular orbital coefficients under a broad class of matrix functions makes it possible to search directly for matrix quantities that reproduce converged results.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach uses program synthesis guided by electronic-structure physics to search for matrices whose eigenvectors match the molecular orbital coefficients from converged Hartree–Fock or density-functional theory calculations. The search exploits the fact that the eigenvectors of the Fock or Kohn–Sham matrix are unchanged for a broad class of matrix functions of that matrix, so candidate algorithms can be expressed as such functions and evaluated without self-consistent field iterations. Generated algorithms compute total energies using a single matrix diagonalization.
schema.research_plan: (1) The first claim is supported by generating algorithms and evaluating total energies for LiCl, LiF, NaCl, NaF, and C1–C4 hydrocarbons, with agreement against converged Hartree–Fock or density-functional theory energies and the number of diagonalizations as criteria. (2) The second claim is supported by further simulations on C8–C20 alkanes testing transferability to larger species. The abstract does not specify a separate failure condition or matched compute details.

items.title: Automated Discovery of Algorithms for Molecular Electronic Structure Calculations Using Physics-Informed Program Synthesis
items.abstract: We demonstrate a physics-informed program synthesis (PIPS) approach that can be used to identify entirely new algorithms that approximate the results of single-reference electronic structure approaches like Hartree–Fock (HF) and density-functional theory (DFT)but without any self-consistent field iterations at all. Our PIPS strategy exploits the fact that the eigenvectors of the Fock matrix F (or Kohn–Sham matrix K) are the same as the eigenvectors of a broad class of matrix functions, f(F). As a result, PIPS can be used to seek matrices M that yield the same molecular orbital coefficients as converged HF or DFT calculations. We demonstrate this approach by generating new algorithms that accurately predict total energies for a series of heterodiatomic molecules (LiCl, LiF, NaCl, NaF) and C1–C4 hydrocarbons; further simulations of C8–C20 alkane species demonstrate further transferability and efficiency of the resulting algorithms. We obtain novel algorithms that can reproduce HF or DFT energies to within 0.1 kcal/mol/atom while requiring only a single matrix-diagonalization operation, rather than an iterative self-consistent field convergence. The approach demonstrated here could be similarly applied to more complex wave function ansatze, opening an interesting optimization-based pathway to identifying accurate yet efficient algorithms for molecular quantum chemistry.

schema.problem: As AI agents begin to automate AI R&D, there is no established way to assess whether their outputs are safe to deploy when the agents themselves may be untrusted.
schema.motivation: Because the deliverable in AI R&D is an artifact that will be deployed and run, it is now necessary to evaluate whether monitoring can catch hidden sabotage before deployment.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework spans four long-horizon tasks: safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, and inference-server optimization. Each main task is paired with two hidden side tasks: an embedded side task that sabotages the submitted model, adapter, kernel, or server, and an independent side task that takes a covert out-of-scope action in the sandbox while leaving the artifact honest. Frontier agents are evaluated as both saboteurs and monitors under four monitor types that vary on whether the monitor may execute and probe the produced artifact and whether it sees the agent's chain-of-thought. The framework is released as a modular framework for evaluating sabotage and control in automated AI R&D.
schema.research_plan: (1) Detection across the two hidden side-task types bears on the claim that training-data sabotage is hardest to catch. (2) Comparisons across the four monitor types code artifact execution/probing against trajectory-only monitoring and chain-of-thought visibility bear on the claim that artifact execution helps but is not enough; missed embedded sabotage is categorized by failure mode to show why monitors still miss it.

items.title: ResearchArena: Evaluating Sabotage and Monitoring in Automated AI R&D
items.abstract: As AI agents begin to automate AI R&D, we need ways to assess whether their outputs are safe to deploy, even when the agents themselves may be untrusted. AI control offers one such approach: rather than trusting the agent, it treats it as a potential adversary and uses a monitor to detect covert sabotage before deployment. We evaluate AI control for automated AI R&D with ResearchArena, a framework spanning four long-horizon tasks: safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, and inference-server optimization. Because the deliverable in AI R&D is an artifact that will be deployed and run, we pair each main task with two kinds of hidden side task: an embedded side task that sabotages the submitted model, adapter, kernel, or server itself, and an independent side task that takes a covert out-of-scope action in the sandbox while leaving the artifact honest. We evaluate frontier agents at both sabotage and monitoring, across four monitor types that vary along two axes: whether the monitor may execute and probe the produced artifact, and whether it sees the agent's chain-of-thought. We find that sabotage hidden in the training data is the hardest to catch, flagged fewer than half the time. Letting the monitor run experiments on the artifact, rather than only read the trajectory, helps, but it is not enough: monitors still miss embedded sabotage by inspecting only the surface, by noticing the anomaly but explaining it away, or by probing the artifact with the wrong test. We release ResearchArena as a modular framework for evaluating sabotage and control in automated AI R&D.

schema.problem: Designing a computational imaging system, including selecting operators, setting parameters, and validating consistency, currently requires weeks of specialist effort per modality, creating an expertise bottleneck that excludes the broader scientific community from prototyping imaging instruments.
schema.motivation: Removing this design bottleneck would free specialist time and make imaging-instrument prototyping accessible to non-specialists across a wider range of modalities.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach comprises a structured specification format and three autonomous agents with planning, judging, and execution roles that translate a one-sentence natural-language description into a validated forward model. An error theorem decomposes the total reconstruction error into five independently bounded terms, each associated with a corrective action. The agents compose primitive operators into chains, including novel chains spanning 3D to 5D.
schema.research_plan: (1) The formal error theorem supports the bounded-error claim by establishing five independently bounded error terms, each tied to a corrective action. (2) Evaluation on six real-data modalities spanning all five carrier families compares the automated pipeline's forward models against expert-designed library quality, with matching quality as the support criterion. (3) Ten novel designs that compose primitive operators into chains from 3D to 5D test whether the pipeline reaches compositional capability beyond any single-modality tool. Support would require matching expert-library quality on all tested modalities and valid novel designs across 3D-5D chains; failure on these would undercut the corresponding claims.

items.title: Designing Any Imaging System from Natural Language: Agent-Constrained Composition over a Finite Primitive Basis
items.abstract: Designing a computational imaging system -- selecting operators, setting parameters, validating consistency -- requires weeks of specialist effort per modality, creating an expertise bottleneck that excludes the broader scientific community from prototyping imaging instruments. We introduce spec.md, a structured specification format, and three autonomous agents -- Plan, Judge, and Execute -- that translate a one-sentence natural-language description into a validated forward model with bounded reconstruction error. A design-to-real error theorem decomposes total reconstruction error into five independently bounded terms, each linked to a corrective action. On 6 real-data modalities spanning all 5 carrier families, the automated pipeline matches expert-library quality (98.1 +/- 4.2%). Ten novel designs -- composing primitives into chains from 3D to 5D -- demonstrate compositional reach beyond any single-modality tool.

schema.problem: Existing evaluations of autonomous agents for scientific research typically assume a pre-configured execution environment, so the capability to resolve software dependencies, align hardware and framework versions, and configure distributed execution remains largely unbenchmarked.
schema.motivation: Benchmarking environment synthesis is necessary for autonomous agents to achieve reproducible scientific research, since progress in code repair and autonomous experimentation may not transfer to research code without this capability.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark defines a task in which, given a research repository, documentation, and a target execution setting, agents must construct an environment that successfully executes at runtime. It is applied to diverse research repositories to evaluate current state-of-the-art agents.
schema.research_plan: The benchmark is evaluated on diverse research repositories with current state-of-the-art agents, using successful runtime execution as the success criterion. Failure modes are categorized, particularly around dependency resolution and version coupling, to characterize the capability gap.

items.title: ResearchEnvBench: Benchmarking Agents on Environment Synthesis for Research Code Execution
items.abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to support scientific research, and recent benchmarks report progress in code repair and autonomous experimentation. However, these evaluations typically assume a pre-configured execution environment, which requires resolving complex software dependencies, aligning hardware and framework versions, and configuring distributed execution, yet this capability remains largely unbenchmarked. We introduce ResearchEnvBench, a benchmark for environment synthesis in research code execution. Given a research repository, documentation, and a target execution setting, agents must construct an environment that successfully executes at runtime. Evaluations on diverse research repositories reveal a substantial gap in current SOTA agents, with failures dominated by incomplete dependency resolution and brittle version coupling. ResearchEnvBench provides a realistic testbed for advancing autonomous agents toward reproducible scientific research.

schema.problem: Existing data-driven methods for discovering mechanical material laws require either stress-strain pairs or full-field displacement measurements, which are often inaccessible in practice, leaving discovery from partial observations such as boundary-only measurements unsolved.
schema.motivation: Advances in technology depend on understanding and predicting mechanical behavior, and discovery from partial observations would make data-driven material modeling practical when full-field stress-strain or displacement data cannot be obtained.
schema.proposed_approach: The method embeds a differentiable finite element solver within the learning loop, directly linking candidate energy functionals to the available measurements. The material law is represented by a structure-preserving neural architecture that enforces frame indifference, material symmetry, polyconvexity, and coercivity by design throughout training. The framework is applied to two- and three-dimensional settings and supports discovery from partial observations, including boundary-only measurements.
schema.research_plan: The paper presents evaluations in two- and three-dimensional settings, including scenarios with boundary-only measurements; it examines generalization across geometries and loading conditions and robustness to measurement noise. The abstract does not name baselines, metrics, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: The internal law of a material can be discovered from its boundary
items.abstract: Since the earliest stages of human civilization, advances in technology have been tightly linked to our ability to understand and predict the mechanical behavior of materials. In recent years, this challenge has increasingly been framed within the broader paradigm of data-driven scientific discovery, where governing laws are inferred directly from observations. However, existing methods require either stress-strain pairs or full-field displacement measurements, which are often inaccessible in practice. We introduce Neural-DFEM, a method that enables unsupervised discovery of hyperelastic material laws even from partial observations, such as boundary-only measurements. The method embeds a differentiable finite element solver within the learning loop, directly linking candidate energy functionals to available measurements. To guarantee thermodynamic consistency and mathematical well-posedness throughout training, the method employs Hyperelastic Neural Networks, a novel structure-preserving neural architecture that enforces frame indifference, material symmetry, polyconvexity, and coercivity by design. The resulting framework enables robust material model discovery in both two- and three-dimensional settings, including scenarios with boundary-only measurements. Neural-DFEM allows for generalization across geometries and loading conditions, and exhibits unprecedented accuracy and strong resilience to measurement noise. Our results demonstrate that reliable identification of material laws is achievable even under partial observability when strong physical inductive biases are embedded in the learning architecture.

schema.problem: Long-horizon planning with learned latent world models requires iteratively composing a one-step transition model, so its errors accumulate in the open-loop, posterior-free regime where the planner operates. Existing multi-step training objectives alter the model's weights but not the planner's query, leaving the autoregressive one-step rollout as the error-compounding operation.
schema.motivation: Since further refining one-step accuracy has diminishing returns, changing the planning-time rollout substrate is a more direct route to reducing latent drift and improving sample efficiency and final returns.
schema.proposed_approach: The method augments a latent world model with a horizon-conditioned predictor that returns the imagined latent states at every horizon in a single forward pass. Training uses a future-anchored regression to bootstrapped exponential-moving-average encodings of genuinely observed future states, and a cross-horizon self-consistency loss that makes the predictor's K-step output agree with composing its own shorter-horizon outputs. At planning time, this direct multi-horizon predictor replaces the composed one-step model as the rollout substrate.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation compares the direct multi-horizon predictor against composed-rollout, reconstruction-free, and direct multi-step baselines on pixel-based continuous control and long-horizon discrete benchmarks, measuring planning-time latent drift and closed-loop return. The core claim would fail if the direct predictor does not reduce planning-time latent drift or improve sample efficiency and final returns relative to composed-rollout planning.

items.title: Direct Latent Horizon Prediction: Redefining the Planning-Time Rollout of Latent World Models
items.abstract: Long-horizon planning with learned latent world models is throttled by compounding error: a transition model trained on one-step supervision must be iteratively composed at planning time, so errors accumulate in precisely the open-loop, posterior-free regime in which the planner operates. Existing multi-step training objectives—latent overshooting , replay overshooting , and scheduled-sampling-style data aggregation —anchor a composed prior against hindsight posteriors and alter the model's weights, but not the planner's query: plans still re-roll an autoregressive one-step operator, the very operation whose error compounds. We propose Direct Latent Horizon Prediction (DLHP), which augments a latent world model with a horizon-conditioned predictor that returns the imagined latent states at every horizon in a single forward pass, trained under (i) a future-anchored regression to bootstrapped (EMA) encodings of genuinely observed future states and (ii) a cross-horizon self-consistency loss that makes its K-step output agree with composing its own shorter-horizon outputs. The core falsifiable claim: switching the planning-time rollout substrate from a composed one-step model to a direct multi-horizon predictor—rather than refining one-step accuracy, which has demonstrably diminishing returns —reduces drift off the encoder-reachable latent manifold and thereby improves sample efficiency and final returns over the same agent planning with composed rollouts. We evaluate on pixel-based continuous control and long-horizon discrete benchmarks against composed-rollout, reconstruction-free, and direct multi-step baselines, measuring both planning-time latent drift and closed-loop return.

schema.problem: In reconstruction-free visual world models based on joint-embedding predictive architectures such as LeWM, candidate action sequences are evaluated by repeated one-step latent rollout, which makes planning computationally expensive and exposes predicted trajectories to accumulated latent errors as the horizon grows.
schema.motivation: Making such world models practical requires reducing the planning cost and long-horizon latent error that currently limit their use.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed fast latent world model builds on a JEPA-style latent representation and replaces repeated local rollout with action-prefix prediction. Given the current latent and a candidate action sequence, it encodes the sequence's prefixes and predicts the future latents reached after executing those prefixes, in parallel. Action prefixes are made the basic prediction unit, and the model is trained with prefix-level supervision to learn continuous state evolution under different action prefixes. During planning, the predictor uses the last prefix token from the encoded action sequence to evaluate the corresponding future latent without explicitly rolling through intermediate imagined states.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed model against LeWM across multiple tasks, measuring average success, planning time, and open-loop latent loss; the growth of open-loop latent loss with rollout horizon is used to assess error accumulation. Support requires higher average success, lower planning time, and lower or slower-growing latent loss than LeWM, though the abstract does not specify task names or matched compute.

items.title: Fast LeWorldModel
items.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), including recent LeWorldModel (LeWM), have become a promising foundation for reconstruction-free visual world models. For visual planning, however, LeWM evaluates candidate action sequences by repeatedly applying a local one-step latent transition model. This autoregressive rollout makes planning computationally expensive and exposes the predicted trajectory to accumulated latent errors as the horizon grows. We propose Fast LeWorldModel (Fast-LeWM), a fast latent world model that replaces repeated local rollout with action-prefix prediction. Given the current latent and a candidate action sequence, Fast-LeWM encodes its prefixes and predicts the future latents reached after executing those prefixes in parallel. By making action prefixes the basic prediction unit, Fast-LeWM directly models action effects accumulated to different extents over multiple horizons. This prefix-level supervision forces the model to learn how states continuously evolve under different action prefixes, rather than only fitting one-step state transitions. During planning, the predictor can use the last prefix token from the encoded action sequence to evaluate the corresponding future latent without explicitly rolling through each intermediate imagined state. Across multiple tasks, Fast-LeWM improves average success over LeWM while substantially reducing planning time, achieving lower open-loop latent loss whose growth becomes significantly slower as the rollout horizon increases.

schema.problem: The field lacks a criterion for when imagined rollouts stop being trustworthy that accounts for the intrinsic divergence of learned latent dynamics; existing remedies rely on fixed schedules, reconstruction error, or epistemic uncertainty and miss cases where even essentially exact one-step world models produce useless long rollouts because latent dynamics amplify representational perturbations exponentially fast.
schema.motivation: Solving this would improve model-based reinforcement learning in chaotic but low-epistemic-error regimes and brings the fixable-vs-intrinsic error distinction from atmospheric-ML error-accumulation research into latent world models.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed algorithm-agnostic rollout scheduler estimates the finite-time divergence of the latent flow along each imagined trajectory and uses this estimate to terminate rollouts, allocate the imagination budget, and anneal model-based value targets before divergence exceeds a tolerance.
