A companion evaluation metric decomposes rollout error into a model-deficiency part and an intrinsic-predictability part, porting the fixable-vs-intrinsic distinction from atmospheric-ML error-accumulation research into latent world models.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the scheduler is the falsifiable comparison: on tasks where chaotic sensitivity and stochasticity are varied independently, the proposed scheduler should beat uncertainty-based truncation (MACURA, Infoprop), accuracy-adaptive rollout (AR-MBPO), and two-horizon scheduling (DHMBPO) specifically in low-epistemic-error, high-divergence regimes and preserve performance in stable, high-stochasticity regimes. The abstract states no separate evaluation for the companion metric.

items.title: Chaos-Bounded Imagination: Scheduling World-Model Rollouts by the Local Predictability Horizon of Latent Dynamics
items.abstract: Compounding error is widely recognized as the central bottleneck of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), and nearly all existing remedies decide how long to trust an imagined rollout using a fixed schedule, reconstruction error, or ensemble-derived epistemic uncertainty . We argue that these criteria miss a distinct failure source: even a world model that is essentially exact one step ahead can produce useless long rollouts because its learned latent dynamics amplify unavoidable representational perturbations — encoder residual, posterior sampling noise, numerical error — exponentially fast. The question "when does an imagined rollout stop being trustworthy?" must therefore be answered with a property of the learned dynamics, its local finite-time divergence rate, not only with a property of model training such as epistemic uncertainty. We propose Chaos-Bounded Imagination (CBI), an algorithm-agnostic rollout scheduler that estimates the finite-time divergence of the latent flow along each imagined trajectory, and uses it to terminate rollouts, allocate the imagination budget, and anneal model-based value targets before divergence exceeds a tolerance. As a companion contribution, we define a useful-horizon evaluation metric that separates rollout error into a model-deficiency part and an intrinsic-predictability part, porting the fixable-vs-intrinsic distinction from atmospheric-ML error-accumulation research into latent world models. The proposal is falsifiable: on tasks where chaotic sensitivity and stochasticity are varied independently, CBI should beat uncertainty-based truncation (MACURA, Infoprop), accuracy-adaptive rollout (AR-MBPO), and two-horizon scheduling (DHMBPO) specifically in low-epistemic-error, high-divergence regimes, while preserving performance in stable, high-stochasticity regimes.

schema.problem: A world model's average error does not say whether a particular rollout can be trusted, or for how long.
schema.motivation: Equivariant structure offers a route to certifiable transfer, making it possible to trust particular rollouts and to decide how long they can be trusted under limited re-observation budgets.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach constructs a computable certification region over configuration, horizon, and resolution for equivariant latent world models. It certifies rollout error under exact equivariance from the k generators of the symmetry monoid, and characterizes equivariance at the function level by requiring orbits over equivariant targets to be flattened. For approximate orbit transfer, it propagates defects using the finite-time Lyapunov spectrum. A certificate based on cones and an adapted metric reads an a-priori horizon directly from the model's Jacobian; for public non-equivariant world models, the tangent spectrum provides a training-free candidate horizon paired with a held-out divergence cross-check.
schema.research_plan: The formal claims are supported by proofs: Theorem A establishes invariance and generator-based certification under exact equivariance; Lemma 2 provides the function-level characterization; Theorem B gives the Lyapunov propagation and charge-value error bounds. Empirically, the plan evaluates an equivariant network on a 40-dimensional learned model, testing whether it recovers the Lyapunov spectrum and comparing against dense and recurrent baselines. The certificate based on cones and an adapted metric is assessed for tightness on uniformly hyperbolic dynamics and for self-abstention elsewhere. A budgeted re-observation decision is used to measure whether the resulting horizon yields better decisions. For public non-equivariant models, the tangent-spectrum candidate horizon is paired with a held-out divergence cross-check designed to abstain or correct when the learned loop over-promises.

items.title: Certified World Models: Predictability Across Configuration, Horizon, and Resolution
items.abstract: Scale buys interpolation; structure buys certifiable transfer. A world model's average error does not say whether a particular rollout can be trusted, or for how long. For equivariant latent world models we give a predictability certificate: a computable region spanning configuration, horizon, and resolution. Under exact equivariance, rollout error is invariant over the monoid generated by k primitive symmetries and is certified from the k generators (Theorem A); universal orbit-flatness over equivariant targets characterizes equivariance at the function level (Lemma 2), so an unconstrained architecture cannot certify the property by construction. Approximate orbit-transfer defects propagate by the finite-time Lyapunov spectrum (Theorem B): expanding channels give a logarithmic horizon $T_j(ε)\sim\log(1/ε)/λ_j$, neutral channels accumulate recurrent defect linearly, and contracting channels accumulate a bounded nonzero floor. Exact conserved charge values are certified to all horizons only at zero defect; with one-step defect $η$, charge-value error grows at most as $Tη$. Empirically, on a 40-dimensional learned model a $\mathbb{Z}_N$-equivariant network recovers the full Lyapunov spectrum ($R^2=0.98$-$0.99$) where dense and recurrent baselines fail. A cone/adapted-metric certificate reads an a-priori horizon off the model's own Jacobian, tight on uniformly hyperbolic dynamics and self-abstaining elsewhere; the resulting horizon improves a budgeted re-observation decision. For public non-equivariant world models the tangent spectrum gives a training-free candidate horizon, paired with a held-out divergence cross-check that abstains or corrects when the learned loop over-promises.

schema.problem: Current learned world models for robotic manipulation largely neglect explicit modeling of contact state—location, normal force, slip state, and friction conditions—which leads to plans and policies that struggle on contact-rich tasks where these dynamics are critical.
schema.motivation: Explicit contact-state modeling could make downstream plans and policies more reliable on contact-rich manipulation tasks and support sample-efficient learning and interpretable failure recovery.
schema.proposed_approach: A world model that jointly predicts visual future states and explicit contact state representations, specifically contact map, force magnitude, and contact mode, trained on multi-modal sensor data including RGB, force/torque, and tactile.
schema.research_plan: The model is evaluated on contact-rich manipulation benchmarks spanning insertion, pushing, and grasping. The evaluation examines whether explicit contact prediction improves downstream RL sample efficiency, reduces failure modes caused by contact misclassification, and enables interpretable failure analysis and recovery. The abstract does not specify comparison baselines, matched compute, or formal failure conditions.

items.title: Explicit Contact-State Prediction in Learned World Models for Robotic Manipulation
items.abstract: Current learned world models for robotic manipulation focus on visual prediction accuracy and downstream task success, but largely neglect explicit modeling of contact state—location, normal force, slip state, and friction conditions. This leads to plans and policies that struggle on contact-rich tasks where these dynamics are critical. We propose ContactWM, a world model that jointly predicts visual future states and explicit contact state representations (contact map, force magnitude, and contact mode), trained on multi-modal sensor data (RGB, force/torque, tactile). We evaluate ContactWM on contact-rich manipulation benchmarks (insertion, pushing, grasping) and show that explicit contact prediction: (i) improves sample efficiency of downstream RL policies by 20–30%, (ii) reduces task failure modes caused by contact misclassification, and (iii) enables more interpretable failure analysis and recovery.

schema.problem: Existing visual world models primarily capture appearance dynamics and overlook tactile states that govern contact-rich interactions, so they can produce imagined futures that appear visually plausible but violate physical dynamics.
schema.motivation: Jointly modeling visual and tactile futures is needed for planning physical interactions, enabling imagined outcomes to respect contact-rich physical dynamics and supporting contact-aware planning.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework jointly predicts future visual latents and three tactile states—contact state, a 3D tactile latent encoding force-related information, and slip state—using a shared latent dynamics model with explicit supervision. A contact-gated asymmetric attention mechanism maintains a visual-only prediction pathway before contact and enables joint visuo-tactile dynamics prediction during contact. Training uses autoregressive rollouts and context noise injection to improve robustness to compounding errors. The predicted contact and slip states support contact-aware planning.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates visual prediction quality via LPIPS at short and long autoregressive rollouts, comparing against a visual-only baseline, with longer rollouts testing robustness to compounding errors. It also assesses zero-shot planning success on chip grasping, fruit grasping, and USB insertion using contact-aware planning from predicted contact and slip states. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched compute/latency constraints.

items.title: FeelWorld: Visuo-Tactile World Model for Hierarchical Contact Prediction and Planning
items.abstract: Humans plan physical interactions by imagining the possible outcomes of candidate actions. However, existing visual world models primarily capture appearance dynamics while overlooking the tactile states that govern contact-rich interactions, potentially producing imagined futures that appear visually plausible but violate physical dynamics. We introduce FeelWorld, a hierarchical visuo-tactile world model that jointly predicts future visual latents and three tactile states. FeelWorld organizes these states hierarchically as contact state, a 3D tactile latent that encodes force-related information, and slip state. These states are jointly predicted by a shared latent dynamics model with explicit supervision. To prevent irrelevant tactile signals during free-space motion from degrading visual prediction, we introduce a contact-gated asymmetric attention mechanism that maintains a visual-only prediction pathway before contact and enables joint visuo-tactile dynamics prediction during contact. The model is further trained with autoregressive rollouts and context noise injection to improve robustness to compounding errors. The predicted contact and slip states also support contact-aware CEM planning. Experiments on chip grasping, fruit grasping, and USB insertion show that FeelWorld reduces 10-step LPIPS from 0.084 to 0.058 and maintains an LPIPS that is 61% lower than that of the visual baseline after an 80-step autoregressive rollout. FeelWorld also achieves an average zero-shot planning success rate of 81.7%, providing an effective approach for incorporating tactile sensing into world models.

schema.problem: Most world models for embodied AI predict pixel-space observations or generic latent codes that do not explicitly encode 3D geometry, so they do not model how object geometry evolves under actions.
schema.motivation: Explicitly grounding predictions in 3D shape could make them more interpretable, generalize better across object shapes, and integrate more naturally with downstream manipulation tasks.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework combines 3D-aware encoders with a latent dynamics model to predict object geometry evolution under actions in a compact geometry-aware latent space, and regularizes the latent dynamics to preserve geometric consistency.
schema.research_plan: The approach is evaluated on deformable and rigid object manipulation, comparing against pixel-based and shape-agnostic world models on long-horizon prediction accuracy and downstream task performance; support requires higher accuracy and task performance than those baselines.

items.title: Geometry-Grounded Latent Dynamics: Explicit 3D Shape Prediction in World Models for Manipulation
items.abstract: World models have become central to planning and control in embodied AI, yet most operate on pixel-space predictions or generic latent codes that do not explicitly encode 3D geometry. We propose a framework that grounds latent dynamics in explicit 3D shape representations—predicting how object geometry evolves under actions in a compact, geometry-aware latent space. By combining 3D-aware encoders with latent dynamics models regularized to preserve geometric consistency, we enable interpretable predictions that generalize better across object shapes and integrate more naturally with downstream manipulation tasks. We implement and evaluate this approach on deformable and rigid object manipulation, demonstrating that explicit 3D shape prediction outperforms pixel-based and shape-agnostic world models on long-horizon prediction accuracy and downstream task performance.

schema.problem: Large video-based dynamics models for robotic control lack explicit 3D spatial structure and produce geometrically inconsistent long-term rollouts with compounding errors; emerging 3D dynamics models based on partial point clouds improve geometric consistency but remain sensitive to occlusions and accumulated prediction drift.
schema.motivation: A task-agnostic world model operating on completed 3D geometry could enable reliable long-horizon rollouts and more accurate cost evaluation for model-based planning, allowing robots to plan and adapt on new manipulation tasks across embodiments and in sim-to-real settings.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed task-agnostic world model operates entirely in 3D space. It first completes partial point clouds to reconstruct missing geometry, then learns action-conditioned dynamics in the completed 3D scene. The completed geometry is used for model-based planning cost evaluation and can support adaptation to new tasks.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of experiments across different robotic embodiments and tabletop manipulation benchmarks assessing long-horizon rollouts, open-loop and closed-loop planning, and sim-to-real transfer; no named baselines, metrics beyond long-horizon reliability, or failure thresholds are specified.

items.title: 3D Point World Models: Point Completion Enables More Accurate Dynamics Learning
items.abstract: Learning predictive models of the world enables robotic control through planning, potentially allowing robots to improvise solutions on new tasks. However, large video-based dynamics models lack explicit 3D spatial structure and suffer from geometrically inconsistent long-term rollouts with compounding errors. Emerging 3D dynamics models based on partial point clouds improve geometric consistency but remain sensitive to occlusions and accumulated prediction drift. To address these challenges, we present 3D Point World Models (3DPWM) - a task-agnostic world model that operates entirely in 3D space by first completing partial point clouds and then learning action-conditioned dynamics in this completed 3D scene. By operating on completed geometry, 3DPWM enables reliable long-horizon rollouts and more accurate cost evaluation for model-based planning while supporting adaptation to new tasks. Experiments across different robotic embodiments and tabletop manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that 3DPWM achieves significantly more reliable long-horizon rollouts (100-300+ steps), supports both open-loop and closed-loop planning, and enables successful sim-to-real transfer.

schema.problem: Existing action-conditioned world models either rely on expensive, densely annotated teleoperation datasets or fail to generalize across heterogeneous embodiments and uncurated web videos because explicit robot kinematics and implicit human actions are misaligned.
schema.motivation: Leveraging widely available internet-scale video instead of costly teleoperation would reduce data requirements and extend video world models to zero-shot policy evaluation and model-based planning across heterogeneous embodiments.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework unifies explicit robot action trajectories with implicit latent actions derived from large-scale internet videos. It introduces a shared multi-modal latent action space regularized by a contrastive alignment loss and a decoupled diffusion decoder, allowing the world model to ingest heterogeneous demonstrations and uncurated video corpora.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is extensive experiments on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks, comparing the proposed framework against single-domain action-conditioned models on video prediction fidelity, policy evaluation correlation with real-world outcomes, and downstream control performance; support would require improvements on these metrics and failure would be no improvement over single-domain action-conditioned models.

items.title: Cross-Modal Latent Action Alignment in Video World Models for Robust Robotic Policy Evaluation and Generalization
items.abstract: Video generative world models have emerged as powerful simulation platforms for robotics, enabling zero-shot policy evaluation and model-based planning. However, existing action-conditioned world models either rely heavily on expensive, densely annotated teleoperation datasets or fail to generalize across heterogeneous embodiments and uncurated web videos due to misalignment between explicit robot kinematics and implicit human actions. To bridge this gap, we propose Cross-Modal Latent Action Alignment (CM-LAA), a novel framework that unifies explicit robot action trajectories with implicit latent actions derived from large-scale internet-scale videos. CM-LAA introduces a shared, multi-modal latent action space regularized by a contrastive alignment loss and a decoupled diffusion decoder, allowing the world model to seamlessly ingest heterogeneous demonstrations and uncurated video corpora. Through extensive experiments on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks, we demonstrate that CM-LAA significantly improves video prediction fidelity, policy evaluation correlation with real-world outcomes, and downstream control performance compared to single-domain action-conditioned models.

schema.problem: Modeling world dynamics for dexterous robotics tasks is challenging due to limited data coverage and scarce action labels.
schema.motivation: Simulating action outcomes in varied environments would enable generalist agents at scale, and large-scale egocentric human video offers a path to train such models from broad daily interactions.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed foundation world model is trained on 44k hours of egocentric human videos spanning daily scenarios, diverse objects, and skills. To handle scarce action labels, it uses a unified continuous proxy action representation that enables transfer of interaction knowledge from unlabeled video. The model is post-trained on small-scale target robot data to improve physics understanding and action controllability. A distillation pipeline then accelerates the model to real-time speed and improves context consistency.
schema.research_plan: The model's physics understanding and action controllability are evaluated after post-training on small-scale target robot data. Systematic evaluation on multiple challenging out-of-distribution benchmarks is used to assess simulation of open-world, contact-rich tasks. The distillation pipeline is assessed by whether it reaches real-time speed and by context consistency. The abstract names applications—live teleoperation, policy evaluation, and model-based planning—as enabled by the generative model, but gives no formal failure condition or matched-control details.

items.title: DreamDojo: A Generalist Robot World Model from Large-Scale Human Videos
items.abstract: Being able to simulate the outcomes of actions in varied environments will revolutionize the development of generalist agents at scale. However, modeling these world dynamics, especially for dexterous robotics tasks, poses significant challenges due to limited data coverage and scarce action labels. As an endeavor towards this end, we introduce DreamDojo, a foundation world model that learns diverse interactions and dexterous controls from 44k hours of egocentric human videos. Our data mixture represents the largest video dataset to date for world model pretraining, spanning a wide range of daily scenarios with diverse objects and skills. To address the scarcity of action labels, we introduce continuous latent actions as unified proxy actions, enhancing interaction knowledge transfer from unlabeled videos. After post-training on small-scale target robot data, DreamDojo demonstrates a strong understanding of physics and precise action controllability. We also devise a distillation pipeline that accelerates DreamDojo to a real-time speed of 10.81 FPS and further improves context consistency. Our work enables several important applications based on generative world models, including live teleoperation, policy evaluation, and model-based planning. Systematic evaluation on multiple challenging out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks verifies the significance of our method for simulating open-world, contact-rich tasks, paving the way for general-purpose robot world models.

schema.problem: Interactive world models must predict future frames conditioned on continuous action streams over long horizons, but applying recent one-step and real-time video generation techniques to this setting suffers from severe compounding errors, exposure bias, and temporal drift.
schema.motivation: Recent breakthroughs in high-fidelity one-step and real-time video synthesis make it timely to adapt these techniques for interactive simulation; robust long-horizon simulators would support real-time planning and reliable policy evaluation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework transforms pre-trained latent video diffusion models into interactive world simulators by integrating a multi-step student-forcing rollout mechanism with a spatio-temporal adversarial discriminator conditioned on action trajectories. Training directly penalizes distributional drift and trajectory divergence over extended rollouts in latent space, targeting long-horizon action-conditioned future-frame prediction.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is empirical evaluation on interactive video benchmarks. Long-horizon consistency and trajectory-drift behavior are assessed through action-conditioned rollouts, while generation speed and policy evaluation are compared against standard teacher-forced diffusion models and distillation baselines; the abstract does not specify ablations, matched controls, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: Action-Conditioned Autoregressive Adversarial Post-Training for Stable Interactive Video World Models
items.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in video generation and diffusion adversarial post-training have enabled high-fidelity one-step and real-time video synthesis. However, applying these techniques to interactive world models—where a model must predict future frames conditioned on continuous action streams over long horizons—remains plagued by severe compounding errors, exposure bias, and temporal drift. In this work, we propose Action-Conditioned Autoregressive Adversarial Post-Training (A3PT), a novel framework that transforms pre-trained latent video diffusion models into robust interactive world simulators. A3PT integrates a multi-step student-forcing rollout mechanism with a spatio-temporal adversarial discriminator conditioned on action trajectories. By directly penalizing distributional drift and trajectory divergence over extended rollouts in latent space, our method eliminates blurriness and structural collapse during long-horizon planning. Extensive evaluations on interactive video benchmarks demonstrate that A3PT achieves superior long-term consistency, real-time generation speeds, and robust policy evaluation capabilities compared to standard teacher-forced diffusion models and distillation baselines.

schema.problem: Existing navigation world models often lack action-conditioned consistency, so visually plausible predictions can drift under multi-step rollout and degrade planning; efficient deployment requires few-step diffusion inference, but existing distillation methods do not explicitly preserve rollout consistency, creating a training-inference mismatch.
schema.motivation: Embodied navigation can benefit from planning in imagined future states, and making world models rollout-consistent under few-step inference is necessary for reliable and efficient deployment.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is a mobile world model for planning-based image-goal navigation. It is trained in two stages: structure pretraining followed by action-conditioned consistency post-training to improve action-conditioned rollout consistency. For efficient deployment, the trained diffusion model is distilled to few-step inference using a state distillation objective that explicitly preserves rollout consistency.
schema.research_plan: (1) The action-conditioned rollout-consistency and planning claims are evaluated on benchmark and real-world image-goal navigation tasks using visual fidelity, trajectory accuracy, and planning success; (2) the few-step distillation/efficiency claim is evaluated by measuring inference efficiency under few-step diffusion, with comparisons implied against existing navigation world models and distillation methods. The abstract does not specify explicit failure conditions, matched compute/parameters, or named baselines.

items.title: MWM: Mobile World Models for Action-Conditioned Consistent Prediction
items.abstract: World models enable planning in imagined future predicted space, offering a promising framework for embodied navigation. However, existing navigation world models often lack action-conditioned consistency, so visually plausible predictions can still drift under multi-step rollout and degrade planning. Moreover, efficient deployment requires few-step diffusion inference, but existing distillation methods do not explicitly preserve rollout consistency, creating a training-inference mismatch. To address these challenges, we propose MWM, a mobile world model for planning-based image-goal navigation. Specifically, we introduce a two-stage training framework that combines structure pretraining with Action-Conditioned Consistency (ACC) post-training to improve action-conditioned rollout consistency. We further introduce Inference-Consistent State Distillation (ICSD) for few-step diffusion distillation with improved rollout consistency. Our experiments on benchmark and real-world tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual fidelity, trajectory accuracy, planning success, and inference efficiency. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/MWM. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/MWM.

schema.problem: Existing driving world models are camera-centric: the latent state encodes the world exactly as the ego-camera sees it, and rollouts are only valid along training trajectories, so generating from novel camera paths requires exemplars or expensive reconstruction.
schema.motivation: Generating from novel camera paths is needed for data synthesis, simulator-in-the-loop planning, and multi-view perception.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed model consists of a factorized latent transition with a scene transition, a camera-motion transition, and a multi-modal residual; a self-supervised structure-from-motion pose head; and a VAE/VDM decoder conditioned on the scene and camera factors. The scene state evolves independently of the camera, and novel viewpoints are rendered by composing the learned camera model with the neural decoder.
schema.research_plan: The claims are evaluated on CARLA and nuScenes under seen, unseen, and held-out camera trajectories. Evidence for the claims comes from comparisons against camera-centric video world models and camera-conditioned view-synthesis pipelines using a newly introduced ratio metric for held-out camera paths and standard FID/FVD, SSIM, and closed-loop planning scores. The claim is treated as falsified if the factorization provides no benefit under trajectory augmentation.

items.title: EgoView-LM: A Camera-Aware Factorized Latent World Model for Viewpoint-Invariant Video Rollout and Closed-Loop Planning in Driving
items.abstract: Driving world models today are camera-centric: the latent state encodes the world exactly as the ego-camera sees it, and rollouts are only valid along training trajectories, so generating from novel camera paths — a requirement for data synthesis, simulator-in-the-loop planning, and multi-view perception — requires exemplars or expensive reconstruction. We hypothesize that explicitly factorizing the world model into a camera-invariant scene state and a learnable camera model yields a generative model closer to the true joint distribution over scenes and camera trajectories: the scene state rolls forward independently of the camera, and novel viewpoints are rendered by composing the camera model with a neural decoder. We introduce EgoView-LM, a video world model with a factorized latent transition (scene transition + camera-motion transition + multi-modal residual), a self-supervised structure-from-motion pose head, and a VAE/VDM decoder conditioned on both factors. We evaluate on CARLA and nuScenes under seen, unseen, and held-out camera trajectories, with a new metric, the novel-view rollout ratio (NVR²), alongside standard FID/FVD, SSIM, and closed-loop planning scores. Against camera-centric video world models and camera-conditioned view-synthesis pipelines , we predict large NVR² gains on held-out trajectories while matching ego-view quality — a result that is directly falsifiable if factorization buys nothing under trajectory augmentation.

schema.problem: Existing video generation models entangle the dynamic content of a scene and the camera motion through which it is observed, so the two factors cannot be controlled independently.
schema.motivation: Disentangling these dimensions would allow video generation from arbitrary pairings of camera and content conditions, greatly expanding creative control.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework explicitly separates dynamic scene content and camera motion, allowing arbitrary combinations of camera and content conditions for video generation. It is trained with a hybrid dataset that combines curated real-world videos and synthetic data to provide diverse paired examples. Training uses a two-level curriculum: at the condition level, control modalities are introduced progressively by difficulty; at the data level, the model is first trained for precise control on synthetic data and then adapted to real data for photorealism.
schema.research_plan: (1) Independent control is evaluated through generated pairings of camera and content conditions, including complex camera movements. (2) Visual quality is compared against existing generation models. The abstract names no metrics, baselines, or failure conditions for the dataset and curriculum components.

items.title: OmniCamera: A Unified Framework for Multi-task Video Generation with Arbitrary Camera Control
items.abstract: Video fundamentally intertwines two crucial axes: the dynamic content of a scene and the camera motion through which it is observed. However, existing generation models often entangle these factors, limiting independent control. In this work, we introduce OmniCamera, a unified framework designed to explicitly disentangle and command these two dimensions. This compositional approach enables flexible video generation by allowing arbitrary pairings of camera and content conditions, unlocking unprecedented creative control. To overcome the fundamental challenges of modality conflict and data scarcity inherent in such a system, we present two key innovations. First, we construct OmniCAM, a novel hybrid dataset combining curated real-world videos with synthetic data that provides diverse paired examples for robust multi-task learning. Second, we propose a Dual-level Curriculum Co-Training strategy that mitigates modality interference and synergistically learns from diverse data sources. This strategy operates on two levels: first, it progressively introduces control modalities by difficulties (condition-level), and second, trains for precise control on synthetic data before adapting to real data for photorealism (data-level). As a result, OmniCamera achieves state-of-the-art performance, enabling flexible control for complex camera movements while maintaining superior visual quality.

schema.problem: Contact is the bottleneck of learned world models for real-world robotics: latent-dynamics models trained purely from pixels capture appearance well but must infer contact implicitly, and existing latent planners either ignore contact structure entirely or require synthetic contact annotations or high-resolution tactile streams.
schema.motivation: Prior work indicates disentangled latent spaces improve linearization and cross-domain dynamics, and onboard proprioception offers a self-supervised contact signal; exploiting it would let contact-rich manipulation policies generalize to novel contact parameters and learn with fewer environment samples without simulator labels or tactile images.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed model is a decoder-free InfoMax-style Dreamer-family world model whose recurrent latent state is factorized into an appearance factor and a contact factor. The contact factor is trained with a self-supervised auxiliary loss for contact onset and force direction, computed from onboard proprioception such as force/torque or joint-torque deviations from a gravity-compensated baseline. No simulator contact labels, 3D annotations, or tactile images are required.
schema.research_plan: The work evaluates the factored model against decoder-free InfoMax and random-split latent controls of identical total dimension on four MuJoCo contact suites: friction-varying push, rail-guided insertion, peg-in-slot with slip detection, and force-locked wall rebound. Ablations over contact-factor dimensionality and auxiliary-loss terms isolate the contribution of the factor and loss components. Linear-probe interpretability of the factored latent tests whether the contact factor captures an identifiable contact subspace. The falsification condition is failure to outperform the identical-capacity baselines on generalization to novel contact parameters and on environment-sample efficiency under these settings.

items.title: Latent Contact Factoring: Disentangling Appearance from Contact Physics in a Decoder-Free Latent World Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation
items.abstract: Contact is the bottleneck of learned world models for real-world robotics: latent-dynamics models trained purely from pixels capture appearance well but must infer contact implicitly, and existing latent planners either ignore contact structure entirely or require synthetic contact annotations or high-resolution tactile streams. We propose latent contact factoring: a decoder-free (InfoMax-style) Dreamer-family world model whose recurrent latent state is explicitly factorized into an appearance factor and an internal-contact factor, where the contact factor is shaped by a self-supervised contact-onset/force-direction auxiliary loss computed from on-board proprioception (force/torque or joint-torque deviations from a gravity-compensated baseline), with no simulator contact labels, no 3D annotations, and no tactile images. Prior work shows disentangled latent spaces improve linearization and cross-domain dynamics , but none has been combined with latent world models for contact-rich manipulation; the closest prior art either predicts contact maps as explicit visual output fed to a rejection-sampling judge or plans in a compressed latent without any contact factor , and classical contact reasoning either optimizes contact locations with known dynamics or assumes planar pushes . Our falsifiable claim: with total latent capacity held fixed, the factored model will generalize to novel contact parameters (mass, friction, payload) better than same-size pixel-only baselines and reach benchmark success with fewer environment samples — because contact dynamics occupy a low-dimensional, identifiable subspace that a dedicated factor can learn without spending scarce capacity on object appearance. We validate on four MuJoCo contact suites (friction-varying push, rail-guided insertion, peg-in-slot with slip detection, force-locked wall rebound) against decoder-free InfoMax and random-split latent controls of identical total dimension, with ablations over contact-factor dimensionality and auxiliary-loss terms, plus linear-probe interpretability of the factored latent.

schema.problem: Existing world-modeling methods struggle to accurately model environments under data scarcity and complex contact-rich dynamic motion.
schema.motivation: Accurate world models of contact-rich dynamics are essential for advancing robotic planning and simulation and can support downstream applications such as data synthesis and real-time model predictive control.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a differentiable physics-grounded rigid-body world model with two core components: a unified Gaussian representation for visual appearance and collision geometry, and an end-to-end differentiable learning pipeline that differentiates through a closed-form physics engine to infer physical properties from sparse visual observations.
schema.research_plan: The claims are evaluated through extensive simulations and real-world evaluations comparing the proposed framework against state-of-the-art methods on learning complex scenarios and generalization. Downstream utility is demonstrated via data synthesis and real-time model predictive control applications. The abstract does not specify quantitative metrics, matched compute or parameter budgets, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: ContactGaussian-WM: Learning Physics-Grounded World Model from Videos
items.abstract: Developing world models that understand complex physical interactions is essential for advancing robotic planning and simulation.However, existing methods often struggle to accurately model the environment under conditions of data scarcity and complex contact-rich dynamic motion.To address these challenges, we propose ContactGaussian-WM, a differentiable physics-grounded rigid-body world model capable of learning intricate physical laws directly from sparse and contact-rich video sequences.Our framework consists of two core components: (1) a unified Gaussian representation for both visual appearance and collision geometry, and (2) an end-to-end differentiable learning framework that differentiates through a closed-form physics engine to infer physical properties from sparse visual observations.Extensive simulations and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ContactGaussian-WM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in learning complex scenarios, exhibiting robust generalization capabilities.Furthermore, we showcase the practical utility of our framework in downstream applications, including data synthesis and real-time MPC.

schema.problem: World models for video generation currently struggle to maintain scene consistency during revisits and tend to forget previously generated environments.
schema.motivation: This is worth solving because it is expected to improve the quality, consistency, and context length of generated videos.
schema.proposed_approach: A geometry-grounded long-term spatial memory mechanism is introduced into world models to retain spatial information over long horizons and support revisits. The mechanism is integrated into state-of-the-art world models.
schema.research_plan: The claimed improvement is assessed by integrating the memory mechanism into state-of-the-art world models and evaluating on the Memory Maze and Minecraft datasets; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

items.title: Enhancing Temporal Consistency in Video Generation with Geometry-Grounded Long-term Spatial Memory
items.abstract: We propose a novel approach to enhance temporal consistency in video generation by introducing a geometry-grounded long-term spatial memory mechanism into world models. Our method addresses the challenges of maintaining scene consistency during revisits and forgetting previously generated environments. We integrate our memory mechanism into state-of-the-art world models and evaluate its effectiveness using Memory Maze and Minecraft datasets. Our approach is expected to improve the quality, consistency, and context length of generated videos.

schema.problem: Existing methods for spatially consistent long-horizon video generation entangle memory modeling with video generation, producing inconsistent content when scenes are revisited and reduced generative capacity when exploring novel regions.
schema.motivation: Decoupling memory conditioning from generation could lower training cost and avoid reliance on extensive annotated data while enabling consistent long-horizon generation along predefined camera trajectories.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework decouples memory conditioning from generation by using a lightweight, independent memory branch that learns spatial consistency from historical observations. The memory branch builds a hybrid memory representation of generated frames to capture complementary temporal and spatial cues, then applies per-frame cross-attention so each frame is conditioned exclusively on the most spatially relevant historical information; the result is injected into the generative model. When generating new scenes, a camera-aware gating mechanism mediates the interaction between memory and generation modules, enabling memory conditioning only when meaningful historical references exist.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation is empirical: the proposed method is compared with an existing method on visual quality and spatial consistency, and data efficiency is examined under limited training data. The abstract does not describe ablations for the memory representation, per-frame cross-attention, or camera-aware gating, nor does it state an explicit failure condition.

items.title: Memorize When Needed: Decoupled Memory Control for Spatially Consistent Long-Horizon Video Generation
items.abstract: Spatially consistent long-horizon video generation aims to maintain temporal and spatial consistency along predefined camera trajectories. Existing methods mostly entangle memory modeling with video generation, leading to inconsistent content during scene revisits and diminished generative capacity when exploring novel regions, even trained on extensive annotated data. To address these limitations, we propose a decoupled framework that separates memory conditioning from generation. Our approach significantly reduces training costs while simultaneously enhancing spatial consistency and preserving the generative capacity for novel scene exploration. Specifically, we employ a lightweight, independent memory branch to learn precise spatial consistency from historical observation. We first introduce a hybrid memory representation to capture complementary temporal and spatial cues from generated frames, then leverage a per-frame cross-attention mechanism to ensure each frame is conditioned exclusively on the most spatially relevant historical information, which is injected into the generative model to ensure spatial consistency. When generating new scenes, a camera-aware gating mechanism is proposed to mediate the interaction between memory and generation modules, enabling memory conditioning only when meaningful historical references exist. Compared with the existing method, our method is highly data-efficient, yet the experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both visual quality and spatial consistency.

schema.problem: Model-based reinforcement learning agents that rely on world models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and lack adversarial robustness.
schema.motivation: Making world models adversarially robust would enhance the resilience of RL agents to adversarial attacks and preserve policy performance.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework integrates adversarial training into the world model learning process, building on existing adversarial training methods for world models. It includes a robust model-based RL algorithm that maintains an auxiliary pessimistic model, updated adversarially, to estimate the worst-case MDP within a Kullback-Leibler uncertainty set. The approach also incorporates identified effective adversarial attack methods for world models in RL settings.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed approach on high-dimensional MuJoCo control tasks, using policy robustness and performance as the stated evidence for the claims. No named baselines, metrics, or explicit failure conditions are given.

items.title: Adversarially Robust World Models for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: We propose a novel framework for developing adversarially robust world models in model-based reinforcement learning (RL). Our approach integrates adversarial training into the world model learning process, enhancing the resilience of RL agents to adversarial attacks. We build upon existing methods for adversarial training of world models and identify effective adversarial attack methods for world models in RL settings. Our framework includes a robust model-based RL algorithm that leverages an auxiliary pessimistic model, updated adversarially, to estimate the worst-case MDP within a Kullback-Leibler uncertainty set. We evaluate our approach on high-dimensional MuJoCo control tasks and demonstrate improved policy robustness and performance.

schema.problem: The adversarial security of world models, and in particular adversarial risk analysis of them, remains underexplored despite their powerful environment modeling in autonomous driving and robotics.
schema.motivation: Safety-critical settings such as autonomous driving and robotics depend on world models, so unexamined adversarial risks may leave learned policies vulnerable; addressing this gap opens a new direction for adversarial research in reinforcement learning systems.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach performs fundamental robustness verification through white-box attack experiments. For the spatial dimension, it decouples model component dependencies and uses a gray-box attack that perturbs only the perception module to mislead policies. For the temporal dimension, it uses a temporally correlated attack with a cross-frame adversarial loss that exploits the model's temporal memory and predictive capabilities to amplify single-frame perturbations into future decisions.
schema.research_plan: The evidence comprises white-box attack experiments for defensive boundaries, a gray-box perturbation of the perception module evaluated by whether it misleads policies, and a temporally correlated attack with cross-frame adversarial loss evaluated by its influence on future decisions. The abstract names no baselines, metrics, or formal failure conditions; support for the gray-box claim would require demonstrating policy misleading without full model access, and support for the temporal claim would require showing future decisions change beyond what single-frame perturbations achieve.

items.title: Adversarial Attacks Against World Models: Hallucination-Driven Policy Failure
items.abstract: World models have demonstrated powerful environment modeling capabilities in scenarios such as autonomous driving and robotics, but their adversarial security issues remain underexplored, in particular, adversarial risk analysis of world models. To bridge this gap, we systematically reveal the adversarial risks of world models through two dimensions: fundamental robustness verification and spatio-temporal vulnerability exploration. Specifically, in the fundamental robustness verification, we quantitatively certify the model’s defensive boundaries via white-box attack experiments; in the spatial dimension, by decoupling model component dependencies, we design a spatial-oriented gray-box attack, Latent Space Attack, that misleads policies by perturbing only the perception module, overcoming traditional requirements for full model access; in the temporal dimension, we propose a novel temporally correlated attack method, Temporal Enhancement Attack, incorporating cross-frame adversarial loss. By leveraging the model’s temporal memory and predictive capabilities, this approach amplifies single-frame perturbations to influence future decisions. This work conducts the first verification of the adversarial robustness of world models, thereby pointing out a new direction for adversarial research in reinforcement learning systems.

schema.problem: Standard latent world models such as PlaNet and Dreamer learn dynamics in an unconstrained latent space, so multi-step latent rollouts accumulate uncontrolled drift in physically conserved quantities like energy and momentum; this drift corrupts imagined trajectories, caps the usable imagination horizon, and degrades sample efficiency on physics-heavy tasks.
schema.motivation: Physics-heavy continuous-control tasks suffer degraded sample efficiency and planning from this drift, and mitigating it would enable longer usable imagination horizons and more sample-efficient control.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework encodes observations into a symplectic latent space with position and momentum coordinates, learns a Hamiltonian function plus an optional Rayleigh dissipation function, and integrates the resulting ODE with a symplectic integrator to generate multi-step latent rollouts. During these rollouts, it computes per-step energy drift and uses that signal online to adaptively truncate imagination horizons, re-weight policy gradients, and regularize the world-model loss.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a controlled comparison on continuous-control tasks with at least one known conserved quantity. Long-horizon rollout fidelity and sample-efficient control are compared against (1) an otherwise-matched Dreamer-style latent world model without symplectic constraints and (2) reconstruction-error-based horizon adaptation. Support for the core claim requires strictly better fidelity and sample-efficient control than both comparisons; failure would be no improvement or worse.

items.title: Symplectic Latent Imagination: Conservation-Aware World Models for Reliable Long-Horizon Planning
items.abstract: Standard latent world models (PlaNet, Dreamer) learn dynamics in an unconstrained latent space and, during multi-step latent rollouts, accumulate uncontrolled drift in physically conserved quantities such as energy and momentum. This drift corrupts the imagined trajectories that drive policy learning and planning, capping the usable imagination horizon and degrading sample efficiency on physics-heavy tasks. We propose Symplectic Latent Imagination (SLI), a world model that (i) encodes observations into a symplectic latent space (q, p), (ii) learns a Hamiltonian H_θ(q,p) plus an optional Rayleigh dissipation function R_θ(p) whose ODE is integrated by a symplectic integrator to generate rollouts, and (iii) uses the per-step energy drift ΔE_k as an online model-reliability signal that adaptively truncates imagination horizons, re-weights policy gradients, and regularizes the world-model loss. The core falsifiable claim is that, on continuous-control tasks with at least one known conserved quantity, enforcing symplectic geometric structure on the latent space and using conservation drift as a trust signal yields strictly better long-horizon rollout fidelity and sample-efficient control than an otherwise-matched Dreamer-style model without these constraints, and outperforms reconstruction-error-based horizon adaptation. Our controlled study bridges two previously disconnected literatures — state-space physics-informed dynamics (HNN/LNN/NODA/SymODEN) and conservation-free latent imagination (Dreamer/PlaNet) — and, to our knowledge, is the first to expose a principled, task-agnostic conservation-drift signal for planning with learned world models.

schema.problem: Current world model research is split among 2D video-generative models that emphasize visual future synthesis, 3D scene-centric models that emphasize spatial reconstruction, and latent predictive models that emphasize abstract representations; each route still struggles to provide physically reliable, action-controllable, and long-horizon stable predictions for embodied decision making.
schema.motivation: Embodied decision-making depends on predicted futures that are physically meaningful and action-useful, so moving beyond realism-only objectives matters for using world-model rollouts in planning.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework encodes observations into a structured latent phase space, evolves the latent state through Hamiltonian-inspired dynamics with control, dissipation, and residual terms, decodes the predicted trajectory into future observations, and uses the resulting rollouts for planning.
schema.research_plan: The abstract offers a conceptual discussion as evidence: it considers how Hamiltonian structure may improve interpretability, data efficiency, and long-horizon stability, and notes practical challenges in real-world robotic scenes involving friction, contact, non-conservative forces, and deformable objects; no experimental, formal, or explicit failure-condition evaluation is described.

items.title: Physically Native World Models: A Hamiltonian Perspective on Generative World Modeling
items.abstract: World models have recently re-emerged as a central paradigm for embodied intelligence, robotics, autonomous driving, and model-based reinforcement learning. However, current world model research is often dominated by three partially separated routes: 2D video-generative models that emphasize visual future synthesis, 3D scene-centric models that emphasize spatial reconstruction, and JEPA-like latent models that emphasize abstract predictive representations. While each route has made important progress, they still struggle to provide physically reliable, action-controllable, and long-horizon stable predictions for embodied decision making. In this paper, we argue that the bottleneck of world models is no longer only whether they can generate realistic futures, but whether those futures are physically meaningful and useful for action. We propose \emph{Hamiltonian World Models} as a physically grounded perspective on world modeling. The key idea is to encode observations into a structured latent phase space, evolve the latent state through Hamiltonian-inspired dynamics with control, dissipation, and residual terms, decode the predicted trajectory into future observations, and use the resulting rollouts for planning. We discuss how Hamiltonian structure may improve interpretability, data efficiency, and long-horizon stability, while also noting practical challenges in real-world robotic scenes involving friction, contact, non-conservative forces, and deformable objects.

schema.problem: Contact-rich manipulation defeats vision because the contact region is occluded, cameras add latency, and the decisive signal is tactile; yet most learned world models for manipulation predict one dominant modality—visual pixels or video, proprioception, or task-specific object states—while vision–touch systems treat the two senses as static policy inputs or fuse them only inside encoders.
schema.motivation: Predicting future tactile and contact-relevant visual states jointly could allow a planner to act through partial occlusion, vision delay, or full vision blackout by anticipating contact rather than relying on immediate visual input.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method builds a joint vision–tactile–proprioceptive world model whose action-conditioned latent dynamics is trained for cross-modal predictive consistency: one objective predicts future tactile latents from vision and proprioception alone, while another predicts future contact-relevant visual latents from touch and proprioception alone. A latent-space MPPI planner then rolls out both imagined futures, enabling planning through partial occlusion, vision delay, or full vision blackout by anticipating contact.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is tested by comparing the joint model against vision-only JEPA world models, modality-separated dynamics models, and matched-size concatenated baselines on peg-in-hole, pushing, and compliant-tool scraping under a graded vision-degradation protocol; outperformance under degradation would support it, while failure to exceed these baselines would falsify it. Claim (2) is tested by ablating the cross-modal prediction objectives and checking that blackout-phase performance falls to the vision-only level; failure to collapse would indicate that other components, not contact anticipation, produce the robustness.

items.title: Anticipating Contact: Cross-Modal Predictive Alignment in a Joint Vision–Touch World Model for Occlusion-Robust Manipulation Planning
items.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is precisely where vision fails: the gripper and object occlude the contact region, cameras add latency, and the physically decisive signal lives in touch. Yet most learned world models for manipulation predict the future in one dominant modality—vision pixels or video , proprioception, or task-specific object states —while vision–touch systems often treat the two senses as static policy inputs or fuse them only inside encoders . We propose a joint vision–tactile–proprioceptive world model whose action-conditioned latent dynamics is trained for cross-modal predictive consistency: “touch imagination” predicts future tactile latents from vision and proprioception alone, and “vision contact imagination” predicts future contact-relevant visual latents from touch and proprioception alone. A latent-space MPPI planner then rolls out both imagined futures, letting the agent plan through partial occlusion, vision delay, or full vision blackout by anticipating contact. Our central falsifiable claim is that this cross-modal predictive alignment—not merely extra input channels—buys occlusion-robust planning: on peg-in-hole, pushing, and compliant-tool scraping, the joint model should outperform vision-only JEPA world models , modality-separated dynamics models , and matched-size concatenated baselines under a graded vision-degradation protocol. Ablating the cross-modal imagination losses should collapse blackout-phase performance to the vision-only level, establishing that anticipating touch, rather than reacting to it, is what enables robust contact-rich manipulation.

schema.problem: Large-scale world-action models do not currently predict future contact together with vision and action, limiting their use for contact-rich manipulation.
schema.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires fine-grained physical interaction, and scaling visuo-tactile training across many embodiments and tasks could make precise tactile and action prediction tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework is a world-action model that predicts future vision and future contact for contact-rich manipulation. It is pretrained with visuo-tactile joint training over tactile-rich demonstrations spanning six embodiments and 450 tasks, using a unified force-based tactile representation to form a physically grounded contact signal that conditions action generation. Tactile contact events are used for task staging and advanced through during execution. For real-time efficiency, an asymmetric mixture-of-transformers architecture pairs a full-width expert for video prediction with slim experts for downstream action and tactile prediction; code and model checkpoints will be made publicly available.
schema.research_plan: (1) Evaluations on real and simulated benchmarks bear on the capability claims across a range of contact-rich tasks. (2) A data-scaling comparison bears on the claim that scaling improves precise tactile and action prediction. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, matched budgets, or failure conditions.

items.title: $N_0$-TWAM: Scaling Tactile-Native World-Action Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation
items.abstract: We present $N_0$-TWAM, a tactile-native world-action model for contact-rich manipulation that predicts both future vision and future contact. To our knowledge, it is the first tactile world-action model trained at large scale, and it shows strong capability on contact-rich tasks. We pre-train $N_0$-TWAM at large scale with visuo-tactile joint training over tactile-rich demonstrations spanning six embodiments and 450 tasks. We use NeoForce, a unified force-based tactile representation, to form a physically grounded contact signal that conditions action generation. To improve long-horizon and multi-stage manipulation, we introduce tactile contact events for task staging and advance through them during execution. For real-time efficiency, we adopt an asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that pairs a full-width expert for video prediction with slim experts for downstream action and tactile prediction. Evaluations on both real and simulated benchmarks justify the capabilities of $N_0$-TWAM across a range of contact-rich tasks, and demonstrate the benefit of data scaling for precise tactile and action prediction. In summary, $N_0$-TWAM endows a world-action model with predictive capabilities to foresee vision, touch and action, building a solid foundation for fine-grained manipulation on open contact-rich tasks. The codebase and model checkpoints will be made publicly available to foster further research and development in tactile-enabled robotic manipulation.

schema.problem: Latent world models for robotics generate rollouts with fixed-timestep, unimodal latent transitions that must integrate through discrete contact events (make/break, stick/slip, flight/stance); this over-smooths the boundaries that determine task success, so imagined trajectories drift exactly at grasp and insertion instants.
schema.motivation: Modeling contact-event timing explicitly and concentrating planning compute at contact boundaries could reduce long-horizon latent drift where task success is decided.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed model is a hybrid latent dynamics model that decomposes latent evolution into a continuous within-regime flow and discrete jump events at contact transitions. It adds a learned hazard head that predicts time-to-next-event, when the regime switch will occur. At rollout time it advances in variable-duration event steps: it integrates the within-regime flow until the predicted hazard fires, then applies a learned jump to the next regime's latent. Planning (model-predictive control or latent tree search) operates over these event-triggered macro-steps, concentrating compute at contact boundaries.
schema.research_plan: The evidence compares (1) boundary-adjacent long-horizon latent error and planning success on contact-rich manipulation and locomotion against fixed-step mixture-of-experts gating and PlaNet-style unimodal dynamics, with parameter count held matched; the claim would fail if the proposed model does not reduce error or improve success relative to these baselines. (2) Ablations isolate the timing contribution from extra capacity. (3) The hazard head is evaluated as a calibrated contact-event predictor against simulator contact onsets.

items.title: Event-Horizon World Models: Hazard-Guided Event-Driven Latent Rollouts for Contact-Rich Robot Planning
items.abstract: Learned latent world models are the substrate for model-based planning in robotics, but their rollouts are generated by fixed-timestep, unimodal latent transitions that must integrate through discrete contact events (make/break, stick/slip, flight/stance). This over-smooths the very boundaries that determine task success, so imagined trajectories drift exactly at grasp and insertion instants. I propose the Event-Horizon World Model (EH-WM), a hybrid latent dynamics model that decomposes latent evolution into (i) a continuous within-regime flow and (ii) discrete jump events at contact transitions, and that adds an explicit learned hazard head predicting the time-to-next-event — when the switch will occur — rather than merely re-gating a mixture-of-experts at each fixed step. At rollout time, EH-WM advances in variable-duration event steps: it integrates the within-regime flow until the predicted hazard fires, then applies a learned jump to the next regime's latent. Planning (MPC / latent tree search) therefore operates over event-triggered macro-steps whose length is chosen by the model, concentrating compute at contact boundaries. The core falsifiable claim is that explicit event timing plus event-driven rollouts reduce boundary-adjacent long-horizon latent error and improve planning success on contact-rich manipulation and locomotion relative to fixed-step MoE gating and PlaNet-style unimodal dynamics at equal parameter count; ablations isolate the timing contribution from extra capacity, and the hazard is evaluated as a calibrated contact-event predictor against simulator contact onsets.

schema.problem: Learned world models predict future latent states under actions, but their transition semantics are implicit: a latent rollout cannot be checked for consistency with what the model claims about its domain, and a trained transition module does not state which other environments it can legitimately be reused in.
schema.motivation: Making transition semantics explicit as a shared declarative ontology enables transfer by ontology matching, auditable reuse decisions, and axiom-satisfaction guarantees at test time.
schema.proposed_approach: In the proposed framework, every latent entity slot carries a type from an explicit OWL 2 EL ontology; the transition module is a typed operator whose pre- and post-conditions are TBox axioms; and each rollout step decodes to an ABox projected onto the models of the TBox, making axiom satisfaction a test-time guarantee inside a declared compiled fragment rather than a soft preference. The shared declarative ontology doubles as an alignment interface: transferring dynamics to a new environment becomes an ontology-matching problem followed by typed module reuse, with every reuse decision auditable as a set of axioms kept, added, or dropped.
schema.research_plan: (1) To test the main claim, the paper compares the proposed model against matched-capacity unconstrained, causal-factorization, and modular world models on environments that preserve the ontology while varying appearance, geometry, or physics parameters; support requires axiom-legal multi-step rollouts and better transfer, and the advantage should be attributable to alignment specifically, disappearing under a reuse-without-matching ablation. (2) For the diagnostic claim, the paper evaluates how well traces of axiom violations from unconstrained models localize distribution shift relative to per-step likelihood, checking whether they predict the entity, axiom family, and timestep at which the model broke; support requires better localization.

items.title: Ontology-Typed World Models: Description-Logic Axioms as a Hard, Shareable Interface for Consistent Rollouts and Cross-Environment Transfer
items.abstract: Learned world models predict future latent states under actions, but their transition semantics are implicit: nothing in a Dreamer-style latent rollout can be checked against what the model claims about its domain, and nothing about a trained transition module states which other environments it could legitimately be reused in. We propose ontology-typed world models (O-CWM), in which (i) every latent entity slot carries a type from an explicit OWL 2 EL ontology, (ii) the transition module is a typed operator whose pre- and post-conditions are themselves TBox axioms, and (iii) each rollout step decodes to an ABox that is projected onto the models of the TBox, so axiom satisfaction is a test-time guarantee inside a declared compiled fragment rather than a soft preference. Because the ontology is shared and declarative, it doubles as an alignment interface: transferring dynamics to a new environment becomes an ontology-matching problem followed by typed module reuse, and every reuse decision is auditable as a set of axioms kept, added, or dropped. The core falsifiable claim is that an ontology-constrained transition model produces axiom-legal multi-step rollouts and transfers better than matched-capacity unconstrained, causal-factorization and modular world models to environments that preserve the ontology while changing appearance, geometry or physics parameters — and that the advantage is attributable to alignment specifically, disappearing under a "reuse without matching" ablation. We additionally claim diagnostic value: for unconstrained models, axiom-violation traces localize distribution shift better than per-step likelihood, predicting the entity, axiom family and timestep at which the model broke. The contribution is the first world model whose dynamics are constrained by, and whose reuse is mediated by, an explicit description-logic ontology, together with the first evaluation of ontology alignment as a world-model transfer mechanism.

schema.problem: Multi-modal world models can represent environment dynamics more richly than single-modality approaches, but indiscriminately predicting all modalities at every timestep is computationally expensive and data-inefficient.
schema.motivation: Different tasks rely on different subsets of available sensor streams, so selective prediction can avoid unnecessary computation and data while retaining task-relevant information.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses a learned router in a latent dynamics model that, for each rollout step and task, decides which modalities must be predicted forward and which can be skipped. Routing is learned via task-conditional meta-learning over a multi-task dataset, enabling the model to discover task-specific modality importance without explicit supervision.
schema.research_plan: Validation on multi-task embodied RL benchmarks in robotics and autonomous driving against baselines that always predict all modalities or jointly fuse them. Evidence includes computational cost and task performance relative to those baselines, and analysis of learned routing patterns against human intuition about modality importance. Support is reduced cost with maintained or improved task performance and routing patterns that align with human intuition; failure is degraded task performance or misaligned routing patterns.

items.title: Task-Conditional Modality Routing in World Models for Efficient Embodied AI
items.abstract: Multi-modal world models can represent environment dynamics more richly than single-modality approaches, but indiscriminately predicting all modalities at every timestep is computationally expensive and data-inefficient. We propose TaskRouter, a task-conditional modality routing framework for latent dynamics models in which a learned router decides, for each rollout step and task, which modalities must be predicted forward and which can be skipped. The key insight is that different tasks rely on different subsets of available sensor streams: a manipulation task may need depth and proprioception but not audio, while audio-guided navigation needs acoustic cues. We show that routing can be learned via task-conditional meta-learning over a multi-task dataset, enabling the model to discover task-specific modality importance without explicit supervision. We validate on multi-task embodied RL benchmarks (robotics, autonomous driving) against baselines that always predict all modalities or jointly fuse them. We demonstrate that selective prediction reduces computational cost by 20-40% while maintaining or improving task performance, and that the learned routing patterns align with human intuition about which modalities matter for which tasks.

schema.problem: Modern world models learn continuous state-space dynamics but often lack interpretable structure and struggle to identify recurring behavioral patterns.
schema.motivation: Discovering discrete, interpretable behavioral modes can make latent dynamics more understandable and more useful for downstream planning.
schema.proposed_approach: A hybrid world modeling approach that augments a learned latent dynamics model with a discrete topic model; LDA and related topic inference are adapted to sequential latent representations to discover discrete behavioral topics corresponding to recurring configurations and action-effect modes.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on visual control benchmarks, including Atari and robotic manipulation, will use metrics for mode interpretability, planning efficiency, and downstream task performance, with comparisons against continuous disentanglement methods and existing discrete-mode discovery methods. The interpretability claim is tested through mode interpretability metrics, while the downstream usefulness claim is tested through planning efficiency and task performance.

items.title: Discovering Discrete Behavioral Modes in World Models via Topic Modeling
items.abstract: We propose TopicDynamics, a hybrid world modeling approach that leverages classical topic modeling techniques to discover discrete, interpretable behavioral modes in latent dynamics. While modern world models excel at learning continuous state-space dynamics, they often lack interpretable structure and struggle to identify recurring behavioral patterns. TopicDynamics augments a learned latent dynamics model with a discrete topic model that discovers recurring configurations and action-effect modes. By adapting Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and related topic inference to sequential latent representations, we enable discovery of discrete behavioral topics that are both interpretable and useful for downstream planning. We evaluate on visual control benchmarks (Atari, robotic manipulation) using metrics for mode interpretability, planning efficiency, and downstream task performance, comparing against continuous disentanglement and existing discrete-mode discovery methods.

schema.problem: Existing dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting frameworks either focus on task-specific robotic policies without explicit shape modeling (e.g., ManiGaussian) or rely on heuristic virtual reality physics engines without learned predictive internal world models of object deformation (e.g., VR-GS).
schema.motivation: Learning to predict future part-level shape states conditioned on continuous actions could enable high-fidelity simulation of complex deformable and articulated objects and downstream control.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an action-conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting world model for modeling, predicting, and interacting with part-level 3D shape dynamics. It integrates structural part-aware segmentation with a learned latent transition model operating over per-Gaussian embeddings and physical contact forces. It predicts future shape states conditioned on continuous actions.
schema.research_plan: The paper outlines an evaluation plan across multi-object deformation and manipulation benchmarks, intended to demonstrate that explicit geometric world modeling enhances predictive foresight and task performance. No named baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are stated.

items.title: ShapeWorld-GS: Action-Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting World Models for Part-Level Deformable Shape Dynamics and Manipulation
items.abstract: World models in robotics and visual graphics have increasingly turned to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to capture scene dynamics and enable interactive simulation. However, existing dynamic 3DGS frameworks either focus on task-specific robotic policies without explicit shape modeling (e.g., ManiGaussian) or rely on heuristic virtual reality physics engines without learning predictive internal world models of object deformation (e.g., VR-GS). In this proposal, we introduce ShapeWorld-GS, an action-conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting world model designed for modeling, predicting, and interacting with part-level 3D shape dynamics. ShapeWorld-GS integrates structural part-aware segmentation with a learned latent transition model operating over per-Gaussian embeddings and physical contact forces. By predicting future shape states conditioned on continuous actions, our framework enables both high-fidelity simulation of complex deformable and articulated objects and robust downstream control. We outline a rigorous evaluation plan across multi-object deformation and manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating how explicit geometric world modeling enhances both predictive foresight and task performance.

schema.problem: Current joint training paradigms that co-evolve latent action models and video-generative world simulators either suffer from representation collapse or require delicate warm-up heuristics due to the unconstrained drift between visual dynamics and action semantics.
schema.motivation: Adapting pretrained video generation models into controllable world models via latent actions is a promising pathway toward generalist embodied agents, making stable co-training of these components important.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework co-evolves latent action models and video world models using two mechanisms: a temporal hierarchy over latent actions that separates fine-grained motion control from abstract long-horizon dynamics, and contrastive mutual-information regularization that aligns the learned latent actions with state transitions across time scales.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the framework on interactive video simulation and downstream visual planning benchmarks, comparing against existing two-stage and naive co-evolution baselines, with evidence for long-horizon consistency and control precision.

items.title: Hierarchically Aligned Co-Evolving Latent Action World Models for Long-Horizon Planning
