items.abstract: Adapting pretrained video generation models into controllable world models via latent actions has emerged as a promising pathway toward generalist embodied agents. However, current joint training paradigms that co-evolve latent action models (LAMs) and video-generative world simulators either suffer from representation collapse or require delicate warm-up heuristics due to the unconstrained drift between visual dynamics and action semantics. In this work, we propose HiCoLA (Hierarchically Aligned Co-Evolving Latent Actions), a novel framework that stabilizes and enhances the joint co-evolution of LAMs and video world models. HiCoLA introduces two key mechanisms: a temporally-hierarchical latent action bottleneck that separates fine-grained motion control from abstract, long-horizon dynamics, and a contrastive mutual information regularizer that aligns the learned latent actions with state transitions across time scales. Extensive evaluations on interactive video simulation and downstream visual planning benchmarks demonstrate that HiCoLA significantly improves long-horizon consistency and control precision compared to existing two-stage and naive co-evolution baselines.

schema.problem: Latent world models leave two properties of the latent state to implicit optimization: the coordinate frame is defined only up to an arbitrary invertible transformation, so structure found in one training run does not transfer to another, and the standard predictive objective does not force the learned latent transition to be stable or certifiable, so planners trained or certified against it can fail in closed loop.
schema.motivation: Two threads that have so far developed separately—identifiable representation learning for latent dynamical systems via controllable-canonical-form structure and contraction-based regularization of learned dynamics—are available to combine, which would make learned latent dynamics transferable across training runs and certifiable for closed-loop planning and control.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed model class parameterizes the learned linearized transition operator in a fixed controllable/observable canonical frame and projects it onto that frame, eliminating rotation/gauge ambiguity. A learned metric regularizer makes the canonical-frame transition contractive with a certifiable rate and yields a forward-invariant ellipsoid. The work also specifies an invariant-set trust-region planner that uses the certificate and invariant ellipsoid.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is organized around the three hypotheses. (1) The coordinate-alignment claim is tested against PlaNet-style and locally-linear latent baselines at matched predictive loss, using a benchmark that measures latent coordinate agreement across random restarts. (2) The certificate claim is tested by computing an online Lyapunov certificate and checking whether it has positive margin. (3) The closed-loop stability claim is tested under compounding model error and injected latent bias, with ablations isolating each mechanism; the number of persistently exciting roll-ins is the stated comparative target. Explicit falsification conditions are specified, though the abstract does not state concrete thresholds or metric names.

items.title: Contraction-Canonicalized Latent World Models: Identifiable Coordinates with Planner-Usable Stability Certificates
items.abstract: Latent world models achieve strong sample efficiency for planning and control, yet two properties of the latent state are left to implicit optimization: (1) the coordinate frame is defined only up to an arbitrary invertible transformation, so structure found in one training run does not transfer to another, and (2) the standard predictive objective does not force the learned latent transition to be stable or certifiable, so planners trained or certified against it can fail in closed loop. This proposal fuses two threads that have so far developed separately—identifiable representation learning for latent dynamical systems via controllable-canonical-form structure, and contraction-based regularization of learned dynamics—into a single trainable model class: contraction-canonicalized latent world models. The learned linearized transition operator is parameterized in (and projected onto) a fixed controllable/observable canonical frame, killing rotation/gauge ambiguity, while a learned metric regularizer makes the canonical-frame transition contractive with a certifiable rate and yields a forward-invariant ellipsoid. We hypothesize that, relative to PlaNet-style and locally-linear latent baselines at matched predictive loss, the canonicalized model recovers trajectories whose latent coordinates align across random restarts, yields an online-computable Lyapunov certificate with positive margin, and keeps closed-loop latent MPC stable under compounding model error and injected latent bias, with strictly fewer persistently exciting roll-ins. We specify the model, the metric-learning contraction regularizer, the invariant-set trust-region planner, a benchmark and ablations isolating each mechanism, and explicit falsification conditions.

schema.problem: Existing latent-dynamics video world models factor appearance from motion, and identity-preserving video diffusion models protect identity through external conditioning or adapters, but no model treats person identity as a persistent predicted state variable inside learned latent dynamics anchored to a face-recognition embedding.
schema.motivation: Long-horizon face video generation requires identity to remain stable without degrading one-step prediction quality, and because deepfake detectors already treat spatio-temporal identity inconsistency as a tampering signal, an identity-stable world model can also serve as a diagnostic for where current generators fail.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework is a sequential latent video world model for human faces whose state is split into an identity factor and a dynamics factor. At each timestep a loss aligns the identity factor with a frozen face-recognition embedding of the observed frame. A regularizer penalizes changes in the identity factor over multi-step imagined rollouts so that the dynamics factor carries expression, pose, and speech. A loop re-projects the identity factor from the model's own decoded future frames every k steps.
schema.research_plan: The main hypothesis (1) is evaluated on MUG and UvA-NEMO plus in-the-wild talking-face sequences with a new benchmark for measuring identity drift over horizon, using baselines that include disentangled video predictors (G3AN, DDPAE, VDSM, SV2P), feature-space world models (DINO-world), and identity-conditioned diffusion models. The evaluation measures face-recognition cosine distance over horizons and one-step prediction quality to test the below-0.05 drift target without prediction degradation. The diagnostic claim (2) is supported by rolling out the model to expose where current generators fail at long horizons; no formal evaluation design for this diagnostic is specified in the abstract.

items.title: Identity-Anchored Latent Dynamics: A Face World Model with a Persistent, Recognizer-Verifiable Identity State
items.abstract: Latent-dynamics video world models successfully factor appearance from motion , and identity-preserving video diffusion models (StableAnimator , LaVieID , Arc2Face ) protect identity through external conditioning or ad-hoc adapters — but no model treats person identity as a persistent, predicted state variable inside learned latent dynamics, anchored to a face-recognition embedding. We propose IALD (Identity-Anchored Latent Dynamics), a sequential latent video world model for human faces in which the state is split into an identity factor z_id and a dynamics factor z_dyn, combining three mechanisms no retrieved baseline jointly has: (i) an identity-anchor loss that aligns z_id at every timestep with the frozen ArcFace embedding of the observed frame ; (ii) an identity-invariance regularizer that penalizes Δz_id over imagined multi-step rollouts, making identity a constant of motion while z_dyn carries expression, pose and speech dynamics; and (iii) a self-correcting rollout loop, in the spirit of Talvitie's compounding-error analysis , that re-projects z_id from the model's own decoded future frames every k steps. We hypothesize that IALD keeps identity drift near zero (ArcFace cosine distance < 0.05 from the initial observation at horizons ≥ 30) without degrading one-step prediction quality. We evaluate on MUG and UvA-NEMO plus in-the-wild talking-face sequences with a new identity-drift-over-horizon benchmark, using disentangled video predictors (G3AN , DDPAE , VDSM , SV2P ), feature-space world models (DINO-world ), and identity-conditioned diffusion models as baselines. Because deepfake detectors such as MINTIME and ICT already treat spatio-temporal identity inconsistency as the tampering signal, an identity-stable world model doubles as a diagnostic: IALD's rollouts expose exactly where current generators fail at long horizons.

schema.problem: Video quality assessment currently has limitations in prediction accuracy and efficiency, especially when training data are limited or diverse.
schema.motivation: Simulation offers a way to generate synthetic training data, making it more tractable to improve video quality assessment under data limitations and diversity.
schema.proposed_approach: A world model that simulates video content dynamics is created to generate synthetic data for training video quality assessment models.
schema.research_plan: The model will be evaluated on existing video quality assessment datasets and compared with state-of-the-art methods. The abstract does not specify evaluation metrics, held-matched conditions, or a failure criterion.

items.title: Leveraging World Models for Enhanced Video Quality Assessment through Simulation
items.abstract: This proposal aims to explore and develop world models that utilize simulation for video quality assessment (VQA), focusing on enhancing accuracy and efficiency in predicting video quality. By modeling the dynamics of video content, these models can improve the prediction capabilities, especially in scenarios with limited or diverse training data. Our approach involves creating a world model that simulates video content and generates synthetic data for training VQA models. We will evaluate the performance of our model on existing VQA datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods.

schema.problem: Efficient techniques for integrating model-based RL with video-generative world simulators for robotics and autonomous driving are lacking; existing approaches struggle with long-term predictions, sim-to-real transfer, and performance evaluation in complex scenarios.
schema.motivation: Combining model-based RL and video-generative simulators could yield more realistic and efficient simulation environments for training autonomous agents.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach will develop efficient techniques for integrating model-based RL with video-generative world simulators for robotics and autonomous driving. It will investigate combinations of existing model-based RL models (World Models, PlaNet, Dreamer) with video-generative simulators such as Sora or Genie, focusing on long-term predictions, sim-to-real transfer, and performance evaluation in complex scenarios.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation will use suitable benchmarks and metrics to assess long-term predictions, sim-to-real transfer, and performance in complex scenarios. No specific benchmarks, metrics, baselines, or failure conditions are named.

items.title: Efficient Integration of Model-Based Reinforcement Learning with Video-Generative World Simulators for Robotics and Autonomous Driving
items.abstract: This proposal aims to develop efficient techniques for integrating model-based reinforcement learning (RL) with video-generative world simulators for robotics and autonomous driving. By combining the strengths of model-based RL and video-generative simulators, we can create more realistic and efficient simulation environments for training autonomous agents. Our approach will focus on addressing the challenges of long-term predictions, sim-to-real transfer, and performance evaluation in complex scenarios. We will investigate the integration of models like World Models, PlaNet, and Dreamer with video-generative simulators such as Sora or Genie, and evaluate their performance using suitable benchmarks and metrics.

schema.problem: Existing driving world model evaluation relies on image-generation metrics such as FID/FVD or Chamfer, or on planner-internal scores that entangle model quality with planner quality; no existing benchmark asks whether a world model preserves the decision-level causal structure of reality, that is, whether it ranks candidate action outcomes as the real world or a ground-truth reference would.
schema.motivation: Evaluation at the decision level would turn qualitative findings of simulator collapse into reproducible numbers, and a decision-level training signal could yield world models that are honest where planning and safety decisions are made.
schema.proposed_approach: The work builds a model-agnostic evaluation protocol that, given one context and a set of candidate actions, compares the world model's outcome ordering to a ground-truth reference using three metrics: Kendall-τ between world-model and ground-truth cost orderings, the probability that the model orders a pair of candidates as reality does, and planning regret, computed as the cost of a plan found by CEM/MPPI in the world model and executed in the reference minus an oracle plan computed with ground-truth costs. It also builds a lightweight training objective that supervises the difference between future latents of paired actions using cached ground-truth outcome labels. The work delivers a benchmark to convert qualitative simulator-collapse findings into reproducible numbers and a training signal for decision-level honesty.
schema.research_plan: For claim (1), the evidence is a correlation study across a suite of state-of-the-art driving world models comparing visual-fidelity and action-fidelity scores with the proposed decision-level metrics; the claim would fail if |ρ| ≥ 0.5 or if no model that wins on FID fails at decision fidelity. For claim (2), the evidence is a controlled training comparison measuring planning regret and visual fidelity, with visual fidelity held unchanged; the claim would fail if the proposed training objective does not reduce planning regret or if the reduction is explained by improved marginals.

items.title: Decision Fidelity: Benchmarking and Training Driving World Models on Counterfactual Action→Outcome Structure
items.abstract: Driving world models are rapidly being promoted from "video predictors" to planning engines, policy trainers, and safety critics, yet they are still evaluated with metrics borrowed from image generation (FID/FVD, Chamfer) or with planner-internal scores that entangle model and planner quality. We ask a question no existing benchmark asks: does the world model preserve the decision-level causal structure of reality, i.e., given one context and a set of candidate actions, does the simulator rank their outcomes the way the real world (or a reference ground-truth simulator) would? We introduce Decision Fidelity, a model-agnostic protocol with three metrics: (i) Ranking Preservation (Kendall-τ between world-model and ground-truth cost orderings over candidate trajectories), (ii) Risk Separation (probability that the model orders a pair of candidates as reality does), and (iii) Planning Regret (cost of a plan found by CEM/MPPI in the world model when executed in the ground-truth reference, minus an oracle plan computed with ground-truth costs). We further propose Counterfactual Outcome Contrast (COC), a lightweight training objective that supervises the difference between future latents of paired actions with cached ground-truth outcome labels, rather than the expert marginal alone. We make two falsifiable claims: (1) visual-fidelity and action-fidelity scores will be weakly correlated (|ρ| < 0.5) with Decision Fidelity across a suite of state-of-the-art driving world models, and at least one FID-winner will fail at decision fidelity; and (2) COC will reduce planning regret at unchanged visual fidelity, an effect not explained by improved marginals. The work delivers a benchmark that converts qualitative "simulator collapse" findings into reproducible numbers, and a training signal for world models that are honest at the level decisions are made.

schema.problem: Current intelligent tutoring decision stacks are fractured: knowledge tracing passively predicts the next student answer, tutor policies are induced model-free or from hand-specified learner POMDPs, and off-policy evaluation of candidate policies is biased or high-variance because knowledge, engagement, and affect are only partially observed.
schema.motivation: Unifying latent-state prediction, policy optimization, and policy evaluation in a single learned model would make tutoring policies more reliable under partial observability, avoid biased or high-variance off-policy estimates, and support subgroup-aware policy selection.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed model is an action-conditioned latent dynamics model of the student trained purely on logged tutor–student interaction. It represents the student's current latent state, predicts state transitions under counterfactual tutoring actions, and exposes calibrated epistemic uncertainty. The architecture is RSSM-style, with a two-stage offline pipeline: first learn the student model from interaction logs, then optimize policies in latent imagination. The same learned model is used for latent-imagination policy optimization, counterfactual off-policy evaluation of policies a student never experienced, and safe subgroup-aware policy selection.
schema.research_plan: (1) Multi-step prediction is compared against passive next-answer knowledge tracing on Probability ITS classroom logs and public tutoring logs. (2) Policy learning gains are compared against the best model-free and OPE-selected policies, with subgroup analysis by pretest. (3) Counterfactual policy-value estimates are compared with importance-sampling, proximal, and structural-causal-model estimators under partial observability, using a semi-synthetic ground-truth generator for counterfactual ground truth. A small controlled online slice tests the policy selected by the method.

items.title: Learning the Learner: Action-Conditioned World Models of Student State for Imagination-Based Policy Optimization and Counterfactual Evaluation in Intelligent Tutoring
items.abstract: Intelligent tutoring systems make sequential pedagogical decisions — which hint to give, which problem to assign, how much feedback — but today's decision stack is fractured: knowledge tracing passively predicts the next student answer, tutor policies are induced model-free or from hand-specified learner POMDPs, and off-policy evaluation of candidate policies is biased or high-variance because knowledge, engagement, and affect are only partially observed. We propose the Learner World Model (LWM): an action-conditioned latent dynamics model of the student, trained purely on logged tutor–student interaction, that (i) represents the student's current latent state, (ii) predicts how that state transitions under counterfactual tutoring actions, and (iii) exposes calibrated epistemic uncertainty. We use one learned object for three jobs no single retrieved system performs together: latent-imagination policy optimization, counterfactual off-policy evaluation of policies a student never experienced, and safe, subgroup-aware policy selection. Our core falsifiable claim is that action-conditioned latent imagination beats passive next-answer knowledge tracing on multi-step prediction, yields policies with learning gains at least as large as the best model-free or OPE-selected policies (with the largest differential for lower-pretest students), and gives counterfactual policy-value estimates with lower error than importance-sampling, proximal, and structural-causal-model estimators under partial observability. We detail an RSSM-style architecture, a two-stage offline pipeline (learn the learner, then optimize in imagination), and an evaluation plan on the Probability ITS classroom logs, public tutoring logs, a semi-synthetic ground-truth generator, and a small controlled online slice.

schema.problem: Current multimodal large language models remain largely restricted to static spatial perception and cannot answer what-if questions about the consequences of object motions in 3D scenes.
schema.motivation: Humans perform this anticipation effortlessly, so exposing the deficiency and its cause is a step toward grounding multimodal reasoning in physical reality.
schema.proposed_approach: The work constructs a diagnostic benchmark with four tasks—collision, compatibility, occlusion, and trajectory—that test whether models can anticipate consequences of object motions. It analyzes model behavior to attribute errors to chain-of-thought reasoning drifting from visual evidence. To address the deficiency, it proposes a framework that externalizes simulation by generating videos of hypothetical dynamics, supplying explicit visual cues of causality intended to keep reasoning grounded in physical reality. The dataset and code are publicly released.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is tested by evaluating current multimodal models and humans on the four benchmark tasks, with failure if models matched human anticipation; the abstract does not state held-matched controls. Claim (2) is supported by analysis of model reasoning, with failure if errors did not correlate with textual drift from visual evidence. Claim (3) is proposed as a remedy, but the abstract does not specify an evaluation or failure condition for the framework.

items.title: CausalSpatial: A Benchmark for Object-Centric Causal Spatial Reasoning
items.abstract: Humans can look at a static scene and instantly predict what happens next -- will moving this object cause a collision? We call this ability Causal Spatial Reasoning. However, current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot do this, as they remain largely restricted to static spatial perception, struggling to answer "what-if" questions in a 3D scene. We introduce CausalSpatial, a diagnostic benchmark evaluating whether models can anticipate consequences of object motions across four tasks: Collision, Compatibility, Occlusion, and Trajectory. Results expose a severe gap: humans score 84% while GPT-5 achieves only 54%. Why do MLLMs fail? Our analysis uncovers a fundamental deficiency: models over-rely on textual chain-of-thought reasoning that drifts from visual evidence, producing fluent but spatially ungrounded hallucinations. To address this, we propose the Causal Object World model (COW), a framework that externalizes the simulation process by generating videos of hypothetical dynamics. With explicit visual cues of causality, COW enables models to ground their reasoning in physical reality rather than linguistic priors. We make the dataset and code publicly available here: https://github.com/CausalSpatial/CausalSpatial

schema.problem: Active inference is not precisely characterized in policy optimization terms: how expected free energy minimization for closed-loop policies relates to standard reinforcement learning, and what role the epistemic value plays, remains unclear.
schema.motivation: Grounding active inference within modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory could provide convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach frames active inference as policy optimization and reformulates expected free energy minimization for closed-loop control policies as a convex Markov decision process. In that formulation, pragmatic terms are linear in predictive state marginals, while epistemic value contributes a nonlinear component. The authors analyze finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations, and derive a mirror descent algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around current state marginals to produce a policy-dependent reward. They argue that coupling world-model learning with this policy optimization yields a reinforcement learning structure with policy-dependent rewards.
schema.research_plan: The support is theoretical: (1) the convex MDP formulation and decomposition are established for closed-loop policies and analyzed across finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations; (2) the mirror descent algorithm derivation supports compatibility with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming; (3) the coupling of world-model learning and policy optimization is argued to enable convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees. The abstract states no explicit failure conditions and describes no empirical experiments or baselines.

items.title: Active Inference as a Convex Markov Decision Process
items.abstract: Active Inference (AIF) frames adaptive behavior as the minimization of expected free energy (EFE), combining epistemic and pragmatic objectives within a single variational principle. We frame AIF as policy optimization and show that, for closed-loop control policies, EFE minimization can be formulated as a convex Markov decision process (MDP). In this formulation, the pragmatic terms are linear in the predictive state marginals and therefore equivalent to reward maximization in a latent MDP, while the epistemic value introduces a nonlinear component that distinguishes EFE minimization from standard reinforcement learning. This perspective further reveals the epistemic drive of active inference as a policy-dependent (performative) reward. We analyze finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations of EFE and derive a mirror descent (MD) algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around the current state marginals, yielding a policy-dependent reward that is compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming. Finally, we argue that coupling world-model learning with policy optimization gives active inference the structure of performative reinforcement learning, providing a route toward grounding active inference within modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory, including convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.

schema.problem: Midbrain dopamine neurons are thought to implement a temporal difference reward prediction error that updates cached striatal values, but dopamine ramps to predictable rewards challenge this account, leaving unclear how such ramps can be reward prediction errors.
schema.motivation: Resolving this would clarify how inferred and cached values interact during goal-directed behaviour and may revise the traditional dichotomy between model-based and model-free learning.
schema.proposed_approach: A dual-process learning system couples a world-model inference process with temporal difference learning of cached values. Inferred values provide the update target for cached value learning but are excluded from the prediction component of the reward prediction error, which produces ramping. The model is used to simulate dopamine signals across behavioural conditions relevant to ramping.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the model by simulating it against key dopamine ramp phenomena: learning dynamics on fast and slow timescales, global updates after changes in reward expectation, transient responses during unexpected state transitions, and sensitivity to state uncertainty manipulations. Support is implied by qualitative reproduction of these patterns; failure would be absence or mismatch of these patterns. The abstract gives no explicit baselines, metrics, or matched control details.

items.title: Dopamine ramps as a normative consequence of dual-process control
items.abstract: Midbrain dopamine neurons are thought to implement a temporal difference (TD) reward prediction error (RPE) that updates cached values stored in striatum. This has been challenged by evidence that dopamine “ramps up” to predictable rewards during goal-directed behaviour. Here, we propose that dopamine ramps are RPEs generated by a dual-process learning system in which values inferred using a world model train cached values via the RPE. Ramps arise because efficient training of cached values requires that inferred values contribute to the update target but not the prediction component of the RPE. The model reproduces key dopamine ramp phenomena, including learning dynamics on fast and slow timescales, global updates following changes in reward expectation, transient responses during unexpected state transitions, and sensitivity to state uncertainty manipulations. We therefore argue that dopamine ramps are a signature of interactions between inferred and cached values that revise the traditional dichotomy between model-based and model-free learning.

schema.problem: Most existing latent action models rely on single-view inputs and operate primarily in 2D pixel space, and simply incorporating multi-view videos into their training does not endow the learned latent actions with 3D-aware perception.
schema.motivation: Achieving 3D-aware perception in latent actions could improve world model generation quality, physical consistency, and generalization for open-world embodied agents.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework introduces three coupled components: a multi-view invariant unified action tokenization scheme; a geometric alignment constraint that anchors intermediate encoder features to a pretrained 3D foundation model to provide cross-view geometric correspondences; and a non-injective RGB-D joint reconstruction objective that prevents future-frame appearance shortcut learning by focusing supervision on geometrically significant motion cues. The components are unified by a single motivation rather than stacked. The framework follows a two-stage paradigm of large-scale human video pretraining followed by robot fine-tuning.
schema.research_plan: (1) The negative claim about naive multi-view training is supported by an analysis attributing failure to future-frame appearance leakage, inter-camera appearance discrepancies, and viewpoint variations. (2) The performance claim is supported by extensive experiments in a two-stage paradigm of large-scale human video pretraining followed by robot fine-tuning, evaluating world model generation quality, physical consistency, and generalization ability against baselines. No explicit failure condition is stated.

items.title: LAWM-3D: Learning 3D-Aware Latent Actions from Human Videos for Generalizable Robot World Models
items.abstract: World models enable agents to perform forward rollout and planning without real-world interaction. However, their application in open-world embodied intelligence remains limited by the high cost of action annotations and the heterogeneity of action spaces across platforms. Recently, latent action models (LAMs) have alleviated this bottleneck by learning action representations directly from unlabeled human videos in a self-supervised manner. Nevertheless, most existing LAMs rely on single-view inputs and operate primarily in 2D pixel space, raising a fundamental question: can simply incorporating multi-view videos into LAM training endow the learned latent actions with 3D-aware perception? Our study shows that the answer is negative. The primary reasons lie in future-frame appearance leakage as well as inter-camera appearance discrepancies and viewpoint variations. To address these issues, we propose LAWM-3D, which introduces three tightly coupled key designs: (1) a multi-view invariant unified action tokenization scheme for learning 3D-aware latent actions; (2) a geometric alignment constraint that anchors intermediate encoder features to a pretrained 3D foundation model, thereby explicitly providing cross-view geometric correspondences; and (3) a non-injective RGB-D joint reconstruction objective that prevents shortcut learning from future-frame appearance information, forcing the LAM to focus supervision on motion cues with geometric significance. Importantly, these components are not simply stacked but are tightly coupled through a unified motivation. Built upon a two-stage paradigm of large-scale human video pretraining followed by robot fine-tuning, extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed 3D-aware latent actions significantly improve world model performance, achieving SOTA results in generation quality, physical consistency, and generalization ability.

schema.problem: Existing aerial tracking benchmarks are based mainly on passive 2D video sequences from fixed camera locations or predefined flight paths, treating drones as passive cameras rather than embodied agents that actively perceive, interact with, and control their motion in dynamic 3D scenes.
schema.motivation: Aerial object tracking has applications in public safety, emergency rescue, and wildlife monitoring; enabling drones to act as embodied agents in interactive 3D scenes is needed to better reflect and support these real deployment conditions.
schema.proposed_approach: The work defines a drone-embodied tracking task in which a drone tracks a target in interactive 3D environments using online egocentric observations and active flight control in a closed loop. It builds a large-scale benchmark of 11,368 target trajectories across diverse scenes, rendering conditions, semantic regions, and moving distractors, with evaluation metrics for target visibility, tracking accuracy, and trajectory success. The proposed framework consists of an altitude-aware perception module and dual world models that imagine future states under both high- and low-altitude regimes; pseudo altitude-aware observations and imagined future states are combined to alleviate the altitude-mediated contradiction between target visibility and flight safety.
schema.research_plan: Benchmark coverage is supported by the scale (11,368 target trajectories) and diversity of scenes, rendering conditions, semantic regions, and moving distractors. The method claim is tested through closed-loop tracking experiments on the proposed benchmark using its metrics for target visibility, tracking accuracy, and trajectory success. The abstract does not name baselines, matched-compute conditions, or explicit failure conditions; support is implied by improvement across all metrics relative to existing methods.

items.title: DeTrack: A Benchmark and Altitude-Aware Dual World Model for Drone-embodied Tracking
items.abstract: Aerial object tracking has broad applications in public safety, emergency rescue, wildlife monitoring, and related fields. However, existing aerial tracking benchmarks are mainly based on passive 2D video sequences captured from fixed camera locations or predefined flight paths, where drones are treated as passive cameras rather than embodied agents that actively perceive, interact, and control their motion in dynamic 3D scenes. In this paper, we define a new drone-embodied tracking task, termed DeTrack, which requires a drone to track a target in interactive 3D environments using online egocentric observations and active flight control in a closed loop. We build a large-scale benchmark containing 11,368 target trajectories across diverse scenes, rendering conditions, semantic regions, and moving distractors, together with evaluation metrics for target visibility, tracking accuracy, and trajectory success. We further propose AaDWorlds, an altitude-aware dual world model framework for drone-embodied tracking. AaDWorlds consists of an altitude-aware perception module and dual world models that imagine future states under both high- and low-altitude regimes. By combining pseudo altitude-aware observations and imagined future states, AaDWorlds alleviates the intrinsic altitude-mediated contradiction between target visibility and flight safety. Experiments on the DeTrack benchmark demonstrate that AaDWorlds improves closed-loop tracking performance across all evaluation metrics.

schema.problem: Contemporary debate over whether large-scale artificial models possess world models presupposes that a world model must be an objective, first-person-independent replica of the world, and lacks a rigorous account of what would count as a functional world model in an artificial system.
schema.motivation: Large-scale models make the question of world models practically urgent for prediction and action, and resolving the conceptual confusion can guide AI research paths toward robust predictive agents.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper synthesizes cognitive-developmental observations and functional analyses to reframe human world models as indexical and inter-subjective, and to treat fully objective, perspective-free world models as a theoretical limit. It constructs a typology of world models, operational criteria for identifying functional world models in artificial systems, and an empirical program to validate these criteria. It also sketches formal desiderata for world-model tests and outlines implications for research on robust predictive agents.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is supported by a synthesis of cognitive-developmental observations and functional analyses; claim (2) by conceptual analysis treating a fully objective, perspective-free model as a limit for finite intelligence; claim (3) by functional analysis of prediction, counterfactual reasoning, and action coordination in artificial systems. The paper also proposes an empirical program to validate the operational criteria, but describes no concrete experiments, baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

items.title: World Models Without Subjectivity: Indexical Cognition, Functional Objectivity, and the Limits of AI Understanding
items.abstract: We revisit the debate over whether contemporary large-scale artificial models (LLMs and related architectures) possess or can possess world models, and we interrogate the presupposition that a world model must be an `objective' , first-person-independent replica of the world. Building on a synthesis of cognitive-developmental observations and functional analyses, we argue: (1) human world models are primarily indexical and inter-subjective-they arise from embodied, perspectival, and social coordination processes rather than from a pre-existing objective representation; (2) the notion of a fully objective, perspective-free world model is a theoretical limit rather than an achievable substrate for any finite intelligence; and (3) AI systems can and do develop functional world models-structures that support prediction, counterfactual reasoning, and action coordination-without inheriting human-style subjectivity or indexicality. We propose a rigorous typology of world models, operational criteria for identifying functional world models in artificial systems, and an empirical program to validate these criteria. The paper clarifies conceptual confusions, sketches formal desiderata for world-model tests, and outlines implications for AI research paths toward robust predictive agents.

schema.problem: Autonomous ultrasound probe guidance typically requires many probe-motion trajectories for training; high-quality demonstrations are labor-intensive, and explicit simulators are hard to build because ultrasound appearance depends on contact, tissue deformation, and view-dependent acoustic artifacts.
schema.motivation: A learned model of ultrasound dynamics could make training goal-directed robotic probe navigation practical without explicit simulators or large demonstration collections.
schema.proposed_approach: The pipeline has two stages: a latent conditional diffusion world model predicts future ultrasound observations from recent context frames, probe motions, and temporal offset; a goal-conditioned temporal transformer predicts ordered probe motions and is fine-tuned using rewards from the frozen world model. The world model is trained on self-collected neck ultrasound data, and the policy is refined in closed loop with frozen dynamics.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the world model on self-collected target-directed scans for preservation of action-dependent anatomical structure, then tests the full framework in real-world closed-loop guidance for carotid and thyroid targets, using success rate as the metric. The abstract reports no baselines, ablations, or explicit failure thresholds.

items.title: Action-Conditioned World Model for Goal Plane Probe Guidance in Robotic Ultrasound
items.abstract: We present an action-conditioned world model framework for goal plane probe guidance in robotic ultrasound, with a focus on neck ultrasound scanning. Autonomous ultrasound tasks often require large numbers of probe-motion trajectories for training, but collecting high-quality demonstrations is labor-intensive and explicit simulators are difficult to build because ultrasound appearance depends on contact, tissue deformation, and view-dependent acoustic artifacts. We address this problem with a two-stage model-based learning pipeline. First, a latent conditional diffusion world model predicts future ultrasound observations from recent context frames, probe motions and temporal offset. Second, a goal-conditioned temporal transformer predicts ordered probe motions and is fine-tuned using rewards from the frozen world model. Experiments on the self-collected dataset show that the world model preserves action-dependent anatomical structure on target-directed scans. In real-world closed loop experiments, the framework achieves success rates of 70.0\% for carotid guidance and 65.0\% for thyroid guidance. These results demonstrate the potential of learned ultrasound dynamics for training goal-directed robotic probe navigation.

schema.problem: Reliable autonomy for underwater robots remains constrained by tightly coupled physical limits: hydrodynamic uncertainty, partial observability, bandwidth-limited communication, and energy scarcity are usually treated as independent challenges even though they interact within the closed perception-planning-control loop and amplify over time.
schema.motivation: The increasing deployment of autonomous underwater robots and rapid advances in learning-based planning and control make this coupling timely to address; internalizing it may shift the field from performance-driven adaptation toward resilient, scalable, and verifiable autonomy.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper develops a perspective that situates planning and control within coupled sensing, communication, coordination, and resource constraints in ocean environments. It synthesizes recent progress in reinforcement learning, belief-aware planning, hybrid control, multi-robot coordination, and foundation-model integration through this perspective. It then examines environmental monitoring, inspection, exploration, and cooperative missions to distinguish stress profiles, introduces a taxonomy of cross-layer failures spanning epistemic, dynamic, and coordination breakdowns to analyze cascading errors, and outlines research directions toward physics-grounded world models, certifiable learning-enabled control, communication-aware coordination, and deployment-aware system design.
schema.research_plan: The paper supports its claims through a conceptual synthesis and domain-structured review rather than new experiments or proofs: it uses representative application domains to illustrate distinct stress profiles of coupling and uses the proposed taxonomy to analyze how epistemic, dynamic, and coordination errors cascade. Support would require the synthesized lines of work to fit the coupled-constraint framing and the domain cases to show distinct coupling profiles; no numerical baselines, metrics, or explicit failure thresholds are specified.

items.title: Underwater Embodied Intelligence for Autonomous Robots: A Constraint-Coupled Perspective on Planning, Control, and Deployment
items.abstract: Autonomous underwater robots are increasingly deployed for environmental monitoring, infrastructure inspection, subsea resource exploration, and long-horizon exploration. Yet, despite rapid advances in learning-based planning and control, reliable autonomy in real ocean environments remains fundamentally constrained by tightly coupled physical limits. Hydrodynamic uncertainty, partial observability, bandwidth-limited communication, and energy scarcity are not independent challenges; they interact within the closed perception-planning-control loop and often amplify one another over time. This Review develops a constraint-coupled perspective on underwater embodied intelligence, arguing that planning and control must be understood within tightly coupled sensing, communication, coordination, and resource constraints in real ocean environments. We synthesize recent progress in reinforcement learning, belief-aware planning, hybrid control, multi-robot coordination, and foundation-model integration through this embodied perspective. Across representative application domains, we show how environmental monitoring, inspection, exploration, and cooperative missions expose distinct stress profiles of cross-layer coupling. To unify these observations, we introduce a cross-layer failure taxonomy spanning epistemic, dynamic, and coordination breakdowns, and analyze how errors cascade across autonomy layers under uncertainty. Building on this structure, we outline research directions toward physics-grounded world models, certifiable learning-enabled control, communication-aware coordination, and deployment-aware system design. By internalizing constraint coupling rather than treating it as an external disturbance, underwater embodied intelligence may evolve from performance-driven adaptation toward resilient, scalable, and verifiable autonomy under real ocean conditions.

schema.problem: Existing work on generative economic simulation remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare, and there is no implementation blueprint for building models whose aggregate dynamics emerge from heterogeneous agents interacting with markets and institutions.
schema.motivation: Such high-fidelity environments could serve as sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents, making their development timely.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper constructs an implementation roadmap that organizes generative economic simulation systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds, through adaptive and large-language-model-based agent worlds and self-evolving agents, to evolving institutional worlds and sim-to-real twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey classifies existing work across these levels. A curated paper list and related resources are released to support future research.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is supported by the construction of the six-level ladder and the systematic classification of surveyed literature onto it. Claim (2) is supported by the same systematic literature survey across levels. Claim (3) is presented as a forward-looking argument supported by the release of curated resources, with no empirical validation or failure condition described.

items.title: From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models
items.abstract: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

schema.problem: Depth sensors lose range inside narrow corridors as ambient illumination drops, and perception-based planning deteriorates rapidly; collisions with obstacles recur even though the downturn can appear small on poorly scaled visualizations.
schema.motivation: Affordable indoor autonomy under considerable lighting variation would avoid such collisions and make low-light cluttered navigation more reliable.
schema.proposed_approach: The method grafts a variational autoencoder onto a feature pyramid attentive mechanism and jointly tunes this encoder with a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient agent. A composite objective drives the latent representation toward geometric features rather than raw intensity values. The learned policy navigates with the tuned representation, and control reverts to a reactive fallback below a set illumination threshold. Code is released.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation uses navigation trials in cluttered Gazebo scenes under low ambient illumination, comparing the jointly tuned policy with a plain DDPG baseline and a frozen-encoder condition, with success rate as the metric. Generalization is assessed through transfer trials in an unseen maze, where the magnitude of the drop in success is used as evidence about texture robustness. No explicit failure threshold is stated, but a large transfer drop would undermine the claim that the latent representation preserves obstacle silhouettes. Deployment feasibility is assessed by processing depth frames on a consumer GPU and by the fallback behavior below an illumination threshold. The abstract does not state whether compute, parameter, or latency budgets are matched across conditions.

items.title: VAE+DDPG: An Attention‐Enhanced Variational Autoencoder for Deep Reinforcement Learning‐Based Autonomous Navigation in Low‐Light Environments
items.abstract: Depth sensors often lose range inside narrow corridors once ambient illumination approaches Lx, and perception planning deteriorates rapidly. Collisions with desks recur, although on semilogarithmic axes, the downturn appears trivial because lower luminance compresses ordinate values. The experiment grafts a variational autoencoder onto a feature pyramid attentive mechanism, then tunes the joint encoder alongside a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) agent. This composite objective drifts the latent representation toward geometric features rather than raw intensity values. After convergence the learned policy achieves roughly % success at Lx and almost % when illumination reaches Lx inside cluttered Gazebo scenes during navigation trials. A plain DDPG stabilises near %, whereas freezing the encoder drags performance, confirming benefits of simultaneous tuning. Transfer trials inside an unseen maze reduce success by three points, implying that the latent space preserves obstacle silhouettes despite texture variation. Deployment processes depth frames at ten hertz on one RTX 4070, occupying GB memory. Control reverts to a reactive fallback once illumination falls below Lx in field experiments suddenly. Collectively, this evidence indicates that affordable indoor autonomy under considerable lighting variation appears attainable. The code can be found at https://github.com/uiseoklee/VAEplusDDPG .

schema.problem: Natural-language governance increasingly constrains strategic systems, but existing agents fail to jointly optimize policy compliance, physical dynamics, and long-horizon adaptation; reward-optimizing reinforcement learning violates governance feasibility while semantically aligned language agents induce unstable downstream physical dynamics, revealing a structural decoupling between governance compliance and physically resilient planning.
schema.motivation: Natural-language governance increasingly constrains strategic systems, making joint policy compliance, physical resilience, and long-horizon adaptation an increasingly urgent requirement.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework grounds policy constraints into executable strategic representations, evaluates candidate actions through latent world-model trajectory rehearsal, and adapts strategy at test time via trajectory-level retrospective policy adaptation. It also includes a benchmark built around policy black swans, adversarial sanctions, and dynamic compliance shocks to instantiate the regime.
schema.research_plan: (1) The failure-regime and decoupling claim is supported by identified failure modes of reward-optimizing reinforcement learning and semantically aligned language agents, though the abstract does not specify the evidence behind that identification. (2) The improvement claim is evaluated against reinforcement learning, planning-based, and agentic LLM baselines on policy compliance and structural stability under macroeconomic turbulence, using the introduced benchmark's policy black swans, adversarial sanctions, and dynamic compliance shocks; no explicit failure condition or matched-compute statement is given. (3) The distinct-regime claim is supported by comparative performance across baseline classes rather than by ablations isolating each component of the proposed coupling.

items.title: From Topology to Trajectory: LLM-driven World Models For Supply Chain Resilience
items.abstract: Natural-language governance increasingly constrains strategic systems, yet existing agents fail to jointly optimize policy compliance, physical dynamics, and long-horizon adaptation. We formalize this challenge as governance-constrained decision intelligence and identify two fundamental failure regimes: reward-optimizing reinforcement learning (RL) violates governance feasibility, while semantically aligned language agents induce unstable downstream physical dynamics. These failures reveal a structural decoupling between governance compliance and physically resilient planning. To bridge this gap, we propose ReflectiChain, a unified framework built on semantic–physical–reflective coupling: policy constraints are grounded into executable strategic representations, candidate actions are evaluated through latent world-model trajectory rehearsal, and strategy evolves at test time via trajectory-level retrospective policy adaptation. To operationalize this regime, we introduce Semi-Sim, a benchmark featuring policy black swans, adversarial sanctions, and dynamic compliance shocks. Across RL, planning-based, and agentic LLM baselines, ReflectiChain improves policy compliance by 23.6 percentage points over classical RL while substantially enhancing structural stability under macroeconomic turbulence. Our findings suggest that governance-constrained environments constitute a distinct decision regime requiring reflective world-model agents beyond reward optimization or semantic reasoning alone.

schema.problem: Estimating environment state from high-dimensional, multimodal, and noisy observations is challenging in reinforcement learning, and existing probabilistic approaches require explicit noise assumptions that limit generalization.
schema.motivation: A geometric representation of uncertainty would avoid explicit probabilistic modeling and allow adaptive integration of multiple sensor modalities without knowing noise distributions.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach learns a structured latent state representation in which distances between states are trained to correspond to the minimum number of actions needed to move between them. It uses a latent transition model capable of handling multiple sensor modalities, and a sensor fusion mechanism that weights modality contributions by inverse distance to adaptively integrate observations without assuming noise distributions. The learned representation is then used by an RL agent on multimodal tasks, with no explicit noise augmentation applied.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed representation empirically across a range of multimodal RL tasks. It compares robustness to sensor noise and state-estimation quality against baseline methods, and assesses downstream RL-agent performance when using the learned representation without explicit noise augmentation. The abstract provides no explicit failure conditions, metrics, or matched compute/parameter controls; support is indicated by relative improvements over baselines rather than by proofs.

items.title: Geometry of Uncertainty: Learning Metric Spaces for Multimodal State Estimation in RL
items.abstract: Estimating the state of an environment from high-dimensional, multimodal, and noisy observations is a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional approaches rely on probabilistic models to account for the uncertainty, but often require explicit noise assumptions, in turn limiting generalization. In this work, we contribute a novel method to learn a structured latent representation, in which distances between states directly correlate with the minimum number of actions required to transition between them. The proposed metric space formulation provides a geometric interpretation of uncertainty without the need for explicit probabilistic modeling. To achieve this, we introduce a multimodal latent transition model and a sensor fusion mechanism based on inverse distance weighting, allowing for the adaptive integration of multiple sensor modalities without prior knowledge of noise distributions. We empirically validate the approach on a range of multimodal RL tasks, demonstrating improved robustness to sensor noise and superior state estimation compared to baseline methods. Our experiments show enhanced performance of an RL agent via the learned representation, eliminating the need of explicit noise augmentation. The presented results suggest that leveraging transition-aware metric spaces provides a principled and scalable solution for robust state estimation in sequential decision-making.

schema.problem: Existing contamination detectors for code-generation benchmarks either operate at text level on prompts (renaming, word perturbation, n-gram overlap) or report a single model-level inflation estimate; none can tell a downstream user which individual benchmark problems are trustworthy for a given model, even though the most dangerous contamination is a leaked canonical solution rather than a leaked prompt alone.
schema.motivation: Code-generation benchmarks are scored by hidden tests, so a model that memorized both prompt and reference solution can pass a problem it never generalized, inflating its leaderboard position and undermining per-problem trust in benchmark results.
schema.proposed_approach: For each problem the proposed black-box probe generates semantically equivalent, oracle-preserving clones: reworded statements bound to the same hidden tests, verified for equivalence by running original and clone solutions against both test suites. It measures a difficulty-normalized solve-rate gap between the original and clones per item and flags statistically significant gaps. The per-item gaps are aggregated into a contamination-calibrated per-model score and a re-ranked leaderboard.
schema.research_plan: (1) The assumption that generalized models solve clones at expected rates while memorizing models collapse is tested by constructing oracle-preserving clones and measuring difficulty-normalized solve-rate gaps. (2) The per-problem identification claim is tested under controlled contamination: open code LLMs are fine-tuned on a random subset of paired prompt–solution items from an unseen benchmark, and per-problem gap labels are checked against the injected contamination labels, with statistically significant gaps flagged. (3) The calibration claim is tested by checking that the contamination-calibrated ranking agrees with a truly fresh benchmark better than the vanilla ranking. Failure is indicated if the per-problem gaps do not recover the injected labels or if the calibrated ranking does not agree more closely with the fresh benchmark.

items.title: CloneGap: Oracle-Preserving Clone Probing for Per-Problem Contamination Detection and Calibrated Code-Benchmark Ranking
items.abstract: Code-generation benchmarks are scored by hidden tests, so the most dangerous form of contamination is not a leaked prompt alone but the leaked canonical solution—a model that memorized both prompt and reference answer can pass a problem it never generalized, inflating its leaderboard position. Existing contamination detectors either operate at text level on the prompt (renaming, word perturbation, n-gram overlap) or report a single model-level inflation estimate; none can tell a downstream user which individual problems on a code benchmark are trustworthy for that model. We introduce CloneGap, a black-box per-problem contamination probe: for each problem we generate semantically equivalent, oracle-preserving clones that are reworded statements bound to the same hidden tests, verified for equivalence by running the original and clone solutions against both test suites. A model that truly generalized the underlying problem should solve clones at roughly the rate its ability and the item's difficulty permit; a model that leaned on a memorized prompt–solution pair should collapse on clones even though the oracle is identical. We measure a difficulty-normalized solve-rate gap between original and clones per item, flag statistically significant gaps, and aggregate them into a contamination-calibrated per-model score and re-ranked leaderboard. We validate CloneGap under controlled contamination by fine-tuning open code LLMs on a random subset of an unseen benchmark's paired prompt–solution items, checking that per-problem gaps recover the injected labels and that the calibrated ranking better agrees with a truly fresh benchmark than the vanilla ranking.

schema.problem: Reliable detection of data leakage is lacking for code large language models: existing approaches either assume access to proprietary training corpora, rely on brittle heuristics such as timestamp filtering, or require external reference sets with manually tuned, non-generalizable thresholds.
schema.motivation: Without reliable leakage detection, benchmark performance of code large language models can be artificially inflated by pre-training exposure, so trustworthy evaluation requires a method that works in both gray-box and black-box settings without manual threshold tuning.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework generates semantically equivalent variants of a benchmark sample and contrasts the model's behavior on the original with its behavior on the variants, flagging cases where the original is disproportionately easier. It supports gray-box operation using model logits and black-box operation using model outputs. A controlled leakage detection testbed is also constructed for evaluation.
schema.research_plan: (1) The detection claim is evaluated in the controlled leakage detection testbed with known leakage labels, comparing the proposed framework against strong baselines in gray-box and black-box settings using average F1. (2) Robustness and threshold independence are assessed across different models and training stages. (3) A gray-box study of 15 widely used code large language models on four popular benchmarks is conducted to examine benchmark-specific leakage patterns beyond prior overlap-based analyses.

items.title: SrDetection: A Self-Referential Framework for Data Leakage Detection in Code Large Language Models
items.abstract: Evaluating code large language models (Code LLMs) requires reliable detection of data leakage, where benchmark performance is artificially inflated by exposure to benchmark data during pre-training. Existing approaches either assume access to proprietary training corpora, rely on brittle heuristics such as timestamp filtering, or use external reference sets with manually tuned, non-generalizable thresholds. To address these limitations, we introduce SrDetection , a unified s elf- r eferential leakage detection framework for both gray-box (access to model logits) and black-box (access to model outputs) settings. SrDetection generates semantically equivalent variants of a benchmark sample and detects leakage by contrasting the model’s behavior on the original versus its variants, flagging cases where the original is disproportionately easier for the model. We further design a controlled leakage detection testbed and evaluate SrDetection in this environment. Across different models and training stages, SrDetection improves average F1 by 21.52 points in the gray-box setting and 14.46 points in the black-box setting over strong baselines, demonstrating robust, threshold-independent leakage detection. Finally, a gray-box study of 15 widely used Code LLMs on four popular benchmarks reveals benchmark-specific leakage patterns beyond prior overlap-based analyses[Source code and data are available at https://github.com/SMinL/SrDetectionCode ].

schema.problem: Automated program repair and LLM-based issue-solving agents are validated by incomplete test suites, so patches that pass all tests may nonetheless be incorrect. Existing patch-correctness-assessment techniques either learn from previously labeled patches, rank patches by static or dynamic similarity, or generate more tests whose oracles are derived from the implemented behaviour of the patched program—exactly the behaviour LLMs tend to encode.
schema.motivation: Using the pre-patch buggy program as an oracle offers a way to specify which behaviours must change and which must be preserved without depending on labelled patches or on the patched program’s own behaviour, enabling machine-checkable evidence of incorrectness.
schema.proposed_approach: Given a buggy program, a bug report, and a patch, an LLM infers an explicit executable two-clause specification: one clause is a predicate over inputs that characterises the bug-triggering region and the behaviour that must change there, and the other clause is a predicate over inputs on which the patched and pre-patch programs must behave identically. A differential executor searches for inputs inside the must-differ region and outside it (must-equal), and an iterative falsification loop feeds discrepancies back to the LLM. Any out-of-frame behavioural divergence is reported as a machine-checkable counterexample certificate naming the violated clause, the input, and the two outputs.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation compares the proposed method against RGT, Poracle, Shibboleth, FixCheck, LLM4PatchCorrect, and a random-selection baseline on curated overfitting corpora and on SWE-bench-Verified-style issue-solving patches; the fraction of patches undecidable from the bug report alone is reported as a first-class result. No explicit failure condition or held-matched quantities are stated for the comparative claims.

items.title: FRAMECHECK: Contract-Guided Differential Patch Validation from Bug Reports
items.abstract: Automated program repair (APR) and LLM-based issue-solving agents are validated by test suites that are incomplete, so patches that pass all tests may nonetheless be incorrect. Existing patch-correctness-assessment techniques either learn from previously labeled patches, rank patches by static or dynamic similarity, or generate more tests whose oracles are derived from the implemented behaviour of the patched program — exactly the behaviour LLMs tend to encode. FRAMECHECK makes the opposite move: it uses the pre-patch (buggy) program as an oracle. Given a buggy program, a bug report, and a patch, an LLM infers a change frame: an explicit, executable two-clause specification consisting of (i) an obligation clause, a predicate over inputs that characterises the bug-triggering region and the behaviour that must change there, and (ii) a preservation clause, a predicate over inputs on which the patched and pre-patch programs must behave identically. A differential executor then searches for inputs inside the frame (must-differ) and outside it (must-equal), and an iterative falsification loop feeds discrepancies back to the LLM. Any out-of-frame behavioural divergence is reported as a machine-checkable counterexample certificate naming the violated clause, the input, and the two outputs. I evaluate FRAMECHECK against RGT, Poracle, Shibboleth, FixCheck, LLM4PatchCorrect, and the random-selection baseline on curated overfitting corpora and on SWE-bench-Verified-style issue-solving patches, reporting as a first-class result the fraction of patches that are undecidable from the bug report alone.

schema.problem: Software patches may unintentionally alter program behavior, and validating a patch against its intended semantics is difficult because regression tests are incomplete and natural-language descriptions of patch intent are informal and non-executable.
schema.motivation: Making patch intent executable would enable automated validation and provide documentation, complementing code review and regression testing; large language models now make it feasible to extract intent from natural-language artifacts.
schema.proposed_approach: Given a pull request, the proposed technique uses large language models to extract developer intent from natural-language artifacts and synthesizes executable patch specifications expressed as runtime assertions in comparison programs that integrate pre- and post-patch versions. The specifications focus on patch-relevant behaviors and support cross-version properties. The technique iteratively refines inferred specifications by comparing pre- and post-patch behaviors, identifies violations, filters inconsistencies via self-review, and generates bug reports.
schema.research_plan: (1) The specification-inference ability is evaluated on 400 recent pull requests from four widely used open-source Python projects, with precision measured against developer-confirmed true positives. (2) The practical usefulness is evaluated by whether reported warnings correspond to confirmed bugs and subsequent fixes, and by per-pull-request time and monetary cost. (3) The technique is compared with the state-of-the-art technique Testora.

items.title: PatchGuru: Patch Oracle Inference from Natural Language Artifacts
items.abstract: As software systems evolve, patches may unintentionally alter program behavior. Validating patches against their intended semantics is difficult due to incomplete regression tests and informal, non-executable natural language (NL) descriptions of patch intent. We present PatchGuru, the first automated technique that infers executable patch specifications from real-world pull requests (PRs). Given a PR, PatchGuru uses large language models (LLMs) to extract developer intent from NL artifacts and synthesizes patch oracles: under-approximate yet practical specifications expressed as runtime assertions in comparison programs that integrate pre- and post-patch versions. Patch oracles focus on patch-relevant behaviors, enable automated validation, and support cross-version properties. PatchGuru iteratively refines inferred oracles by comparing pre- and post-patch behaviors, identifies violations, filters inconsistencies via self-review, and generates bug reports. We evaluate PatchGuru on 400 recent PRs from four widely used open-source Python projects. PatchGuru reports 39 warnings with a precision of 0.62, yielding 24 confirmed true positives, including 12 previously unknown bugs, 11 of which were subsequently fixed by developers. Compared to the state-of-the-art technique Testora, PatchGuru detects 17 more bugs (24 vs. 7) while improving precision from 0.32 to 0.62. PatchGuru incurs an average cost of 8.9 minutes and USD 0.07 per PR. These results suggest that PatchGuru complements code review and regression testing by providing executable documentation and automated validation of patch intent.

schema.problem: Large language models fail when natural language requirements are ambiguous, incomplete, or under-specified, and existing clarification-seeking methods treat clarification as an isolated post-hoc behavior rather than integrating it into a unified dialogue framework.
schema.motivation: Interactive clarification improves code generation outcomes, and LLMs can now be taught to recognize ambiguity and ask clarifying questions, making a systematically integrated clarification-to-code dialogue both feasible and valuable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework combines three components: an ambiguity detector that classifies requirement ambiguity at semantic, pragmatic, and structural levels; a fine-tuned clarification-question generator that asks focused, context-aware follow-up questions tailored to the ambiguity type; and a dialogue-aware code generator that maintains multi-turn context to synthesize code from clarified specifications. Evaluation uses a new benchmark of 500+ naturally ambiguous requirements from Stack Overflow and real development tasks, annotated with ambiguity type, effective clarifications, and ground-truth code solutions.
schema.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated on the new benchmark of 500+ naturally ambiguous requirements. Annotated ambiguity types support assessing whether the detector and generated questions are tailored to each type, and ground-truth code solutions support assessing the dialogue-aware code generator's outputs. The abstract does not name baselines, metrics, or failure thresholds, so what would count as supporting or failing evidence is not specified.

items.title: Interactive Code Generation through Clarification-Aware Dialogue and Ambiguity Feedback
items.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated strong code generation capabilities, yet they often fail when natural language requirements are ambiguous, incomplete, or under-specified. Recent work has shown that LLMs can be taught to recognize ambiguity and ask clarifying questions, and that interactive refinement improves outcomes. However, existing approaches treat clarification-seeking as a post-hoc model behavior (via prompting or fine-tuning) without systematically integrating it into a unified dialogue framework. We propose ClarificationFlow, a framework that combines three novel components: (1) an ambiguity detector that classifies requirement ambiguity types at multiple levels (semantic, pragmatic, structural); (2) a clarification-question generator fine-tuned to ask focused, context-aware follow-up questions tailored to the ambiguity type; and (3) a dialogue-aware code generator that maintains multi-turn context to synthesize code from clarified specifications. We will evaluate on a new benchmark, ClarifyBench, comprising 500+ naturally ambiguous requirements from Stack Overflow and real development tasks, annotated with ambiguity type, effective clarifications, and ground-truth code solutions.

schema.problem: Text-to-CAD systems that synthesize parametric CAD programs from natural-language prompts often receive under-specified or internally inconsistent geometric descriptions, with missing critical dimensions or conflicting constraints, and existing fine-tuned models reactively follow instructions and hallucinate dimensions when the text is ambiguous.
schema.motivation: Resolving specification issues before code synthesis would make text-to-CAD more robust to ambiguous prompts and reduce invalid programs, while keeping the interaction burden of clarification low.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework pairs a proactive clarifying agent with a CAD coding agent. The clarifying agent audits the prompt and asks targeted clarification questions only when necessary, producing a self-consistent specification; the coding agent then translates this specification into an executable CadQuery program. The coding agent is fine-tuned on a curated high-quality text-to-CadQuery dataset, and the clarifying agent is trained via supervised fine-tuning on clarification trajectories. Code and datasets are released publicly.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes experiments comparing the proposed framework to frontier closed-source models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 on mean Chamfer distance and invalidity ratio, with additional measurement of interaction overhead for ambiguous prompts. The abstract does not specify held-matched conditions, ablations, or failure thresholds.

items.title: Clarify Before You Draw: Proactive Agents for Robust Text-to-CAD Generation
items.abstract: Large language models have recently enabled text-to-CAD systems that synthesize parametric CAD programs (e.g., CadQuery) from natural-language prompts. In practice, however, geometric descriptions can be under-specified or internally inconsistent: critical dimensions may be missing and constraints may conflict. However, existing fine-tuned models tend to reactively follow the user instructions and hallucinate dimensions when the text is ambiguous. To address this, we propose a proactive agentic framework for text-to-CadQuery generation, named as ProCAD, that resolves specification issues before code synthesis. Our framework pairs a proactive clarifying agent, which audits the prompt and asks targeted clarification questions only when necessary to produce a self-consistent specification, with a CAD coding agent that translates the specification into an executable CadQuery program. We fine-tune the coding agent based on a curated high-quality text-to-CadQuery dataset and train the clarifying agent via agentic SFT on clarification trajectories. Experiments show that proactive clarification significantly improves robustness to ambiguous prompts while keeping interaction overhead low. ProCAD outperforms frontier closed-source models, including Claude Sonnet 4.5, reducing the mean Chamfer distance by 79.9% and lowering the invalidity ratio from 4.8% to 0.9%. Our code and datasets are made publicly available on https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/Pro-CAD.

schema.problem: Large language models often misunderstand natural language specifications when generating code because they work directly with flat text, producing code that is not aligned with requirement intent.
schema.motivation: Making the semantic structure of a specification explicit before code generation could improve alignment, increase robustness to paraphrased or ambiguous requirements, and allow specification understanding to be validated separately from synthesis.
