schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method parses natural language specifications into a structured semantic graph that captures predicates, entities, control flow, and data dependencies, analogous to Abstract Meaning Representation but adapted for imperative code. A large language model then generates code from this explicit semantic representation rather than from raw specification text.
schema.research_plan: The evidence for the three claims is experimental evaluation on HumanEval, MBPP, and competitive programming benchmarks. Comparisons are made against baselines that use semantic prompting post-hoc and baselines that learn implicit semantic features in embeddings. The abstract does not specify failure conditions, metrics, or matched compute or latency controls.

items.title: Bridging Specification and Code: Explicit Semantic Intermediate Representation for LLM-Based Code Generation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle to align generated code with natural language specifications, often misunderstanding requirement intent because they work directly with flat text. We propose SEMIR (Semantic Intermediate Representation), a method that explicitly parses natural language specifications into a structured semantic graph capturing predicates, entities, control flow, and data dependencies—analogous to Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) but adapted for imperative code. An LLM then generates code from this explicit semantic representation rather than raw specification text. We demonstrate that explicit semantic parsing (1) improves alignment between specification and generated code, (2) increases robustness to paraphrased and ambiguous requirements, and (3) enables tractable validation of specification understanding before code synthesis. Experiments on HumanEval, MBPP, and competitive programming benchmarks show consistent improvements over baselines that either use semantic prompting post-hoc or learn implicit semantic features in embeddings.

schema.problem: Existing code generation approaches focus on reasoning strategies or post-refinement methods but share a common assumption that the LLM correctly understands the given requirement, which does not always hold.
schema.motivation: Because downstream reasoning and refinement cannot recover correctness when the initial requirement understanding is wrong, explicitly aligning requirements offers a way to improve code generation for advanced LLMs.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach first identifies requirement content that does not align with the LLM and aligns the requirements. Based on the aligned requirements, the LLM generates code, and the method then verifies whether the generated code aligns with the requirements. It iterates requirement alignment and code generation until correct code is produced or a maximum number of iterations is reached.
schema.research_plan: To support the effectiveness claim, the paper compares the proposed approach with all advanced baselines on four LLMs across five programming benchmarks and reports average improvements per benchmark. The abstract does not specify metrics, failure conditions, matched compute or parameter settings, or ablations isolating the alignment and verification components.

items.title: Bridging the Gap between User Intent and LLM: A Requirement Alignment Approach for Code Generation
items.abstract: Code generation refers to automatically producing executable programs from user requirements. Recently, researchers have explored approaches to enhance the correctness of generated code with advanced large language models. Although achieving improvements, existing approaches focus on designing reasoning strategies or post-refinement methods to enhance code generation performance. Despite their differences, all these methods share a common assumption: the LLM can correctly understand the given requirement. However, this assumption does not always hold. To fill this gap, we propose REA-Coder, a requirement alignment approach to enhance the code generation performance of LLMs. REA-Coder involves first identifying the requirement content that does not align with LLMs and aligning the requirements. Then, based on the aligned requirements, LLMs generate code and further verify whether the generated code aligns with the requirements, iterating this process of requirement alignment and code generation until generating correct code or achieving the maximum number of iterations. Experimental results show that REA-Coder outperforms all advanced baselines on four LLMs across five programming benchmarks. Concretely, REA-Coder achieves average improvements of 7.93%, 30.25%, 26.75%, 8.59%, and 8.64% on the five benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of requirement alignment for improving the code generation performance of LLMs.

schema.problem: Long-horizon repository-level code generation from natural-language requirements currently lacks a systematic mechanism for translating high-level requirements into hierarchical, executable contracts prior to implementation, leaving agents prone to premature termination, loss of global coherence, and fragile cross-file dependencies.
schema.motivation: A pre-implementation contract mechanism would let autonomous coding agents preserve global coherence and cross-file dependencies across long-horizon, multi-module tasks.
schema.proposed_approach: A multi-agent framework enforces a specification-to-test-to-code pipeline: it decomposes a monolithic requirement into a hierarchical dependency graph of module-level contracts, automatically generates executable unit test suites before writing any implementation code, and executes an iterative feedback-driven refinement loop across module boundaries.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation on the NL2Repo-Bench benchmark, comparing the framework against standard repository-level baselines on long-horizon test pass rates and global coherence. The abstract does not state ablations, matched compute budgets, or explicit failure thresholds.

items.title: SpecTest-Agent: Specification-to-Test-Driven Long-Horizon Repository Generation via Hierarchical Micro-Contracts
items.abstract: Long-horizon repository-level code generation remains a severe bottleneck for autonomous coding agents, which frequently suffer from premature termination, loss of global coherence, and fragile cross-file dependencies when given only a natural-language requirements document. While recent frameworks like TENET introduce test-driven development (TDD) for existing repository patch tasks, and benchmarks like NL2Repo-Bench highlight the failure modes of greenfield multi-module generation, there is currently no systematic mechanism for translating high-level natural language requirements into hierarchical, executable micro-contracts prior to implementation. We propose SpecTest-Agent, a multi-agent framework that bridges this gap by enforcing a rigorous specification-to-test-to-code pipeline. Specifically, SpecTest-Agent decomposes a monolithic requirement into a hierarchical dependency graph of module-level contracts, automatically generates executable unit test suites (micro-specs) before writing any implementation code, and executes an iterative feedback-driven refinement loop across module boundaries. Experiments on NL2Repo-Bench demonstrate that SpecTest-Agent significantly improves long-horizon test pass rates and global coherence compared to standard repository-level baselines.

schema.problem: LLM-based code synthesis remains unreliable: models may hallucinate features, generated tests and code may diverge, and repairs often require manual effort.
schema.motivation: LLMs show promise for synthesizing software directly from natural-language problem descriptions; making that synthesis reliable would reduce manual repair effort and support automated software construction.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is a test-driven pipeline that extracts functional requirements from a natural-language problem description, resolves dependencies among them, maps them into a modular Model-View-Controller structure, generates tests before generating code, and then applies bounded execution-driven refinement.
schema.research_plan: Execution reliability is evaluated with Pass@1 and refine@k, and faithfulness of functional-requirement extraction is assessed using NLI-based entailment. The execution-reliability claim is supported by the Pass@1 and refine@k evaluations; the extraction-faithfulness claim is supported by the NLI-based entailment assessment. No explicit failure conditions, ablations, or matched-resource controls are stated.

items.title: Requirement-Guided Test-Driven Development for Modular Code Generation with Large Language Model
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for synthesizing software directly from natural-language problem descriptions. However, LLM-based code synthesis remains unreliable: models may hallucinate features, generated tests and code may diverge, and repairs often require manual effort. We present a test-driven pipeline that extracts functional requirements (FR) from a problem description, resolves dependencies, maps them into a modular Model-View-Controller (MVC) structure, and generates tests before code, followed by bounded, execution-driven refinement. We evaluate execution reliability with Pass@1 and refine@k, and assess the faithfulness of FR extraction using NLI-based entailment.

schema.problem: Most LLM-based automated program repair agents rely on static context retrieval and iterative trial-and-error patch generation, with test execution failures guiding the process only post hoc; on complex, repository-scale bugs this reactive paradigm can trap agents in combinatorial search.
schema.motivation: Proactively deriving executable test specifications could avoid those search traps and give the repair process a fine-grained verification oracle, reducing redundant search steps and improving localization for repository-scale bugs.
schema.proposed_approach: A proactive, test-driven multi-agent framework that decouples bug formalization from patch synthesis. One agent actively probes the repository, constructs minimal reproduction scripts, and isolates runtime behavior divergences; the resulting synthesized failing tests serve as an executable specification and fine-grained verification oracle that continuously constrains a patch-generation agent through execution-trace feedback.
schema.research_plan: The abstract indicates a conceptual evaluation and outlines experiments on benchmarks such as SWE-bench Lite and SWT-Bench, comparing the framework against existing post-hoc reactive repair methods. Claim (1) would be assessed through redundant search steps and claim (2) through localization precision. No explicit failure conditions, ablations, or matched controls are stated.

items.title: ProTest: Pre-Patch Test Synthesis and Execution-Grounded Verification for Repository-Level Program Repair
items.abstract: Automated program repair (APR) using Large Language Models (LLMs) has increasingly adopted agentic workflows, yet most coding agents rely on static context retrieval and iterative trial-and-error patch generation guided only post-hoc by test execution failures. This reactive paradigm often leads agents into combinatorial search traps when tackling complex, repository-scale bugs. In this proposal, we introduce ProTest, a proactive, test-driven multi-agent framework that decouples bug formalization from patch synthesis. Instead of directly generating code modifications, ProTest first deploys a Test Specification Agent to actively probe the repository, construct minimal reproduction scripts, and isolate runtime behavior divergences. These synthesized failing tests serve as an executable specification and a fine-grained verification oracle that continuously constrains a Patch Generation Agent via execution-trace feedback. We evaluate ProTest conceptually and outline experiments across benchmarks such as SWE-bench Lite and SWT-Bench, demonstrating how proactive test synthesis reduces redundant search steps and improves localization precision compared to existing post-hoc reactive repair methods.

schema.problem: Existing LLM-based repair systems treat tests as fixed post-hoc filters within a linear pipeline, reducing repository-level issue resolution to optimization under static and potentially misaligned behavioral constraints, which leads to under-constrained search and brittle or overfitted fixes.
schema.motivation: Software engineers already refine code and tests together during issue resolution, so enabling repair agents to co-evolve implementation and specification may make issue resolution more reliable and less overfit.
schema.proposed_approach: A coevolutionary multi-agent framework jointly explores and iteratively refines candidate code patches and test patches. Tests are modeled as dynamic constraints that both guide and are revised by the repair process. Code and test candidates undergo mutual evaluation and semantic recombination, progressively narrowing the space of behavior consistent with the issue description.
schema.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on SWE-bench Lite and SWT-bench Lite against state-of-the-art agent-based and agentless baselines, with repair success and test reproduction quality as the measured dimensions. The framing claim is argued from observed software-engineering practice, and the superiority and criticality claims are supported by this benchmark evaluation. No explicit failure conditions or matched compute/latency controls are described.

items.title: Beyond Fixed Tests: Repository-Level Issue Resolution as Coevolution of Code and Behavioral Constraints
items.abstract: Software engineers resolving repository-level issues do not treat existing tests as immutable correctness oracles. Instead, they iteratively refine both code and the tests used to characterize intended behavior, as new modifications expose missing assumptions or misinterpreted failure conditions. In contrast, most existing large language model (LLM)-based repair systems adopt a linear pipeline in which tests or other validation signals act mostly as post-hoc filters, treating behavioral constraints as fixed during repair. This formulation reduces repair to optimizing code under static and potentially misaligned constraints, leading to under-constrained search and brittle or overfitted fixes. We argue that repository-level issue resolution is fundamentally not optimization under fixed tests, but search over evolving behavioral constraints. To operationalize this view, we propose Agent-CoEvo, a coevolutionary multi-agent framework in which candidate code patches and test patches are jointly explored and iteratively refined. Rather than treating tests as immutable oracles, our framework models them as dynamic constraints that both guide and are revised by the repair process. Through mutual evaluation and semantic recombination, code and test candidates progressively narrow the space of behavior consistent with the issue description. Evaluated on SWE-bench Lite and SWT-bench Lite, Agent-CoEvo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art agent-based and agentless baselines in both repair success and test reproduction quality. Our findings suggest that enabling repair agents to revise behavioral constraints during search is critical for reliable issue resolution, pointing toward a shift from code-only optimization to coevolution of implementation and specification.

schema.problem: There is no cheap per-sample signal that tells a developer whether a specific generated program is correct before execution-based certification, and existing likelihood-based execution-free heuristics are known to mis-rank.
schema.motivation: A reliable execution-free per-sample correctness signal would give developers immediate feedback and avoid reliance on expensive hidden-test execution; LLM rewriting now makes semantically equivalent requirement paraphrases available to construct such a signal.
schema.proposed_approach: For a single coding instance, the proposal generates several semantically equivalent paraphrases of the same requirement using LLM rewriting plus a semantic-equivalence filter following prior work, then generates code under each paraphrase under a fixed sample budget. It measures agreement among the resulting programs at textual, AST-level structural, and identifier/role-level. The construction also includes the paraphrase/equivalence filter and an abstention study comparing against selective generation with unit-test validation.
schema.research_plan: The proposal tests the main hypothesis with a sign test comparing the per-instance paraphrase-agreement signal against likelihood baselines and other execution-free signals for Pass@1, under a fixed sample budget that isolates paraphrase agreement from sampling noise. Paraphrase-quality ablations diagnose failure modes if agreement under remote-but-equivalent paraphrases fails to separate correct from incorrect code; an abstention study evaluates the signal against selective generation with unit-test validation.

items.title: SpecPar-Con: Per-Instance Specification-Paraphrase Consistency as an Execution-Free Predictor of Functional Correctness in LLM Code Generation
items.abstract: Code generation benchmarks rely on executing hidden tests to certify functional correctness, but no cheap per-sample signal tells a developer whether a specific generated program is right before that certificate is available, and likelihood-based heuristics are known to mis-rank , . We propose specification-paraphrase consistency (SpecPar): for a single coding instance, generate code under several semantically equivalent paraphrases of the same requirement (produced with LLM rewriting plus a semantic-equivalence filter following ) and measure agreement between the resulting programs — textual, AST-level structural, and identifier/role-level. Our falsifiable hypothesis is that per-instance SpecPar agreement out-predicts existing execution-free signals (max-likelihood, mean log-prob, internal correctness representations, uncertainty estimates, LLM-as-judge scores) for that instance's Pass@1, because correct code must anchor deterministically to the requirement across independently worded specs, whereas wrong code follows spurious surface cues , . The proposal includes the exact construction of the paraphrase/equivalence filter, a fixed sample budget that isolates paraphrase agreement from sampling noise, a careful sign test against likelihood baselines, and an abstention study against selective generation with unit-test validation . If agreement under remote-but-equivalent paraphrases fails to separate correct from incorrect code, the hypothesis is refuted and the failure modes are precisely diagnosed by our paraphrase-quality ablations.

schema.problem: LLM-generated code quality is still questionable, and code validation remains a challenging problem.
schema.motivation: The observation that correct code pieces exhibit intrinsic consistency while flawed code pieces may not provides a signal by which flaws can be detected.
schema.proposed_approach: The method varies a given prompt into multiple paraphrased prompts and asks an LLM to generate multiple versions of code. It then cross-validates whether the semantic relations still hold among the acquired code versions, treating inconsistencies as signals of flaws.
schema.research_plan: The method is initially evaluated on the HumanEval benchmark using erroneous programs generated by GPT-4o, with detection of erroneous programs and false positive rate as the quality measures; no explicit failure threshold or baseline comparisons are stated.

items.title: Automatic Validation of LLM-Generated Code with Prompt Paraphrasing
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used for code generation. However, the quality of generated code is still questionable, and code validation remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose a novel solution called paraphrase prompt testing. Our intuitive observation is that intrinsic consistency always exists among correct code pieces but may not exist among flawed code pieces, so we can detect flaws in the code by detecting inconsistencies. Therefore, we can vary a given prompt to multiple prompts with paraphrasing, and to ask the LLM to acquire multiple versions of generated code, so that we can validate whether the semantic relations still hold in the acquired code through cross-validation. Our initial evaluation on HumanEval shows that paraphrase prompt testing is able to detect 70.6% of the erroneous programs generated by GPT-4o, with a false positive rate of 6.1%.

schema.problem: Test-based benchmarks treat test suites as the arbiter of correctness, but even strengthened test suites presuppose that test success equals specification fidelity, so programs may pass tests while still violating the problem specification.
schema.motivation: Compiling natural-language specifications into executable clauses offers a way to expose test-blind specification violations and improve sample selection for LLM code generation beyond test agreement.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework compiles a benchmark problem's natural-language specification into executable specification clauses—signal predicates over generated programs such as input-domain constraints, example-consistent output invariants, and keyword-grounded behavioral constraints—filters those clauses for agreement with the problem's examples and gold solution, and uses them as an executable specification oracle. It builds a filtered clause dataset over HumanEval and MBPP.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the specification-violation claim, the paper uses the filtered clause dataset to measure the share of LLM-generated programs that pass gold and test-strengthened suites yet violate executable specification clauses, and quantifies which specification clauses test suites never witness. (2) For the reranking claim, it evaluates oracle-first selection of k samples against majority voting and test-discriminating selection methods on pass@1, with a pre-registered null-result threshold.

items.title: SpecFidelity: Executable Specification Oracles for Finding and Fixing Test-Blind Correctness Gaps in LLM-Generated Code
items.abstract: Test-based benchmarks treat test suites as the arbiter of correctness for code generation: EvalPlus strengthened tests shown to hide wrong code, but even strengthened suites presuppose that test success equals specification fidelity . We propose SpecFidelity, a framework that compiles a benchmark problem's natural-language specification into executable intent clauses — signal predicates over generated programs such as input-domain constraints, example-consistent output invariants, and keyword-grounded behavioral constraints — filters them for agreement with the problem's examples and gold solution, and uses them as an executable spec oracle. Its two claims are falsifiable: (H1) a measurable share of LLM-generated programs passes gold and test-strengthened suites yet violates some executable spec clause (the spec-fidelity gap); (H2) spec-oracle-first reranking of k samples improves pass@1 over majority voting and over test-discriminating selection methods . We build a filtered clause dataset over HumanEval and MBPP, quantify clause-test coverage (which spec clauses test suites never witness), and evaluate oracle-first selection against consistency-based baselines, with a pre-registered null-result threshold.

schema.problem: Standard benchmarks for LLM-generated code measure only whether code passes stated tests, leaving unmeasured whether code honors a developer's implicit intentions under ambiguous prompts.
schema.motivation: Because pass rates may overstate how well generated code reflects developer intent, measuring hidden intent violations can reveal a consequential blind spot in current evaluations.
schema.proposed_approach: The work constructs a 49-problem pilot benchmark derived from HumanEval+ by stripping implicit constraints from clarified prompts and encoding them as hidden constraint tests. It defines a metric as the fraction of generated solutions that pass the stated visible tests but fail hidden tests that capture unstated intent. The benchmark is applied to code generated by Claude Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI GPT 4.1.
schema.research_plan: Evidence comes from benchmark measurements on 49 problems across the two named models: visible-test pass rates and hidden-constraint failure rates are compared to support the claim that passing code still violates intent, and consistency across models is inspected to support the systematic bimodal pattern claim. No explicit failure condition or matched-compute design is stated.

items.title: DevIntent: How Much Does LLM-Generated Code Violate Developer Intent?
items.abstract: Code generated by LLMs can violate a developer's implicit intentions when given an ambiguous prompt, yet standard benchmarks measure only whether code passes its stated test. We introduce the Intent Violation Rate (IVR) and a 49-problem pilot benchmark derived from HumanEval+. Each problem strips implicit constraints from a clarified prompt and encodes them as hidden constraint tests. IVR measures the fraction of LLM-generated solutions that pass the stated (visible) tests yet fail hidden constraint tests that capture unstated intent. Evaluating Claude Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI GPT 4.1, we find both pass over 92\% of stated tests yet violate intent in over half of problems (54.5\% and 63.5\%), following a systematic, bimodal pattern consistent across both models. Out findings indicate that pass rates overstate how well generated code reflects developer intent.

schema.problem: Code generation models are not robust against adversarial attacks, and their vulnerability remains a significant concern.
schema.motivation: As code generation models are increasingly used to automate software engineering tasks, their susceptibility to adversarial attacks limits reliable use.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed work will develop and study adversarial training methods for code generation models, building on existing adversarial attacks including CodeAttack and Discrete Adversarial Attack. It will investigate gradient-based and structure-aware adversarial training techniques and evaluate model resistance to discrete and continuous adversarial attacks.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation will use the existing attack methods to attack code generation models trained with the studied adversarial training techniques, measuring whether robustness against discrete and continuous attacks improves. The abstract does not specify metrics, baselines, or failure thresholds.

items.title: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness of Code Generation Models through Adversarial Training
items.abstract: Code generation models have shown remarkable capabilities in automating software engineering tasks. However, their robustness against adversarial attacks remains a significant concern. This proposal aims to enhance the adversarial robustness of code generation models by investigating and developing effective adversarial training methods. We will build upon existing adversarial attack methods, such as CodeAttack [D054b6aa3e562] and Discrete Adversarial Attack [Dd122098fc9ca], to evaluate and improve the robustness of code generation models. Our approach involves a comprehensive study of various adversarial training techniques, including gradient-based and structure-aware methods. We will evaluate the effectiveness of these methods in enhancing the model's resistance to different types of adversarial attacks, including discrete and continuous attacks.

schema.problem: Recent secure code generation methods claim to prevent LLMs from producing insecure code, but their robustness under adversarial conditions remains untested, and current evaluations decouple security from functionality, potentially inflating reported gains.
schema.motivation: Realistic prompt perturbations can be introduced inadvertently by developers or deliberately by adversaries, so unverified robustness may create a false sense of security; a joint security-and-functionality evaluation is needed because non-functional but analyzer-flagged secure code is not useful.
schema.proposed_approach: Three state-of-the-art secure code generation methods (SVEN, SafeCoder, PromSec) are subjected to realistic prompt perturbations: paraphrasing, cue inversion, and context manipulation. All methods are evaluated under consistent conditions, with security and functionality assessed jointly using multiple static analyzers and executable tests. Based on the audit findings, best practices for building and evaluating robust secure code generation methods are proposed, and the audit code is released.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the analyzer-overestimation claim comes from comparing static-analyzer security verdicts against executable functionality tests on generated code. Evidence for the adversarial-robustness claim comes from applying paraphrasing, cue inversion, and context manipulation to all three methods under the same pipeline. Holding conditions consistent across methods enables the comparison; the abstract does not state an explicit numerical threshold for robustness failure. Best practices are proposed but no separate evaluation of their efficacy is described.

items.title: How Secure is Secure Code Generation? Adversarial Prompts Put LLM Defenses to the Test
items.abstract: Recent secure code generation methods, using vulnerability-aware fine-tuning, prefix-tuning, and prompt optimization, claim to prevent LLMs from producing insecure code. However, their robustness under adversarial conditions remains untested, and current evaluations decouple security from functionality, potentially inflating reported gains. We present the first systematic adversarial audit of state-of-the-art secure code generation methods (SVEN, SafeCoder, PromSec). We subject them to realistic prompt perturbations such as paraphrasing, cue inversion, and context manipulation that developers might inadvertently introduce or adversaries deliberately exploit. To enable fair comparison, we evaluate all methods under consistent conditions, jointly assessing security and functionality using multiple analyzers and executable tests. Our findings reveal critical robustness gaps: static analyzers overestimate security by 7 to 21 times, with 37 to 60% of ``secure'' outputs being non-functional. Under adversarial conditions, true secure-and-functional rates collapse to 3 to 17%. Based on these findings, we propose best practices for building and evaluating robust secure code generation methods. Our code is available.

schema.problem: Current code generation models have limitations in handling complex systems and ensuring accuracy when producing program code from high-level specifications.
schema.motivation: Automating code production from high-level specifications is valuable, and integrating recent code LLMs with formal methods offers a feasible path toward more reliable automation.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach automates program code production from high-level specifications by integrating logic, computability theory, and AI algorithms. It uses code LLMs and incorporates formal specifications and reactive program synthesis. A benchmark is also planned to test the approach and compare it with existing methods.
schema.research_plan: The paper plans to evaluate the approach on a benchmark it develops, comparing it against existing methods; the abstract does not specify metrics, compute or parameter matching, or failure criteria.

items.title: A Novel Approach to Code Generation: Integrating Logic, Computability, and AI Algorithms
items.abstract: We propose a novel approach to automate program code production from high-level specifications by integrating logic, computability theory, and AI algorithms. Our approach leverages code Large Language Models (LLMs) and incorporates formal specifications and reactive program synthesis to enhance accuracy and efficiency. We aim to develop a benchmark to test our approach and compare it with existing methods, addressing the limitations of current code generation models in handling complex systems and ensuring accuracy.

schema.problem: Large language models perform well at function-level code generation, but output quality declines significantly for repository-level systems; current workflows that rely only on natural-language prompts are ambiguous and difficult to verify.
schema.motivation: Using structured specification artifacts as inputs could make high-quality repository-level code generation a tangible goal while offering superior verifiability and significant potential for improvement.
schema.proposed_approach: The work proposes a paradigm in which structured specification artifacts guide LLM code generation instead of relying only on natural-language prompts. A pilot study investigates feasibility by generating Model-View-Controller business logic for three software systems using five LLMs, after which the authors outline potential, challenges, and a future roadmap.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of a pilot study that generates Model-View-Controller business logic for three software systems using five LLMs; the abstract does not specify baselines, evaluation metrics, or failure conditions that would distinguish support from failure for the stated claims.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Repository-Level Generation with Structured Spec-Driven Engineering
items.abstract: State-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in code generation at the function level. However, the output quality significantly declines when scaling to repository-level systems. Current workflows relying only on natural language prompts suffer from inherent ambiguity and a lack of verifiability. To address this, we propose structured spec-driven engineering (SSDE), a paradigm that leverages structured artifacts to guide LLM generation. We argue that structured specifications as LLM inputs make high-quality, repository-level code generation a tangible goal, while at the same time offering superior verifiability, leading to significant potential for improvement. We first investigate the feasibility of this vision through a pilot study generating Model-View-Controller (MVC) business logic for three software systems using five LLMs, and then highlight the potential, challenges, and future roadmap for SSDE.

schema.problem: Execution feedback such as test verdicts, error messages, and traces tells the repair model what broke, not which generated statement counterfactually produced the failure. Recent findings show frontier LLMs are much less reliable at identifying necessary causes from observed output than at forward execution simulation, and full-trace conditioning gives limited repair gains.
schema.motivation: As LLM-based self-repair and coding agents increasingly rely on execution signal, causally localized evidence may make repair more effective without overwhelming the model with complex traces; raw-trace gains are limited and diminish with complexity.
schema.proposed_approach: For a generated program that fails a test, the proposed framework instruments the program, records its execution, and runs a counterfactual minimality search; angelic interventions overwrite individual trace values and replay execution to find the minimal set of program points whose counterfactually-correct values flip the test from failing to passing. The repair model is then conditioned on this short, dense evidence bundle (localized lines, actual vs. counterfactual values, and the specific perturbation that repairs the symptom) rather than on the full trace.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the repair-effectiveness claim, compare causal-evidence conditioning against no-trace, error-message-only, raw-full-trace, coarse-execution-state, and flow-relevance baselines on NL2code repair, measuring patch correctness on held-out tests, irrelevant-line churn, and repair-iteration count. (2) For the localization claim, compare the computed causal set against the flow-relevant chop on injected faults in the same test. (3) The proposal is falsified if the causal-minimal evidence is no better than a plain dynamic slice plus raw trace, reducing the contribution to prompt compression.

items.title: CausalTrace: Counterfactually-Minimal Execution Traces as Localized Causal Evidence for LLM Code Self-Repair
items.abstract: LLM-based self-repair and coding agents increasingly feed execution signal — test verdicts, error messages, stack traces, even full execution traces — back into the model to fix programs the model itself generated. Yet a failing test or a raw trace is a symptom, not a cause: it tells the model what broke, not which generated statement counterfactually produced the failure. Two recent findings sharpen the problem: frontier LLMs simulate executions forward with ~96% accuracy but fall to ~32% when asked to identify the necessary causes of an observed output (the SIM/MIN gap) , and simply appending full traces to repair prompts yields limited gains in only 2 of 6 dataset/model configurations, diminishing as trace complexity grows . We propose CausalTrace, which offloads causal attribution from the LLM to a deterministic external procedure: given a generated program that fails a test, CausalTrace instruments the program, records its execution, and runs a counterfactual minimality search — angelic interventions that overwrite individual trace values and replay execution (TOD-style omniscient replay ) — to find the minimal set of program points whose counterfactually-correct values flip the test from failing to passing; the repair LLM is then conditioned on this short, dense causal evidence packet (localized lines, actual vs. counterfactual values, and the specific perturbation that repairs the symptom) instead of the full trace. Our central falsifiable claim: on NL2code repair, causal-evidence conditioning yields higher patch correctness on held-out tests, lower irrelevant-line churn, and fewer repair iterations than no-trace, error-message-only, raw-full-trace, coarse-execution-state (DynaFix-style ), and classical failure-inducing-chop (flow-relevance) baselines — and the computed causal set localizes injected faults more precisely than the flow-relevant chop for the same test. The proposal is explicitly falsified if the causal-minimal evidence is no better than a plain dynamic slice plus raw trace, reducing the contribution to prompt compression.

schema.problem: Large language model agents frequently fail on multi-step tasks involving reasoning, tool use, and environment interaction; these failures are typically logged or retried heuristically, and the structured signals about where execution broke down are not systematically converted into reusable supervision.
schema.motivation: Such failures contain structured signals about where execution broke down, and using them systematically can avoid costly manual retries and provide training signal for offline preference optimization or reward modeling.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework models failed execution traces as sequential chains of dependent steps and computes a per-step measure of how much each step contributes to failure by counterfactually intervening on steps to identify failure-inducing steps. For those steps, it generates minimally edited repairs that flip the final outcome to success and validates them as contrastive pairs of the form (wrong step, corrected step). The resulting repairs support targeted test-time recovery with minimal behavioral drift and can be used as training-time supervision for offline preference optimization or reward modeling.
schema.research_plan: The method is evaluated across four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, question answering, and medical browsing. (1) The repair-quality claim is assessed by measuring repair minimality and agreement of causal attribution on converted failed executions. (2) The necessity of causal attribution and localization claim are tested by comparing against heuristic refinement, with localization of repairs and reliability improvement across diverse agent tasks as evaluation targets. The abstract does not specify held-matched compute or exact failure conditions; support is inferred from qualitative comparisons rather than explicit thresholds.

items.title: CausalFlow: Causal Attribution and Counterfactual Repair for LLM Agent Failures
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents frequently fail on multi-step tasks involving reasoning, tool use, and environment interaction. While such failures are typically logged or retried heuristically, they contain structured signals about where execution broke down. We introduce CausalFlow, an interventional framework that converts failed agent traces into minimal counterfactual repairs and reusable supervision. CausalFlow models execution traces as sequential chains of dependent steps and computes Causal Responsibility Scores(CRS) via step-level counterfactual intervention to identify failure-inducing steps. For these steps, we generate minimally edited repairs that flip the final outcome to success, producing validated contrastive pairs of the form (wrong step, corrected step). CausalFlow supports two complementary uses: targeted test-time repair that recovers from failures with minimal behavioral drift, and training-time supervision suitable for offline preference optimization or reward modeling. Across four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, question answering, and medical browsing, CausalFlow converts failed executions into validated minimal repairs with high minimality and causal-consensus scores, and demonstrates that causal attribution is necessary for reliable improvement across diverse agent tasks, outperforming heuristic refinement in complex retrieval settings while producing more localized repairs throughout. These results demonstrate that interventional analysis over structured execution traces provides a principled and scalable mechanism for transforming agent failures into reliability gains and learning-ready supervision.

schema.problem: Reinforcement learning for software engineering agents is dominated by terminal binary outcome rewards: a multi-turn trajectory is scored 1 only if its final patch passes all fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass unit tests, leaving long, low-pass-rate regimes with almost no directional learning signal.
schema.motivation: The environment already contains a dense, verifiable progress signal—how many of the target tests the current patch passes—but existing pipelines read it only at trajectory end, so exploiting it per-step could provide directional signal and avoid learned verifier or execution-free bias.
schema.proposed_approach: The per-step reward is the change in a test-execution progress function: newly passing target tests, weighted by static test specificity, minus regressions among previously passing tests, gated by compile/import checks. It is computed by incrementally re-running only tests whose import closure intersects the edited files. Because the shaping is potential-based it preserves the optimal policy in the noise-free limit, and because it uses the same ground-truth tests as evaluation it requires no learned verifier and inherits no execution-free bias.
schema.research_plan: (1) The main falsifiable claim is tested by training agents with GRPO on SWE-Gym and SWE-rebench task pools using open-weight 7–32B bases, matched against terminal-only RL at matched compute, and evaluating on SWE-bench Verified and a contamination-free fresh-task holdout; sample efficiency, resolve rate, regression rate, and test-hacking rate are compared, with success or failure tied to the specified improvement thresholds and to whether regression or test-hacking increases. (2) A head-to-head against a matched-compute, learned execution-free outcome reward model of the SWE-RM style determines whether verifiable process shaping outperforms learned outcome scoring when both are available.

items.title: Execution-Grounded Progress Rewards: Potential-Based Dense Reward Shaping from Incremental Test Execution for SWE-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for software engineering (SWE) agents is dominated by terminal, binary outcome rewards: a multi-turn trajectory is scored 1 only if its final patch passes all fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass unit tests, leaving long, low-pass-rate regimes with almost no directional learning signal. We observe that the environment already contains a dense, verifiable progress signal — how many of the target tests the current patch state passes — and that existing pipelines read it only at trajectory end. We propose Execution-Grounded Progress Rewards (EGPR), a potential-based process reward in which the per-step reward is the change in a test-execution progress function: newly passing target tests, weighted by static test specificity, minus regressions among previously passing tests, gated by compile/import checks, computed cheaply by incrementally re-running only the tests whose import closure intersects the edited files. Because the shaping is potential-based it preserves the optimal policy in the noise-free limit , and because it uses the same ground-truth tests as evaluation it requires no learned verifier and inherits no execution-free bias. Our falsifiable claim: at matched compute, EGPR-trained agents (GRPO on SWE-Gym/SWE-rebench task pools with open-weight 7–32B bases) achieve at least 2× faster sample efficiency and at least 3 points higher resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and a contamination-free fresh-task holdout than terminal-only RL, with the largest gains at the lowest base pass rates, and without increased regression or test-hacking rates. We also run a head-to-head against a matched-compute, SWE-RM-style learned execution-free outcome reward model — a comparison no retrieved work performs — settling whether verifiable process shaping beats learned outcome scoring when both are available.

schema.problem: In RL for code generation, reward design currently relies on sparse test-suite-level outcome rewards or dense external reward models that are misaligned and costly; intrinsic partial success from passing subsets of test cases is verifiable but not systematically converted into reliable dense supervision.
schema.motivation: Because partial success is natively verifiable in code evaluation, it can provide dense supervision without external models, avoiding misalignment, added latency, and GPU memory overhead while reducing reward sparsity.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework formulates partial-success rewards as a weighted sum of test-case outcomes and analyzes the resulting policy update to expose a bias associated with cardinality. It then applies a dynamic local reward calibrated by test density to correct that bias and provide robust dense supervision from partial success. The corrected local dense reward is combined with global execution outcomes so the policy optimizes toward end-to-end functional correctness.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim about bias is supported by a theoretical analysis of the weighted-sum formulation; support requires showing the bias arises from cardinality weighting and can be removed by the density calibration. (2) The local-reward and integration claims are tested through extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and settings against outcome-driven and reward-model-based baselines, using pass@1 as the primary metric; support is higher pass@1 at negligible time cost and no GPU memory overhead, while failure would be if the local reward does not improve frontier-test progress or the global integration reduces end-to-end correctness. (3) The efficiency claim is checked through reported time cost and GPU memory overhead relative to the baselines.

items.title: Beyond Binary: Turning Partial Success into Dense Verifiable Rewards for Reinforcement Learning in Code Generation
items.abstract: Effective reward design is a central challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for code generation. Mainstream test-suite-level outcome rewards enforce functional correctness but induce sparsity, while external Reward Models (RMs) provide dense supervision at the cost of misalignment and additional overhead. Since code evaluation naturally yields multiple test-case-level outcomes, partial success, i.e., passing a subset of test cases, offers an intrinsic, verifiable source of dense supervision. In this paper, we propose VeRPO (Verifiable Dense Reward Policy Optimization), an RL framework that systematically turns verifiable partial success into reliable dense rewards. We analyze partial-success rewards using a weighted sum formulation, theoretically identifying a critical cardinality bias that causes policy updates to disproportionately favor gains from easy-test successes over progress on frontier tests. Based on this, VeRPO introduces a dynamic, density-calibrated local reward that explicitly corrects this bias and provides robust dense supervision from partial success. To enhance alignment with end-to-end functional correctness, VeRPO further integrates the local dense reward with global execution outcomes. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and settings demonstrate that VeRPO outperforms outcome-driven and RM-based baselines, achieving up to +8.83 pass@1 gain with negligible time cost (< 0.02%) and zero GPU memory overhead.

schema.problem: For code LLMs sampled multiple times, post-hoc scoring must choose among superficially plausible programs, but existing uncertainty estimators, semantic-consistency methods, and test-consensus selectors treat executed evidence as fixed and do not ask which input would most reduce uncertainty about the actual candidate set.
schema.motivation: Making input selection adaptive would let a fixed execution and query budget be spent on the most uncertainty-reducing tests, improving selection and abstention while flagging irreducibly wrong candidate sets.
schema.proposed_approach: Given a sampled set of programs, the approach maintains the partition induced on those programs by the inputs executed so far. Each round, candidate inputs are synthesized by an LLM from the current class structure, each candidate is scored exactly by simulating how it would refine the weighted partition, and the maximally informative input is executed. The loop stops when disagreement-based evidence is exhausted; this stopping condition also flags an irreducibly jointly-wrong blind spot where only an external oracle could help. From the final partition, a class-level selection rule and a partition-derived confidence are used in a risk-calibrated selective or abstention policy.
schema.research_plan: (1) The adaptive loop is compared with passive semantic-entropy, CodeT/AutoTest-style consensus, B4, and LLM-oracle selection on HumanEval, MBPP+, and a LiveCodeBench subset, using hidden-test pass@1 at matched execution and query budget to test the claim of higher cost-matched accuracy. (2) The partition-derived confidence is compared with passive scores on risk-coverage and expected calibration error to test the claim of dominance. (3) The stopping condition is assessed by whether a measurable fraction of remaining failures is identifiable in advance, and whether escalating only flagged tasks to a pairwise oracle recovers them. Budgets are held matched across execution and query counts where the trade-off claim is tested; support for each claim would fail if the corresponding comparison or recovery test did not show the asserted advantage.

items.title: Testing-to-Trust: Adaptive Behavioral Partitioning for Calibrated Code Generation
items.abstract: A code LLM sampled K times for one problem returns a near-uniform distribution of superficially plausible programs, and post-hoc scoring must decide which one to ship or whether to abstain. Existing uncertainty estimators , semantic-consistency methods , and test-consensus selectors all treat the evidence as fixed: they score a sample drawn once, or run a passively generated test pool once, and never ask which executed input would have most reduced our uncertainty about the actual candidate set. We argue that the right state for code-trust decisions is neither a scalar entropy estimate nor a static pass/fail matrix, but the behavioral partition induced on the sampled programs by the inputs executed so far — this partition is partial, exact to compute, and queryable. We propose to maintain it adaptively: each round, candidate inputs are synthesized by an LLM from the current class structure, scored exactly (by simulating their refinement of the weighted partition), and the maximally informative one is executed; the loop stops when disagreement-based evidence is exhausted (a plateau), which also flags the irreducible jointly-wrong blind spot where only an external oracle could help. From the final partition we derive a class-level selection rule and a partition-based confidence used in a risk-calibrated selective/abstention policy. We evaluate on HumanEval, MBPP+, and a LiveCodeBench subset, measuring hidden-test pass@1 at matched execution+query budget, and risk-coverage/calibration, against passive semantic-entropy, CodeT/AutoTest-style consensus, B4, and LLM-oracle selection. We claim three falsifiable results: adaptive partitioning achieves strictly higher cost-matched pass@1 than non-adaptive selectors; partition-derived confidence dominates passive scores on risk-coverage and ECE; and a measurable fraction of remaining failures is identifiable in advance by the plateau flag, recoverable by escalating only those tasks to a pairwise oracle.

schema.problem: LLM-based code generation for databases is evaluated for logical correctness on static schemas, but a large class of real database code is mutating migrations over existing, populated stores; one-shot migration scripts can parse and pass validity checks while silently dropping or corrupting stored rows, and no retrieved benchmark treats stored data as the correctness target.
schema.motivation: Because mutating migrations are common and silent data corruption is costly, making data preservation a first-class correctness target for generated storage-mutating code is important.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed work has two parts. The first is a benchmark of roughly 140 data-preservation migration tasks over populated SQLite instances drawn from realistic schemas, spanning eight edit families (column rename, type widening/narrowing, NOT NULL with derived default, column split/merge, 1–N table extraction, denormalization, FK-crossing moves) and using property-based, executable ground truth. The second is an agent that generates every migration as a forward script plus an inverse back-out script, gates acceptance on an executed round-trip check (forward on a shadow copy, inverse on a copy, then full-table content-digest comparison against the pre-migration snapshot), and uses structured feedback for bounded repair turns.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on the proposed benchmark supports claims as follows: (1) compare one-shot and validity-only-corrected migrations with the round-trip agent on value-transforming tasks using round-trip fidelity measured by full-table content digest; (2) test whether the round-trip agent reaches the hypothesized fidelity threshold; (3) isolate the executed preservation check from general execution feedback to test whether the fidelity gap remains. Failure conditions would be if baselines do not show low fidelity, if the agent does not reach the threshold, or if removing the preservation check while retaining execution feedback does not reduce the gap. The abstract does not state matched compute, parameter, or latency budgets.

items.title: SchemaMorph: Data-Preserving Natural-Language-to-Migration Synthesis over Populated Databases
items.abstract: LLM-based code generation for databases is evaluated almost entirely against logical correctness on static schemas — text-to-SQL benchmarks measure whether a generated SELECT returns the right answer, and schema-synthesis work builds new schemas onto empty databases. But a large class of real database code is mutating code: DDL plus backfill migrations that restructure an existing, populated store to satisfy a changed requirement. When an LLM's one-shot migration script splits a column, narrows a type, or adds a NOT NULL constraint, it frequently parses, executes, and "passes" validity checks while silently dropping or corrupting stored rows — an error class that no retrieved benchmark measures because none defines stored data as the correctness target. We introduce SchemaMorph, consisting of (a) SchemaMorph-Bench, a benchmark of roughly 140 data-preservation migration tasks over populated SQLite instances drawn from realistic schemas, with eight edit families (column rename, type widening/narrowing, NOT NULL with derived default, column split/merge, 1–N table extraction, denormalization, FK-crossing moves) and property-based, executable ground truth; and (b) SchemaMorph-Agent, which generates every migration as a forward script plus an inverse back-out script and gates acceptance on an executed round-trip check — forward on a shadow copy, inverse on a copy, then full-table content-digest comparison against the pre-migration snapshot, with structured feedback driving bounded repair turns. We hypothesize that one-shot and validity-only-corrected migrations achieve low round-trip fidelity on value-transforming tasks, while the round-trip gate raises fidelity above 95%, and that this gap is driven by the executed preservation check rather than by execution feedback in general — establishing data preservation as a first-class, executable correctness signal for generated code that mutates storage.

schema.problem: Large language models for code generation suffer significant performance degradation on out-of-distribution examples, including novel code patterns and rare syntactic constructs unseen during pretraining, and no prior work exploits curriculum learning specifically to improve out-of-distribution robustness in code generation.
schema.motivation: Out-of-distribution failures in code reflect systematic gaps between the training distribution and new code patterns rather than merely hard problems, so addressing them directly can improve robustness on novel code.
schema.proposed_approach: The system detects distribution-shift characteristics in code—syntactic novelty, semantic divergence, and cross-language constructs—and dynamically constructs a learned curriculum that prioritizes training on shifted examples.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on HumanEval, MBPP, ResearchCodeBench, and out-of-distribution test sets from CodeS compares pass rate on out-of-distribution examples against baseline curricula, with particular attention to rarely-seen language constructs; no explicit failure condition or matched-budget controls are stated.

items.title: Curriculum Learning for Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Code Generation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) for code generation suffer significant performance degradation on out-of-distribution examples, including novel code patterns and rare syntactic constructs unseen during pretraining. While curriculum learning has proven effective in NLP, and robustness evaluation frameworks exist for code, no prior work exploits curriculum learning specifically to improve OOD robustness in code generation. We propose CurricOOD, a system that detects distribution shift characteristics in code (syntactic novelty, semantic divergence, cross-language constructs) and dynamically constructs a learned curriculum that prioritizes training on shifted examples. Our key insight is that OOD failures in code are not simply "hard" problems amenable to standard easier→harder curricula; instead, they reflect systematic gaps between the training distribution and new code patterns. We evaluate CurricOOD on multiple code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, ResearchCodeBench) and OOD test sets from CodeS. We expect CurricOOD to improve robustness (measured by pass rate on OOD examples) by 15–25% over baseline curricula, with particular gains on rarely-seen language constructs.

schema.problem: Although multi-stage code generation improves over direct generation, it remains unknown which type of intermediate representation—sketch, pseudo-code, natural-language plan, type signature, or formal specification—is most effective for different problem classes.
schema.motivation: Since multi-stage generation already yields substantial gains, representation choice is a practical lever, and systematic evidence would give practitioners and researchers actionable guidance rather than ad hoc choices.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed study evaluates intermediate representation types (sketches, pseudo-code, natural-language plans, type signatures, formal specifications) across problem complexity, programming language, required reasoning depth, and code structure. It uses controlled experiments on multiple benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests). It measures final code correctness and intermediate representation quality—clarity, executability, completeness—and examines whether representation choice should be task-adaptive or model-dependent.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of controlled experiments on multiple benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests). The study measures final code correctness and intermediate representation quality metrics across dimensions and investigates task-adaptive versus model-dependent representation choice. The abstract does not state baselines, model comparisons, matching conditions, or failure thresholds that would define support or failure.

items.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Intermediate Representations for LLM-Based Code Generation: A Systematic Study
items.abstract: While multi-stage code generation approaches have demonstrated substantial improvements over direct generation, the literature lacks a systematic comparison of what types of intermediate representations (sketches, pseudo-code, natural-language plans, type signatures, formal specifications) are most effective for different problem classes. We propose a comprehensive empirical study that evaluates intermediate representations across diverse dimensions: problem complexity, programming language, required reasoning depth, and code structure. Using controlled experiments on multiple benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests), we measure not only final code correctness but also intermediate representation quality metrics—clarity, executability, completeness—and investigate whether representation choice should be task-adaptive or model-dependent. This work establishes a design space for intermediate representations and provides practitioners and researchers with evidence-based guidance on when to apply which representation.

schema.problem: Automatically generating reliable robot control and localization routines from natural language specifications remains unsolved due to unmodeled sensor noise, environmental ambiguities, and out-of-distribution execution states; existing LLM-based code generation techniques fail under high sensor uncertainty because they treat synthesis as a static text-prediction task disconnected from real-time perceptual variance.
schema.motivation: Reliable routine generation under sensor degradation would avoid unsafe behavior and enable robust autonomy when sensing is compromised; real-time sensor covariance estimation makes it possible to connect uncertainty to code generation.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework tightly couples continuous sensor uncertainty estimation with grammar-constrained code LLM generation and counterexample-guided inductive synthesis. Real-time sensor covariance bounds are projected into syntax-guided symbolic constraints; these dynamically steer code generation to synthesize fallback routines and robust observation-update loops whenever localization confidence drops.
schema.research_plan: Evaluations across simulated and real-world robotics tasks compare the framework against unguided code LLMs and static environment synthesis baselines, measuring safety, robustness, and trajectory adherence under extreme sensor degradation. No explicit failure condition or matched compute/parameter statement is provided.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Sensor-Guided Neural Program Synthesis for Robust Robotic Localization Code Generation
items.abstract: Automatically generating reliable robot control and localization routines from natural language specifications remains a grand challenge due to unmodeled sensor noise, environmental ambiguities, and out-of-distribution execution states. Existing LLM-based code generation techniques for robotics often fail under high sensor uncertainty because they treat code synthesis as a purely static text-prediction task disconnected from real-time perceptual variance. In this proposal, we introduce US-Synth, an uncertainty-aware neural program synthesis framework that tightly couples continuous sensor uncertainty estimation with grammar-constrained code LLM generation and counter-example-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS). By projecting real-time sensor covariance bounds into syntax-guided symbolic constraints, US-Synth dynamically steers the code generation process to synthesize fallback routines and robust observation-update loops whenever localization confidence drops. Extensive evaluations across simulated and real-world robotics tasks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms unguided code LLMs and static environment synthesis baselines in safety, robustness, and trajectory adherence under extreme sensor degradation.

schema.problem: LLM code generation agents rely on iterative self-debugging loops, but debugging effectiveness decays severely within a few attempts, and existing multi-turn debuggers treat execution feedback as monolithic streams, accumulating redundant failures that misguide the generator.
schema.motivation: Addressing this decay is necessary for autonomous code generation agents to keep correcting runtime errors and failing tests across iterative attempts.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework structures execution history into a counterfactual memory graph instead of feeding accumulated raw stack traces. It isolates successful sub-modules, dynamically masks irrelevant error noise, and injects contrastive counterfactual execution paths that highlight the variable states causing divergence from expected behavior.
schema.research_plan: Evidence will come from experiments on standard benchmarks comparing the proposed framework against standard self-debugging baselines, with pass rate as the intended success measure. The abstract does not specify named benchmarks, baseline implementations, ablations isolating the memory graph components, or a failure condition.

items.title: Counterfactual Memory-Augmented Program Repair for Code Generation Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) code generation agents rely heavily on iterative self-debugging loops to correct runtime errors and failing test cases. However, recent findings demonstrate a severe "debugging effectiveness decay," where most models lose 60-80% of their debugging capability within 2-3 iterative attempts due to error trace noise, context window saturation, and path confirmation bias. Existing multi-turn debuggers treat execution feedback as monolithic streams, accumulating redundant failures that misguide the generator. In this proposal, we introduce Counterfactual Memory-Augmented Program Repair (CM-Repair), a framework that mitigates debugging decay by structuring execution history into a counterfactual memory graph. Instead of feeding accumulated raw stack traces, CM-Repair isolates successful sub-modules, dynamically masks irrelevant error noise, and injects contrastive counterfactual execution paths—highlighting precisely what variable states caused divergence from expected behavior. Experiments across standard benchmarks will demonstrate that CM-Repair rescues agent convergence and significantly improves pass rates over standard self-debugging baselines.

schema.problem: Existing text-to-SQL systems for EHRs can produce syntactically valid and execution-successful queries that are clinically wrong—mixing SNOMED CT, ICD-10, and LOINC code namespaces or silently undercounting or overcounting patient cohorts—while current metrics treat the task as purely syntactic rather than clinical.
schema.motivation: Clinicians increasingly query EHRs in natural language, and clinical errors in generated SQL can distort patient cohort counts and terminology predicates; a clinically aware decoding and evaluation approach is needed to reduce this risk.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed constrained decoder extends incremental-parsing schemes such as PICARD: whenever the parser state opens a predicate over a terminology-coded column, the admissible-token set is restricted to literals belonging to that column's code namespace and semantically contained under the question's requested concept subtype. The decoder is paired with an ontology-aware beam reranker that penalizes cross-namespace substitutions using open terminology vocabularies, and with a check that flags queries whose returned patient count becomes unstable under small, semantically-equivalent reformulations of the temporal and join logic. The work also constructs a clinician-graded clinical error taxonomy for text-to-SQL execution (covering namespace mixing, temporal/incidence mis-scoping, patient undercount/overcount, semantic drift, and unanswerable mishandling) and a generalized class-weighted reliability score that decomposes failures by error type. Experiments use T5-3B and open-weight Llama3 models.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation applies the proposed taxonomy to EHRSQL 2024 and MIMICSQL outputs from T5-3B and open-weight Llama3 models and to unconstrained decoding, PICARD, grammar-based decoding, graph-structure injection, ProbGate filtering, and answerability-gating baselines. (1) Support for the first claim is whether observed taxonomy failure rates for systems scoring 90%+ execution accuracy fall within the hypothesized 10–25% range. (2) Support for the second claim is whether namespace-mixing errors approach zero and unpenalized execution accuracy drops by no more than 3–5 points when using the proposed decoder compared with the baselines.

items.title: T-ECoND: Terminology-Grounded, Patient-Safe Constrained Decoding for Clinical Text-to-SQL, with a Clinician-Graded Error Taxonomy for SQL Execution
items.abstract: Clinicians increasingly query Electronic Health Records (EHRs) in natural language through text-to-SQL systems, yet a query can be syntactically valid and execution-successful while remaining clinically wrong: it may mix SNOMED CT, ICD-10, and LOINC code namespaces, or silently undercount or overcount the patient cohort it targets. All metrics the community currently reports — exact match, execution accuracy, the EHRSQL reliability score, and even expert-emulation metrics such as FLEX — treat the problem as syntactic, never as clinical. We propose T-ECoND (Terminology-Encoded Conditioned decoding), a constrained-decoding mechanism that extends incremental-parsing schemes such as PICARD with terminology-scoped decoding: whenever the parser state opens a predicate over a terminology-coded column, the admissible-token set is restricted to literals belonging to that column's code namespace and semantically contained under the question's requested concept subtype. T-ECoND pairs the decoder with (i) an ontology-aware beam reranker that penalizes cross-namespace substitutions using open terminology vocabularies and (ii) a cohort-stability check that flags queries whose returned patient count becomes unstable under small, semantically-equivalent reformulations of the temporal and join logic. We evaluate on EHRSQL 2024 and MIMICSQL with T5-3B and open-weight Llama3 models against unconstrained decoding, PICARD, grammar-based decoding, graph-structure injection, ProbGate filtering, and answerability-gating systems. We additionally introduce the first clinician-graded clinical error taxonomy for text-to-SQL execution (namespace mixing, temporal/incidence mis-scoping, patient undercount/overcount, semantic drift, unanswerable mishandling), adapted from clinical safety assessment practice for medical text generation, and report a generalized, class-weighted reliability score that decomposes failures by error type. We hypothesize that systems scoring 90%+ execution accuracy nonetheless fail on 10–25% of queries under this taxonomy, and that T-ECoND drives namespace-mixing errors to near zero at no more than a 3–5 point cost to unpenalized execution accuracy.

schema.problem: Iterative LLM-based code repair typically presents the model with all failures at once, so it remains unknown whether a deliberate policy for choosing which oracle failure to expose per iteration changes repair yield under a fixed candidate budget when a program fails several tests simultaneously.
schema.motivation: Recent evidence suggests self-repair is feedback-bottlenecked and that diagnosis degrades as oracle content grows, so isolating the exposure policy may improve cost-adjusted repair yield and, if not, can redirect effort toward more promising feedback design.
schema.proposed_approach: The work runs a training-free repair loop over off-the-shelf LLMs. Each iteration exposes a single failing-test oracle instead of the full failing-test bundle, with the failing test chosen by a static selection policy: locality-ranked, coverage-ranked, or random. A strict pass-to-pass regression budget rejects any candidate that flips currently passing tests. Evaluation uses a screened multi-failure subset of the LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench repair benchmarks used in recent self-repair studies.
schema.research_plan: The study evaluates the claim on a screened multi-failure subset of LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench under a fixed candidate budget, comparing per-candidate acceptance yield between single-oracle locality-ranked exposure and whole-suite batch exposure while requiring equal final full-suite pass rates and measuring token cost. The selection-policy comparison and regression budget isolate the exposure policy from candidate rejection. Support is specified as an increase of at least 5 percentage points in per-candidate acceptance yield with equal final pass rates and lower token cost. A loss under single-oracle exposure is specified in advance as an informative negative result that redirects effort toward salience-tagging within batch feedback.

items.title: Orchestrated Oracles: Test-Selection and Pass-to-Pass Budget-Aware LLM Self-Repair for Multi-Failure Programs
items.abstract: Iterative LLM-based code repair typically hands the model everything that failed at once: the full failing-test bundle, traceback, and feedback are fed back unchanged on every round. We ask a narrower, falsifiable question about the control knob this literature under-studies: when a program fails several tests simultaneously, does a deliberate policy for choosing which oracle failure to expose per repair iteration change repair yield under a fixed candidate budget? We isolate three mechanisms in a training-free repair loop over off-the-shelf LLMs: (i) single-test oracle exposure instead of batch exposure, (ii) a static selection policy for which failing test to show (locality-ranked vs. coverage-ranked vs. random), and (iii) a strict pass-to-pass regression budget that rejects any candidate that flips currently-passing tests. We hypothesize that, on a screened multi-failure subset of the repair benchmarks of LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench used in recent self-repair studies, one-oracle-at-a-time presentation with a locality-ranked policy yields ≥5 percentage points higher per-candidate acceptance yield than whole-suite batch exposure, at equal final full-suite pass rates and lower token cost — consistent with evidence that self-repair is feedback-bottlenecked, that diagnosis degrades as oracle content grows, and that repair claims must be cost-adjusted. If single-oracle exposure loses, the negative result itself is informative and redirects effort toward salience-tagging within batch feedback; we spec these outcomes and the pivot in advance.

schema.problem: The application of code LLMs to automate clinical decision support systems remains underexplored, despite LLM integration in CDSS having shown promise.
schema.motivation: Given that LLM integration in CDSS has shown promise, extending this to fine-tuned code LLMs could improve the accuracy and efficiency of clinical decision-making.
schema.proposed_approach: Fine-tune code LLMs on healthcare-specific datasets and develop a framework that uses the fine-tuned models for clinical decision support, then evaluate the framework.
schema.research_plan: The abstract indicates a planned evaluation of the proposed framework to support the claim about improved accuracy and efficiency, but it does not specify baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

items.title: Fine-Tuning Code LLMs for Clinical Decision Support Systems
items.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical decision support systems (CDSS) has shown promise in improving healthcare outcomes. However, the application of code LLMs in automating CDSS remains underexplored. This proposal aims to investigate the potential of fine-tuning code LLMs on healthcare-specific datasets to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of clinical decision-making. We plan to develop and evaluate a novel framework that leverages fine-tuned code LLMs for CDSS, addressing existing gaps in current research.

schema.problem: Code generation models often struggle with accuracy and efficiency, particularly in complex domains.
schema.motivation: Improving these models would broaden their reliable use in complex-domain code generation tasks.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach integrates program synthesis and domain-specific knowledge incorporation into code generation models. It will evaluate various techniques for incorporating domain-specific knowledge and investigate the role program synthesis plays in improving accuracy and efficiency.
schema.research_plan: The planned evaluation compares various domain-specific knowledge incorporation techniques and examines how program synthesis affects code generation accuracy and efficiency. No baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified in the abstract.

items.title: Enhancing Code Generation Models with Program Synthesis and Domain-Specific Knowledge Incorporation
items.abstract: Code generation models have shown remarkable capabilities in generating code from natural-language specifications. However, they often struggle with accuracy and efficiency, particularly in complex domains. This proposal aims to investigate the integration of program synthesis and domain-specific knowledge incorporation to enhance code generation models. We will evaluate the effectiveness of various domain-specific knowledge incorporation techniques and investigate the role of program synthesis in improving code generation accuracy and efficiency.
