schema.problem: Code LLM self-debugging repeatedly stalls on hard problems because the tests, explanations, and patches are all produced by the same model and therefore reinforce the same faulty assumption; self-generated tests capture the model's actual, often wrong, behavior rather than the expected behavior implied by the specification.
schema.motivation: The bottleneck is the oracle rather than the repair operator, so repairing against a specification-derived and independently validated test oracle should avoid self-confirming wrong tests and improve true pass rates on hard problems.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed pipeline is test-first: a unit-test oracle is synthesized blind to any candidate implementation directly from the natural-language specification. Candidate tests are validated without trusting the program to be repaired: one stage keeps only tests whose pass/fail outcomes discriminate across a diverse ensemble of independently sampled candidate programs and fall in a plausibility band, flagging likely specification misreads; a second stage keeps only tests that kill a quota of mutants, dropping vacuous or implementation-entangled assertions; optionally, a cross-model entailment check re-checks borderline assertions against the specification. The surviving oracle is frozen and drives self-repair of a held-out candidate, which can never rewrite its own grading criteria.
schema.research_plan: (1) The main true-pass-rate claim is tested against self-consistency, vanilla self-debugging, and unvalidated test-guided repair under a matched test-execution and LLM-call budget, using held-out ground-truth tests; support requires higher true pass rate, with the largest gains expected on problems that survive one self-repair round, and failure would be no improvement or worse. (2) The overfitting-rate safety claim is audited by an overfitting-rate safety metric, with support requiring the frozen test oracle not to raise overfitting relative to the comparison conditions. Ablations isolate the contribution of test-first independence, the diversity/plausibility validation stage, the mutation-strength stage, and the entailment probe by removing each. The design is controlled and budget-matched across conditions.

items.title: Frozen Oracle: Test-First, Mutation-Validated Test Oracles for LLM Self-Repair
items.abstract: Code LLM self-debugging repeatedly stalls on the same hard problems because the tests, explanations, and patches are all produced by the same model and therefore reinforce one and the same faulty assumption. We argue the bottleneck is not the repair operator but the oracle: self-generated tests capture the model's actual (often wrong) behavior rather than the expected behavior implied by the specification. We propose Frozen Oracle, a test-first pipeline in which the unit-test oracle is synthesized blind to any candidate implementation directly from the natural-language specification, and is then validated without trusting the program to be repaired: (i) a differential filter keeps only tests whose pass/fail outcomes discriminate across a diverse ensemble of independently sampled candidate programs and fall in a plausibility band, which also flags likely spec misreads; (ii) a mutation-strength filter keeps only tests that kill a quota of mutants, dropping vacuous or implementation-entangled assertions; and (iii) an optional cross-model entailment probe re-checks borderline assertions against the spec. The surviving oracle is frozen and drives self-repair of a held-out candidate, which can never rewrite its own grading criteria. Our central, falsifiable claim: at a matched test-execution and LLM-call budget, repairing against a frozen, spec-derived, mutation-and-differentially validated oracle yields a higher true pass rate against held-out ground-truth tests than self-consistency, vanilla self-debugging, and unvalidated test-guided repair, with the largest gains on problems that survive one self-repair round. We detail the method and a controlled, budget-matched experimental design with ablations that isolate test-first independence, the differential filter, the mutation filter, and the entailment probe, plus an overfitting-rate safety metric that a frozen oracle should lower rather than raise.

schema.problem: Unguarded self-debugging for NL2code uses execution feedback from the same small visible test set used for evaluation, and recent work documents that self-generated tests are biased, noisy, and encode actual rather than intended behavior; this causes systematic overfitting to visible tests and inflated reported accuracy while harming held-out correctness.
schema.motivation: Because self-debugging is now the standard recipe for improving NL2code pass@1, distinguishing genuine code repairs from visible-test overfitting is necessary before these improvements can be trusted.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method treats every failed-execution signal as noisy evidence and accepts a repair only when it passes a triple acceptance gate: the repair fixes the failing counterexample; it preserves behavior on an automatically generated differential test suite (difference-exposing inputs on which the pre-repair program and a consensus of independently sampled candidate implementations, or spec-derived expected behavior, agree); and it does not violate a small set of executable spec-derived invariants. If no gate-passing repair exists, the loop stops and rolls back.
schema.research_plan: The claims are tested on function-level benchmarks with explicit visible/hidden splits: HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench, and the contamination-controlled LBPP. Baselines are unguarded self-debugging methods—direct retry, rubber-duck the proposed method, PyCapsule-style iterative self-debugging, UTDebug-style multi-test backtracking, and CodeTree-style tree search—under matched LLM-call and token budgets. The primary evidence is hidden/holdout pass@1 and the size of the visible–hidden gap; success-vs-budget curves are reported. Ablations remove each acceptance gate, replace the consensus oracle with an LLM oracle, and vary mutation-augmented input generation. Failure is inferred if hidden/holdout pass@1 is not improved or the visible–hidden gap is not strictly reduced relative to the baselines under the matched budget.

items.title: Guarded Self-Debugging: Differential Preservation Gates for Closing the Visible–Hidden Gap in LLM NL2code Self-Debugging
items.abstract: Self-debugging with LLMs has become the standard recipe for improving NL2code pass@1, but the execution feedback that drives it comes from the same small visible test set used for evaluation, and recent work documents that self-generated tests are biased, noisy, and prone to encoding the actual rather than the intended behavior of code. We argue that unguarded self-debugging therefore systematically overfits the visible tests, inflating reported accuracy while harming correctness on held-out tests. We propose Guarded Self-Debugging (GSD), a method that treats every failed-execution signal as noisy evidence and admits a repair only when it passes a triple acceptance gate: (i) it fixes the failing counterexample, (ii) it preserves behavior on an automatically generated differential test suite — difference-exposing inputs on which the pre-repair program and a consensus of independently sampled candidate implementations (or the spec-derived expected behavior) agree, in the spirit of preservation conditions — and (iii) it does not violate a small set of executable spec-derived invariants; the loop stops and rolls back when no gate-passing repair exists. Our core, falsifiable claim is that GSD improves pass@1 on hidden/holdout tests and strictly reduces the visible–hidden pass gap relative to unguarded self-debugging baselines (direct retry, rubber-duck Self-Debugging, PyCapsule-style iterative self-debugging, UTDebug-style multi-test backtracking, and CodeTree-style tree search) under a matched LLM-call and token budget. We evaluate on function-level benchmarks with explicit visible/hidden splits (HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench) plus the contamination-controlled LBPP, report success-vs-budget curves, and ablate each gate, the consensus oracle versus an LLM oracle, and mutation-augmented input generation.

schema.problem: Porting legacy CPU codes to GPUs remains a major challenge, and code-generation AI—though promising—is so new that it has not been sufficiently evaluated for this task.
schema.motivation: GPU-equipped supercomputers have become commonplace and GPU use in simulation is increasingly important, while rapidly advancing code-generation AI makes AI-assisted porting tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The work uses Claude Code to generate GPU-oriented code for GeoFEM, a Fortran finite element application parallelized with MPI+OpenMP. It systematically investigates methods to achieve high-performance GPU code generation and to streamline the code-generation process itself. The approach includes automated test execution to assess correctness and performance of the generated GPU code.
schema.research_plan: The study systematically investigates generation and process-streamlining methods; evidence is automated test execution for correctness and performance, with no baselines, metrics, or failure thresholds stated.

items.title: Evaluating Claude Code’s Coding and Test Automation for GPU Acceleration ofa Legacy Fortran Application: A GeoFEM Case Study
items.abstract: With the rise of AI research, supercomputers equipped with GPUs by default have become commonplace, and the use of GPUs in simulation has become even more important. At the same time, porting legacy codes developed for CPUs to GPUs remains a major challenge. A promising way to address this issue is to leverage rapidly advancing code-generation AI; however, because this approach is very new, it has not been sufficiently evaluated. In this study, we attempt GPU-oriented code generation using Claude Code—one such code-generation AI—for GeoFEM, a Fortran-based finite element application parallelized with MPI+OpenMP. We systematically investigate methods to achieve both the generation of high-performance GPU code and the streamlining of the code-generation process itself, including automated test execution to assess correctness and performance of the generated GPU code.

schema.problem: Manual memory management in C remains error-prone, and memory management errors are a leading source of software vulnerabilities. Existing automated program repair for such errors is dominated by rule- and template-based techniques that require expert specifications and generalize poorly, while LLM-based repair still faces interprocedural reasoning and context-window limits for codebase-level fixes.
schema.motivation: Reducing memory-management vulnerabilities in large C codebases is valuable because it avoids expert-crafted repair rules and scales repair beyond isolated snippets. The recent availability of LLMs that can synthesize context-dependent fixes makes program-analysis-guided, retrieval-augmented repair timely.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework augments LLM-based automated program repair with typestate-guided context retrieval. A finite typestate automaton tracks error-propagation paths and memory state transitions across procedures, and the retrieved, focused context is provided to the LLM to support codebase-level memory error repair. The design targets interprocedural reasoning and LLM context-window limitations by selecting semantically relevant paths rather than requiring expert-crafted repair specifications.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates on 49 real-world memory errors from 14 open-source projects totaling approximately 1.57 million lines of code. It compares against memory-error APR tools (SAVER, ProvenFix, and the crash-constraint-driven CrashRepair on a double-free/use-after-free subset) and open-source LLM-based repair tools (SWE-agent 1.0 and Sand2Patch). The measured evidence is number of correctly repaired errors and number of harmful patches introduced. Zero-day memory error cases are evaluated by submitting fixes to original developers. No explicit matched-compute, model, or latency conditions are stated, and the abstract does not specify a failure threshold.

items.title: TLR: Codebase-Level C Memory Management Error Repair with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Memory management errors in C remain a leading source of software vulnerabilities due to the inherent complexity of manual memory handling. Traditional Automated Program Repair (APR) largely relies on rule- or template-based techniques, which require expert-crafted specifications and often struggle to generalize. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a complementary approach, leveraging broad exposure to codebases and programming idioms to synthesize fixes that can extend beyond existing templates and rules. This paper introduces TLR, a novel framework that augments LLM-based repair with typestate-guided context retrieval. By using a finite typestate automaton to track error-propagation paths and memory state transitions, our approach provides the LLM with focused, semantically rich context for codebase-level memory error repair, effectively addressing both interprocedural reasoning and LLM context window limitations. Our framework has successfully repaired 37 out of 49 real-world memory errors derived from 14 open-source projects that collectively comprise approximately 1.57 million lines of code. Compared to state-of-the-art memory error APR tools, SAVER and ProvenFix, our approach correctly fixes 14.50× and 2.36× more errors, respectively; and on the double-free and use-after-free subset, TLR repairs all 7 cases whereas the crash-constraint-driven CrashRepair repairs only 1. Moreover, TLR outperforms current open-source state-of-the-art LLM-based repair tools, repairing more errors than SWE-agent 1.0 and the tree-of-thought agent Sand2Patch, while introducing far fewer harmful patches. We have also successfully repaired three critical zero-day memory errors, with fixes that have been accepted and implemented by the original developers. These results highlight a promising paradigm for codebase-level program repair through program analysis-guided, retrieval-augmented LLMs, combining formal verification strengths with neural model adaptability.

schema.problem: It is not well established how open-source foundation models perform and compare in translating natural-language requests into executable, semantically appropriate SQL queries and business-oriented interpretations in single-agent and multi-agent LLM systems for analytics-intensive environments.
schema.motivation: Open-source foundation models offer a deployable alternative for structured analytics, and realistic evaluation combining semantic and efficiency criteria is needed to determine when they can support business decision-making.
schema.proposed_approach: The study instantiates single-agent and multi-agent LLM systems using open-source foundation models (Mistral, Devstral, Qwen2.5-Coder, and Qwen3) that take natural-language requests, generate executable SQL, and produce business-oriented interpretations. It constructs a custom SQL test suite of realistic marketing and e-commerce analytics tasks and also evaluates on the public Spider benchmark. Evaluation on the custom suite uses exact match, safe SQL rate, and an independent semantic judge; Spider evaluation uses execution accuracy, exact match, and latency. Prompting strategy and agent architecture are treated as configuration factors in the analysis.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim that strict query-level matching is too conservative in domain-specific settings is tested on the custom SQL test suite by comparing exact match, safe SQL rate, and independent semantic judge scores; support would show semantic appropriateness even when exact query-level matching is low, and failure would occur if semantic and exact-match judgments closely track each other. (2) The claim of open-source agent effectiveness and model-family dependence is tested on the public Spider benchmark using execution accuracy, exact match, and latency, with comparison against prior text-to-SQL research; support would show effective performance and clear model-family differences, while failure would show uniform weakness or no dependence. (3) The architectural claim is tested by varying single-agent and multi-agent decomposition and measuring execution accuracy, exact match, latency, and token consumption; the abstract does not state a held-matched compute or prompt condition, so trade-off interpretation is limited.

items.title: Evaluating Open-Source LLM Agents for SQL Generation and Structured Analytics on Relational Databases
items.abstract: This study examines the potential of open-source foundation models for structured data analytics, with particular emphasis on SQL generation and business-oriented interpretation in single-agent and multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. The proposed framework addresses a practical problem in analytics-intensive environments, where natural-language requests must be translated into executable, semantically appropriate SQL queries and subsequently interpreted in a form useful for business decision-making. The system is evaluated in two complementary settings: a custom SQL test suite designed around realistic marketing and e-commerce analytics tasks, and the public Spider benchmark, which supports comparison with prior text-to-SQL research and enables assessment of cross-domain generalization. The analysis includes Mistral, Devstral, Qwen2.5-Coder, and Qwen3. On the custom SQL test suite, performance was assessed using exact match, safe SQL rate, and an independent semantic judge score. Qwen2.5-Coder achieved the strongest overall result, reaching an independent semantic score of 90.14% while maintaining a 98.59% safe SQL rate. Qwen3 followed with a semantic score of 77.46% and completely safe SQL generation. These results indicate that in domain-specific analytics settings, strict query-level matching alone is too conservative to capture practical model usefulness, since semantically appropriate SQL queries may differ substantially from the reference formulation. The Spider benchmark results provide complementary evidence regarding broader model behavior. Qwen2.5-Coder achieved the highest single-agent execution accuracy (72.44%), whereas Devstral obtained the strongest single-agent exact-match score (28.14%). Qwen3 remained competitive and delivered the lowest single-agent latency (0.41 s) among the evaluated models. At the architectural level, the effect of multi-agent decomposition was not uniform: it yielded modest gains in execution accuracy for some model families, but reduced performance for others, while consistently increasing latency and token consumption. Taken together, the findings show that open-source LLM agents can provide effective support for structured analytics, but that their performance depends strongly on model family, prompting strategy, and agent architecture. More broadly, the study demonstrates that the evaluation of text-to-SQL systems benefits from combining benchmark-based metrics, domain-oriented semantic assessment, and efficiency-aware analysis, thereby offering a more realistic basis for the deployment of open-source LLM systems in analytics-intensive environments.

schema.problem: Directly generating reliable mathematical models and executable code from unstructured natural-language logistics requirements remains challenging, because large language models tend to produce invalid constraints or syntactically incorrect code; traditional logistics optimization methods also require manual expert intervention to adjust warehouse rules or operational goals.
schema.motivation: A natural-language interface would make logistics optimization more agile by allowing dynamic adjustment of warehouse rules and operational goals without manual expert intervention, while preserving the rigor of classical models and solvers.
schema.proposed_approach: The pipeline starts from unstructured natural-language requirements and automatically translates them into optimization algorithm code. It uses task-specific agents to construct mathematical models, then synchronizes model changes into executable code through semantic mapping and an ensemble-based difference analysis. A multi-layered verification stage checks for logical inconsistencies between the model and code and corrects them before execution.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation tests the pipeline on the capacitated vehicle routing problem using the Augerat benchmark dataset across six difficulty levels and 54 cases. Evidence consists of whether the generated code passes execution validation and how closely the resulting solutions match expert-designed baselines. Support is high pass rates and small solution deviations; failure is frequent invalid code or large quality gaps.

items.title: Semantic-Driven Mathematical Modeling and Adaptive Refactoring for Logistics Optimization: A Language-Model Orchestrated Optimization Pipeline
items.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) offer a convenient natural language interface for logistics optimization problems, it remains challenging to directly generate reliable mathematical models and executable code from unstructured text requirements. LLMs tend to produce invalid constraints or syntactically incorrect code. In addition, traditional logistics optimization methods lack the flexibility to adjust warehouse rules or operational goals without manual expert intervention. To address these issues, we propose LOOP (a Language-Model Orchestrated Optimization Pipeline), which automatically translates natural-language requirements into optimization algorithm code while retaining the rigor of classical models and solvers. LOOP leverages task-specific agents to construct accurate mathematical models and adopts a difference-driven code generation approach. First, it synchronizes model changes into executable code via semantic mapping and ensemble difference analysis. Second, it incorporates a multi-layered verification mechanism to detect and correct pre-execution logical inconsistencies between the model and code. We evaluate LOOP on the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) using the Augerat benchmark dataset (six difficulty levels). Experimental results show that the final code achieves a 96.3% pass rate across 54 cases, and generated solutions differed by only 1.5% from expert baselines. These findings confirm that LOOP improves the agility of dynamic constraint solution development without sacrificing quality.

schema.problem: Large language models achieve near-ceiling performance on code generation benchmarks, but the programming languages used by popular benchmarks are largely in-distribution, so their performance on unfamiliar programming languages remains unknown.
schema.motivation: A benchmark of unfamiliar languages can test whether frontier models generalize algorithmic problem-solving outside their training distribution, and it avoids the contamination and ceiling effects that limit current code benchmarks.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark comprises 80 algorithm problems expressed in five Turing-complete esoteric languages (Brainfuck, Befunge-98, Whitespace, Unlambda, and Shakespeare), with equivalent Python and JavaScript versions. The languages are chosen for hard-to-use primitives, substantially lower public code representation than Python, and negligible deployment value, reducing post-training contamination. Five frontier models are evaluated under five prompting strategies, including few-shot learning and self-reflection.
schema.research_plan: The evidence compares accuracy on the same 80 problems across familiar and esoteric language versions under five prompting strategies, using five frontier models. Claim (1) is tested by the accuracy gap between familiar and esoteric versions; claim (2) is tested by whether few-shot and self-reflection change esoteric-language accuracy; claim (3) is supported by corpus-representation counts and deployment-value reasoning indicating low contamination risk. The design holds the problem set fixed across languages to isolate language familiarity.

items.title: EsoLang-Bench: Evaluating Genuine Reasoning in Large Language Models via Esoteric Programming Languages
items.abstract: Large language models achieve near-ceiling performance on code generation benchmarks, yet most of the programming languages used by popular benchmarks such as SWE-bench and HumanEval (e.g. Python, JavaScript) are squarely in-distribution. They appear at scale in pre-training corpora and are heavily reinforced during post-training. To study LLM performance on unfamiliar programming languages, we introduce EsoLang-Bench, a benchmark using five esoteric programming languages (Brainfuck, Befunge-98, Whitespace, Unlambda, and Shakespeare). All five of our chosen esoteric languages are Turing-complete, so the same algorithmic problems that are solvable in Python or JavaScript are in principle solvable in each of them. Yet, they are unfamiliar to LLMs which makes them a good proxy for evaluating out-of-distribution performance. The unfamiliarity of esoteric languages comprises of: (i) the hard-by-design primitives comprising the language; (ii) substantially less representation in pre-training corpora (340x to over 60,000x fewer public GitHub repositories than Python); (iii) negligible deployment value, which makes targeted inclusion in post-training data economically irrational. We evaluate five frontier models across five prompting strategies and find a dramatic capability gap. The same 80 problems expressed in Python or JavaScript reach 100% accuracy on top frontier models, while the equivalent esoteric versions score only 0-11%. Few-shot learning and self-reflection also fail to close this gap. EsoLang-Bench therefore provides a contamination-resistant testbed for measuring how well frontier models generalise algorithmic problem-solving to programming languages outside their training distribution.

schema.problem: There is a lack of representative and scalable datasets for automated Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SATD) repayment, no reliable way to filter irrelevant repayment samples from repository histories, and evaluation metrics such as BLEU and CrystalBLEU assess whole code rather than the actual code changes, limiting meaningful measurement.
schema.motivation: Automating SATD repayment would reduce maintenance costs and developer effort, while large language models' success in code generation and repair makes them a plausible basis for automated repayment.
schema.proposed_approach: Adopt a language-independent SATD tracing tool and a ten-step filtering pipeline that extracts SATD repayments from repository commit histories, using an LLM-as-judge step to filter irrelevant repayments, producing 58,722 Python and 97,347 Java SATD repayment items. Introduce two diff-based metrics that measure code changes rather than whole code, extending BLEU and CrystalBLEU, plus a line-level exact-match metric on diffs for fine-grained quality assessment. Use the resulting benchmarks and metrics to evaluate two automated repayment approaches: fine-tuning models of a few hundred million parameters and prompt engineering with large-scale models, including four open-source state-of-the-art LLMs and GPT-4o-mini.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the dataset claim, the evidence is the construction trace: repayments are extracted from commit histories by a language-independent tracing tool, passed through a ten-step filtering pipeline, and relevance-filtered by an LLM-as-judge; adequacy is supported by resulting dataset sizes. (2) For the metric claim, the paper compares the proposed diff-based and line-level diff metrics against exact match and against whole-code BLEU and CrystalBLEU, using correlation with exact match as the validity check; failure would be low correlation between the proposed metrics and exact match. (3) For the comparison claim, the paper evaluates fine-tuned smaller models and prompt-engineered large-scale models on the same datasets using exact match, whole-code BLEU and CrystalBLEU, and the proposed diff-based and line-level metrics, holding the evaluation setup fixed across models; the prior Java-only study serves as historical context.

items.title: A Large-Scale Empirical Evaluation of LLMs for Automated Self-Admitted Technical Debt Repayment
items.abstract: Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SATD), cases where developers intentionally acknowledge suboptimal solutions in code through comments, poses a significant challenge to software maintainability. Left unresolved, SATD can degrade code quality, increase maintenance costs, and hinder long-term software sustainability. Manually identifying and resolving SATD is time-consuming and error-prone, often competing with feature development and release deadlines. Automating SATD repayment is therefore essential to alleviate developer burden. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in tasks like code generation and program repair, their potential in automated SATD repayment remains underexplored. In this paper, we identify three key technical challenges in training and evaluating LLMs for SATD repayment: (1) dataset representativeness and scalability, (2) removal of irrelevant SATD repayment samples, and (3) limitations of existing evaluation metrics, i.e., BLEU and CrystalBLEU. To address the first two dataset-related challenges, we adopt a language-independent SATD tracing tool and design a 10-step filtering pipeline to extract SATD repayments from repository commit histories, leveraging LLM-as-judge for relevance filtering. This results in two new large-scale SATD repayment datasets: 58,722 items for Python and 97,347 items for Java. To improve evaluation, we introduce two diff-based metrics, BLEU-diff and CrystalBLEU-diff, which measure code changes rather than whole code, thereby mitigating the impact of SATD-irrelevant source code. Additionally, we propose a new metric, Line-Level Exact Match on Diff (LEMOD), which is both interpretable and informative, providing fine-grained insights into SATD repayment quality. Using our new benchmarks and evaluation metrics, we evaluate two types of automated SATD repayment methods: fine-tuning smaller models (a few hundred million parameters) and prompt engineering with large-scale models, including four SOTA open-source LLMs and GPT-4o-mini. Our results reveal that while fine-tuned smaller models achieve Exact Match (EM) scores comparable to prompt-based approaches, they underperform on BLEU-based metrics and LEMOD. The best EM performance is achieved by Gemma-2-9B, correctly addressing 10.1% of Python SATDs and 8.1% of Java SATDs with a simple prompt. The only previous study in this domain focused solely on Java, achieving an EM score of 2.3%. When using BLEU-diff, CrystalBLEU-diff, and LEMOD metrics, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and GPT-4o-mini deliver the highest performance. While our three proposed metrics demonstrate strong correlations with EM (0.65~0.84), both BLEU and CrystalBLEU show almost no correlation with this intuitive metric (0.01~0.08), highlighting their largely unpredictable behavior when applied directly to the entire code rather than the diff. Our work contributes a robust benchmark, improved evaluation metrics, and a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs, advancing research on automated SATD repayment.

schema.problem: While prompt wording and structure are known to influence model performance, the impact of psychologically inspired prompt framings remains unexplored.
schema.motivation: LLMs are increasingly integrated into software engineering workflows, so understanding whether psychology-based communication strategies change code generation quality can inform transparent and interpretable human-AI interactions.
schema.proposed_approach: Eight influence tactics from Yukl & Falbe's taxonomy were operationalized as reproducible prompt templates. The templates were applied to five leading open-weight LLMs on LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Verified, and the generated code was assessed on functional correctness, quality, maintainability, and security.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a benchmark evaluation in which eight influence-tactic prompt templates are run across five leading open-weight LLMs on LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Verified, and generated code is scored on functional correctness, quality, maintainability, and security. The analysis compares how these quality dimensions vary across prompt framings and tactics, with particular attention to whether any tactics such as urgency are associated with different outcomes. The abstract does not state a formal failure condition or what was held matched across runs.

items.title: Do influence tactics matter? investigating prompt framing effects in LLM code generation
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering workflows, helping developers write, debug, test, and maintain code. While prompt wording and structure are known to influence model performance, the impact of psychologically inspired prompt framings remains unexplored. This study investigates whether different psychology-based communication strategies that humans use to persuade or motivate others can lead to more effective prompt framing, which may, in turn, affect LLM behaviour in coding tasks. Drawing on Yukl & Falbe’s well-known taxonomy, we operationalized eight influence tactics (like rational persuasion, ingratiation, and exchange) into reproducible prompt templates. These prompt templates were evaluated across five leading open-weight LLMs using two widely adopted benchmarks: LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Verified. We assessed the resulting code output on four key software quality dimensions: functional correctness, quality, maintainability, and security. Our results show that certain influence-induced prompt framings, particularly those emphasizing urgency, were associated with reduced correctness and security. This work presents the first large-scale empirical study of influence-induced prompt framing in software engineering tasks, offering insights into how linguistic cues may shape LLM outputs. We conclude with practical insights for designing transparent and interpretable human-AI interactions in code generation.

schema.problem: Most existing CAD approaches rely on task-specific models that require structural modifications for new tasks, and they predominantly handle point clouds or images rather than the industry-standard Boundary Representation (B-rep) format.
schema.motivation: Large language models' code-generation capabilities make it possible to convert CAD modeling sequences into code and align them with B-rep, enabling a unified model for multiple CAD tasks.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach uses a unified multimodal large language model that performs diverse CAD tasks from B-rep inputs. CAD modeling sequences are converted into Python-like code and aligned with B-rep by leveraging the code-generation capabilities of large language models. Training is two-stage: pre-training on reverse engineering to learn geometric features and design logic, then extending the model to downstream tasks such as completion, error correction, and CAD-QA. B-rep is interpreted as structural code.
schema.research_plan: Evidence consists of downstream task performance on completion, error correction, and CAD-QA; the abstract does not state baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

items.title: BrepCoder: A Unified Multimodal Large Language Model for Multi-task B-rep Reasoning
items.abstract: Recent advancements in deep learning have actively addressed complex challenges within the Computer-Aided Design (CAD) domain.However, most existing approaches rely on task-specifi c models requiring structural modifi cations for new tasks, and they predominantly focus on point clouds or images rather than the industry-standard Boundary Representation (B-rep) format. To address these limitations, we propose BrepCoder, a unifi ed Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that performs diverse CAD tasks from B-rep inputs. By leveraging the code generation capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), we convert CAD modeling sequences into Python-like code and align them with B-rep. We then adopt a two-stage training strategy: First, pre-training on reverse engineering to learn geometric features and design logic. Second, eff ectively extending the model to various downstream tasks such as completion, error correction, and CAD-QA. Consequently, by interpreting B-rep as structural code, BrepCoder achieves superior generalization across diverse tasks, demonstrating its potential as a general-purpose CAD agent.

schema.problem: Constructing simulation scenarios manually is time-consuming and often depends on platform-specific modeling experience; existing LLM methods for interpreting operational documents still struggle with long-document parsing, incomplete platform interfaces, auditable task execution, and cross-lingual equipment-name normalization.
schema.motivation: Automating scenario generation from operational documents would reduce manual effort and lower the barrier of platform-specific modeling expertise.
schema.proposed_approach: The method standardizes Word-based scenario inputs, extracts scenario elements into a schema-constrained JSON intermediate representation, and decomposes generation into planning and execution. A dual-channel planning agent assigns basic object and scenario-property operations to a C# object model, while allocating fine-grained unit, mission, and environment operations to Lua-based scripting interfaces. An execution agent integrates two-stage hot-pluggable tool loading, side-effect-aware read/write-separated scheduling, and a matching module that combines BM25 retrieval, multilingual vector retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, and low-confidence LLM reranking.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on representative red-blue simulation scenarios evaluate (1) average end-to-end generation time, first-round planning success rate, and post-replan success rate to support the generation-pipeline and recovery claims, and (2) Top-1/Top-5 equipment matching performance to support the cross-lingual normalization claim. The abstract does not specify baselines, ablations, or matched conditions; success rates and matching performance serve as the implied pass/fail signals, though no explicit thresholds are given.

items.title: A Large-Language-Model-Oriented Dual-Channel Agent Framework for Intelligent Generation of Simulation Scenarios
items.abstract: Constructing simulation scenarios manually is time-consuming and often depends on platform-specific modeling experience. Existing large-language-model (LLM) methods are promising for interpreting operational documents, but they still struggle with long-document parsing, incomplete platform interfaces, auditable task execution, and cross-lingual equipment-name normalization. This paper proposes a dual-channel LLM-agent framework for intelligent generation of simulation scenarios. The method standardizes Word-based scenario inputs, extracts scenario elements into a schema-constrained JSON intermediate representation, and decomposes the generation process into planning and execution. A DLL/Lua dual-channel Plan Agent assigns basic object and scenario-property operations to a C# object model, while allocating fine-grained unit, mission, and environment operations to Lua-based scripting interfaces. An Exec Agent further integrates two-stage hot-pluggable tool loading, side-effect-aware read/write-separated scheduling, and a Smart-Matcher module that combines BM25 retrieval, multilingual vector retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, and low-confidence LLM reranking. Experiments on representative red-blue simulation scenarios show an average end-to-end generation time of 168 s, a first-round planning success rate of 92.0%, a post-Replan success rate of 100.0%, and Top-1/Top-5 equipment matching performance of 95.6% and 98.4%, respectively.

schema.problem: There is no established way to measure coding agents' stamina—how many consecutive change requests they can handle before failing—because prevailing evaluation focuses on the fraction of tasks solved in short interactions.
schema.motivation: Real vibe-coding sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns, so a benchmark matching this sustained multi-turn setting is needed to study coding-agent behavior under realistic workloads.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark presents agents with a REST API server and a sequence of procedurally generated follow-up change requests; the reported setup uses 100 turns and result in codebases up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or an LLM-driven sampler, both restricted to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and server run in an isolated environment and communicate over HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. The benchmark and the generated tasks are released.
schema.research_plan: Six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs are evaluated across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each, with the benchmark recording how many turns pass. Claim (1) is supported if agents fail early on long sessions in the no-thorough-testing condition; it would fail if agents routinely survived many turns. Claim (2) is tested by comparing passed-turn counts with and without test feedback and retry; it would fail if feedback did not raise the passed-turn count. Claim (3) is tested by holding models fixed across harnesses and comparing performance; it would fail if strong models performed similarly across harnesses or weak models succeeded in some harnesses.

items.title: StaminaBench: Stress-Testing Coding Agents over 100 Interaction Turns
items.abstract: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing. Unlike the prevailing fraction-of-tasks-solved metric, this matches real vibe-coding where sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns. In StaminaBench, agents implement a REST API server and modify it across a tunable number of procedurally generated follow-up change requests - 100 in our experiments, resulting in codebases of up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement, ensuring reproducibility and reliability; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, both constrained to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and the server run in an isolated environment and communicate with the benchmark through HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. We evaluate six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each and find that: (1) all the tested models fail within 5-6 turns, confirming that vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent and allowing it to retry improves passed turn count by up to 12x; and (3) a good harness is required for strong performance: stronger models exhibit up to a 6x gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail with any harness. We release the benchmark and the generated tasks to enable further research into multi-turn coding agent behavior. Benchmark code and data: github.com/amazon-science/StaminaBench.

schema.problem: Large-scale architectural refactorings that dismantle a central invariant across a large interdependent codebase are considered effectively infeasible through incremental refactoring and conventionally call for a rewrite; it is not established whether an AI coding agent can perform such a change without human review or a pre-existing oracle.
schema.motivation: Such changes conventionally require a rewrite; an agent-executed alternative would avoid that rewrite.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach uses an AI coding agent with no human review of the generated code and no pre-existing oracle. The agent writes a formal specification, refined over 14 audit cycles against the source code; implementation is atomic; a compile/test feedback loop follows; then 17 verification cycles audit the code against the frozen specification. The target behaviour is that a streaming generation survives the closing of its UI panel and can be reattached to the same live stream without loss or duplication. The full specification and raw session logs are published for inspection.
schema.research_plan: (1) The capability claim is examined through a single fully instrumented case study on a 717,725-line TypeScript application, with no human review of generated code and no pre-existing oracle. (2) Specification adequacy is audited over 14 refinement cycles against the source code before implementation. (3) Code/specification consistency is audited over 17 verification cycles against the frozen specification, with convergence accepted only after two consecutive verification passes return zero findings. (4) Behavioural conformance is checked across the first and roughly thirty later sessions against the specified target behaviour. (5) Transparency is provided by publishing the full specification and raw session logs for independent inspection and consistency checking.

items.title: Specification-first convergence with an AI coding agent: a case study of dismantling a core architectural invariant across 189 files in a 717k-line codebase with no test oracle and no human code review
items.abstract: This paper reports a single, fully instrumented case study of a large-scale architectural refactoring by an AI coding agent under a specification-first protocol, with no human review of the generated code and no pre-existing oracle to validate the target behaviour. The task, dismantling a central invariant across a large interdependent codebase, was assessed by the author as effectively infeasible through incremental refactoring, the kind of change that conventionally calls for a rewrite instead. Under the protocol described here, the agent completed it successfully. The system is a 717,725-line production TypeScript application across 3,648 files. The task required dismantling a core lifetime invariant: the guarantee that a UI panel remains open for the duration of an AI request. The target behaviour was that a streaming generation survives the closing of its panel and can be reattached, on reopening, to the same live stream with no loss or duplication. The protocol: formal specification by the agent, 14 refinement cycles auditing that specification against the source code, atomic implementation, a compile/test feedback loop, then 17 verification cycles auditing the code against the frozen specification. Across 31 audit passes, 201 defects were corrected before any human executed the program. The convergence criterion was empirical: two consecutive verification passes returning zero findings. The change touched 189 files (31 new); with the extraction phase, the two commits total 288 files, 34,770 insertions, 16,422 deletions. Across the first and roughly thirty later sessions, the software behaved as specified, no bug observed. Elapsed: three days; cost: USD 2,430. The full specification and raw session logs, 1,500+ pages in French, are published as evidence, allowing inspection of the process and submission to a language model for consistency checking.

schema.problem: Existing repository-level code completion benchmarks focus almost exclusively on software code and largely overlook hardware description languages.
schema.motivation: Strong LLM performance on code completion in general-purpose programming languages makes repository-level evaluation in hardware description languages a timely next step.
schema.proposed_approach: The work constructs a benchmark with training and evaluation splits for repository-level multilingual hardware code completion. It targets completion tasks across three major hardware design coding styles. Each completion target is annotated with code-structure-level and hardware-oriented semantic labels derived from concrete syntax tree analysis.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the coverage and annotation claims is the benchmark construction itself, including concrete syntax tree-derived labels. Evidence for the adequacy claim is a comprehensive evaluation of models on the evaluation split and subsequent analysis. The abstract does not specify the models, baselines, metrics, or a failure condition.

items.title: MHRC-Bench: A Multilingual Hardware Repository-Level Code Completion benchmark
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on code completion tasks in general-purpose programming languages. However, existing repository-level code completion benchmarks focus almost exclusively on software code and largely overlook hardware description languages. In this work, we present \textbf{MHRC-Bench}, consisting of \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Train} and \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Eval}, the first benchmark designed for multilingual hardware code completion at the repository level. Our benchmark targets completion tasks and covers three major hardware design coding styles. Each completion target is annotated with code-structure-level and hardware-oriented semantic labels derived from concrete syntax tree analysis. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of models on MHRC-Bench-Eval. Comprehensive evaluation results and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of MHRC-Bench.

schema.problem: Current multi-LoRA serving engines are built for hot/cold task routing and static adapters, and do not model population-level cultural-evolution simulations in which tens to hundreds of fine-tuned agents share a static prefix, interact densely over many generations, and refit adapters every generation; the natural one-adapter-per-agent implementation consequently duplicates prefix KV storage and invalidates caches across refits.
schema.motivation: As LLM cultural-evolution research shifts from probing single models to running population simulations, efficiently serving many fine-tuned agents over generations would avoid the cost and cache invalidation of current engines and allow larger populations and more generations for the scientific measurements these experiments produce.
schema.proposed_approach: Prefill the shared prefix once with the base model and store, per agent, only the rank-r features needed to reconstruct that agent's K/V as base KV plus a low-rank adapter correction; this reduces per-agent cache from Θ(2d L) to Θ(2r L) per token and the adapter contribution to prefill compute from a d² pass to rank-r matmuls. Because multi-layer LoRA perturbs the hidden states feeding later layers, the reconstruction is approximate. The engine also includes a cache versioned by generation, invalidated by adapter lineage and measured drift, and a scheduler over the agent interaction graph that keeps lineage prefixes resident.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the fidelity claim, the decisive evaluation is an error-compounding test: an exact engine and the approximate engine run the same population experiment from the same seeds over many generations, and the comparison asks whether the approximate evolutionary trajectories diverge more than seed-to-seed variation does; the outputs measured are semantic diversity, transmission drift, and compositionality over 20 generations. (2) The implied failure condition is that approximate trajectories diverging beyond the seed-to-seed noise band, or those measured outputs falling outside that band, would falsify the fidelity claim. (3) For the scalability claim, the evidence is agent capacity and episodes-per-GPU-hour as M grows, testing close-to-linear scaling; the abstract does not state what compute, parameter, or precision controls are held fixed for that test.

items.title: LineageKV: Base-Anchored Delta-KV Serving for Population-Scale Cultural Transmission Experiments with LoRA Agent Societies
items.abstract: Cultural-evolution research with LLMs has moved from probing a single model's cultural knowledge to running populations: iterated-learning chains, transmission bottlenecks, and multi-agent cultural simulations in which tens to hundreds of agents, each a fine-tuned variant of one base model, repeatedly transmit text to one another over many generations. The natural implementation — one LoRA adapter per agent on a shared base model — is a serving workload that current multi-LoRA engines do not model: a static population-wide prefix that every agent must prefill with its own weights (M-fold KV duplication), a dense interaction graph rather than a hot/cold task-routing graph, and adapters that are re-fit every generation, invalidating caches. We propose LineageKV, a serving engine whose core mechanism is base-anchored delta KV: prefill the shared prefix once with the base model, and store per agent only the rank-r post-A features needed to reconstruct that agent's K/V as k_base + s·B_k(A_k h_base); per-agent cache shrinks from Θ(2d L) to Θ(2r L) per token, and the adapter's contribution to prefill compute from a d² pass to rank-r matmuls. Because multi-layer LoRA perturbs the hidden states feeding later layers, the reconstruction is approximate; our falsifiable claim is that the induced attention-output perturbation, evaluated not on perplexity but on the scientific measurements these experiments exist to produce (semantic diversity, transmission drift, compositionality), stays inside the seed-to-seed noise band over 20 generations, while agent capacity and episodes-per-GPU-hour scale close to linearly in M. We add a generation-versioned cache that invalidates by adapter lineage and measured drift, and an interaction-graph scheduler that keeps lineage prefixes resident. The decisive evaluation is an error-compounding test: exact and approximate engines run the same population experiment for many generations from the same seeds, and we ask whether evolutionary trajectories diverge more than seeds do.

schema.problem: In multi-LLM agent systems using multi-LoRA role specialization, agents share a pretrained backbone but each independently constructs and stores KV caches for the same long tool-augmented trajectories, causing substantial memory and compute overhead; existing KV cache sharing methods largely overlook this multi-LoRA setting.
schema.motivation: Avoiding redundant per-agent cache storage and computation would lower deployment cost for long agentic trajectories while retaining adapter-based specialization.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework decomposes each agent's KV cache into a shared base component derived from pretrained weights and an adapter-dependent component derived from LoRA weights. The base component is shared across agents, and the adapter-dependent component is stored in its inherent low-rank form. An architecture that shares the low-rank cache avoids redundant computations for contexts already processed by other agents, and a custom kernel reorders attention computation to reconstruct adapter contributions at runtime without materializing the low-rank cache to full dimension.
schema.research_plan: (1) No separate evidence protocol is stated for the observation that cache differences are dominated by adapter outputs. (2) Memory reduction and accuracy preservation are evaluated against a non-shared caching baseline on agentic question-answering benchmarks. (3) Throughput and time-to-first-token latency are compared against fully shared caching. The abstract states no explicit failure thresholds or held-matched compute budgets.

items.title: LRAgent: Efficient KV Cache Sharing for Multi-LoRA LLM Agents
items.abstract: Role specialization in multi-LLM agent systems is often realized via multi-LoRA, where agents share a pretrained backbone and differ only by lightweight adapters. Despite sharing base model weights, each agent independently builds and stores its own KV cache for the same long, tool-augmented trajectories, incurring substantial memory and compute overhead. Existing KV cache sharing methods largely overlook this multi-LoRA setting. We observe that, cache differences across agents are dominated by adapter outputs, while activations from the shared pretrained backbone remain highly similar. Based on this observation, we propose LRAgent, a KV cache sharing framework for multi-LoRA agents. It decomposes the cache into two components, a shared base component derived from pretrained weights and an adapter-dependent component derived from LoRA weights. LRAgent reduces memory overhead by sharing the base component across agents and storing the adapter component in its inherent low-rank form. It also reduces computational overhead by sharing the low-rank cache, enabled by a shared-A multi-LoRA architecture. This avoids redundant computations for contexts that have already been processed by other agents. To efficiently reconstruct adapter contributions at runtime, we introduce Flash-LoRA-Attention, a kernel that reorders attention computation to avoid materializing the low-rank cache to full dimension. LRAgent achieves throughput and time-to-first-token latency close to fully shared caching, while preserving accuracy near the non-shared caching baseline across agentic question-answering benchmarks.

schema.problem: Under load, reasoning LLM serving lacks a way to treat thinking-token budgets as a shared finite resource: scheduler-level SLO systems treat output length as an exogenous stochastic quantity, while reasoning-efficiency systems optimize thinking length per request in isolation, assuming each request can spend its individually optimal amount.
schema.motivation: Because thinking-token length is the dominant knob for both accuracy and latency, and its marginal accuracy return collapses under load, cross-request allocation can convert capacity shortage into graceful accuracy degradation instead of SLO violations or dropped requests.
schema.proposed_approach: The serving controller allocates thinking-token budgets across concurrent requests under end-to-end latency SLOs. It estimates each request's accuracy-vs-thinking-tokens curve at runtime by probing for answer-stabilization plateaus, then runs a marginal-value allocation that grants budget to requests with the highest unharvested accuracy gain per unit of decode time until their deadlines bind. It is implemented on a budget-elastic reasoning model that remains accurate when thinking is truncated at tranche boundaries.
schema.research_plan: The work evaluates the controller on a mixed-difficulty reasoning workload under arrival rates that cross the full-thinking saturation point, using a budget-elastic reasoning model. Evidence for the main comparative claim comes from holding end-to-end SLO attainment fixed and comparing accuracy against per-request early exit, difficulty-adaptive budgeting, and SLO schedulers; the claim fails if cross-request allocation does not produce a measurable accuracy margin over the per-request-optimal schemes.

items.title: Thinking Budgets Are a Contention Resource: Congestion-Aware Reasoning-Length Control for SLO-Bound LLM Serving
items.abstract: o1-style reasoning LLMs turn every request into a variable, quality-bearing workload: the number of thinking tokens the model spends is the single dominant knob determining both accuracy and latency. Today's serving systems treat that knob in one of two disconnected ways: scheduler-level SLO systems treat output length as an exogenous stochastic quantity to predict and serve, while reasoning-efficiency systems (early exit, budget training) optimize thinking length per request in isolation, assuming the request can always spend its individually optimal amount. Neither side exploits the fact that under load, thinking tokens are a shared finite resource whose marginal accuracy return collapses past each request's answer-stabilization plateau . We propose a serving controller that allocates thinking-token budgets across concurrent requests under end-to-end latency SLOs, converting capacity shortage into a measurable, graceful accuracy degradation instead of SLO violations or dropped requests. The system estimates each request's accuracy-vs-thinking-tokens curve at runtime via plateau probing, then runs a marginal-value allocation that gives budget to requests with the highest unharvested accuracy gain per unit of decode time until their deadlines bind. We implement this on a budget-elastic reasoning model that remains accurate when thinking is truncated at any tranche boundary , and evaluate against per-request early exit, difficulty-adaptive budgeting, and SLO schedulers on a mixed-difficulty reasoning workload under arrival rates that cross the full-thinking saturation point. The falsifiable claim: at fixed SLO attainment, congestion-aware cross-request budget allocation beats every per-request-optimal scheme by a measurable accuracy margin — because per-request optimality cannot capture the congestion shadow price that couples all requests.

schema.problem: Inference-time scaling improves LLM performance, but real deployments have strict computational budgets, and it is not well formulated how to allocate a finite global budget across a stream of queries to maximize aggregate reasoning performance.
schema.motivation: Under tight computational budgets, principled global allocation can avoid wasting compute on queries that cannot be solved and direct it to queries that are near solvability, improving cost-accuracy tradeoffs.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach formulates inference budget allocation as a global constrained optimization problem. It models each query's reasoning utility with a utility function that rises sharply after a query-specific threshold and derives an optimal allocation policy from a global shadow price that equalizes marginal utility under the resource constraint. The resulting procedure abandons queries deemed unable to benefit and reallocates their budget to solvable queries near their emergence thresholds.
schema.research_plan: The theoretical claim is supported by deriving the optimal allocation policy from the stated utility model. The empirical claims are supported by experiments on several reasoning tasks with different traffic streams, measuring total token cost versus mean accuracy and comparing against uniform allocation. The resource-scarce claim is evaluated by comparing global accuracy to uniform allocation under resource-scarce regimes. The abstract does not state ablation conditions, matched compute, or a pre-specified failure condition.

items.title: The Shadow Price of Reasoning: Economic Perspective on Optimal Budget Allocation for LLMs
items.abstract: Inference-time scaling has emerged as a critical avenue for enhancing Large Language Models' performance, yet real-world deployment is constrained by strict computational budgets. In this work, we formulate inference budget allocation as a global constrained optimization problem governed by economic principles. By modeling per-query reasoning utility with a shifted-surge function, we derive an optimal allocation policy based on a global shadow price that equilibrates marginal utility under resource scarcity. Based on this theory, we propose Constrained Latent-utility Equilibrium Allocation for Reasoning (CLEAR). It performs rational abandonment and reallocates resources from insolvent queries to solvable queries near their emergence thresholds. Extensive experiments on several reasoning tasks with different traffic streams demonstrate that CLEAR significantly improves the Pareto frontier of total token cost versus mean accuracy. In resource-scarce regimes, CLEAR achieves up to a 3x improvement in global accuracy compared to uniform allocation.

schema.problem: KV-cache memory grows linearly with sequence length and dominates long-context LLM inference, while existing work on KV-cache pruning, precision quantization, and adaptive budgeting remains largely decoupled.
schema.motivation: Jointly optimizing token retention and precision assignment can reduce KV-cache memory and enable longer-context serving under GPU constraints.
schema.proposed_approach: The system predicts per-token attention importance at inference time using lightweight attention logits, retains tokens based on that importance, and assigns mixed-precision quantization (INT2, INT4, INT8) to retained tokens according to importance rank. A feedback loop adjusts layer budgets dynamically in response to memory pressure.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on LongBench and L-Eval compare the proposed system against baseline quantization, measuring KV-cache memory reduction and accuracy; support requires memory reduction with accuracy maintained, and failure would be accuracy degradation at comparable memory.

items.title: Attention-Guided Mixed-Precision KV-Cache Management for Long-Context LLM Inference
items.abstract: Efficient long-context LLM inference requires careful management of the KV-cache, which grows linearly with sequence length and dominates memory consumption. While recent work has explored KV-cache pruning, precision quantization, and adaptive budgeting independently, they remain largely decoupled. We propose ATTUNE, a system that jointly optimizes token retention and precision assignment by predicting per-token attention importance and allocating dynamic layer-wise memory budgets. ATTUNE uses lightweight attention logits to estimate token importance at inference time, then assigns mixed-precision quantization (INT2, INT4, INT8) to retained tokens based on their importance rank. A feedback loop adjusts layer budgets dynamically in response to memory pressure. Experiments on long-context benchmarks (LongBench, L-Eval) show ATTUNE achieves 3–4× KV-cache memory reduction relative to baseline quantization while maintaining accuracy, enabling longer-context serving under GPU constraints.

schema.problem: Most existing KV cache compression methods rely on either quantization or eviction alone based on importance estimation, and are limited by coarse compression choices and inaccurate importance assessment, leading to suboptimal inference quality in long-context settings.
schema.motivation: Reducing KV cache memory overhead while preserving inference quality under strict memory budgets is valuable for long-context LLM serving, and automatic per-element compression decisions could remove the low-level tuning burden from end users.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework combines quantization and eviction in a hybrid KV cache compression scheme. It offers fine-grained compression options that adapt smoothly to the varying importance of cached key-value pairs. An integrated optimizer automatically chooses the best compression action for each cached element, maximizing quality while insulating end users from low-level tuning. A joint key-value importance metric drives the optimizer's decisions, and flexible conversion policies across multiple quantization precision levels reduce quality degradation.
schema.research_plan: Experimental evaluation compares the framework's output quality under matched memory constraints against state-of-the-art KV cache compression alternatives.

items.title: HqeKV: Towards Hybrid Quantization and Eviction for KV Cache in Long-Context LLM Inference
items.abstract: The autoregressive inference in large language models requires repeated computation across transformer layers.While caching intermediate key-value (KV) pairs eliminates redundancy, it introduces severe memory overhead, particularly in long-context settings.Most existing cache compression methods operate solely on either quantization or eviction, based on importance estimation of cached data.However, they are limited by coarse compression choices and inaccurate importance assessment, leading to suboptimal inference quality.To address this, we propose HqeKV, a hybrid compression framework built on both quantization and eviction, offering finer-grained compression options that adapt smoothly to the varying importance of cached KV pairs.An integrated optimizer automatically selects the best compression action for each cached element, maximizing quality while insulating end-users from tedious low-level tuning details.We further design a joint K-V importance metric to provide more accurate importance assessment results so that the optimizer can make smarter decisions.Additionally, HqeKV supports flexible conversion policies across multiple quantization precision levels, to further reduce quality degradation.Extensive experiments show that HqeKV improves output quality under the same memory constraints, outperforming stateof-the-art alternatives.Code is available at https://github.com/skywclouds/HqeKV.

schema.problem: Existing privacy mechanisms for multi-tenant LLM inference, such as those preventing timing side-channels from KV-cache sharing, incur significant latency and throughput overhead.
schema.motivation: Safe and selective KV-cache sharing could reduce this overhead if formal privacy guarantees and quantifiable privacy-utility-efficiency trade-offs can be maintained.
schema.proposed_approach: A joint privacy-efficiency optimization framework uses differential privacy noise injection on attention patterns to decouple privacy enforcement from memory management. It comprises a differential-privacy-aware cache replacement policy, a privacy-preserving attention computation strategy, and a runtime scheduler that maximizes throughput under differential privacy budgets. The design enables selective and safe KV-cache sharing across inference requests.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on multi-tenant LLM serving compare the framework against full cache isolation, measuring throughput, ε-DP privacy guarantees, and downstream-task accuracy. Support would be higher throughput while maintaining formal privacy guarantees and no downstream accuracy loss; failure would be violating the privacy guarantee or degrading accuracy. The abstract does not state matched compute/parameters or ablation conditions.

items.title: Privacy-Efficient KV-Cache Management for Multi-Tenant LLM Inference
items.abstract: Private LLM inference in multi-tenant settings faces a fundamental efficiency challenge: mechanisms that prevent privacy attacks (such as timing side-channels from KV-cache sharing) incur significant latency and throughput overhead. We propose DP-KVCache, a joint privacy-efficiency optimization framework that uses differential privacy to enable selective and safe KV-cache sharing across inference requests while meeting formal privacy guarantees. Unlike prior work that achieves privacy through isolation (SafeKV) or MPC-compatibility (MPCache), DP-KVCache uses differential privacy noise injection on attention patterns to decouple privacy enforcement from memory management, enabling fine-grained cache reuse with quantifiable privacy-utility-efficiency trade-offs. We co-design a DP-aware cache replacement policy, a privacy-preserving attention computation strategy, and a runtime scheduler that maximizes throughput under differential privacy budgets. Experiments on multi-tenant LLM serving show 1.5–2.2× throughput improvements over full cache isolation while maintaining ε-DP privacy guarantees, with no accuracy loss on downstream tasks.

schema.problem: Unrestricted cross-user KV cache sharing in LLM serving introduces side-channel vulnerabilities that allow an adversary to infer user inputs by probing for cache reuse, while existing defenses disable sharing entirely and thereby forgo reuse of privacy-irrelevant prompt segments.
schema.motivation: Prompts often include large privacy-irrelevant portions such as system instructions or publicly accessible material, so enabling fine-grained reuse of only non-sensitive KV entries can preserve much of the sharing benefit while preventing leakage.
schema.proposed_approach: A privacy-aware KV cache sharing mechanism that performs token-level cache management, deriving reusable KV segments via sensitivity masking and retrieving them over variable-length spans. It is implemented as an extension on top of the vLLM serving system. The design centers on two components: deriving reusable segments accurately and efficiently, and retrieving variable-length reusable spans efficiently.
schema.research_plan: The mechanism is implemented on vLLM and evaluated on three datasets. The security claim is tested by checking for direct leakage through KV-cache reuse side channels, and the performance claims are tested by measuring time-to-first-token and cache hit rate against state-of-the-art approaches. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched-control settings for the comparison.

items.title: CachePrune: Privacy-Aware and Fine-Grained KV Cache Sharing for Efficient LLM Inference
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Key-Value (KV) caching to accelerate inference, and many serving systems further share the KV cache across users' requests to reduce redundant computation. While widely adopted, unrestricted cross-user sharing introduces side-channel vulnerabilities, allowing an adversary to infer user inputs by probing for cache reuse. Existing defenses disable sharing entirely to prevent leakage; yet such a coarse-grained strategy sacrifices substantial reuse potential, since prompts often include large portions of privacy-irrelevant segments, such as system instructions or publicly accessible materials. Building on this, we present CachePrune, a privacy-aware KV cache sharing mechanism that enables fine-grained reuse of KV entries across requests. Realizing such fine granularity requires token-level cache management, as reusable segments vary in length and position due to sensitivity masking, making reuse more complex than the fixed-size or sentence-level chunking used in existing coarse-grained schemes. Specifically, CachePrune makes fine-grained reuse practical by addressing two key challenges: accurately and efficiently deriving reusable KV segments and efficiently retrieving them over variable-length spans. We implement CachePrune on top of vLLM and evaluate it on three datasets, showing that it eliminates direct leakage through KV cache reuse side channels while reducing TTFT by 4.5x and increasing cache hit rates by 44% compared with state-of-the-art approaches.

schema.problem: In disaggregated LLM serving, transferring large KV caches between prefill and decode nodes introduces substantial latency and network bandwidth bottlenecks. Existing KV cache compression and eviction techniques target local GPU memory or single-node offloading, while current disaggregated transport frameworks treat KV cache payloads as uncompressed raw tensors or apply static, uniform compression.
schema.motivation: Adapting compression and transfer decisions to real-time network bandwidth and downstream task sensitivity can reduce transfer overhead and congestion while preserving generation quality, making the throughput benefits of disaggregated inference more attainable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework provides network-aware adaptive KV cache compression and co-designed transfer for disaggregated LLM serving. It dynamically co-optimizes on-the-fly KV cache quantization/compression ratios and transfer schedules based on real-time network bandwidth availability and downstream task sensitivity. Bandwidth-adaptive lossy compression is integrated directly into the prefill-to-decode serialization pipeline.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the framework experimentally against state-of-the-art disaggregated serving baselines, measuring transfer overhead and end-to-end request throughput. It also assesses preservation of generation quality under the bandwidth-adaptive compression.

items.title: NetCo: Network-Aware Adaptive KV Cache Compression and Co-Designed Transfer for Disaggregated LLM Serving
items.abstract: Disaggregated LLM inference, which separates prefill and decode phases across distinct GPU nodes, significantly improves overall hardware utilization and reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT). However, transferring large KV caches over the network between prefill and decode nodes introduces substantial latency and network bandwidth bottlenecks, often negating the throughput benefits of disaggregation. Existing KV cache compression and eviction techniques focus primarily on saving local GPU memory or single-node offloading, while current disaggregated transport frameworks treat KV cache payloads as uncompressed raw tensors or apply static, uniform compression. In this paper, we propose NetCo, a network-aware adaptive KV cache compression and co-designed transfer framework for disaggregated LLM serving. NetCo dynamically co-optimizes on-the-fly KV cache quantization/compression ratios and transfer schedules based on real-time network bandwidth availability and downstream task sensitivity. By integrating bandwidth-adaptive lossy compression directly into the prefill-to-decode serialization pipeline, NetCo minimizes transfer latency and alleviates network congestion while preserving generation quality. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that NetCo substantially reduces transfer overhead and improves end-to-end request throughput compared to state-of-the-art disaggregated serving baselines.

schema.problem: In prefill-decode disaggregated serving, prefill workers produce a KV cache that must be transferred to decode workers on different physical systems; this transfer is a significant bottleneck for serving LLMs at scale, especially for long-input and agentic workloads. Existing lossless codecs are unsuitable because they primarily target offline weight compression, run on CPUs, or use variable-length coding whose compression cannot keep up with KV production during prefill.
schema.motivation: A GPU-friendly lossless compressor matched to prefill throughput would remove the KV transfer bottleneck and improve time-to-first-token and request throughput in disaggregated serving.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed GPU-friendly lossless compressor for KV cache transfer preserves KV tensors bitwise and integrates into existing serving frameworks without modifying model execution. It exploits redundancy in the floating-point exponents of KV activations by encoding frequent exponent values with fixed-length codes and routing rare exponents through a sparse escape stream of (position, value). A calibrated top-16 exponent codebook removes the need for online histogramming, and the regular dense path with sparse escape correction makes both encoding and decoding efficient on GPUs. The implementation is released as open-source code, and the same approach extends to FP8 KV caches.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on real BF16 activation tensors measures compression and decompression throughput against prior lossless compressors on the critical codec path. End-to-end transfer experiments compare transfer speed, time-to-first-token, and request throughput. FP8 KV caches are evaluated for compression relative to native E5M2. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched resource controls.

items.title: SplitZip: Ultra Fast Lossless KV Compression for Disaggregated LLM Serving
