items.abstract: Contemporary systems serving large language models (LLMs) have adopted prefill-decode disaggregation to load-balance between the compute-bound prefill phase and the memory-bound decode phase. Under this design, prefill workers generate a KV cache that must be transferred to decode workers before generation can begin. With these workers residing on different physical systems, this transfer becomes a significant bottleneck to serving LLMs at scale, especially for long-input and agentic workloads. Existing lossless codecs are unsuitable here as they primarily target offline weight compression, run on CPUs, or use variable-length coding whose compression cannot keep up with KV production during prefill. We introduce SplitZip, a GPU-friendly lossless compressor for KV cache transfer that preserves KV tensors bitwise and integrates into existing serving frameworks without modifying model execution. SplitZip exploits redundancy in floating-point exponents of KV activations, encoding frequent exponent values with fixed-length codes and routing rare exponents through a sparse escape stream of (position, value). A calibrated top-16 exponent codebook eliminates online histogramming, while the regular dense path and sparse escape correction make both encoding and decoding efficient on GPUs. On real BF16 activation tensors, SplitZip achieves $613.3$ GB/s compression throughput and $2181.8$ GB/s decompression throughput, outperforming prior lossless compressors on the critical codec path. End-to-end transfer experiments show up to $1.32\times$ speedup for BF16 KV cache transfer, $1.30\times$ speedup for TTFT, and $1.23\times$ increase in Request Throughput. The same approach extends to FP8 KV caches, providing up to $1.14\times$ compression over native E5M2. Code is available at https://github.com/Intelligent-Microsystems-Lab/SplitZip

schema.problem: Existing KV-cache reuse approaches for RAG (e.g., Cache-Craft and CacheBlend) optimize static or single-turn retrieval, but multi-turn RAG sessions involve chunk re-ordering, document substitution, and query reformulation that invalidate prefix matching and cause expensive prefill recomputation.
schema.motivation: RAG systems are increasingly deployed in multi-turn interactive search and conversational settings, making the cost of redundant prefill recomputation a growing concern for serving latency and GPU memory.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework maintains a retrieval provenance graph across conversation turns to track chunk lineage and predict cross-chunk attention shifts. It uses the graph to enable lightweight localized cache correction when retrieved chunks are re-ordered, substituted, or queries are reformulated, rather than full re-execution. The system-algorithm co-design includes a provenance-guided attention approximation kernel and a session-aware cache eviction policy.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on multi-turn RAG benchmarks are designed to measure Time-to-First-Token and GPU memory consumption, with generation quality held as a constraint to ensure it is not sacrificed.

items.title: Dynamic Retrieval-Aware Chunk KV-Cache Orchestration for Multi-Turn RAG Serving
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in multi-turn interactive search and conversational settings, where users progressively refine queries and retrieve overlapping or evolving sets of text chunks. While recent systems like Cache-Craft and CacheBlend optimize KV-cache reuse for static or single-turn retrieval, they fail to handle the complex dynamics of multi-turn search sessions—specifically, chunk re-ordering, document substitution, and query reformulation—which invalidate prefix matching and trigger expensive prefill recomputations. This proposal introduces TurnCache, a dynamic, retrieval-aware KV-cache orchestration framework for multi-turn RAG serving. TurnCache maintains a retrieval provenance graph across conversation turns to track chunk lineage and predict cross-chunk attention shifts, enabling lightweight localized cache correction rather than full re-execution. We outline a system-algorithm co-design featuring a provenance-guided attention approximation kernel and a session-aware cache eviction policy. Experiments on multi-turn RAG benchmarks are designed to demonstrate significant reductions in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and GPU memory consumption without sacrificing generation quality.

schema.problem: RAG systems face prefill efficiency bottlenecks due to attention, and traditional KV caches only accelerate decoding; reusing document-level KV caches across queries and sessions would amortize computation but raises correctness challenges from position and context misalignment.
schema.motivation: Amortizing document-specific prefill computation would remove quadratic complexity and enable faster RAG without changing existing architectures or retraining models.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework reuses document-level KV caches computed in prior sessions during prefill and resolves position misalignment and context misalignment across queries and sessions in multi-document RAG workloads. It includes a theoretical analysis establishing conditions under which multi-document KV cache reuse remains stable and close to full recomputation. The approach is designed to integrate into existing RAG pipelines without architectural changes or model retraining.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the stability and correctness claim, the theoretical analysis establishes conditions under which multi-document KV cache reuse remains stable and close to full recomputation. (2) For the efficiency and accuracy claims, empirical validation is planned beyond standard benchmarks using noise-robustness tests and domain-specific workloads such as legal, checking prefill speedups against task-level performance with no material degradation as the support criterion.

items.title: Thesis Proposal: Efficient KV Cache Reuse for Multi-Document Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems face efficiency bottlenecks in prefill due to attention mechanism, and traditional KV cache only accelerates decoding.In this context, reusing document-level KV cache computed for retrieved documents in previous sessions during the prefill stage appears to be a natural way to amortize computation, but it raises serious correctness challenges due to position and context misalignment across queries and sessions.This research proposes a multi-document KV cache reuse framework for multi-document RAG workloads across queries and sessions to resolve position misalignment and context misalignment, preserving accuracy while eliminating document-specific quadratic complexity in prefill.Theoretical analysis will establish conditions under which multidocument KV cache reuse remains stable and close to full recomputation, providing principled guarantees for both efficiency and accuracy.These results will enable deployment in existing RAG pipelines without architectural changes or model retraining.Crucially, to ensure robustness in real-world deployments, validation will extend beyond standard benchmarks to include noise-robustness tests and domain-specific workloads (e.g., legal).The research aims to empirically confirm these guarantees and demonstrate that substantial prefill speedups can be achieved without materially degrading task-level performance.

schema.problem: For Mixture-of-Experts speculative decoding under memory pressure, verification cost is position-dependent and submodular in the experts fired, including staging bytes and all-to-all volume, so selecting drafts for expected acceptance alone is latency-suboptimal.
schema.motivation: Serving large Mixture-of-Experts targets under memory constraints requires staging experts from host memory; making verification cost-aware avoids wasted expert staging and all-to-all traffic, improving tokens per output time for offloaded serving.
schema.proposed_approach: Before each verification round, the policy predicts each draft position's acceptance probability from a target-conditioned entropy bound and its marginal verification latency from a cheap router-cost probe plus profiled per-expert byte/latency tables with incremental union accounting. It then truncates the draft to the prefix maximizing predicted expected accepted prefix length divided by predicted verification latency. Expert prefetching follows the chosen prefix, jointly determined by truncation rather than prefetching the full draft.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the central tokens-per-output-time claim, evaluate the proposed policy against acceptance-optimal multi-draft verification and entropy-only draft-length policies on offloaded Mixture-of-Experts serving workloads in single-node validation, measuring tokens per output time. (2) For the cost-awareness claim, run an all-experts-GPU-resident ablation where the measured advantage must collapse to zero; this zero-delta endpoint is the falsification condition for confounded cost-awareness. (3) Defer comparison of the contention term against serving grids to follow-up work.

items.title: Cost-Aware Verification Budgeting for Speculative Decoding of MoE LLMs under Partial Expert Residency
items.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates LLM inference by drafting multiple tokens with a cheap model and verifying them in parallel against the target model. For dense targets, a verification round has approximately uniform cost, so maximizing the expected number of accepted tokens per round is a good proxy for maximizing wall-clock throughput. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) targets under memory pressure — where only a subset of experts is GPU-resident and the rest must be staged from host memory — the cost of verifying a draft is a submodular union over the experts the router fires across draft positions, plus per-expert staging bytes and all-to-all volume; the marginal cost of each additional draft position depends on which experts are still cold and how much of the expert pool the already-drafted prefix has touched. We argue that acceptance-optimal verification is therefore latency-suboptimal for MoE SD, and propose a cost-aware verification-budgeting policy that, before issuing the verification round, predicts (i) the acceptance probability of each draft position via a target-conditioned entropy bound, and (ii) the marginal verification latency of each position via a cheap router-cost probe plus profiled per-expert byte/latency tables with incremental union accounting, then truncates the draft to the prefix n* = argmax_n E[L_n]/t(n), where E[L_n] is the predicted expected accepted prefix length and t(n) the predicted verification latency. The decision jointly determines which experts to prefetch, so prefetching follows the chosen prefix rather than the full draft. Our central falsifiable claim is that this policy strictly improves tokens-per-output-time (TPOT) over acceptance-optimal multi-draft verification and entropy-only draft-length policies on offloaded MoE serving workloads, while its measured advantage must collapse to zero when all experts are GPU-resident — a zero-delta endpoint we enforce as an ablation, so the protocol itself falsifies any confounded cost-awareness claim. Scope: single-node validation first, with the contention term compared against serving grids in follow-up work.

schema.problem: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by verifying multiple draft candidates in parallel, but this advantage weakens for sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models because different draft-tree branches activate different experts, expanding the union of activated experts and increasing target-side verification cost.
schema.motivation: Reducing target-side verification cost would preserve the parallel-verification advantage of speculative decoding for sparse MoE serving and avoid unnecessary expert activations.
schema.proposed_approach: The method truncates the draft tree before target verification and retains only the cost-effective prefix. It uses fine-grained drafter signals to estimate candidate benefit and combines this estimate with offline-profiled target-side verification cost. The approach requires no training and no hyperparameter tuning, maintains lossless decoding, and is integrated with the SGLang graph-based serving framework.
schema.research_plan: The method is evaluated on diverse MoE backbones and benchmarks. Experiments compare decoding speed against autoregressive decoding and the state-of-the-art baseline EAGLE-3, and measure reduction in unnecessary expert activations during verification. Support would be consistent speedups across backbones and benchmarks with reduced expert activations; failure would be no speedup or degradation of output quality relative to the lossless claim.

items.title: Making Every Verified Token Count: Adaptive Verification for MoE Speculative Decoding
items.abstract: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by verifying multiple draft candidates in parallel, but this advantage weakens for sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. As the draft tree grows, different branches activate different experts, expanding the union of activated experts and substantially increasing target-side verification cost. We propose EVICT, a training-free, hyperparameter-free, and lossless adaptive verification method for MoE speculative decoding. EVICT makes every verified token count by truncating the draft tree before target verification and retaining only the cost-effective prefix. It leverages fine-grained drafter signals to estimate candidate benefit, combines them with offline-profiled verification cost, and remains highly compatible with the high-performance graph-based serving framework SGLang. Extensive experiments on diverse MoE backbones and benchmarks show that EVICT achieves up to 2.35x speedup over autoregressive decoding and an average 1.21x speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline EAGLE-3, while significantly reducing unnecessary expert activations during verification.

schema.problem: KV cache compression is split into quantizers that preserve every token at reduced precision but cap attainable compression, and structural pruners that drop tokens outright, leaving the attention softmax on a heavily biased subset of context and surrendering much of full-cache accuracy even at modest retention.
schema.motivation: A mechanism that recovers most of the accuracy gap left by token-retention methods at very low KV-cache memory would make low-memory long-context serving practical without the bias of hard eviction.
schema.proposed_approach: When tokens are evicted from a layer's KV cache, they are aggregated with the model's own attention weights into a small number of super-token K/V pairs that serve as moment-preserving sketch tokens; these tokens carry an unbiased approximation of the evicted mass into every future softmax. The mechanism replaces hard eviction, is agnostic to the saliency policy, and slots into existing page-centric layouts and serving systems that place, compress, and evict caches across tiers. The construction targets operation at under 1% of total KV-cache memory.
schema.research_plan: Two falsifiable claims are tested on standard long-context benchmarks: (1) at equal byte budgets, the proposed method beats token-retention baselines by a positive margin across retention levels; (2) the sketch layer's value saturates as its byte share grows. Support requires a positive margin against token-retention baselines at matched byte budgets, and non-decreasing then saturating value from the sketch layer as more bytes are allocated to it; failure is the absence of such a margin or saturation. Comparisons are made against token-retention baselines and full-cache performance on standard long-context benchmarks.

items.title: SketchKV: Moment-Preserving Sketch Tokens for Softmax-Calibrated Extreme KV Cache Compression
items.abstract: KV cache compression research has split into two families — quantizers that preserve every token at reduced precision but cap the attainable compression, and structural pruners that drop tokens outright, leaving the attention softmax to operate on a heavily biased subset of the context and surrendering a large fraction of full-cache accuracy even at modest retention. We propose SketchKV, a third mechanism that replaces hard eviction with moment-preserving sketch tokens: when tokens are evicted from a layer's KV cache, they are aggregated with the model's own attention weights into a small number of super-token K/V pairs that carry an unbiased approximation of the evicted mass into every future softmax. SketchKV targets the explicit accuracy gap that token-retention methods concede (e.g., DynamicKV keeps 1.7% of the cache at only ~85% of full-cache LongBench performance), aiming to recover a majority of that gap at under 1% of total KV-cache memory. The construction is agnostic to the saliency policy, slots into existing page-centric layouts, and flows naturally into serving systems that already place, compress, and evict caches across tiers. We define concrete falsifiable claims: at equal byte budgets, SketchKV must beat token-retention baselines by a positive margin across retention levels, and the sketch layer must saturate in value as its byte share grows, both testable with standard long-context benchmarks.

schema.problem: The key-value cache is the primary memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference; existing eviction methods permanently discard tokens and degrade when a discarded token later proves essential, while quantization methods retain all tokens at low precision but offer limited compression.
schema.motivation: Compressing the cache without discarding tokens would preserve full-context fidelity while reducing memory cost for long-context inference.
schema.proposed_approach: The cache is represented by a small set of anchors stored exactly; every other token is expressed through its most similar anchor, and only those approximated tokens whose approximation most affects the model's output are refined. The scheme compresses the cache without discarding any token.
schema.research_plan: (1) The no-discard compression claim is demonstrated by the representation design itself. (2) The accuracy-preservation claim is tested by comparing the method's scores against full-cache inference across multiple models and datasets, including a 70B-parameter setting; significant accuracy degradation relative to the full cache is the implied failure condition.

items.title: AnchorKV: Anchor-Residual KV Cache Compression
items.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache is the primary memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference. Existing approaches attack it from opposite ends: eviction methods permanently discard tokens, degrading performance whenever a discarded token later proves essential, while quantization methods retain all tokens at low precision but offer limited compression. We propose AnchorKV, a compression scheme that shrinks the cache by $20\times$ without discarding a single token. AnchorKV represents the cache using a small set of anchors stored exactly, expresses every other token through its most similar anchor, and refines only those whose approximation most affects the model's output. AnchorKV consistently preserves accuracy across models and datasets, retaining 99% of the full-cache score at the 70B scale, while keeping the entire context at a fraction of its cost.

schema.problem: Large language models rely on KV caches for efficient inference, but the growing demand for longer context lengths creates significant memory bottlenecks. Existing KV cache compression techniques are mostly model-specific or rely on heuristics, limiting their adaptability and generalizability across different models and tasks.
schema.motivation: Longer context lengths make KV-cache memory increasingly costly, so a general compression method that reduces memory while preserving inference accuracy across models and tasks is valuable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework develops a model-agnostic dynamic KV-cache compression method that adjusts compression based on model sensitivity to KV-cache loss. It uses a unified utility function to quantify the trade-off between memory reduction and inference accuracy, and optimizes KV cache allocation for each layer and task. The framework is intended for evaluation on a wide range of long-context tasks and LLMs.
schema.research_plan: Evidence consists of evaluation across a wide range of long-context tasks and LLMs, using metrics of latency, throughput, and memory consumption; the stated goal is state-of-the-art performance, though no baselines, ablations, or explicit failure conditions are named.

items.title: AdaptiveKV: A Model-Agnostic Framework for Dynamic KV-Cache Compression in LLMs
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely heavily on Key-Value (KV) cache for efficient inference, but the growing demand for longer context lengths has led to significant memory bottlenecks. While KV cache compression techniques have been proposed, most existing methods are either model-specific or rely on heuristics, limiting their adaptability and generalizability across different models and tasks. This proposal introduces AdaptiveKV, a model-agnostic framework for dynamic KV-cache compression that adjusts based on model sensitivity to KV-cache loss. By developing a unified utility function that quantifies the trade-off between memory reduction and inference accuracy, AdaptiveKV aims to optimize KV cache allocation for each layer and task, ensuring minimal performance degradation while maximizing memory efficiency. Our approach will be evaluated on a wide range of long-context tasks and LLMs, with the goal of achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of latency, throughput, and memory consumption.

schema.problem: On-device LLM inference is constrained by the memory capacity and bandwidth required by growing key-value (K/V) caches.
schema.motivation: Dedicated mobile video hardware is available in mobile SoCs and may offload memory and I/O pressure from CPU/GPU resources.
schema.proposed_approach: The project characterizes K/V-cache tensor distributions across models and tasks, develops lossless and controlled-lossy HEVC-compatible compression methods for VPU acceleration and disk offloading, and evaluates them using GPU servers and a mobile SoC testbed. Key metrics include compression ratio, reconstruction fidelity, model accuracy, encode/decode throughput, storage capacity, latency, and energy consumption. Reproducibility is supported through versioned code, configurations, manifests, random seeds, software versions, and machine-readable results.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation uses GPU servers and a mobile SoC testbed to measure compression ratio, reconstruction fidelity, model accuracy, encode/decode throughput, storage capacity, latency, and energy consumption. (1) The claim that mobile video hardware can reduce CPU/GPU memory and I/O pressure without unacceptable quality degradation is examined across K/V-cache tensor distributions from different models and tasks. The implied failure condition is unacceptable quality degradation or no reduction in memory and I/O pressure. Reproducibility is supported by versioned code, configurations, manifests, random seeds, software versions, and machine-readable results.

items.title: Magician: VPU-Accelerated KV Cache Disk Offloading for On-Device Large Language Model Inference
items.abstract: On-device LLM inference is constrained by the memory capacity and bandwidth required by growing key-value (K/V) caches. Magician investigates VPU-accelerated compression and disk offloading for K/V-cache data. It characterizes tensor distributions across models and tasks, develops lossless and controlled-lossy HEVC-compatible compression methods, and evaluates them using GPU servers and a mobile SoC testbed. Key metrics include compression ratio, reconstruction fidelity, model accuracy, encode/decode throughput, storage capacity, latency, and energy consumption. The project aims to determine when dedicated mobile video hardware can reduce CPU/GPU memory and I/O pressure without unacceptable quality degradation. Reproducibility is supported through versioned code, configurations, manifests, random seeds, software versions, and machine-readable results.

schema.problem: LLM inference serving workloads are heterogeneous and unpredictable, and current serving approaches may not achieve optimal end-to-end efficiency or low latency.
schema.motivation: Optimizing end-to-end efficiency, reducing latency, and improving handling of heterogeneous and unpredictable requests would make LLM inference serving more effective.
schema.proposed_approach: A hybrid scheduling framework for LLM inference serving that integrates learning-based request length prediction with dynamic resource allocation.
schema.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated using real-world datasets and performance metrics; no specific baselines, metrics, or held-matched conditions are stated.

items.title: Efficient LLM Inference Serving with Adaptive Scheduling and Learning-Based Request Length Prediction
items.abstract: This proposal aims to develop a novel hybrid scheduling framework for Large Language Model (LLM) inference serving, integrating learning-based request length prediction with dynamic resource allocation. The goal is to optimize end-to-end efficiency, reduce latency, and improve the handling of heterogeneous and unpredictable requests. The proposed framework will be evaluated using real-world datasets and performance metrics.

schema.problem: Under cloud-native high-concurrency, multi-tenant deployment, LLM inference services exhibit large differences in input length, long autoregressive generation, high KV cache usage, GPU memory pressure, and request queue fluctuation, which cause increased average and tail latency, uneven GPU resource utilization, and inefficient model replica scheduling.
schema.motivation: The move to cloud-native high-concurrency deployment for enterprise LLM services makes tail latency and GPU utilization pressing operational constraints, while service mesh governance and centralized model pooling capabilities make it tractable to address these issues.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses a service mesh for service discovery, distributed tracing, rate limiting and circuit breaking, and canary routing. A central model pool manages model instances, GPU resources, queue status, and model versions. The resource-aware scheduling algorithm operates within this pool to identify request features, score instance status, split long and short requests, and perform dynamic scaling.
schema.research_plan: Simulation experiments construct scenarios with different concurrency levels, burst traffic, and instance failures, and compare the proposed scheduling with round-robin, least-connections, and Kubernetes HPA scheduling on average response time, P95/P99 tail latency, GPU utilization, and system throughput. (1) The stability/scalability claim is supported by behavior under these stress and failure scenarios, and would fail if the framework degrades under them. (2) The scheduling improvement claim is supported by head-to-head comparisons under the same simulated conditions, and would fail if it does not match or exceed the baselines on the measured metrics.

items.title: A High-Concurrency Inference Service Framework for Large Language Models Based on Service Mesh and Model Pooling
items.abstract: For applications such as enterprise knowledge question answering, intelligent customer service, code generation, educational question answering, and industryassisted decision-making, large language model inference services are shifting from single-point interface calls to cloudnative, high-concurrency, and multi-tenant deployment models. Compared with traditional deep learning inference services, large language models are characterized by large differences in input length, long autoregressive generation time, high KV cache usage, strong GPU memory pressure, and significant request queue fluctuations. Therefore, under high concurrency conditions, they are prone to problems such as increased average response time, worsened P95/P99 tail latency, uneven GPU resource utilization, and inefficient model replica scheduling. To address these issues, this paper proposes a highconcurrency inference service framework for large language models based on service mesh and model pooling. This framework utilizes a service mesh for service discovery, distributed tracing, rate limiting and circuit breaking, and canary routing governance capabilities. A model pool centrally manages model instances, GPU resources, queue status, and model versions. A model pooling resource-aware scheduling algorithm, MP-RAS, is designed to achieve request feature identification, instance status scoring, long and short request splitting, and dynamic scaling. Simulation experiments construct scenarios with different concurrency levels, burst traffic, and instance failures, and are compared with roundrobin scheduling, least-connections scheduling, and Kubernetes HPA scheduling. Results show that in a scenario with 1000 concurrent requests, the proposed method reduces the average response time to 1.82 s, the P95 latency to 2.94 s, increases the average GPU utilization to 82.4%, and achieves a system throughput of 428 req/s. These results demonstrate that the integration of service mesh and model pooling can provide a more stable, scalable, and manageable high-concurrency service solution for online inference of large language models.

schema.problem: Existing LLM serving schedulers consume output-length or execution-time forecasts but treat them as point estimates, fixed buckets, or input-agnostic min–max intervals, leaving them without calibrated per-request predictive distributions that remain valid under prompt-distribution shift.
schema.motivation: Calibrated posterior predictive distributions would let schedulers explicitly trade SLO violation risk against wasted KV cache, make deadline-aware admission decisions, and sustain SLO goodput when exchangeability-based coverage and fixed intervals fail.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework replaces the forecast layer with an online, sparse, heteroscedastic Gaussian process over prompt features; for each request it maintains a calibrated posterior predictive distribution over remaining output length, combining aleatoric (heteroscedastic noise) and epistemic (distance-to-data) uncertainty and updating after every observed token. A scheduler then consumes the full posterior: KV cache is provisioned at request-specific predictive quantiles chosen by an explicit tradeoff between expected SLO-violation probability and expected wasted memory; admission is granted when the posterior probability of meeting a deadline exceeds a load-dependent threshold; and preemptions are chosen by maximizing expected reduction in SLO-violation probability net of swap/recompute cost. The paper specifies a vLLM-based implementation and an evaluation protocol on ShareGPT/MTBench/production-style traces.
schema.research_plan: The paper specifies an evaluation protocol that compares the proposed scheduler against seven baselines plus a clairvoyant upper bound on ShareGPT/MTBench/production-style traces, using an explicit prompt-distribution-shift protocol. The central falsifiable claim is tested under shift, where success requires sustained calibration and strictly higher SLO goodput than the listed baselines, and under stationary workloads, where success requires matching the best baseline within a small margin at lower wasted KV memory.

items.title: CalibServe: Calibrated Online Gaussian-Process Length Forecasting for Risk-Aware Scheduling of LLM Inference Serving
items.abstract: Modern LLM serving schedulers increasingly consume forecasts of per-request output length or execution time to approximate shortest-job-first (SJF) service, provision KV cache, and set preemption windows, yet nearly all of them treat these forecasts as point estimates, fixed buckets, or crude input-agnostic min–max intervals. We propose CalibServe, which replaces the forecast layer with an online, sparse, heteroscedastic Gaussian process over prompt features that maintains, per request, a calibrated posterior predictive distribution over remaining output length — combining aleatoric (heteroscedastic noise) and epistemic (distance-to-data) uncertainty, and updating after every observed token. We then show how a scheduler can exploit the full posterior rather than a summary: KV cache is provisioned at request-specific predictive quantiles chosen by an explicit tradeoff between expected SLO-violation probability and expected wasted memory; admission is granted when the posterior probability of meeting a deadline exceeds a load-dependent threshold; and preemptions are chosen by maximizing expected reduction in SLO-violation probability net of swap/recompute cost. Our central falsifiable claim is that, under prompt-distribution shift — where exchangeability-based conformal coverage degrades and fixed intervals fail — CalibServe sustains calibration and achieves strictly higher SLO goodput than FCFS, point-forecast SJF/SRTF/LTR schedulers, min–max interval policies, and a conformal-quantile-interval baseline, while closing a larger fraction of the gap to clairvoyant SJF; under stationary workloads it should match the best of these within a few points at a fraction of the wasted KV memory. We specify the method, a vLLM-based implementation plan, and an evaluation protocol on ShareGPT/MTBench/production-style traces with an explicit shift protocol, against seven baselines plus a clairvoyant upper bound.

schema.problem: LLM inference requests have unknown output lengths beforehand and are both compute- and memory-intensive; existing schedulers rely on simple heuristics or focus purely on compute, resulting in suboptimal performance.
schema.motivation: Efficient LLM inference scheduling is crucial for user experience, so properly handling demand uncertainty and workload hybridity can improve overall efficiency.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed scheduler predicts an output-length distribution for each request by combining its prompt contents with past inference results, aiming for lightweight and accurate estimation. It models the true service cost of a request with both compute and memory aspects, and uses an uncertainty-aware scheduling policy over request cost distributions to improve overall scheduling efficiency.
schema.research_plan: The paper reports testbed experiments over diverse setups to evaluate efficiency; no baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are stated.

items.title: SageSched: Efficient LLM Scheduling Confronting Demand Uncertainty and Hybridity
items.abstract: Efficient LLM inference scheduling is crucial for user experience. However, LLM inferences exhibit remarkable demand uncertainty (with unknown output length beforehand) and hybridity (being both compute and memory intensive). Existing LLM schedulers rely on simple heuristics or focus purely on compute resource, suffering suboptimal performance. In this work, we propose SageSched, an efficient LLM scheduler that properly handles demand uncertainty and hybridity of inference workloads. SageSched combines prompt contents with the past inference results to predict output-length distribution in a light-weight and also accurate manner. Meanwhile, it models the true service cost of an inference request with both compute and memory aspects considered. Finally, SageSched employs an uncertainty-aware scheduling policy that can yield the best overall efficiency given the request cost distributions. Testbed experiments over diverse setups confirm that SageSched can attain an efficiency improvement of over 28.7%.

schema.problem: Long-context LLM serving is bottlenecked by a KV cache that grows linearly with context length. Existing remedies—eviction/selection, quantization, offloading, and recurrent-compression approaches such as AHN, Trellis, and ATLAS—either keep token-level states that still grow with history, rely on heuristics, or require gradient training at fine-tuning or test-time optimization cost, leaving no constant-memory attention augmentation for existing frozen LLMs.
schema.motivation: Bounded memory and per-token compute are needed for long-context serving; a drop-in constant-memory augmentation fit offline in minutes on one GPU avoids billions of tokens of distillation or fine-tuning and provides a clean target for a fused attention kernel or small dedicated accelerator.
schema.proposed_approach: Per attention head-group, a fixed random echo-state reservoir of dimension R recursively absorbs every token's key/value features via s_t = tanh(W_in·[k_t;v_t] + W_res·s_{t-1}), with W_res frozen random and spectral radius ≤ 1. A linear readout maps s_t to a single synthetic memory token (k*,v*), which is added to the usual softmax attention over a small sliding window plus attention-sink anchors. The backbone is never trained; the readout is fit offline by closed-form ridge regression to the residual attention contribution of the dropped context over a small corpus (<1k long-context examples). Memory and per-token FLOPs are O(R+W) regardless of context length, realized as one bf16 matvec plus one extra KV pair per token.
schema.research_plan: (1) The performance claim is tested on NIAH/RULER retrieval accuracy and long-context perplexity at 128k context, with success defined by the stated thresholds at ≤5% full KV memory and zero per-request learning. (2) It is falsified if depth-dependent recall collapses below window-only baselines—the memory-capacity law is measured directly—or if the trained-SSM alternative dominates at equal compute budget. (3) The complexity claim is supported by inspection of the fixed-size state and per-token operations, compared against surveyed eviction/quantization methods.

items.title: EchoKV: Frozen Echo-State Reservoirs as Constant-Memory KV Caches for Long-Context LLM Serving
items.abstract: Long-context LLM serving is bottlenecked by the KV cache, which grows linearly with context length. Existing remedies — eviction/selection , quantization, and offloading — either keep storing token-level KVs that still grow with history or rely on heuristics, and the closest recurrent-compression approaches (AHN , Trellis , ATLAS ) train their fixed-size memory with gradients, at fine-tuning-scale or test-time optimization cost. We propose EchoKV, a drop-in, constant-memory attention augmentation for existing frozen LLMs: per attention head-group, a fixed random echo-state reservoir (ESN ) of dimension R recurrently absorbs every token's key/value features (s_t = tanh(W_in·[k_t;v_t] + W_res·s_{t-1}), W_res frozen random with spectral radius ≤ 1), and a linear readout maps s_t to a single synthetic "memory token" (k*,v*) that joins the usual softmax attention over a small sliding window plus attention-sink anchors . The backbone is never trained: the readout is fit offline by closed-form ridge regression to the residual attention contribution of the dropped context over a small corpus (<1k long-context examples), which takes minutes on one GPU rather than the billions of tokens MOHAWK-style distillation or self-distillation requires. Memory and per-token FLOPs are strictly O(R + W) regardless of context length, versus O(L) for every eviction/quantization method we surveyed. Falsifiable claim: at 128k context, EchoKV attains ≥95% of full-attention NIAH/RULER retrieval accuracy and within 15% relative long-context perplexity at ≤5% of full KV memory, with zero per-request learning; it is falsified if depth-dependent recall collapses below window-only baselines (a memory-capacity law we measure directly ) or if the trained-SSM alternative dominates at equal compute budget. The frozen-sparse reservoir is also a clean target for a fused attention kernel (one bf16 matvec + one extra KV pair per token) and, per physical-RC precedent , for a small dedicated accelerator.

schema.problem: Standard Transformers have quadratic time complexity and an indefinitely growing key-value cache, which makes long-context processing prohibitively expensive.
schema.motivation: Long-context processing is needed for practical LLM applications, and making it possible with constant memory and linear time would avoid the prohibitive growth of standard attention while allowing pre-trained models to be extended with minimal fine-tuning.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture is an efficient plug-in module for LLMs that processes sequential data chunks. It maintains a temporary memory on a FIFO queue for recent events and a global memory with a gated update rule for long-range dependencies. These memories act as a dynamic soft prompt for the next chunk. A layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy is introduced to enable efficient fine-tuning on extremely long contexts, and the implementation is released publicly.
schema.research_plan: The paper reports empirical evaluations: (1) passkey retrieval after fine-tuning on 32k contexts, tested with passkeys at any position in a 1M-token sequence; (2) SCROLLS benchmark summarization tasks, compared against other efficient methods and a full-attention baseline; and (3) real-world agent and user behavior QA tasks. The abstract does not state a separate proof or measurement for the constant-memory/linear-time complexity claim, and no explicit failure conditions are given.

items.title: CoMeT: Collaborative Memory Transformer for Efficient Long Context Modeling
items.abstract: The quadratic complexity and indefinitely growing key-value (KV) cache of standard Transformers pose a major barrier to long-context processing. To overcome this, we introduce the Collaborative Memory Transformer (CoMeT), a novel architecture that enables LLMs to handle arbitrarily long sequences with constant memory usage and linear time complexity. Designed as an efficient, plug-in module, CoMeT can be integrated into pre-trained models with only minimal fine-tuning. It operates on sequential data chunks, using a dual-memory system to manage context: a temporary memory on a FIFO queue for recent events, and a global memory with a gated update rule for long-range dependencies. These memories then act as a dynamic soft prompt for the next chunk. To enable efficient fine-tuning on extremely long contexts, we introduce a novel layer-level pipeline parallelism strategy. The effectiveness of our approach is remarkable: a model equipped with CoMeT and fine-tuned on 32k contexts can accurately retrieve a passkey from any position within a 1M token sequence. On the SCROLLS benchmark, CoMeT surpasses other efficient methods and achieves performance comparable to a full-attention baseline on summarization tasks. Its practical effectiveness is further validated on real-world agent and user behavior QA tasks. The code is available at: https://github.com/LivingFutureLab/Comet

schema.problem: Multi-LoRA serving systems treat the adapter library as a fixed, pre-trained artifact: they schedule requests across known adapters, cache them, or make offline training cheaper, but they do not answer whether a request to a new domain with only a few labeled examples should be served immediately or deferred for training.
schema.motivation: A domain-adaptation user may face a new domain with 16 labeled examples and a latency SLO; answering per request can avoid the delay and cost of training before serving and can amortize repeated traffic to the new domain.
schema.proposed_approach: When a request targets a domain with no adapter, the runtime first composes an adapter on the fly from the existing library by routing inputs to relevant existing adapters and merging adapter ranks with weights derived from the support examples. It then verifies the composed adapter using leave-one-out loss over the support examples plus label-free transferability features. If a regret predictor calibrated with conformal methods predicts the composition will fall short, the runtime escalates to actual LoRA synthesis as a bounded, warm-started micro-fine-tune initialized from the composed adapter. The synthesized adapter is cached and indexed back into the library so later requests to that domain can reuse it.
schema.research_plan: Evidence would compare composed-only serving against a plain multi-LoRA forward pass for latency and against a freshly trained adapter for quality on unseen-domain requests, while tracking per-domain GPU-hours and SLO attainment. Support requires that composition resolves the majority of unseen-domain requests within the target latency overhead and recovers most of a freshly trained adapter's quality while reducing per-domain GPU cost at equal SLO attainment; failure would be falling short on these conditions.

items.title: Conform or Create: Deadline-Aware Adapter Composition with Escalation to On-Demand LoRA Synthesis for Unseen Domains
items.abstract: Multi-LoRA serving systems assume the adapter library is a fixed, pre-trained artifact: they schedule requests across known adapters, cache them, or make offline training cheaper. They do not answer the operational question a domain-adaptation user actually asks — "a new domain just arrived with 16 labeled examples and a 2-second SLO; do I serve it now, or schedule a training job?" This proposal builds a serving runtime that answers that question per request. When a request targets a domain with no adapter, the runtime first composes an adapter on the fly from the existing library (input-aware routing plus support-set-weighted rank-wise merging), verifies the composition via leave-one-out loss over the k support examples plus label-free transferability features, and escalates to actual LoRA synthesis — a bounded, warm-started micro-fine-tune initialized from the composed adapter — only when a conformally calibrated regret predictor says composition will fall short. The synthesized adapter is cached and indexed back into the library, so repeated traffic to a new domain amortizes. The falsifiable core claim is that support-set-verifiable composition resolves the majority of unseen-domain requests within 1.35× the latency of a plain multi-LoRA forward pass while recovering most of the quality of a freshly trained adapter, cutting GPU-hours per new domain by an order of magnitude at equal SLO attainment.

schema.problem: Prefix KV cache managers currently decide what to retain or evict from access statistics alone (recency, frequency, or runtime-derived hotness), but these signals are blind at the decisive moment when a prefix node is first written: a recurring system template and a one-off user suffix are indistinguishable until repeated hits accumulate, even though real-traffic studies show cross-request reuse concentrates in structured, templated prefixes whose text already marks them as reusable.
schema.motivation: Reducing Time-to-First-Token in production LLM serving remains important, and making retention decisions from content at insertion time could exploit template reuse immediately, including under workload drift and cold-start template emergence where no access history yet exists.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a learned reuse-value policy for exact-match prefix KV caches. It scores every radix-cache node at insertion and refresh using cheap content features of the node's stored token segment (hashed n-grams, chat/role markers, template structure, and cluster identity over previously recurring segments) combined with multiperspective access statistics. The resulting scores drive admission, eviction, and CPU-tier placement. Reuse remains strictly exact-token-match, so the policy changes only which KV tensors are retained, never their contents or outputs.
schema.research_plan: The abstract carries a falsifiable comparison design: (1) hold GPU KV memory fixed and compare against access-statistics-only, hotness-based, non-learned reuse-forecast, and LRU-family policies, measuring token hit-rate and P95/P99-TTFT; evidence is statistical significance of gains, with the largest expected gap under workload drift and cold-start template emergence. The claim would fail if no statistically significant gains over these baselines are observed at fixed memory. The abstract does not specify ablations, dataset composition, or model scale.

items.title: CacheSight: Content-Aware Learned Reuse-Value Prediction for Exact-Match Prefix KV Caches in LLM Serving
items.abstract: Prefix KV caching is the dominant mechanism for cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) in production LLM serving, yet today's cache managers decide what to retain or evict from access statistics alone — recency, frequency, or runtime-derived "hotness." These signals are blind at the decisive moment: when a prefix node is first written, a recurring system template and a one-off user suffix are indistinguishable until repeated hits accumulate, whereas real-traffic studies show cross-request reuse concentrates in structured, templated prefixes whose text already marks them as reusable . We propose CacheSight, a learned reuse-value policy for exact-match prefix KV caches that scores every radix-cache node at insertion and refresh from (a) cheap content features of the node's stored token segment (hashed n-grams, chat/role markers, template structure, cluster identity over previously recurring segments) combined with (b) multiperspective access statistics, using the scores for admission, eviction, and CPU-tier placement. Because reuse remains strictly exact-token-match, CacheSight changes only which KV tensors are retained, never their contents or outputs. Our falsifiable claim: at fixed GPU KV memory, content features yield statistically significant token hit-rate and P95/P99-TTFT gains over access-statistics-only, hotness-based , non-learned reuse-forecast , and LRU-family policies , with the largest gap under workload drift and cold-start template emergence, where no access history exists yet.

schema.problem: Large language models in privacy-sensitive settings require differential privacy guarantees, but existing approaches allocate privacy budgets uniformly across inference requests, leaving latency-relevant heterogeneity unexploited while still needing to respect strict DP composition bounds.
schema.motivation: Making per-request privacy budget allocation responsive to serving conditions can reduce end-to-end latency without weakening privacy, which is important for practical privacy-compliant LLM serving in multi-tenant clusters.
schema.proposed_approach: An online scheduling and budget allocation framework dynamically assigns per-request privacy budgets to minimize end-to-end latency while respecting strict DP composition bounds. It integrates privacy budget allocation with speculative decoding and KV-cache management, treating privacy as a first-class scheduling dimension. The work presents an online algorithm with formal privacy guarantees and a system implementation targeting multi-tenant inference clusters.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes a formal privacy guarantee for the online algorithm, a system implementation targeting multi-tenant inference clusters, and experiments comparing end-to-end latency against uniform budget allocation while maintaining equivalent privacy levels. Support for the latency claim requires lower latency under the same privacy composition; the formal guarantee requires the budget allocation to remain within the DP composition bound.

items.title: DP-Aware Inference Serving: Dynamic Privacy Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Inference
items.abstract: Large language models deployed in privacy-sensitive settings require differential privacy (DP) guarantees, but current approaches allocate privacy budgets uniformly across inference requests. We propose DP-Aware Serving (DAS), an online scheduling and budget allocation framework that dynamically assigns per-request privacy budgets to minimize end-to-end latency while respecting strict DP composition bounds. DAS integrates differential privacy budget allocation with modern LLM inference optimizations—speculative decoding and KV-cache management—treating privacy as a first-class scheduling dimension. We present an online algorithm with formal privacy guarantees, a system implementation targeting multi-tenant inference clusters, and experiments demonstrating 1.5–3.2× latency reduction compared to uniform budget allocation while maintaining equivalent privacy levels.

schema.problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting offers fast novel-view synthesis, but inference-time serving remains inefficient for large scenes and mobile deployment because current systems treat all Gaussians equally, causing redundant computation on off-screen or imperceptible Gaussians and poor memory bandwidth utilization.
schema.motivation: Efficient serving is needed to make large-scale and mobile novel-view synthesis practical by reducing latency and increasing throughput without sacrificing visual quality.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system dynamically prioritizes Gaussians by combining view-frustum culling with learned priority scores, exits rendering early when cumulative opacity saturates, and uses a GPU memory-aware scheduler to batch heterogeneous multi-view requests.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation compares the proposed system against naive per-view rendering on large-scale scenes, measuring inference latency, throughput, and visual quality; support would be lower latency and higher throughput with maintained visual quality, while degradation or quality loss would count against the claims.

items.title: Efficient Multi-View 3D Reconstruction via Adaptive Gaussian Prioritization and Inference Scheduling
items.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a fast alternative to NeRF for novel-view synthesis, but inference-time serving remains inefficient for large scenes and mobile deployment. Current 3DGS systems treat all Gaussians equally during rendering, leading to redundant computation on off-screen or imperceptible Gaussians and poor memory bandwidth utilization. We propose AdaGauss, a system that dynamically prioritizes Gaussians based on view frustum, opacity, and screen-space coverage, coupled with a view-aware inference scheduler that batches multi-view requests intelligently. AdaGauss combines view-frustum culling with learned priority scores, early-exit rendering when cumulative opacity saturates, and GPU memory-aware batching of heterogeneous view requests to maximize throughput. We demonstrate 2–4× latency reduction and 3–6× throughput improvement on large-scale scenes compared to naive per-view rendering, while maintaining visual quality.

schema.problem: Existing batched speculative decoding frameworks assume standard, dense KV cache memory management and therefore suffer from severe synchronization and memory footprint overheads when applied to long contexts or quantized KV hierarchies.
schema.motivation: Removing these alignment overheads and VRAM pressure would make batched speculative decoding practical for long-context and quantized-KV serving workloads.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a co-designed system integrating hierarchical quantized KV caching with batched speculative decoding. It introduces a paged, multi-tier KV cache manager that natively handles speculative draft-target tree expansions and 4-bit quantized states under ragged batched execution. The design is intended to eliminate alignment overheads and reduce VRAM pressure relative to dense-KV batched speculative decoding frameworks.
schema.research_plan: The abstract specifies an evaluation plan comparing end-to-end throughput against state-of-the-art batched speculative decoding and serving engines under varying batch sizes and context lengths; no named baselines, ablations, or failure conditions are given.

items.title: BatchQuantSpec: Batched Hierarchical Speculative Decoding with Paged Quantized KV Cache Management
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive LLM generation, and recent advances have extended it to batched serving and long-context single-sequence inference using hierarchical or quantized KV caches. However, existing batched speculative decoding frameworks assume standard, dense KV cache memory management and suffer from severe synchronization and memory footprint overheads when applied to long contexts or quantized KV hierarchies. In this work, we propose BatchQuantSpec, a co-designed system that integrates hierarchical quantized KV caching with authentic batched speculative decoding. By introducing a paged, multi-tier KV cache manager that natively handles speculative draft-target tree expansions and 4-bit quantized states under ragged batched execution, BatchQuantSpec eliminates alignment overheads and reduces VRAM pressure. Our evaluation plan demonstrates significant end-to-end throughput improvements over state-of-the-art batched speculative decoding and serving engines across varying batch sizes and context lengths.

schema.problem: Existing low-bit KV-cache quantization methods for LLM inference focus exclusively on benign memory-throughput trade-offs, leaving their security and adversarial robustness unexamined.
schema.motivation: As aggressive quantization is adopted for memory savings, its potential to heighten vulnerability to prompt injection and cache inversion makes it necessary to secure compressed KV caches rather than treating compression as a purely performance-oriented trade-off.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework co-designs low-bit KV-cache quantization with adversarial defense by protecting outliers identified through quantization sensitivity and constraining values with bounds that are resilient to adversarial perturbation, aiming to retain high memory savings while defending against cache-based adversarial manipulation and leakage.
schema.research_plan: The abstract describes evidence only at a high level: existing low-bit quantization is examined under prompt injection and cache inversion attacks to show worsened vulnerability with aggressive compression, and the proposed framework is evaluated for memory savings and defense against cache-based adversarial manipulation and leakage; no detailed baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions are specified.

items.title: RobustKV: Adversarially Robust and Efficient KV-Cache Quantization under Adversarial Attacks
items.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is a foundational mechanism for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference over long context lengths, prompting extensive research into memory-efficient low-bit quantization techniques such as KIVI and KVQuant. However, existing KV-cache compression methods focus exclusively on benign memory-throughput trade-offs, leaving their security and adversarial robustness completely unexamined. In this work, we investigate the security implications of low-bit KV-cache quantization, demonstrating that aggressive compression exacerbates vulnerability to adversarial exploits such as prompt injection and cache inversion attacks. To address this gap, we propose RobustKV, a novel co-designed quantization framework that incorporates sensitivity-guided outlier protection and perturbation-resilient bounds to simultaneously achieve high-compression memory savings and robust defense against cache-based adversarial manipulation and leakage.

schema.problem: Neural topic models such as the embedded topic model (ETM) require only two fused matrix multiplications at inference, yet production serving stacks treat per-document topic assignment as CPU-era one-shot work. Existing multi-tenant LLM serving systems reduce TTFT and KV-cache footprint via literal prefix matching, attention-aware semantic reuse, and whole-cache cross-tenant sharing, but they key caches on literal request identity rather than the semantic group of documents, so they under-reuse for chunk-reordered cross-tenant workloads.
schema.motivation: Making amortized neural topic inference a first-class serving substrate would allow semantic-group-based KV-cache sharing across literal-different requests, reducing TTFT and cache footprint, while batched kernel fusion and quantization make low-latency per-document topic assignment tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system comprises a batched kernel-fused runtime for ETM-style inference that performs INT8/FP16-quantized embedding and softmax matmuls with one-time calibration, targeting per-document topic-ID assignment at batch sizes 1–64. A serving router uses topic assignments and contextualized topic embeddings as the key for KV-cache admission, aliasing, and eviction: cached KV entries are admitted per topic, the top-1 topic ID acts as an alias for admission control, and a residual-deviation bound gates eviction. A topic-segment scheduler batches documents by topic segment and dispatches prefill to GPU fractions, amortizing topic-mixing switch cost.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the kernel runtime comes from comparing per-document topic-ID assignment latency against the streaming-inference baselines of Yao et al. at batch sizes 1–64. Evidence for the router comes from evaluating TTFT on topic-aligned multi-tenant serving traces against cited serving baselines, including a no-regression check against KVShare on adversarial heavy-tail tenants. Failure would be shown by failing to reduce TTFT on topic-aligned traces or regressing against KVShare on adversarial tenants.

items.title: TopicServe: Amortized Neural Topic Inference as a Serving Substrate — Topic-ID Cache Keys and Topic-Segment Batch Routers for Multi-Tenant LLM Serving
items.abstract: Neural topic models such as the embedded topic model (ETM) require, at inference time, only two fused matrix multiplications — a bag-of-words embedding lookup and a softmax over the topic-word matrix — yet production serving stacks treat per-document topic assignment as CPU-era, one-shot work. Meanwhile, multi-tenant LLM serving research has reduced Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and KV-cache footprint through literal prefix matching , attention-aware semantic reuse , and whole-cache cross-tenant sharing , but every one of these systems keys its cache on the literal request identity, not on the semantic group of documents a request belongs to. We propose TopicServe, a two-part system that makes amortized neural topic inference a first-class serving substrate. (1) TopicServe-Kernel: a batched, kernel-fused runtime for ETM-style inference — INT8/FP16-quantized embedding and softmax matmuls with one-time calibration — targeting sub-millisecond per-document topic-ID assignment at batch sizes 1–64, versus the streaming-inference baselines of Yao et al. that were orders of magnitude slower per document. (2) TopicServe-Router: a serving component that uses topic assignments and contextualized topic embeddings as the key for KV-cache admission, aliasing, and eviction: cached KV entries are admitted per topic (instead of per literal request), the top-1 topic ID acts as an alias for admission control, and a residual-deviation bound gates eviction, generalizing SmartCache and KVShare to chunk-reordered, cross-tenant workloads where literal prefix matching provably under-reuses . A topic-segment scheduler batches documents by topic segment and dispatches prefill to GPU fractions, amortizing the topic-mixing switch cost. On topic-aligned multi-tenant serving traces we expect up to 3.1× TTFT reduction versus the cited serving baselines, with a no-regression floor against KVShare on adversarial heavy-tail tenants.

schema.problem: LLM-powered intelligent tutoring systems require per-student persistent state across sessions, but existing LLM serving systems either retain KV state only within a session or cache multi-request state under generic recency/frequency heuristics that ignore why a given state must survive.
schema.motivation: Forgetting-driven retention could avoid evicting exactly the students with long inter-session gaps and high mastery-decay risk, sustaining full-history personalization for more concurrent students under fixed memory and interactive latency service-level objectives.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework materializes each student's state as an identity-bound, pinned, multi-tier KV-cache prefix in HBM/DRAM managed by page tables and asynchronously offloaded. Placement and eviction are scored by predicted return time multiplied by mastery-decay rather than LRU/LFU. Per-student knowledge-tracing updates are co-scheduled into decode idle gaps under a hard latency watchdog. The work specifies the retention policy, the page-table/scheduling mechanisms, and a systems-first evaluation protocol.
schema.research_plan: The paper specifies a systems-first evaluation protocol in which tutoring-quality outcomes are measured as evidence rather than as the optimization objective. Comparisons include in-session stateless prefix caching and LRU multi-tiering, with full-history tutoring prediction quality measured by next-response correctness AUC under fixed total KV memory and an interactive p95 TTFT/TBT service-level objective. The falsifiable claim is evaluated on concurrent student capacity and multi-week histories. A pre-registered null-result path is reported: if knowledge-tracing-driven and recency-driven policies tie, the added complexity is unjustified and the paper reports the null.

items.title: SessTutor: Forgetting-Aware, Long-Lived Student-State Management for Multi-Tenant LLM Tutoring Serving
items.abstract: LLM-powered intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) require per-student persistent state — dialogue history, learner profile, and an updatable student model — to personalize across sessions spanning days to weeks. Existing LLM serving systems either retain KV state only within a session, or cache multi-request state under generic recency/frequency heuristics that ignore why a particular state must survive. We propose SessTutor, a student-state serving stack in which retention decisions are driven by the learner's knowledge-tracing (KT) forgetting dynamics: each student's state is materialized as an identity-bound, pinned, multi-tier KV-cache prefix (HBM/DRAM, page-table managed, asynchronously offloaded); placement and eviction are scored by predicted return time × mastery-decay rather than LRU/LFU; and the per-student KT update — orders of magnitude cheaper than the fine-tuning iterations co-scheduled by prior work — is co-scheduled into decode idle gaps under a hard latency watchdog. Falsifiable claim: at fixed total KV memory and an interactive p95 TTFT/TBT service-level objective (SLO), forgetting-guided retention sustains full-history tutoring prediction quality (LLMKT-style next-response correctness AUC) for 3–5× more concurrent students than in-session stateless prefix caching or LRU multi-tiering, and for multi-week histories — because the students evicted by recency-driven policies are exactly those with long inter-session gaps and high mastery-decay risk. We specify the policy, the page-table/scheduling mechanisms, and a systems-first evaluation protocol in which tutoring-quality outcomes are measured evidence, not the optimization objective; we pre-register the null-result path (if KT-driven and recency-driven policies tie, the added complexity is unjustified and the paper reports the null).

schema.problem: Existing blockchain-based distributed machine learning protocols face efficiency and security limitations, particularly when homomorphic encryption is used.
schema.motivation: Blockchain-based distributed ML can ensure data privacy and security, so resolving efficiency and security limitations with homomorphic encryption is necessary to make such training practical.
schema.proposed_approach: The work will evaluate existing protocols, identify key challenges, and develop a proof-of-concept implementation of blockchain-based distributed ML training with homomorphic encryption to demonstrate feasibility.
schema.research_plan: Evidence will come from evaluating existing protocols to identify challenges and from a proof-of-concept implementation serving as feasibility evidence for the claim. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: Efficient and Secure Blockchain-Based Distributed Machine Learning with Homomorphic Encryption
items.abstract: Blockchain-based distributed machine learning (ML) has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential to ensure data privacy and security. However, existing protocols face efficiency and security limitations, particularly when using homomorphic encryption. This proposal aims to investigate the trade-offs between efficiency and security in blockchain-based distributed ML training protocols with homomorphic encryption. We will evaluate existing protocols, identify key challenges, and develop a proof-of-concept implementation to demonstrate the feasibility of efficient and secure blockchain-based distributed ML.

schema.problem: Existing adversarial training methods for large language models are computationally expensive and often require significant resources.
schema.motivation: Reducing the computational cost of adversarial training for LLMs would make robustness to textual adversarial examples more practical and scalable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method integrates adversarial training for large language models with multi-task learning and auxiliary losses to improve robustness while reducing computational cost.
schema.research_plan: The paper reports extensive experiments on various NLP tasks and adversarial attacks to support effectiveness; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: Efficient Adversarial Training for Large Language Models using Multi-Task Learning and Auxiliary Losses
items.abstract: Adversarial training is a promising method to improve the robustness of large language models (LLMs) against carefully crafted textual adversarial examples. However, existing adversarial training methods for LLMs are computationally expensive and often require significant resources. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages multi-task learning and auxiliary losses to enhance the efficiency of adversarial training for LLMs. Our approach, called Efficient Adversarial Training with Multi-Task Learning (EAT-MTL), integrates adversarial training with multi-task learning and auxiliary losses to improve the robustness of LLMs while reducing computational costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EAT-MTL through extensive experiments on various NLP tasks and adversarial attacks.

schema.problem: Long-horizon LLM agent-society simulations are run on serving stacks designed for chat and DAG-shaped agent workflows, which treat the request prefix as the main reusable prompt unit; in cultural-evolution simulations the dominant reusable prompt unit is instead an instance of a propagating cultural artifact that recurs across agents and turns while mutating, and existing caches do not exploit this structure.
schema.motivation: These simulations are becoming a primary substrate for studying language and cultural evolution, so serving that exploits artifact reuse could reduce compute and latency while making the serving layer a measured and accountable part of the experiment rather than an invisible source of bias.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is a KV-cache serving layer that detects artifact spans during prefill and keys cache entries by a graph of mutation relationships between instances rather than by request prefix. It provides three reuse tiers: prefix-exact reuse; lossless span reuse through value-copy plus key rotation by the relative rotary-position delta; and mutation-tolerant reuse with localized recompute and deviation-based recalibration. Eviction is based on predicted future reach of cached artifacts under online-fit diffusion dynamics instead of LRU or time-to-live. It is deployed in S³-style propagation and GovSim-style governance simulations with 10²–10³ agents, 10²–10³ turns, and 7–8B open models.
schema.research_plan: (1) The structural claim and reuse advantage are evaluated by running the proposed serving layer on S³-style propagation and GovSim-style governance simulations and comparing prefill-FLOP and time-to-first-token against prefix-caching baselines and static cross-agent sharing. (2) The lossless tier is checked by requiring it to reproduce seed-matched cultural-metric trajectories; the mutation-tolerant tier is evaluated by measuring how artifact reach/frequency curves, consensus time, and sustainability rate change as reuse aggressiveness increases, producing a curve over the perturbation of emergent dynamics. (3) The trade-off claim is examined by holding the simulation settings fixed (10²–10³ agents, 10²–10³ turns, 7–8B open models) and reporting performance reduction jointly with the measured cost to emergent-dynamics preservation.

items.title: MemeKV: Lineage-Keyed KV-Cache Serving for Long-Horizon LLM Agent-Society Simulations
items.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agent-society simulations — hundreds to thousands of agents over hundreds of thousands of turns, exchanging rules, norms, and coined terms as they propagate and mutate — are becoming a primary substrate for studying language and cultural evolution, yet they run on serving stacks designed for chat and DAG-shaped agent workflows. We argue the mismatch is structural: in such simulations, the dominant reusable unit in a prompt is not a request prefix but an instance of a propagating cultural artifact that recurs across agents and turns while mutating as it diffuses. We propose MemeKV, a KV-cache serving layer that (i) detects artifact spans in prefill, (ii) keys cache entries by artifact lineage — a graph of mutation relationships between instances — rather than by request prefix, (iii) offers three reuse tiers (prefix-exact; lossless span reuse via value-copy plus RoPE-delta rotation of keys; mutation-tolerant reuse with localized recompute and deviation-based recalibration), and (iv) evicts by predicted cultural utility (expected future reach under online-fit diffusion dynamics) instead of LRU or time-to-live. Crucially, we introduce a new evaluation axis: serving behavioral fidelity. The lossless tier must reproduce seed-matched cultural-metric trajectories, and we report the first fidelity curve quantifying how much lossy KV reuse perturbs emergent dynamics (artifact reach/frequency curves, consensus time, sustainability rate) as reuse aggressiveness increases. On S³-style propagation and GovSim-style governance simulations (10²–10³ agents, 10²–10³ turns, 7–8B open models), MemeKV targets ≥2× prefill-FLOP and TTFT reduction over prefix-caching baselines and static cross-agent sharing, at a measured and controllable fidelity cost — making the serving layer an accountable part of the scientific experiment instead of an invisible one.

schema.problem: Gigascale 3D Gaussian Splatting captures (city blocks, campuses, digital twins) contain 40M–100M+ Gaussians that exceed a single large GPU's HBM; once rasterization is optimized and the scene file is compressed, the dominant remaining serving cost is unaddressed: memory-hierarchy management of which spatial tiles at which LOD reside in HBM vs DRAM vs NVMe, when they are fetched, and how they are shared and evicted across concurrent clients.
schema.motivation: Making photorealistic real-time 3D serving of gigascale scenes to concurrent VR/AR users possible requires managing this multi-tier memory hierarchy under multi-client load, not just accelerating rasterization or compression.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed serving runtime treats a 3DGS scene as a large, spatially structured parameter set served from a unified 3-level cache: an LOD octree of quantized Gaussian tiles with graceful coarse-level degradation on a miss; asynchronous NVMe→DRAM and DRAM→HBM pipelines built on GPU-Direct-Storage-style transfers and multipath host-GPU movement; and a per-client camera-trajectory predictor that drives geometry-aware prefetch over an adaptive lookahead window. It also uses cost-aware eviction with cross-client refcounting to keep shared viewpoints resident and a per-client SLO scheduler over frame deadlines, residency, and bandwidth. It builds on the FlashGS rasterizer and Octree-GS/H-3DGS tiles.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes a first-of-kind bandwidth feasibility study for the NVMe tier and ablations isolating each lever (prediction, lookahead, tiering depth, sharing, scheduling). The falsifiable test is the stated claim: under scenes 10–20× HBM and 1–16 concurrent clients, support requires sustaining the 90 FPS @ 1080p deadline with near-zero miss-induced frame drops and sub-linear HBM residency growth; failure would show one or more baselines match or the scaling/deadline conditions are not met. Baselines are resident, synchronous-LOD, cache-centric single-scene, and naive-LRU streaming.

items.title: SplatServe: Trajectory-Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management and Multi-Client Serving for Gigascale 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
items.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the dominant format for photorealistic real-time 3D, but gigascale captures — city blocks, campuses, digital twins — contain 40M–100M+ Gaussians that exceed the HBM of a single large GPU. We argue that once the rasterizer is optimized (order-of-magnitude speedups are already demonstrated) and the scene file is compressed, the dominant remaining cost in serving such scenes is memory-hierarchy management under a multi-client workload: which spatial tiles, at which level of detail, reside in GPU HBM vs. host DRAM vs. NVMe, when they are fetched, and how they are shared and evicted across concurrent VR/AR users. We present SplatServe, a serving runtime that treats a 3DGS scene as a large, spatially structured parameter set served from a unified 3-level cache: an LOD octree of quantized Gaussian tiles with graceful coarse-level degradation on a miss; asynchronous NVMe→DRAM and DRAM→HBM pipelines built on GPU-Direct-Storage-style transfers and multipath host-GPU movement; a per-client camera-trajectory predictor that drives geometry-aware prefetch over an adaptive lookahead window; cost-aware eviction with cross-client refcounting that keeps shared viewpoints resident; and a per-client SLO scheduler over frame deadlines, residency, and bandwidth. Our falsifiable claim: on scenes 10–20× HBM with 1–16 concurrent clients, SplatServe sustains a 90 FPS @ 1080p frame deadline with near-zero miss-induced frame drops and sub-linear growth of total HBM residency in client count — which resident, synchronous-LOD, cache-centric single-scene, and naive-LRU streaming baselines cannot. We build on the FlashGS rasterizer and Octree-GS/H-3DGS tiles, and evaluate with a first-of-kind bandwidth feasibility study for the NVMe tier plus ablations isolating each lever (prediction, lookahead, tiering depth, sharing, scheduling).

schema.problem: The claim that predicting job duration and scheduling on that prediction reduces average job completion time in production GPU clusters is widely relied upon but has only been validated on pre-2022 traces or private testbeds.
