schema.motivation: Publicly available 2023-era GPU cluster traces and the need to design LLM-era cluster schedulers make it both possible and timely to subject this claim to rigorous statistical testing.
schema.proposed_approach: The evaluation is a trace-driven discrete-event simulation over Alibaba's 2023 GPU cluster release and all four clusters of the Helios trace. It compares strict FIFO, FIFO-with-backfilling, two predicted-shortest-remaining-time variants, a Hilbert-curve placement baseline, and the proposed scheduler with its fragmentation-aware placement constraint.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the backfilling-versus-prediction claim comes from a 19-point cluster-size sweep and a 300-replicate job-level bootstrap on Alibaba's 2023 GPU cluster release, with a separate cross-trace bootstrap on all four Helios clusters. Replication is assessed by confidence intervals on the job-completion-time difference across clusters, with a finding treated as non-replicating if a cluster's interval does not exclude zero. Prediction's added value on top of backfilling is isolated by comparing backfilling-only against prediction-plus-backfilling ordering, with bootstrap replicates on the two traces used to decide trace-dependence. The proposed fragmentation-aware placement constraint is evaluated against backfilling on both traces, with support requiring it to match backfilling rather than merely improve on unconstrained scheduling.

items.title: Backfilling, Not Prediction: A Cluster-Size Sweep and Cross-Trace Bootstrap of Forecast-Driven GPU Scheduling in the LLM Era
items.abstract: Prior work claims that predicting job duration and scheduling on that prediction reduces average job completion time (JCT) on production GPU clusters (Hu et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2025), a claim that has shaped scheduler design for LLM-era GPU clusters despite being validated only on pre-2022 traces or private testbeds. This paper tests that claim with the statistical rigor it has not yet received: a 19-point cluster-size sweep, a 300-replicate job-level bootstrap, and a separate cross-trace bootstrap on a second, independent trace. Using Alibaba&apos;s 2023 GPU cluster release and all four clusters of the Helios trace, we compare six scheduling policies, strict FIFO, FIFO-with-backfilling, two predicted-shortest-remaining-time variants, a Hilbert-curve placement baseline, and the proposed PredSched-LLM, via trace-driven discrete-event simulation. The result inverts the premise it set out to test: on both traces, strict FIFO&apos;s average JCT collapses under contention, up to ninefold worse on Alibaba and further still on Helios, but the mechanism responsible is backfilling, not prediction, and that finding replicates cleanly across all five clusters tested (95 percent CI excludes zero everywhere). The two traces disagree on what prediction-informed ordering adds on top of backfilling: no distinguishable advantage on Alibaba, but a real directional signal on Helios (90-100 percent of bootstrap replicates favor it). The proposed fragmentation-aware placement constraint does not clear backfilling&apos;s bar on either trace. Backfilling is the one effect that is large and reproduces across every cluster tested; prediction&apos;s value is genuinely trace-dependent, not simply absent.

schema.problem: Deploying deep neural networks on mobile devices remains challenging due to limited computing resources, and although CPU and GPU could jointly reduce inference latency, collaborative execution is obstructed by significant synchronization overhead for combining partial results and by difficulty predicting execution times of CPU/GPU tasks under dynamic implementation and parallelism selection.
schema.motivation: Mobile devices offer unified memory and a narrower CPU-GPU performance gap, making CPU-GPU co-execution a newly tractable way to reduce inference latency if the synchronization and prediction obstacles can be addressed.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach assigns DNN layer tasks to both CPU and GPU and combines partial results using a lightweight synchronization mechanism built on OpenCL fine-grained shared virtual memory. Machine learning models predict the execution time of tasks on CPU and GPU, incorporating GPU kernel performance characteristics and dispatch times. These predictions are used to quickly select CPU-GPU co-execution strategies.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is a comprehensive evaluation on four mobile platforms. The evaluation measures speedups for linear and convolutional layers, comparing the selected CPU-GPU co-execution strategies against an exhaustive grid search over possible co-execution strategies on one platform (Pixel 5) as a reference for the achievable maximum. Support is implied when the selected strategies approach that reference; no explicit failure condition is stated.

items.title: Accelerating Mobile Inference Through Fine-Grained CPU-GPU Co-Execution
items.abstract: Deploying deep neural networks on mobile devices is increasingly important but remains challenging due to limited computing resources. On the other hand, their unified memory architecture and narrower gap between CPU and GPU performance provide an opportunity to reduce inference latency by assigning tasks to both CPU and GPU. The main obstacles for such collaborative execution are the significant synchronization overhead required to combine partial results, and the difficulty of predicting execution times of tasks assigned to CPU and GPU (due to the dynamic selection of implementations and parallelism level). To overcome these obstacles, we propose both a lightweight synchronization mechanism based on OpenCL fine-grained shared virtual memory (SVM) and machine learning models to accurately predict execution times. Notably, these models capture the performance characteristics of GPU kernels and account for their dispatch times. A comprehensive evaluation on four mobile platforms shows that our approach can quickly select CPU-GPU co-execution strategies achieving up to 1.89x speedup for linear layers and 1.75x speedup for convolutional layers (close to the achievable maximum values of 2.01x and 1.87x, respectively, found by exhaustive grid search on a Pixel~5 smartphone).

schema.problem: The Winograd algorithm reduces multiplicative complexity in convolutions but often suffers from memory inefficiency and limited scalability on modern CPUs.
schema.motivation: Making Winograd scale efficiently on multicore CPUs would improve convolution throughput for deep learning workloads.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed parallelization applies SIMD vectorization to maximize instruction-level parallelism. It uses a locality-aware data reuse strategy in which one input tile serves multiple filters. A modular architecture with deep loop fusion minimizes overhead and is intended to ensure scalability on multicore CPUs.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the claims is experimental benchmarking on Intel Xeon CPUs against Winograd implementations in PyTorch and TensorFlow, with convolution configurations C ≤ 16 and VGG16; the VGG16 comparison also includes MKL-DNN-accelerated PyTorch. The abstract does not state an explicit failure condition or matched-budget constraints.

items.title: OSOW: A Resource-Efficient Parallelization of the Winograd Algorithm on Multicore CPUs
items.abstract: The Winograd algorithm reduces multiplicative complexity in convolutions but often suffers from memory inefficiency and limited scalability on modern CPUs. This paper presents OSOW, a resource-efficient parallelization of Winograd designed to maximize throughput on multicore CPUs. Our methodology includes three optimizations: SIMD vectorization to maximize instruction-level parallelism; a locality-aware data reuse strategy enabling one input tile to serve multiple filters; and a modular architecture with deep loop fusion to minimize overhead and ensure scalability. Experiments on the Intel Xeon CPU show OSOW outperforms Winograd implementations in PyTorch and TensorFlow. For convolutions with $$C \le 16$$ C ≤ 16 , OSOW achieves speedups of 1.92 $$\times $$ × over TensorFlow and 3.37 $$\times $$ × over PyTorch. On VGG16, OSOW delivers 1.48 $$\times $$ × over TensorFlow and 1.25 $$\times $$ × over MKL-DNN-accelerated PyTorch.

schema.problem: Existing LLM-agent safety guards rely on separate fine-tuned models that generate tokens, and application-layer classifiers sit above the sandbox where they can be circumvented; no primitive gives kernel-level access to an agent model's own next-token distribution before generation.
schema.motivation: Reading the same base model's logits removes the cost and latency of a second guard model, and enforcing safety below the sandbox boundary makes governance harder to bypass as agents proliferate.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed kernel-level operation runs inside an OS kernel that executes LLM inference and performs a single forward pass, reading specific next-token logits to classify an agent's action as safe or dangerous with zero learned parameters. The check reuses the same base model the agent already runs, so no separate guard model is required. Because agent actions pass through kernel-mediated host functions, enforcement operates below the WASM sandbox boundary rather than as an application-layer classifier. The operation is implemented within a bare-metal x86-64 kernel written in Rust, and a calibration strength parameter serves as a deployment-time policy knob that trades recall for precision per operation class.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed operation on Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Mistral-7B across HarmBench, XSTest, and ToxicChat, reporting block rates, F1 against Llama Guard 3 on ToxicChat (n=1,000) with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and classification latency relative to Llama Guard 3. The evidence is structured to show (1) safe/dangerous classification from logit reads, (2) parity-or-better relative to a fine-tuned guard, (3) lower latency from a single-logit read rather than token generation, and (4) enforcement below the sandbox boundary through kernel-mediated host functions. Baseline and evaluation settings are held to the same three base models and external benchmarks.

items.title: ProbeLogits: Kernel-Level LLM Inference Primitives for AI-Native Operating Systems
items.abstract: An OS kernel that runs LLM inference internally can read the model's own next-token logit distribution before any text is generated, and act on it as a governance primitive. I present ProbeLogits, a kernel-level operation that performs a single forward pass and reads specific token logits to classify an agent's action as safe or dangerous, with zero learned parameters. Because the probe reads a logit from the same base model the agent already runs, it removes the second model a fine-tuned guard requires: the marginal cost of a safety check becomes a single logit read. I evaluate ProbeLogits on three base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B) across three external benchmarks (HarmBench, XSTest, ToxicChat). On HarmBench non-copyright, all three reach a 97-99% block rate. On ToxicChat (n=1,000), ProbeLogits attains F1 parity-or-better against Llama Guard 3: Qwen2.5-7B Safe/Dangerous reaches F1=0.812 (+13.7 pp, bootstrap 95% CIs disjoint), Llama-3 matches within CI (+0.4 pp), and Mistral exceeds by +4.4 pp. Classification is a measured 2.4-3.4x faster than Llama Guard 3 (332-556 ms vs. 851-1,142 ms), because it reads a single logit position instead of generating tokens. A calibration strength alpha acts as a deployment-time policy knob rather than a learned hyperparameter, trading recall for precision per operation class. I implement ProbeLogits within Anima OS, a bare-metal x86-64 kernel written in ~285,000 lines of Rust. Because agent actions must pass through kernel-mediated host functions, enforcement operates below the WASM sandbox boundary, making it substantially harder to circumvent than application-layer classifiers.

schema.problem: Modern large language model training is no longer limited by data availability, but existing preprocessing pipelines cannot simultaneously achieve massive scale and high data quality; current approaches either filter aggressively and lose many tokens or retain large volumes with substantial noise.
schema.motivation: Breaking this scale–quality trade-off matters because it enables training on larger high-quality corpora without excessive token loss, reducing compute and improving model quality at web scale.
schema.proposed_approach: The work builds a web-scale preprocessing pipeline designed to maximize usable token retention while enforcing quality control; it is applied to Common Crawl dumps and produces curated training corpora, including a base-scale dataset.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the model-quality claim, a 3B-parameter model is trained on 60B tokens curated by the proposed pipeline and compared with DCLM and FineWeb on MMLU accuracy; success requires beating those baselines, while failure would be parity or lower. (2) For compute efficiency, the pipeline is evaluated by the number of tokens required to reach the same aggregate score as DCLM. (3) For data retention, usable tokens extracted from a single Common Crawl dump are compared with DCLM. (4) For base-scale corpus quality and scale, the pipeline's base dataset is compared with FineWeb.

items.title: FLUX: Data Worth Training On
items.abstract: Modern large language model training is no longer limited by data availability, but by the inability of existing preprocessing pipelines to simultaneously achieve massive scale and high data quality. Current approaches are forced to sacrifice one for the other: either aggressively filtering to improve quality at the cost of severe token loss, or retaining large volumes of data while introducing substantial noise. In this work, we introduce FLUX, a preprocessing pipeline specifically designed to break this long-standing trade-off by maximizing token retention while enforcing rigorous quality control. Models trained on FLUX-curated data consistently outperform prior methods. A 3B-parameter model trained on 60B tokens with FLUX achieves 32.14% MMLU accuracy, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art pipeline DCLM (31.98%) and significantly outperforming FineWeb (29.88%). FLUX achieves the same aggregate score as a model trained on DCLM data using only 39B tokens, resulting in a 34.4% reduction in training compute. At the data level, FLUX extracts 50B usable tokens from a single dump (CC-MAIN-2025-51), compared to 40B from DCLM (+25% retention). FLUX-Base yields 192B tokens, exceeding FineWeb's 170B while still maintaining superior quality. Overall, FLUX establishes a new state of the art in web-scale data preprocessing by demonstrating that high retention, strong quality control, and computational efficiency can be achieved simultaneously, redefining the limits of scalable dataset construction for modern language models.

schema.problem: Auto-tuning mechanisms designed primarily for NVIDIA GPUs fail to effectively exploit the architectural features of SIMD CPUs, creating a significant performance gap on SIMD platforms for Triton kernels.
schema.motivation: Modern AI workloads increasingly rely on Python-based kernel frameworks such as Triton for usability and automatic tuning, while SIMD platforms are widely adopted from high-performance computing to AI inference; closing this gap would combine these benefits with improved performance and development efficiency.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is composed of a front-end for user intent recognition and a back-end for user-guided, SIMD-aware tuning. It captures high-level SIMD optimization intent from human users and integrates it seamlessly into machine framework tuning for Triton kernels on SIMD platforms.
schema.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on x86 and RISC-V platforms, with performance and tuning cost compared against native Triton tuning. The abstract does not state matched compute budgets, ablations, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: A Human–Machine Collaborative Tuning Framework for Triton Kernel Optimization on SIMD Platforms
items.abstract: Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) technology enhances performance through parallel data processing on CPUs. SIMD platforms are widely adopted across domains ranging from high-performance computing to AI inference. As modern AI workloads increasingly rely on Python-based kernel frameworks to maintain usability and benefit from automatic tuning, Triton has emerged as a representative solution. However, Triton’s auto-tuning mechanism, designed primarily for NVIDIA GPUs, fails to effectively exploit the architectural features of SIMD CPUs, creating a significant performance gap on these platforms.To address this problem, we introduce a human–machine collaborative design tailored for Triton kernel tuning on SIMD platforms. This design improves both development efficiency and performance by capturing high-level SIMD optimization intent from human users and integrating it seamlessly into machine framework tuning. Based on this collaborative design, we develop a tuning framework composed of a front-end for user intent recognition and a back-end for user-guided, SIMD-aware tuning. Experiments on x86 and RISC-V platforms show an average performance improvement of 31.7% over native Triton tuning, with tuning cost reduced by up to 75.0%.

schema.problem: Finding effective compiler flag combinations for programs under constrained resources is a fundamental challenge; the problem is NP-hard and requires searching an extremely high-dimensional discrete space, while traditional heuristic search methods, though effective, are often computationally expensive.
schema.motivation: The availability of pre-trained small language models capable of capturing expert optimization knowledge makes it tractable to replace costly heuristic search with efficient inference, enabling practical and low-cost automated performance tuning in industrial compilers.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is integrated into the industrial-strength GCC compiler and uses pre-trained small language models—typically hundreds of millions to a few billion parameters—to predict near-optimal compiler flag combinations for generating high-performance executables on SW Processors. It transforms the costly search problem into an efficient inference task.
schema.research_plan: The approach is evaluated by comparing the predicted compiler flag combinations against the current state-of-the-art -O3 optimization level in GCC using the SPEC CPU 2017 integer speed benchmark on a test set independent of the training data; support requires the predicted combinations to improve performance over -O3.

items.title: Automating Compiler Flags Selection for SW Processors via Small Language Models
items.abstract: Finding effective compiler flag combinations for programs under constrained resources is a fundamental challenge in compiler optimization. The problem is inherently NP-hard, requiring a search within an extremely high-dimensional discrete space. While traditional heuristic search methods can be effective, they are often computationally expensive. We propose a machine learning framework, AutoCFS-SLMs , integrated into the industrial-strength GCC compiler, to predict near-optimal compiler flag combinations for generating high-performance executables on SW Processors. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate Small Language Models (SLMs)—typically ranging from hundreds of millions to a few billion parameters—into an industrial compiler for performance optimization. By transforming the costly search problem into an efficient inference task, our approach is compared against the current state-of-the-art -O3 optimization level in GCC using the SPEC CPU 2017 integer speed benchmark. Experimental results on a test set independent of the training data show that our method achieves an average performance improvement of 7.6% compared to -O3. This study demonstrates that pre-trained SLMs can effectively capture expert optimization knowledge, offering a practical and efficient solution for low-cost, automated performance tuning in industrial compilers.

schema.problem: Existing work has proposed various KV cache transfer paths for disaggregated LLM serving, but there is no systematic benchmarking comparing their latency, throughput, and energy efficiency; the performance and energy implications of optimization techniques such as frequency scaling have also not been rigorously characterized.
schema.motivation: Such characterization can guide deployment choices between colocated and disaggregated serving and support SLO-aware energy-efficient configurations across workloads, transfer media, and model sizes.
schema.proposed_approach: The work benchmarks multiple KV cache transfer paths for disaggregated LLM serving under synthetic inference workloads, measuring latency, throughput, and energy consumption and comparing them with a colocated serving baseline. It also applies DVFS to evaluate disaggregated serving at different GPU frequencies and to explore independent frequency scaling on prefill and decode GPUs. From the resulting tradeoff insights, it proposes a prototype framework for SLO-aware energy-efficient LLM serving and discusses its design challenges and evaluation methodology.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim that disaggregation gains depend on multiple factors is investigated by benchmarking multiple KV transfer paths under synthetic inference workloads and comparing their latency, throughput, and energy consumption with a colocated baseline while varying workload characteristics, transfer media, and model sizes. (2) The claim about bandwidth is investigated by studying performance as KV transmission bandwidth varies, with the stated threshold serving as the point beyond which further performance gains are not expected. (3) The claim about independent frequency scaling is investigated by applying DVFS at different GPU frequencies and independently scaling prefill and decode GPUs, checking energy consumption against latency SLO constraints. The abstract does not specify formal failure conditions beyond the bandwidth threshold and the SLO constraint.

items.title: Revisiting Disaggregated Large Language Model Serving for Performance and Energy Implications
items.abstract: Different from traditional Large Language Model (LLM) serving that colocates the prefill and decode stages on the same GPU, disaggregated serving dedicates distinct GPUs to prefill and decode workload. Once the prefill GPU completes its task, the KV cache must be transferred to the decode GPU. While existing works have proposed various KV cache transfer paths across different memory and storage tiers, there remains a lack of systematic benchmarking that compares their performance (e.g., latency and throughput) and energy efficiency. Meanwhile, although optimization techniques such as frequency scaling have been utilized for disaggregated serving, their performance and energy implications have not been rigorously characterized. In this paper, we address this gap through comprehensive benchmarking of disaggregated LLM serving. We evaluate multiple KV transfer paths under synthetic inference workloads, measuring latency, throughput, and energy consumption, and compare them against a colocated serving baseline. Through dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), we further investigate the performance and energy consumption of disaggregated serving configurations under different GPU frequencies, and explore the benefits of independently frequency scaling on the prefill and decode GPUs. Our results show that performance gains from prefill-decode disaggregation are not guaranteed, but depend on multiple factors including the workload characteristic, KV transfer medium, and LLM model size. We also observe diminishing performance returns from increasing KV transmission bandwidth beyond a certain threshold. Moreover, we demonstrate that stage-wise independent frequency scaling provides additional opportunities to improve energy efficiency while satisfying latency SLO constraints. Based on these insights, we propose a prototype framework for SLO-aware energy-efficient LLM serving and discuss its design challenges and evaluation methodology.

schema.problem: Existing Mixture-of-Experts approaches for large vision-language models apply symmetric architectures to visual and linguistic modalities, ignoring an inherent processing asymmetry. This causes two issues: text and vision form hierarchical containment relationships that Euclidean expert spaces cannot encode, and language experts in deeper layers drift toward parametric memory, losing grounding in provided visual and linguistic information.
schema.motivation: As large vision-language models scale, Mixture-of-Experts offers computational efficiency, but preserving cross-modal grounding and hierarchical alignment is needed to avoid hallucination and maintain multimodal performance.
schema.proposed_approach: An MoE large vision-language model architecture explicitly models visual-linguistic asymmetry through three specialized expert groups: one group handles modality-specific processing; a second group uses hyperbolic negative-curvature geometry for cross-modal relationships to encode hierarchical containment; a third group biases language processing toward contextual evidence and suppresses parametric memory activation to maintain grounding throughout network depth.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation compares the proposed architecture against MoE variant baselines and dense models on multimodal tasks, including hallucination-sensitive tasks, and reports parameter activation. The abstract does not state named metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: Hyperbolic and Evidence-Prioritized Experts for Large Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance on multimodal tasks through scaled architectures and extensive training. Recent studies introduce Mixture of Experts (MoE) into LVLMs for improved computational efficiency. However, existing MoE approaches treat visual and linguistic modalities with symmetric architectures, overlooking the inherent asymmetry in how these two modalities are processed. This asymmetry causes two critical issues. First, text and vision form hierarchical rather than parallel relationships, as text queries typically describe partial aspects of complete visual scenes. Euclidean expert space struggles to encode such containment structures. Second, language experts in deeper layers progressively shift from evidence-based processing to parametric memory dependence, losing grounding in the provided visual and linguistic information. To address these issues, we propose AsyMoE, a novel architecture that explicitly models this asymmetry through three specialized expert groups. Intra-modality experts handle modality-specific processing. Hyperbolic inter-modality experts capture hierarchical cross-modal relationships through negative curvature geometry. Evidence-priority language experts suppress parametric memory activation and maintain contextual grounding throughout network depth. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AsyMoE achieves consistent improvements over baseline methods, with average gains of 1.5% over MoE variants and up to 3.8% on hallucination-sensitive tasks. AsyMoE activates 25.45% fewer parameters compared to dense models.

schema.problem: The standard estimator of loss-singularity complexity, the local learning coefficient, requires per-task calibration and 10^4–10^6 forward-backward passes per checkpoint, and it yields only an integrated Bayesian scalar rather than a directional, layer-local view of singular structure.
schema.motivation: A closed-form spectral reading would make singular-structure geometry cheaper to compute across many checkpoints and layers, and would provide complementary directional, layer-local access to dead directions.
schema.proposed_approach: At a chosen layer, the method computes closed-form spectral readings from either the network's activation matrix or its per-sample-gradient Fisher-Gram, replacing an SGLD posterior chain with spectral linear algebra. The readings are grounded in a dead-direction framework that predicts structural correlation between activation-side and Fisher-side spectra at singular minima. A rank-multiplicative volume identity is used, with the active-volume log-determinant-positive slope treated as the monitor of dead directions rather than single-eigenvalue monitors. The approach is applied to reduced-rank regression and a non-linear modular-addition transformer.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the framework predictions, the paper states a dead-direction framework and a rank-multiplicative volume identity; support is the predicted slope-rank relation across rank deficits, with the smallest eigenvalue as a rank-blind control. (2) On reduced-rank regression with a closed-form real log canonical threshold, the proposed observables are checked for the framework-predicted sign of rank-tracking, using calibrated local learning coefficient as reference. (3) On a non-linear modular-addition transformer, the proposed observables are tested for rank-sensitive separation across model dimension in a regime where calibrated local learning coefficient at the protocol budget is rank-flat; failure would be absence of such separation.

items.title: Dead-Direction Signatures: A Cheap Spectral Reading of Singular Complexity
items.abstract: Singular learning theory characterises the complexity of a deep network through the geometry of its loss singularities. The local learning coefficient (LLC), the standard estimator of Watanabe's real log canonical threshold (RLCT, $λ$), reads this geometry as an integrated Bayesian scalar through SGLD, which needs per-task calibration and $10^4$-$10^6$ forward-backward passes per checkpoint. We introduce Dead-Direction Signatures (DDS), a family of cheap closed-form spectral readings of singular structure: each reads a network's activation matrix or per-sample-gradient Fisher-Gram at a chosen layer, replacing the SGLD posterior chain with spectral linear algebra. The readings rest on a dead-direction framework that predicts a structural correlation between activation- and Fisher-side spectra at any singular minimum, and a rank-multiplicative volume identity that single-eigenvalue monitors cannot produce: the active-volume $\log\det^{+}(G)$ slope counts the dead directions, tracking the rank-deficit $r$ across $r \in \{1,2,3,4\}$ (slope ratios $2.0, 3.1, 4.0$ at $r{=}2,3,4$ against the predicted $2,3,4$), where the smallest eigenvalue is rank-blind. On reduced-rank regression with closed-form $λ$, calibrated LLC recovers $λ$ at $99\%$ mean and the DDS observables rank-track it at the framework-predicted sign; on a non-linear modular-addition transformer DDS separates $d_{\mathrm{model}}$ across eighteen orders of magnitude where calibrated LLC at the protocol budget is rank-flat. Complementary to LLC's integrated posterior reading, DDS gives a directional, layer-local handle on a network's dead directions, read in closed form from its activation and gradient spectra.

schema.problem: The overhead of WebGPU per-operation dispatch for browser-based LLM inference remains poorly characterized, and naive single-operation measurements conflate dispatch overhead with synchronization.
schema.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed to browsers and edge devices where WebGPU is a modern cross-platform standard, and browser-based inference engines have proliferated; understanding and reducing dispatch overhead is needed for practical browser-based inference.
schema.proposed_approach: A sequential-dispatch measurement method for WebGPU per-operation dispatch cost, designed to separate dispatch overhead from synchronization, unlike naive single-operation measurement. The method measures per-dispatch cost across data types and isolates dispatch count as the cause at batch size 1.
schema.research_plan: The evidence compares sequential-dispatch measurements with naive single-operation measurements to separate dispatch from synchronization and identify overestimation. It measures per-dispatch cost across different data types to test whether cost depends on data type, and analyzes batch size 1 to compare dispatch overhead against kernel quality and isolate dispatch count as the cause.

items.title: Measuring and Reducing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead for LLM Inference
items.abstract: Large Language Models are deployed to multiple types of environments, from internet browsers to edge devices, and WebGPU serves as a modern cross-platform standard. The engines for browser-based LLM inference have proliferated, yet the overhead of WebGPU per-operation dispatch remains poorly characterized. In this work, we introduce a sequential-dispatch measurement method and show that naive single-operation measurements overestimate per-dispatch cost by conflating dispatch with synchronization. Using our method, we measure the per-dispatch cost and show that it is independent of data type used. We show that the dispatch overhead, not kernel quality, is the bottleneck at batch size 1, and isolate the dispatch count as the cause. Therefore, we conclude that at batch size 1, the effective approach to LLM inference optimization in WebGPU is reducing dispatch count. Our findings point to dispatch amortization, in the inference engines and in the WebGPU specification, as a path to practical browser-based inference.

schema.problem: Residual connections with PreNorm are standard in modern LLMs, yet they accumulate all layer outputs with fixed unit weights, causing uncontrolled hidden-state growth with depth and progressively diluting each layer's contribution.
schema.motivation: Deeper modern LLMs make this dilution and hidden-state growth more consequential, limiting effective use of depth and motivating aggregation mechanisms that better preserve each layer's contribution.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method replaces fixed accumulation with softmax attention over preceding layer outputs, allowing each layer to selectively aggregate earlier representations with learned, input-dependent weights. For large-scale training, a block-level variant partitions layers into blocks and attends over block-level representations instead of all earlier layer outputs. The block-level variant is combined with cache-based pipeline communication and a two-phase computation strategy to serve as a practical drop-in replacement for standard residual connections. The approach is integrated into the Kimi Linear architecture (48B total / 3B activated parameters) for pre-training on 1.4T tokens.
schema.research_plan: (1) Scaling law experiments across model sizes test whether the proposed mechanism's improvement is consistent with scale; failure would be inconsistency across sizes. (2) Ablations test the benefit of content-dependent depth-wise selection relative to fixed aggregation, with failure if learned input-dependent weights contribute no benefit. (3) A 48B-total/3B-activated linear architecture is pre-trained on 1.4T tokens to assess whether the mechanism mitigates PreNorm dilution, indicated by more uniform output magnitudes and gradient distributions across depth, and whether downstream performance improves across evaluated tasks; failure would be no such mitigation or no improvement over standard residual connections.

items.title: Attention Residuals
items.abstract: Residual connections with PreNorm are standard in modern LLMs, yet they accumulate all layer outputs with fixed unit weights. This uniform aggregation causes uncontrolled hidden-state growth with depth, progressively diluting each layer's contribution. We propose Attention Residuals (AttnRes), which replaces this fixed accumulation with softmax attention over preceding layer outputs, allowing each layer to selectively aggregate earlier representations with learned, input-dependent weights. To address the memory and communication overhead of attending over all preceding layer outputs for large-scale model training, we introduce Block AttnRes, which partitions layers into blocks and attends over block-level representations, reducing the memory footprint while preserving most of the gains of full AttnRes. Combined with cache-based pipeline communication and a two-phase computation strategy, Block AttnRes becomes a practical drop-in replacement for standard residual connections with minimal overhead. Scaling law experiments confirm that the improvement is consistent across model sizes, and ablations validate the benefit of content-dependent depth-wise selection. We further integrate AttnRes into the Kimi Linear architecture (48B total / 3B activated parameters) and pre-train on 1.4T tokens, where AttnRes mitigates PreNorm dilution, yielding more uniform output magnitudes and gradient distribution across depth, and improves downstream performance across all evaluated tasks.
